cards.front:
The Constitution of India has been amended through three different procedures depending on the subject matter. Which article lays down this amendment procedure?

(A) Article 352
(B) Article 368
(C) Article 356
(D) Article 370
cards.back:
(B) Article 368

Constitution & Preamble — Article 368 lays down the amendment procedure. THREE methods: (1) SIMPLE MAJORITY of Parliament — for matters like creation of new states (Art 4), admission of states (Art 3), abolition of LC (Art 169), 5th & 6th Schedules — technically outside Art 368; (2) SPECIAL MAJORITY under Art 368(2) — 2/3 of members present & voting + majority of total membership of each House. Used for most amendments. (3) SPECIAL MAJORITY + RATIFICATION BY 1/2 OF STATE LEGISLATURES — for matters affecting the federal structure: election of President (Art 54, 55), executive power of Union/States (73, 162), SC/HC (Parts V-VII), distribution of legislative powers, 7th Schedule, representation in Parliament.

cards.front:
Which is the FIRST Constitutional Amendment of India (1951), and what did it primarily do?

(A) Added the 9th Schedule + restrictions on Article 19 freedoms
(B) Lowered voting age from 21 to 18
(C) Added Fundamental Duties
(D) Abolished right to property as a Fundamental Right
cards.back:
(A) Added the 9th Schedule + restrictions on Article 19 freedoms

Constitution & Preamble — The FIRST Amendment (18 June 1951) — passed by the PROVISIONAL Parliament before the first general elections — did three major things: (1) Added the NINTH SCHEDULE (laws immune from judicial review — originally for land reforms like zamindari abolition, after SC struck some down in Champakam Dorairajan 1951). (2) Added 'REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS' under Article 19(2) — public order, friendly foreign relations, incitement to offence. (3) Amended Article 15 to allow special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs). Proposed by Nehru — the FIRST-EVER amendment to the Constitution. Also: provided safeguards for State-run trading against Article 19(1)(g). 9th Schedule immunity was later qualified by IR Coelho (2007) to basic-structure review.
cards.option3: Abolished right to property as a Fundamental Right

(2) Added 'REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS' under Article 19(2) — public order, friendly foreign relations, incitement to offence. (3) Amended Article 15 to allow special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs). Proposed by Nehru — the FIRST-EVER amendment to the Constitution. cards.front:
Which Constitutional Amendment is called the 'MINI-CONSTITUTION' due to the sweeping changes it brought during the Emergency?

(A) 24th Amendment (1971)
(B) 42nd Amendment (1976)
(C) 44th Amendment (1978)
(D) 52nd Amendment (1985)
cards.back:
(B) 42nd Amendment (1976)

Constitution & Preamble — 42nd Amendment (1976), passed during the Emergency under Indira Gandhi, was called the MINI-CONSTITUTION for its extensive changes: (1) Added SECULAR, SOCIALIST, INTEGRITY to the Preamble; (2) Added FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Part IV-A, Article 51-A — 10 duties, later 11); (3) DPSP given PRIMACY over FRs in certain cases; (4) JUDICIAL REVIEW restricted; (5) Terms of LS/SLA extended from 5 to 6 years (later reversed by 44th); (6) President bound by Cabinet advice (Art 74) — this remained; (7) Administrative tribunals via Art 323A/B added; (8) Education, Forests, Weights & Measures, Protection of Wild Animals moved from State to Concurrent List. Swaran Singh Committee recommendations. Many provisions were reversed by the 43rd and 44th Amendments (Janata govt 1977-79).

cards.front:
Which Constitutional Amendment implemented GST (Goods and Services Tax) in India, effective 1 July 2017?

(A) 99th Amendment
(B) 101st Amendment
(C) 103rd Amendment
(D) 105th Amendment
cards.back:
(B) 101st Amendment

Constitution & Preamble — 101st Amendment (2016, effective 1 July 2017) — implemented GST. Key changes: (a) Added Article 246A — concurrent power to Union and States on GST; (b) Added Article 269A — distribution of IGST between Union & States; (c) Added Article 279A — GST COUNCIL (FM + State FMs; 2/3 votes by States + 1/3 by Centre, total 3/4 for decisions). Excluded from GST: alcoholic liquor for human consumption, 5 petroleum products (until notified by Council). Subsumed: Central Excise, Service Tax, VAT, Octroi, Luxury Tax, Entry Tax, etc. Four-slab structure: 5/12/18/28% + cess on sin/luxury goods. 99th (2014) = NJAC (struck down by SC 2015); 103rd (2019) = 10% EWS reservation; 105th (2021) = restored state power to identify OBCs.

Key changes: (a) Added Article 246A — concurrent power to Union and States on GST; (b) Added Article 269A — distribution of IGST between Union & States; (c) Added Article 279A — GST COUNCIL (FM + State FMs; 2/3 votes by States + 1/3 by Centre, total 3/4 for decisions). cards.front:
Which amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years?

(A) 42nd Amendment (1976)
(B) 52nd Amendment (1985)
(C) 61st Amendment (1989)
(D) 73rd Amendment (1992)
cards.back:
(C) 61st Amendment (1989)

Constitution & Preamble — 61st Amendment (1989, effective March 1989): amended Article 326 to lower the voting age for Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections from 21 to 18 years. Proposed by Rajiv Gandhi govt to enfranchise ~5 crore young voters. First general election with 18+ age: 1989. Previously 21 since 1950. Globally, most democracies now use 18 too. Fun fact: until the amendment, young adults could marry (even earlier, per pre-1978 laws) but couldn't vote.

cards.front:
The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) created a THIRD TIER of governance. Which local bodies do they govern, respectively?

(A) 73rd: Panchayats (rural); 74th: Municipalities (urban)
(B) 73rd: Municipalities; 74th: Panchayats
(C) Both cover rural bodies only
(D) 73rd: Gram Sabhas; 74th: State Finance Commissions
cards.back:
(A) 73rd: Panchayats (rural); 74th: Municipalities (urban)

Constitution & Preamble — 73rd AMENDMENT (1992, effective 24 April 1993 — celebrated as NATIONAL PANCHAYATI RAJ DAY): added Part IX + Articles 243-243-O + 11th SCHEDULE (29 subjects devolved to Panchayats). Three-tier panchayat: GRAM, MANDAL/BLOCK/PANCHAYAT SAMITI (intermediate), ZILA PARISHAD (district). Reservations: 1/3 seats for women (many states now 50%), proportional for SC/ST. 5-year term. State Election Commission + State Finance Commission (every 5 years). 74th AMENDMENT (1992, effective 1 June 1993): added Part IX-A + Articles 243-P to 243-ZG + 12th SCHEDULE (18 subjects). Three types of urban bodies: NAGAR PANCHAYAT, MUNICIPAL COUNCIL, MUNICIPAL CORPORATION. Both amendments largely based on Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) + Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) + L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommendations.

cards.front:
The 103rd Amendment (2019) provided 10% reservation for which category?

(A) OBCs in private educational institutions
(B) Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) among the unreserved category
(C) Transgender persons in public employment
(D) Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha
cards.back:
(B) Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) among the unreserved category

Constitution & Preamble — 103rd AMENDMENT (January 2019): inserted Article 15(6) + 16(6), providing 10% reservation in EDUCATION and GOVT EMPLOYMENT to ECONOMICALLY WEAKER SECTIONS (EWS) of citizens NOT covered by SC/ST/OBC reservations (i.e., poor among 'general' category). EWS eligibility: family income < ₹8 lakh/year; does not own >5 acres agri land, >1000 sq ft flat etc. Upheld by SC in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (November 2022, 3:2 majority). India's total reservation thus exceeds 50% Indra Sawhney (1992) cap, but SC said 50% cap doesn't apply to EWS. 93rd (2005) = Article 15(5) OBC reservation in private educational institutions. 104th (2020) = removed Anglo-Indian nomination from LS + State Assemblies; extended SC/ST reservation till 2030.

cards.front:
Which amendment added the word 'SECULAR' to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution?

(A) 1st Amendment (1951)
(B) 24th Amendment (1971)
(C) 42nd Amendment (1976)
(D) 44th Amendment (1978)
cards.back:
(C) 42nd Amendment (1976)

Constitution & Preamble — 42nd Amendment (1976) added THREE words to the Preamble: SOCIALIST, SECULAR, and INTEGRITY (in 'sovereignty, unity and INTEGRITY of the Nation'). The original 1950 Preamble described India as a 'SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC'; after 42nd, 'SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC'. 'SECULAR' is debated — India follows 'principled distance' from religion (not strict French laïcité separation). SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994) declared secularism part of the BASIC STRUCTURE. 44th Amendment (1978) could not undo these additions — they remain. Constituent Assembly had deliberately NOT included 'secular' and 'socialist' originally; they felt it was implicit.

cards.front:
The 44th Amendment (1978) made three key reversals of the 42nd Amendment. Which of the following was NOT part of the 44th Amendment?

(A) Removed 'Right to Property' from Fundamental Rights; made it a legal right (Article 300-A)
(B) Restored Lok Sabha/Assembly term to 5 years (from 6 under 42nd)
(C) Safeguarded Articles 20 and 21 — now never suspendable even during Emergency
(D) Added Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A)
cards.back:
(D) Added Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A)

Constitution & Preamble — FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Article 51-A, Part IV-A) were added by the 42nd AMENDMENT (1976), NOT the 44th. Originally 10 FDs; the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th (parents' duty to educate children 6-14). 44th Amendment (1978, Janata Party govt) REVERSALS: (1) Removed RIGHT TO PROPERTY (from Art 19(1)(f) + 31 → made it a legal right under Art 300-A, not a FR); (2) Restored LS/SLA term to 5 years; (3) ART 352 'armed rebellion' (replaced 'internal disturbance') + written Cabinet recommendation required for emergency; (4) ARTS 20 + 21 NEVER SUSPENDABLE even during emergency; (5) Restricted Ordinance-making; (6) Repealed judicial-review restrictions. Core 42nd provisions like Preamble changes + FDs SURVIVED the 44th.

cards.option2: Restored Lok Sabha/Assembly term to 5 years (from 6 under 42nd)
cards.option3: Safeguarded Articles 20 and 21 — now never suspendable even during Emergency

cards.front:
The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the 10th Schedule dealing with:

(A) Anti-defection law
(B) Panchayat subjects
(C) Official languages
(D) Scheduled tribal areas of NE India
cards.back:
(A) Anti-defection law

Constitution & Preamble — 52nd Amendment (1985, Rajiv Gandhi govt) added the TENTH SCHEDULE — ANTI-DEFECTION LAW. Disqualifies MPs/MLAs for: (1) Voluntarily giving up membership of their party; (2) Voting against party whip (or abstaining) on any motion. Originally allowed 'SPLIT' (if 1/3 defected together) — STRIKED DOWN by 91st Amendment (2003) which now requires 2/3 merger for exemption. Decision-making authority: Speaker (LS) / Chairman (RS) — their decision subject to judicial review per Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1993). 91st Amendment (2003) also limited CoM size to 15% of LS strength (min 12). The Anti-Defection Law was a response to 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' political culture (origin: Haryana 1967 — Gaya Lal changed parties 3 times in a fortnight). disqualification on grounds of defection.
cards.option3: Scheduled tribal areas of NE India

cards.front:
The amendment procedure of the Indian Constitution is laid down in:

(A) Article 356
(B) Article 368
(C) Article 370
(D) Article 372
cards.back:
(B) Article 368

Constitution & Preamble — Article 368 prescribes three modes of amendment: simple majority (for a few provisions), special majority of Parliament, and special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures (for federal-structure provisions). The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) held that Parliament cannot amend the 'basic structure'.
cards.storedExplanation: Article 368 prescribes three modes of amendment: simple majority (for a few provisions), special majority of Parliament, and special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures (for federal-structure provisions). The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) held that Parliament cannot amend the 'basic structure'.

cards.front:
The words 'SOCIALIST', 'SECULAR' and 'INTEGRITY' were added to the Preamble by the:

(A) 42nd Amendment (1976)
(B) 44th Amendment (1978)
(C) 73rd Amendment (1992)
(D) 86th Amendment (2002)
cards.back:
(A) 42nd Amendment (1976)

Constitution & Preamble — 42nd Amendment (the 'mini-Constitution' during the Emergency, 1976) expanded the Preamble, added Fundamental Duties (Art 51A), widened DPSP, curbed judicial review. Many of its excesses were rolled back by the 44th Amendment (1978).

cards.front:
The 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to:

(A) Urban Local Bodies (Municipalities)
(B) Panchayati Raj Institutions (rural)
(C) Union Territories
(D) Lokpal institutions
cards.back:
(B) Panchayati Raj Institutions (rural)

Constitution & Preamble — 73rd Amendment — Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) + 11th Schedule (29 subjects). Set up three-tier Panchayati Raj (Gram / Block / Zilla), mandatory elections every 5 years, reservation for SC/ST/women (33%). 74th Amendment (also 1992) did the same for urban bodies — Part IX-A + 12th Schedule.

cards.front:
The 86th Amendment (2002) made RIGHT TO EDUCATION a Fundamental Right under Article:

(A) Article 19
(B) Article 21
(C) Article 21A
(D) Article 29
cards.back:
(C) Article 21A

Constitution & Preamble — Article 21A — free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14. The RTE Act, 2009 operationalised this. Fundamental Duty 51A(k) was added simultaneously: parents must provide opportunities for education of their children between 6-14.
cards.storedExplanation: Article 21A — free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14. The RTE Act, 2009 operationalised this. Fundamental Duty 51A(k) was added simultaneously: parents must provide opportunities for education of their children between 6-14.

cards.front:
Consider the following statements about the 101ST CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. 1. It introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) from 1 July 2017. 2. It inserted Article 279A creating the GST Council. 3. It added a new Article 246A giving concurrent powers to the Union and States to levy GST. 4. It abolished all state sales-tax entries from the Constitution. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 2 and 3 only
(D) 1 and 4 only
cards.back:
(A) 1, 2 and 3 only

Constitution & Preamble — Statement 4 is WRONG — alcohol for human consumption and five petroleum products remain outside GST (still under state VAT/excise). 1, 2, 3 correctly describe the 101st Amendment, which enabled the dual GST (CGST + SGST + IGST) structure.
cards.storedExplanation: Statement 4 is WRONG — alcohol for human consumption and five petroleum products remain outside GST (still under state VAT/excise). 1, 2, 3 correctly describe the 101st Amendment, which enabled the dual GST (CGST + SGST + IGST) structure.

cards.front:
The 103rd Amendment (2019) provides 10% reservation in government jobs and educational institutions to:

(A) Scheduled Castes
(B) Scheduled Tribes
(C) Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) of the general category
(D) Other Backward Classes
cards.back:
(C) Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) of the general category

Constitution & Preamble — 103rd Amendment — inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6). Provides 10% reservation for EWS among the 'general' (non-SC/ST/OBC) category. Upheld by the Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan (2022). Definition of EWS is by executive notification (annual family income threshold).
cards.storedExplanation: 103rd Amendment — inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6). Provides 10% reservation for EWS among the 'general' (non-SC/ST/OBC) category. Upheld by the Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan (2022). Definition of EWS is by executive notification (annual family income threshold).

cards.front:
Which of the following CANNOT be amended merely by a SPECIAL majority of Parliament — i.e., requires ratification by half the state legislatures also?

(A) Fundamental Duties
(B) Distribution of legislative powers between Centre and States
(C) Directive Principles of State Policy
(D) Preamble
cards.back:
(B) Distribution of legislative powers between Centre and States

Constitution & Preamble — Federal-structure provisions need state ratification: 7th Schedule (Union/State/Concurrent Lists), election of President, extent of executive power of Union/States, Supreme Court and High Courts, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself. The other items need only a special majority of Parliament.

The other items need only a special majority of Parliament.

cards.front:
Which Part and Articles of the Indian Constitution deal with Citizenship?

(A) Part I, Articles 1–4
(B) Part II, Articles 5–11
(C) Part III, Articles 12–35
(D) Part IV, Articles 36–51
cards.back:
(B) Part II, Articles 5–11

Constitution & Preamble — Citizenship is covered in Part II of the Constitution, comprising Articles 5 to 11. Part I (Articles 1–4) deals with the Union and its territories; Part III (Articles 12–35) covers Fundamental Rights; Part IV covers the Directive Principles of State Policy — common distractor choices students mix up.

Part I (Articles 1–4) deals with the Union and its territories; Part III (Articles 12–35) covers Fundamental Rights; Part IV covers the Directive Principles of State Policy — common distractor choices students mix up.

cards.front:
Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, which of the following is NOT a recognised mode of acquiring Indian citizenship?

(A) Citizenship by birth
(B) Citizenship by descent
(C) Citizenship by investment
(D) Citizenship by naturalisation
cards.back:
(C) Citizenship by investment

Constitution & Preamble — The 1955 Act recognises FIVE modes of acquisition: by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation, and by incorporation of territory. 'Citizenship by investment' (a concept used by some Caribbean states) has NO place in Indian law. This is the intended 'exception' framing — the distractors name real modes.

'Citizenship by investment' (a concept used by some Caribbean states) has NO place in Indian law. This is the intended 'exception' framing — the distractors name real modes.

cards.front:
Arrange the following Citizenship Amendment Acts in the correct chronological order of enactment: (I) 2019, (II) 2003, (III) 1986, (IV) 1992

(A) III → IV → II → I
(B) IV → III → II → I
(C) III → II → IV → I
(D) II → III → IV → I
cards.back:
(A) III → IV → II → I

Constitution & Preamble — Correct chronology: 1986 (III, tightened citizenship-by-birth requirements after the Assam Accord) → 1992 (IV, permitted citizenship by descent through mothers, not only fathers) → 2003 (II, introduced the concept of Overseas Citizen of India and National Register of Citizens) → 2019 (I, CAA providing expedited citizenship to persecuted religious minorities from Afghanistan/Bangladesh/Pakistan). The distractors shuffle these.

The distractors shuffle these.

cards.front:
Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition, termination and all other matters relating to citizenship?

(A) Article 5
(B) Article 9
(C) Article 11
(D) Article 13
cards.back:
(C) Article 11

Constitution & Preamble — Article 11 grants Parliament plenary power over citizenship matters — the Citizenship Act 1955 and all subsequent amendments draw their authority from this provision. Article 5 lays down criteria for citizenship at the Constitution's commencement. Article 9 says persons voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship cease to be Indian citizens. Article 13 deals with laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights — unrelated.

Article 5 lays down criteria for citizenship at the Constitution's commencement. Article 9 says persons voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship cease to be Indian citizens. Article 13 deals with laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights — unrelated.

cards.front:
India follows the principle of single citizenship, unlike the United States which has dual citizenship (federal and state). Which of the following statements regarding Indian single citizenship is CORRECT?

(A) Indian states can independently grant citizenship for residence-based purposes
(B) A citizen of one Indian state enjoys fewer Fundamental Rights in another state
(C) All Indians are citizens of India alone; no separate state citizenship exists
(D) The President may grant separate state citizenship in emergencies
cards.back:
(C) All Indians are citizens of India alone; no separate state citizenship exists

Constitution & Preamble — The single-citizenship principle means every Indian is a citizen of India only — NOT of any particular state. This was a deliberate design choice by the framers to strengthen national unity (contrast with the US 14th Amendment's dual citizenship). cards.front:
Under Article 9 of the Indian Constitution, a person who voluntarily acquires citizenship of a foreign state:

(A) Retains Indian citizenship unless Parliament terminates it
(B) Automatically ceases to be an Indian citizen
(C) Must obtain Presidential assent to retain Indian citizenship

cards.front:
Under the Indian citizenship regime, the 'termination' of citizenship (by order of the Central Government) is DISTINCT from 'deprivation' of citizenship. Which of the following is the primary distinction?

(A) Termination applies only to women; deprivation applies to men
(B) Termination is automatic on foreign-citizenship acquisition; deprivation is an order by government on grounds like fraud, disloyalty, or imprisonment abroad
(C) Both terms mean the same thing — mere drafting variations
(D) Termination requires Parliamentary approval; deprivation is Presidential discretion
cards.back:
(B) Termination is automatic on foreign-citizenship acquisition; deprivation is an order by government on grounds like fraud, disloyalty, or imprisonment abroad

Constitution & Preamble — CORRECT distinction: TERMINATION (Section 9 of the 1955 Act) kicks in AUTOMATICALLY when an Indian voluntarily acquires foreign citizenship — no investigation, no order needed. DEPRIVATION (Section 10) is an order BY the Central Government on specific grounds: (a) citizenship obtained by fraud/misrepresentation, (b) unlawful communication with the enemy during war, (c) disloyalty to the Constitution, (d) a 2-year imprisonment within 5 years of naturalisation, or (e) 7 years of continuous residence abroad. A and D are pure fabrications; C conflates two legally-distinct mechanisms.

cards.option2: Both terms mean the same thing — mere drafting variations
cards.option3: Termination requires Parliamentary approval; deprivation is Presidential discretion

cards.front:
Indian citizenship by Constitution is dealt with under:

(A) Articles 1-4
(B) Articles 5-11 (Part II)
(C) Articles 12-35
(D) Articles 80-81
cards.back:
(B) Articles 5-11 (Part II)

Constitution & Preamble — Part II — Articles 5-11. Art 5 — citizens at commencement of Constitution (those domiciled or born in India + parents born in India + 5-yr ordinary residents). Art 6 — migrants from Pakistan. Art 7 — those who migrated TO Pakistan. Art 8 — Indians abroad. Art 9 — voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship → Indian citizenship lost. Art 10 — continuance of citizenship. Art 11 — Parliament's power to legislate (resulted in Citizenship Act 1955). India follows JUS SANGUINIS (parental ancestry) primarily, with limited JUS SOLI (birth on territory).

(B) A lifelong visa giving most rights of NRIs except voting, agricultural-land purchase, and political/government office

The Prime Minister's Office (PMO) is:

(A) A constitutional body
(B) An executive body, not created by the Constitution
(C) A statutory body created by Parliament
(D) A regulatory commission
cards.back:
(B) An executive body, not created by the Constitution

Constitution & Preamble — The PMO is an executive office that evolved from the PM's Secretariat; it is not a creation of the Constitution. Its head — the Principal Secretary to the PM (IAS officer). Unlike the Cabinet Secretariat (serves the entire Cabinet) the PMO works directly for the PM.

Consider the following statements about the FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES. 1. They were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. 2. (A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 2 and 3 only

(D) A is false, R is true
cards.back:

Art 356 is the single strongest centralising lever — correctly given as the reason.

cards.front:
The 7th Schedule of the Constitution divides legislative powers into:

(A) States, Districts, Villages
(B) Union List, State List, Concurrent List
(C) Civil, Criminal, Defence
(D) Direct, Indirect
cards.back:
(B) Union List, State List, Concurrent List

Constitution & Preamble — 7th Schedule — three lists. UNION List (List I) — 100 subjects (originally 97); only Parliament can legislate (defence, foreign affairs, currency, atomic energy, posts, telecom, RBI, etc.). STATE List (List II) — 61 subjects (originally 66); only state legislature (police, public health, agriculture, local govt). CONCURRENT List (List III) — 52 subjects (originally 47); both can legislate (criminal law, marriage, succession, education — moved from State to Concurrent by 42nd Amendment). RESIDUARY POWERS rest with Centre (Art 248). Conflict in Concurrent → Union law prevails (Art 254).

The Preamble to the Indian Constitution describes India as:

(A) Sovereign Democratic Republic only
(B) Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic (latter 2 added by 42nd Amendment, 1976)
(C) Federal Sovereign State
(D) Constitutional Monarchy

SC in Kesavananda (1973) and Berubari (1960) cases said Preamble is part of Constitution and reflects basic structure but is not justiciable.

cards.front:
The Preamble to the Indian Constitution begins with which words?

(A) 'We, the People of India'
(B) 'We, the Representatives of India'
(C) 'We, the Citizens of India'
(D) 'The Constitution of India hereby declares'
cards.back:
(A) 'We, the People of India'

Constitution & Preamble — The Preamble OPENS with 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC...' This echoes the opening of the US Constitution ('We the People'). 'WE THE PEOPLE' emphasises POPULAR SOVEREIGNTY — the Constitution derives its authority from the people, not from any monarch or external power. The Preamble was LAST TO BE ADOPTED by the Constituent Assembly (on 26 November 1949), after all articles were finalised. It was AMENDED ONCE (42nd Amendment, 1976) — adding SOCIALIST, SECULAR, and INTEGRITY. Ends with: '...HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.' Based on Jawaharlal Nehru's OBJECTIVES RESOLUTION (13 Dec 1946), adopted by Constituent Assembly on 22 Jan 1947. Preamble is the KEY to the Constitution (K.M. Munshi), reflects its 'soul and spirit' (Thakurdas Bhargava).

cards.front:
The OBJECTIVES RESOLUTION — which later became the Preamble in slightly modified form — was moved in the Constituent Assembly by:

(A) Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
(B) Pt. JAWAHARLAL NEHRU
(C) Dr. Rajendra Prasad
(D) Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
cards.back:
(B) Pt. JAWAHARLAL NEHRU

Constitution & Preamble — OBJECTIVES RESOLUTION — moved by JAWAHARLAL NEHRU on 13 DECEMBER 1946 in the Constituent Assembly. Adopted unanimously on 22 JANUARY 1947. It outlined the key vision of the future Indian Constitution: (1) India as a SOVEREIGN INDEPENDENT REPUBLIC; (2) Territories of British India + Indian States acceding to form a UNION; (3) All powers derived from the PEOPLE; (4) Guaranteed rights including Justice (social/economic/political), Equality, Freedom (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship, vocation, association), Fraternity, + safeguards for minorities, backward classes, tribes; (5) Maintenance of territorial integrity; (6) Contribution to world peace + welfare of mankind. This became the philosophical foundation + is directly reflected in the PREAMBLE. The Constituent Assembly was ELECTED by Provincial Assemblies; first sat 9 Dec 1946; adopted Constitution 26 Nov 1949; it came into force 26 Jan 1950.

cards.front:
Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976) during the Emergency?

(A) Sovereign, Republic, Democratic
(B) SOCIALIST, SECULAR, and INTEGRITY
(C) Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
(D) Justice, Fraternity, Unity
cards.back:
(B) SOCIALIST, SECULAR, and INTEGRITY

Constitution & Preamble — 42nd Amendment (1976) added THREE words to the Preamble: (1) 'SOCIALIST' — reflecting Indira Gandhi's policy direction (nationalisation of banks/coal; welfare state orientation); (2) 'SECULAR' — though the Constitution was already in practice secular, explicit mention added. Secularism here is the 'principled distance' from all religions (neither Indian nor French-style laïcité); (3) 'INTEGRITY' — added to the phrase 'unity and INTEGRITY of the Nation' (original: just 'unity'). All three were retained even after the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many 42nd provisions. Today: 'SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC' in the Preamble. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) ruled the Preamble IS PART of the Constitution (reversing Berubari Union Case 1960 which said it was NOT). Thus, the Preamble CAN BE AMENDED (subject to basic structure doctrine).

cards.front:
The Preamble guarantees its citizens JUSTICE — in which three forms?

(A) Civil, Criminal, Administrative
(B) Social, Economic, Political
(C) Equal, Fair, Due
(D) Individual, Collective, Institutional
cards.back:
(B) Social, Economic, Political

Constitution & Preamble — Preamble's exact phrasing on Justice: 'JUSTICE, social, economic and political'. These three forms: (1) SOCIAL — end of inequalities based on caste, colour, race, sex, religion; inspired by the Russian Revolution; manifest in reservations, abolition of untouchability (Art 17), protection of SC/ST/OBC/minorities. (2) ECONOMIC — ending economic inequalities; freedom from hunger, poverty, exploitation; reflected in DPSP (equal pay for equal work, right to work, living wages, distribution of wealth). (3) POLITICAL — universal adult franchise (18+), equal political rights, no discrimination in political participation, Article 326. All three derive from the RUSSIAN REVOLUTION of 1917 (via USSR Constitution's influence). The Preamble continues: 'LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation'. Liberty/Equality/Fraternity from the French Revolution (1789).

These three forms: (1) SOCIAL — end of inequalities based on caste, colour, race, sex, religion; inspired by the Russian Revolution; manifest in reservations, abolition of untouchability (Art 17), protection of SC/ST/OBC/minorities. (2) ECONOMIC — ending economic inequalities; freedom from hunger, poverty, exploitation; reflected in DPSP (equal pay for equal work, right to work, living wages, distribution of wealth). (3) POLITICAL — universal adult franchise (18+), equal political rights, no discrimination in political participation, Article 326. All three derive from the RUSSIAN REVOLUTION of 1917 (via USSR Constitution's influence). The Preamble continues: 'LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation'. Liberty/Equality/Fraternity from the French Revolution (1789).

AMBEDKAR's 125th birth anniversary year (he was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee). Previously also called 'LAW DAY' by the Bar Council. cards.front:
The Preamble declares India as a 'REPUBLIC'. What does this specifically signify?

(A) India is ruled by a monarch
(B) The Head of State (President) is ELECTED (not hereditary) and holds office for a fixed term
(C) India is a dominion of the British Commonwealth
(D) India has a single-party dictatorship
cards.back:
(B) The Head of State (President) is ELECTED (not hereditary) and holds office for a fixed term

Constitution & Preamble — REPUBLIC = a form of government where the HEAD OF STATE is ELECTED (directly or indirectly), NOT HEREDITARY. India's President is INDIRECTLY ELECTED by an electoral college of MPs + MLAs for 5-year terms. Contrasts with a MONARCHY (hereditary king/queen — e.g., UK, Japan, Saudi Arabia). India was a DOMINION (under British Crown) from 15 Aug 1947 till 26 Jan 1950, when the Constitution came into force and India became a REPUBLIC. Other Preamble-defining terms: SOVEREIGN — independent, not subject to any external authority (not a dominion, not under the British monarch). DEMOCRATIC — government by the people, via free/fair elections, universal adult franchise, rule of law, independent judiciary. SOCIALIST — commitment to economic justice (added 1976). SECULAR — state has NO official religion, all religions equally treated (added 1976). The FULL DESCRIPTION: 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'.

cards.front:
'The PREAMBLE IS A PART OF THE CONSTITUTION.' This was SETTLED LAW in which Supreme Court case?

(A) Berubari Union Case (1960) — held Preamble NOT part of the Constitution
(B) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — reversed Berubari, held Preamble IS PART
(C) Shankari Prasad Case (1951)
(D) Golaknath Case (1967)
cards.back:
(B) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — reversed Berubari, held Preamble IS PART

Constitution & Preamble — Evolution of the question 'Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?': (1) BERUBARI UNION CASE (1960 — 8-judge SC bench on India-Pakistan land cession to Pakistan): held Preamble is NOT a part of the Constitution — 'it is a key to the mind of the makers'. (2) KESAVANANDA BHARATI v. STATE OF KERALA (1973 — 13-judge bench, landmark Basic Structure Doctrine case): OVERRULED Berubari; held the Preamble IS PART of the Constitution AND can be amended (but basic structure cannot be destroyed). This remains the settled position. Thus the 42nd Amendment's additions to the Preamble (1976) were constitutionally valid. (3) LIC OF INDIA CASE (1995): reaffirmed Preamble as 'integral part'. Preamble is NOT enforceable in court (unlike articles), but is a KEY to interpreting ambiguous provisions. Preamble reflects the IDEALS / PHILOSOPHY / OBJECTIVES of the Constitution makers. Called the 'SOUL OF THE CONSTITUTION' by Thakurdas Bhargava, 'BIRTH CERTIFICATE OF THE CONSTITUTION' by K.M. Munshi.

cards.front:
The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration of:

(A) Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states OTHER than the north-eastern states covered by the Sixth Schedule
(B) Tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
(C) Panchayati Raj Institutions across all states
(D) Salaries of High Court judges
cards.back:
(A) Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states OTHER than the north-eastern states covered by the Sixth Schedule

Constitution & Preamble — The Fifth Schedule provides for the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states OTHER THAN Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram — the latter four are governed by the Sixth Schedule's autonomous-district-council model. States covered by the Fifth Schedule include Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan and Telangana. Option B describes the Sixth Schedule, option C describes the Eleventh, option D describes the Second.
cards.option1: Tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
cards.option2: Panchayati Raj Institutions across all states
cards.storedExplanation: The Fifth Schedule provides for the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states OTHER THAN Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram — the latter four are governed by the Sixth Schedule's autonomous-district-council model. States covered by the Fifth Schedule include Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan and Telangana. Option B describes the Sixth Schedule, option C describes the Eleventh, option D describes the Second.

cards.front:
Which Schedule originally contained provisions concerning the territories of the Indian Union, and what did the 7th Amendment (1956) change about it?

(A) The First Schedule; the 7th Amendment reorganised states on linguistic lines into Part A, B, C, D states
(B) The First Schedule; the 7th Amendment abolished the Part A/B/C/D classification and created the present States and Union Territories listing
(C) The Fourth Schedule; the 7th Amendment re-allocated Rajya Sabha seats
(D) The Second Schedule; the 7th Amendment changed salaries of governors
cards.back:
(B) The First Schedule; the 7th Amendment abolished the Part A/B/C/D classification and created the present States and Union Territories listing

Constitution & Preamble — The First Schedule contains the names of States and Union Territories of India along with their territorial extent. Pre-1956, the Constitution classified states into Part A (former governors' provinces), Part B (former princely states), Part C (chief-commissioner provinces) and Part D (other territories). The 7th Amendment Act 1956 — following the States Reorganisation Act — abolished this A/B/C/D classification and reorganised India into 14 States and 6 Union Territories (the current structure has since evolved to 28 States + 8 UTs). Option A describes the pre-1956 layout but mis-attributes the change. Options C and D describe different Schedules.
cards.option1: The First Schedule; the 7th Amendment reorganised states on linguistic lines into Part A, B, C, D states
cards.option2: The Fourth Schedule; the 7th Amendment re-allocated Rajya Sabha seats
cards.option3: The Second Schedule; the 7th Amendment changed salaries of governors

Pre-1956, the Constitution classified states into Part A (former governors' provinces), Part B (former princely states), Part C (chief-commissioner provinces) and Part D (other territories). The 7th Amendment Act 1956 — following the States Reorganisation Act — abolished this A/B/C/D classification and reorganised India into 14 States and 6 Union Territories (the current structure has since evolved to 28 States + 8 UTs). cards.front:
Fundamental Rights are enshrined in which Part of the Indian Constitution?

(A) Part II
(B) Part III
(C) Part IV
(D) Part IV-A
cards.back:
(B) Part III

Fundamental Rights — Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Constitution is the 'Fundamental Rights' section — enforceable against the State. Part II (Arts 5-11) is Citizenship. Part IV (Arts 36-51) is DPSP (non-justiciable). Part IV-A (Art 51-A) is Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment, 1976).
cards.storedExplanation: Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Constitution is the 'Fundamental Rights' section — enforceable against the State. Part II (Arts 5-11) is Citizenship. Part IV (Arts 36-51) is DPSP (non-justiciable). Part IV-A (Art 51-A) is Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment, 1976).

cards.front:
The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) was described by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar as:

(A) 'The conscience of the Constitution'
(B) 'The heart and soul of the Constitution'
(C) 'The crown of the Constitution'
(D) 'The backbone of federalism'
cards.back:
(B) 'The heart and soul of the Constitution'

Fundamental Rights — Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' because without it, the Fundamental Rights would be unenforceable. Article 32 grants citizens the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of FRs via writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto). Article 32 itself IS a Fundamental Right. 'The conscience of the Constitution' is sometimes used for the DPSP+FR combination; 'crown' is used loosely for the Preamble.

Article 32 grants citizens the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of FRs via writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto). Article 32 itself IS a Fundamental Right. 'The conscience of the Constitution' is sometimes used for the DPSP+FR combination; 'crown' is used loosely for the Preamble.

cards.front:
Which Fundamental Right was removed from the list by the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978)?

(A) Right to Equality
(B) Right to Freedom of Religion
(C) Right to Property
(D) Right to Constitutional Remedies
cards.back:
(C) Right to Property

Fundamental Rights — The Right to Property (originally Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978) during the Janata Party government. It was relocated as a LEGAL right under Article 300-A (Part XII). This reduced the number of FRs from 7 to 6. The other FRs have never been removed, though their scope has been modified.

It was relocated as a LEGAL right under Article 300-A (Part XII). This reduced the number of FRs from 7 to 6. The other FRs have never been removed, though their scope has been modified.

cards.front:
The 'Right to Education' was added as a Fundamental Right (Article 21-A) by which Constitutional Amendment?

(A) 73rd Amendment, 1992
(B) 86th Amendment, 2002
(C) 93rd Amendment, 2005
(D) 101st Amendment, 2016
cards.back:
(B) 86th Amendment, 2002

Fundamental Rights — The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21-A guaranteeing the right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years. Implementing legislation: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 — came into force on 1 April 2010. 73rd=Panchayati Raj; 93rd=OBC reservation in educational institutions; 101st=GST.
cards.storedExplanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21-A guaranteeing the right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years. Implementing legislation: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 — came into force on 1 April 2010. 73rd=Panchayati Raj; 93rd=OBC reservation in educational institutions; 101st=GST.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT one of the six Fundamental Rights in the current Indian Constitution?

(A) Right to Equality (Arts. 14-18)
(B) Right to Freedom (Arts. 19-22)
(C) Right to Property (Art. 300-A)
(D) Right against Exploitation (Arts. 23-24)
cards.back:
(C) Right to Property (Art. 300-A)

Fundamental Rights — Six FRs today: (1) Right to Equality (Arts. 14-18); (2) Right to Freedom (Arts. 19-22); (3) Right against Exploitation (Arts. 23-24); (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Arts. 25-28); (5) Cultural & Educational Rights (Arts. 29-30); (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Arts. 32-35). Right to Property was DEMOTED to a legal right (Art. 300-A) by the 44th Amendment (1978) — so it is NOT a Fundamental Right anymore.
cards.storedExplanation: Six FRs today: (1) Right to Equality (Arts. 14-18); (2) Right to Freedom (Arts. 19-22); (3) Right against Exploitation (Arts. 23-24); (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Arts. 25-28); (5) Cultural & Educational Rights (Arts. 29-30); (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Arts. 32-35). Right to Property was DEMOTED to a legal right (Art. 300-A) by the 44th Amendment (1978) — so it is NOT a Fundamental Right anymore.

cards.front:
Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees:

(A) Right to life and personal liberty
(B) Equality before law AND equal protection of laws
(C) Freedom of speech and expression
(D) Right to education
cards.back:
(B) Equality before law AND equal protection of laws

Fundamental Rights — Article 14: 'The State shall not deny to any person equality BEFORE the law or the equal PROTECTION of the laws within the territory of India.' Note two distinct guarantees: (1) 'equality before law' — British/Dicey concept, negative — no one is above the law; (2) 'equal protection of the laws' — American concept, positive — equal treatment under equal circumstances. Article 21 is life/liberty. Article 19(1)(a) is speech. Article 21-A is education.
cards.option1: Right to life and personal liberty
cards.storedExplanation: Article 14: 'The State shall not deny to any person equality BEFORE the law or the equal PROTECTION of the laws within the territory of India.' Note two distinct guarantees: (1) 'equality before law' — British/Dicey concept, negative — no one is above the law; (2) 'equal protection of the laws' — American concept, positive — equal treatment under equal circumstances. Article 21 is life/liberty. Article 19(1)(a) is speech. Article 21-A is education.

cards.front:
The Right to Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?

(A) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
(B) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
(C) K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
(D) Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
cards.back:
(C) K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

Fundamental Rights — The 9-judge bench in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (August 2017) unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21, and is protected under Part III of the Constitution. This case was a reference from the Aadhaar challenges. Kesavananda (1973) = basic structure doctrine. Maneka Gandhi (1978) = expanded Article 21 ('procedure established by law' → must be just, fair, reasonable). Navtej Johar (2018) = decriminalised consensual same-sex relations (Sec 377).
cards.option1: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
cards.option2: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
cards.option3: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
cards.storedExplanation: The 9-judge bench in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (August 2017) unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21, and is protected under Part III of the Constitution. This case was a reference from the Aadhaar challenges. Kesavananda (1973) = basic structure doctrine. Maneka Gandhi (1978) = expanded Article 21 ('procedure established by law' → must be just, fair, reasonable). Navtej Johar (2018) = decriminalised consensual same-sex relations (Sec 377).

cards.front:
The writ of 'Habeas Corpus' is used to:

(A) Direct a lower court to produce records of a case
(B) Challenge the legality of a person's detention and demand their production before court
(C) Prevent a public servant from exercising an office they have no right to
(D) Direct a public authority to perform its statutory duty
cards.back:
(B) Challenge the legality of a person's detention and demand their production before court

Fundamental Rights — HABEAS CORPUS (Latin: 'let you have the body') — the court directs the detaining authority to PRODUCE the detained person and justify the detention. If the detention is illegal, the person is released. Used primarily against illegal police detention, preventive detention, etc. Other writs: CERTIORARI = challenge lower court/tribunal order; QUO WARRANTO = challenge authority to hold office; MANDAMUS = command to public authority; PROHIBITION = prevent lower court from exceeding jurisdiction.
cards.option1: Direct a lower court to produce records of a case
cards.option2: Prevent a public servant from exercising an office they have no right to
cards.option3: Direct a public authority to perform its statutory duty
cards.storedExplanation: HABEAS CORPUS (Latin: 'let you have the body') — the court directs the detaining authority to PRODUCE the detained person and justify the detention. If the detention is illegal, the person is released. Used primarily against illegal police detention, preventive detention, etc. Other writs: CERTIORARI = challenge lower court/tribunal order; QUO WARRANTO = challenge authority to hold office; MANDAMUS = command to public authority; PROHIBITION = prevent lower court from exceeding jurisdiction.

cards.front:
Article 17 of the Constitution deals with:

(A) Abolition of titles
(B) Abolition of untouchability
(C) Prohibition of human trafficking
(D) Prohibition of child labour
cards.back:
(B) Abolition of untouchability

Fundamental Rights — Article 17: 'Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.' Its enforcement was operationalised through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Article 18 abolishes titles (hereditary honours); Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits child labour under 14 in factories, mines, and hazardous employment.

Its enforcement was operationalised through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. cards.front:
During a National Emergency (Article 352), which of the following Fundamental Rights CANNOT be suspended?

(A) Right to Freedom under Article 19
(B) Rights under Articles 20 and 21
(C) Right to Equality under Article 14
(D) Right against Exploitation
cards.back:
(B) Rights under Articles 20 and 21

Fundamental Rights — Article 359 (as amended by 44th Amendment, 1978) specifies that during Emergency, the enforcement of FRs (except Articles 20 and 21) may be suspended by Presidential order. Art 20 = protection against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination. Art 21 = life and personal liberty. After the ADM Jabalpur (1976) fiasco — where the SC held Art 21 COULD be suspended — the 44th Amendment explicitly immunised Arts 20 and 21. Today these two rights are NEVER suspendable. Protection in respect of conviction; Life & Liberty.

Art 20 = protection against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination. Art 21 = life and personal liberty. After the ADM Jabalpur (1976) fiasco — where the SC held Art 21 COULD be suspended — the 44th Amendment explicitly immunised Arts 20 and 21. Today these two rights are NEVER suspendable. cards.front:
Consider the following statements regarding the RIGHT TO EQUALITY (Articles 14-18). 1. Article 14 applies to both citizens and non-citizens. 2. Article 15 prohibits discrimination against 'any person' on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. 3. Article 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment) is available only to citizens. 4. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and is enforceable against both the State and private individuals. Which of the statements is/are correct?

(A) 1 and 2 only
(B) 1, 3 and 4 only
(C) 2 and 4 only
(D) All four statements
cards.back:
(B) 1, 3 and 4 only

Fundamental Rights — Statement 2 is WRONG — Article 15's protection is given to 'any CITIZEN', NOT 'any person' (that wider language appears in Art. 14). Statement 1 is correct (Art. 14 protects 'any person'). Statement 3 is correct (Art. 16 is citizen-only). Statement 4 is correct — Art. 17 runs against both State and private actors (horizontal application, enforced via the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955).
cards.storedExplanation: Statement 2 is WRONG — Article 15's protection is given to 'any CITIZEN', NOT 'any person' (that wider language appears in Art. 14). Statement 1 is correct (Art. 14 protects 'any person'). Statement 3 is correct (Art. 16 is citizen-only). Statement 4 is correct — Art. 17 runs against both State and private actors (horizontal application, enforced via the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955).

cards.front:
ASSERTION (A): The writ of Habeas Corpus lies even against private individuals. REASON (R): It is a remedy against unlawful detention, regardless of who is detaining. Which is correct?

(A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false
(D) A is false but R is true
cards.back:
(A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

Fundamental Rights — Habeas Corpus (produce the body) is UNIQUE among the five writs — it lies against BOTH the State and private individuals. The reason given is exactly the doctrinal rationale: its purpose is freedom from any illegal detention. The other four writs (Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto) lie only against public authorities.
cards.option1: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
cards.option2: A is true but R is false
cards.option3: A is false but R is true
cards.storedExplanation: Habeas Corpus (produce the body) is UNIQUE among the five writs — it lies against BOTH the State and private individuals. The reason given is exactly the doctrinal rationale: its purpose is freedom from any illegal detention. The other four writs (Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto) lie only against public authorities.

cards.front:
Match List-I (Fundamental Right) with List-II (seminal case). List-I: A. Right to privacy recognised as part of Article 21. B. Doctrine of 'basic structure' laid down. C. 'Procedure established by law' expanded to 'due process'. D. Right to free legal aid read into Article 21. List-II: 1. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). 2. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). 3. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). 4. Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).

(A) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4
(B) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(C) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4
(D) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1
cards.back:
(A) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4

Fundamental Rights — Puttaswamy (2017) — privacy as Art. 21 right (9-judge bench). Kesavananda (1973) — basic-structure doctrine, 13-judge. Maneka Gandhi (1978) — 'procedure established by law' read as fair-just-reasonable, importing due process. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) — legal aid and speedy trial as part of Art. 21. These four cases anchor modern Art. 21 jurisprudence.
cards.storedExplanation: Puttaswamy (2017) — privacy as Art. 21 right (9-judge bench). Kesavananda (1973) — basic-structure doctrine, 13-judge. Maneka Gandhi (1978) — 'procedure established by law' read as fair-just-reasonable, importing due process. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) — legal aid and speedy trial as part of Art. 21. These four cases anchor modern Art. 21 jurisprudence.

cards.front:
Which of the following Fundamental Rights is NOT available to non-citizens?

(A) Article 21 — protection of life and personal liberty
(B) Article 20 — protection in respect of conviction for offences
(C) Article 19 — six freedoms (speech, assembly, movement, etc.)
(D) Article 14 — equality before law
cards.back:
(C) Article 19 — six freedoms (speech, assembly, movement, etc.)

Fundamental Rights — Article 19's six freedoms are available ONLY to citizens (and only to natural persons, not corporations per Bennett Coleman). Articles 14, 20, 21 protect 'any person' — including foreigners. Article 15 (like 16) is also citizen-only. Negative-stem trap: the student must remember which are 'any person' vs 'any citizen'.
cards.option1: Article 21 — protection of life and personal liberty
cards.option2: Article 20 — protection in respect of conviction for offences
cards.storedExplanation: Article 19's six freedoms are available ONLY to citizens (and only to natural persons, not corporations per Bennett Coleman). Articles 14, 20, 21 protect 'any person' — including foreigners. Article 15 (like 16) is also citizen-only. Negative-stem trap: the student must remember which are 'any person' vs 'any citizen'.

cards.front:
Arrange the following events in the evolution of the Right to Property in correct chronological order. 1. 44th Amendment removed Right to Property from Part III. 2. 1st Amendment inserted Art. 31A and 9th Schedule to protect land-reform laws. 3. Kesavananda Bharati held 'basic structure' binds even 42nd-era amendments. 4. Minerva Mills struck down clauses of 42nd Amendment that barred judicial review.

(A) 2 → 3 → 1 → 4
(B) 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
(C) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
(D) 3 → 2 → 1 → 4
cards.back:
(A) 2 → 3 → 1 → 4

Fundamental Rights — 1st Amendment = 1951 (land reforms). Kesavananda = 1973 (basic structure). 44th Amendment = 1978 (property demoted to a legal right under Art. 300A). Minerva Mills = 1980 (reaffirmed judicial review as basic structure). Sequence: 1951 → 1973 → 1978 → 1980. Chronological-ordering pattern.
cards.storedExplanation: 1st Amendment = 1951 (land reforms). Kesavananda = 1973 (basic structure). 44th Amendment = 1978 (property demoted to a legal right under Art. 300A). Minerva Mills = 1980 (reaffirmed judicial review as basic structure). Sequence: 1951 → 1973 → 1978 → 1980. Chronological-ordering pattern.

cards.front:
A law made by Parliament authorises preventive detention for up to 4 months without advisory-board review. Which of the following is correct?

(A) The law is valid; Art. 22 permits up to 3 months without review and Parliament may extend
(B) The law is invalid; Art. 22(4) caps detention beyond 3 months unless an Advisory Board recommends extension
(C) The law is valid only during a National Emergency
(D) The law is valid only for foreigners
cards.back:
(B) The law is invalid; Art. 22(4) caps detention beyond 3 months unless an Advisory Board recommends extension

Fundamental Rights — Article 22(4) is strict: no preventive-detention law shall authorise detention for a period longer than THREE months unless an Advisory Board (of High Court Judges-qualified persons) reports sufficient cause within that period. A 4-month-no-review law violates this cap. Not dependent on Emergency or citizenship. 44th Amendment tried to reduce 3 months to 2 but that provision was not brought into force.
cards.option1: The law is valid; Art. 22 permits up to 3 months without review and Parliament may extend
cards.option2: The law is valid only during a National Emergency
cards.option3: The law is valid only for foreigners
cards.storedExplanation: Article 22(4) is strict: no preventive-detention law shall authorise detention for a period longer than THREE months unless an Advisory Board (of High Court Judges-qualified persons) reports sufficient cause within that period. A 4-month-no-review law violates this cap. Not dependent on Emergency or citizenship. 44th Amendment tried to reduce 3 months to 2 but that provision was not brought into force.

cards.front:
Consider the following FRs and the ground on which the State may restrict them. Which pairing is INCORRECT?

(A) Art. 19(1)(a) freedom of speech — 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground
(B) Art. 19(1)(d) freedom of movement — 'interest of any Scheduled Tribe' as a ground
(C) Art. 19(1)(g) freedom of profession — 'public interest' as a ground
(D) Art. 25 freedom of religion — 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground
cards.back:
(D) Art. 25 freedom of religion — 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground

Fundamental Rights — Art. 25 permits reasonable restrictions only on grounds of PUBLIC ORDER, MORALITY, HEALTH and OTHER PROVISIONS OF PART III. 'Sovereignty and integrity of India' is a ground for Art. 19(1)(a)/(b)/(c)/(d) (added by 16th Amendment, 1963), not for Art. 25. All other pairings in the question are correct. Negative-stem pattern.

cards.option2: Art. 19(1)(d) freedom of movement — 'interest of any Scheduled Tribe' as a ground
cards.option3: Art. 19(1)(g) freedom of profession — 'public interest' as a ground

'Sovereignty and integrity of India' is a ground for Art. 19(1)(a)/(b)/(c)/(d) (added by 16th Amendment, 1963), not for Art. 25. All other pairings in the question are correct. Negative-stem pattern.

cards.front:
ASSERTION (A): During a Proclamation of Emergency under Art. 352, all Fundamental Rights stand suspended. REASON (R): Art. 359 empowers the President to suspend the right to move any court for enforcement of FRs specified in the order.

(A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(C) A is false but R is true
(D) Both A and R are false
cards.back:
(C) A is false but R is true

Fundamental Rights — A is FALSE: post 44th Amendment (1978), Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended, even during Emergency. R is TRUE: Art. 359 lets the President suspend ENFORCEMENT of specified FRs (not the rights themselves, and not 20/21). The trap is the word 'all' in A — a single counter-example falsifies it.

cards.option3: Both A and R are false

R is TRUE: Art. 359 lets the President suspend ENFORCEMENT of specified FRs (not the rights themselves, and not 20/21). The trap is the word 'all' in A — a single counter-example falsifies it.

cards.front:
Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees two distinct rights. Identify them correctly.

(A) Equality before law AND equal protection of laws
(B) Equality of status AND equality of opportunity
(C) Equality before law AND freedom of speech
(D) Equal protection of laws AND right to property
cards.back:
(A) Equality before law AND equal protection of laws

Fundamental Rights — Article 14 guarantees TWO distinct-but-related ideas: (1) 'Equality before law' — a British/Dicey concept meaning nobody is above the law, all are equally subject to it; (2) 'Equal protection of laws' — an American 14th-Amendment concept meaning like should be treated alike (reasonable classification allowed). Option B refers to the Preamble's phrasing of equality; C mixes Art 14 with Art 19; D injects the now-repealed right to property.
cards.option1: Equality of status AND equality of opportunity
cards.option2: Equality before law AND freedom of speech
cards.option3: Equal protection of laws AND right to property

Option B refers to the Preamble's phrasing of equality; C mixes Art 14 with Art 19; D injects the now-repealed right to property.

cards.front:
Which Supreme Court case established that 'arbitrariness is antithetical to Article 14' and thereby introduced the doctrine of non-arbitrariness into equality jurisprudence?

(A) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
(B) E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)
(C) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
(D) A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
cards.back:
(B) E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)

Fundamental Rights — E.P. Royappa (1974, per Bhagwati J.) introduced the revolutionary 'arbitrariness test': where a state action is arbitrary, it is by nature unequal and violates Article 14 — even without needing to find a comparator. This freed Article 14 from the strict 'classification' test alone. Maneka Gandhi (1978) BUILT on Royappa, famously linking Articles 14-19-21 into the 'golden triangle'. Kesavananda is the basic-structure case (unrelated). A.K. Gopalan is the pre-Maneka case whose narrow reading was later overruled.
cards.option1: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)

cards.front:
Article 15 of the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on five specific grounds. Which of the following is NOT one of those grounds?

(A) Religion
(B) Race
(C) Language
(D) Caste
cards.back:
(C) Language

Fundamental Rights — Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds ONLY of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. 'Language' is notably ABSENT — this surprises many students given India's linguistic sensitivity. Language-based safeguards exist elsewhere (Articles 29-30 for minorities, the Eighth Schedule), but Article 15's enumerated list is these five alone. Memorising the 5 (religion-race-caste-sex-birthplace) is a high-ROI drill.

cards.front:
The 50 % ceiling on reservations (with exceptions for extraordinary circumstances) was laid down in which landmark judgment?

(A) M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963)
(B) Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
(C) Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951)
(D) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
cards.back:
(B) Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)

Fundamental Rights — The Indra Sawhney (or 'Mandal') judgment of 1992 is the leading case fixing the 50 % ceiling on reservations under Article 16, introducing the 'creamy layer' doctrine for OBCs, and upholding reservations for socially-and-educationally-backward classes in public employment. M.R. Balaji (1963) DID suggest a 50 % cap earlier but in the context of educational institutions and had limited force; Indra Sawhney is the authoritative ruling. Champakam Dorairajan led to the 1st Constitutional Amendment adding Article 15(4). Kesavananda is the basic-structure case.

cards.front:
Article 18 of the Constitution deals with abolition of titles. Which of the following is CORRECTLY permitted under Article 18?

(A) Accepting a foreign title without Presidential consent
(B) A State conferring a hereditary title of nobility on a citizen
(C) A citizen accepting an academic or military distinction
(D) An Indian national holding office of profit under a foreign State without Presidential consent
cards.back:
(C) A citizen accepting an academic or military distinction

Fundamental Rights — Article 18 abolishes titles EXCEPT academic and military distinctions — so 'Dr.', 'Professor', 'Major', 'Colonel' etc. are all permitted and widely used. Article 18(1) bars the State from conferring any title other than military/academic; 18(2) bars citizens from accepting foreign titles; 18(3)-(4) regulate non-citizens holding office under the State and citizens holding office under foreign States. Crucially, civilian awards like Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are NOT considered 'titles' per the Supreme Court (Balaji Raghavan, 1996) — they're just recognitions and cannot be used as prefixes/suffixes to names. e.g. 'Dr.', 'Lt. Col.'.

cards.option2: A State conferring a hereditary title of nobility on a citizen

cards.front:
Article 16 deals with equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. Which clause of Article 16 specifically enables reservations in PROMOTIONS for SCs and STs?

(A) Article 16(2)
(B) Article 16(4)
(C) Article 16(4A)
(D) Article 16(5)
cards.back:
(C) Article 16(4A)

Fundamental Rights — Article 16(4A) — added by the 77th Constitutional Amendment Act 1995 — empowers the State to make reservations in PROMOTIONS in favour of SCs/STs (not OBCs). Subsequent amendments (81st, 82nd, 85th) refined this: carry-forward of unfilled vacancies, relaxation in qualifying marks, consequential seniority. Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination in employment on grounds like religion/sex; Article 16(4) enables reservations in INITIAL appointments (not promotions); Article 16(5) allows religious-denomination-specific posts. Distinguishing 16(4) from 16(4A) is a classic exam trap.

cards.front:
The 'reasonable classification' test under Article 14 requires two conditions to be satisfied simultaneously. These are:

(A) (i) the classification must advance public policy AND (ii) it must be approved by Parliament
(B) (i) intelligible differentia distinguishing the group from others AND (ii) rational nexus between that differentia and the objective of the law
(C) (i) the classification must have been upheld by a previous Supreme Court judgment AND (ii) it must not cost the state exchequer beyond 2% of GDP
(D) (i) absolute equality in outcome AND (ii) absolute equality in treatment
cards.back:
(B) (i) intelligible differentia distinguishing the group from others AND (ii) rational nexus between that differentia and the objective of the law

Fundamental Rights — The classical test — laid down in State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and refined across cases — has exactly two limbs: (1) INTELLIGIBLE DIFFERENTIA: the group created by the classification is distinguishable on some clear basis from those excluded, and (2) RATIONAL NEXUS: the differentia has a reasonable connection with the purpose of the law. Both MUST be satisfied. Absolute equality (D) is neither required nor possible. Options A and C invent criteria. Note: post-Royappa, arbitrariness is a parallel test.

cards.option2: (i) the classification must have been upheld by a previous Supreme Court judgment AND (ii) it must not cost the state exchequer beyond 2% of GDP
cards.option3: (i) absolute equality in outcome AND (ii) absolute equality in treatment

cards.front:
Article 17 abolishes 'untouchability' and makes its practice in any form a punishable offence. The relevant enforcement legislation is:

(A) The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955)
(B) The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 only
(C) The Indian Penal Code, Chapter XIV only
(D) The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
cards.back:
(A) The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955)

Fundamental Rights — The enabling legislation for Article 17 is the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 — renamed Protection of Civil Rights Act via a 1976 amendment. The SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989 (option B) is supplementary and deals with broader atrocities, but Article 17's direct enforcement statute is option A. IPC Chapter XIV covers offences related to religion (not untouchability specifically). The Equal Remuneration Act (1976) deals with wage equality on gender lines — completely different domain.

cards.front:
The 'creamy layer' doctrine — which excludes the more affluent members of Other Backward Classes (OBCs) from the benefit of reservations — was judicially crafted in Indra Sawhney (1992). Which of the following statements regarding its subsequent application is CORRECT?

(A) The creamy layer doctrine applies to SCs and STs in the same manner as to OBCs
(B) The creamy layer doctrine applies to OBCs for reservations, and
(C) The creamy layer concept was abolished by the 117th Amendment
(D) The creamy layer threshold is automatically pegged to 50% of per-capita GDP
cards.back:
(B) The creamy layer doctrine applies to OBCs for reservations, and

Fundamental Rights — Correct nuance: Indra Sawhney mandated creamy-layer exclusion for OBCs but explicitly SAID the concept did NOT apply to SC/STs. HOWEVER, in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) the Supreme Court extended creamy-layer exclusion to SC/ST PROMOTIONS (not to initial appointments). So the rule today is: OBC initial appointments — creamy layer applies; SC/ST initial appointments — creamy layer does NOT apply; SC/ST promotions — creamy layer DOES apply (Jarnail Singh). Options C and D are fiction. per Jarnail Singh (2018) — also to SC/ST PROMOTIONS.

cards.front:
The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act (2019) introduced a NEW clause enabling reservations for 'Economically Weaker Sections' (EWS). Which Articles were amended?

(A) Articles 14 and 17
(B) Articles 15 and 16
(C) Articles 16 and 17
(D) Articles 14 and 18
cards.back:
(B) Articles 15 and 16

Fundamental Rights — The 103rd Amendment Act 2019 inserted Article 15(6) and Article 16(6) to enable up to 10 % reservation for EWS in educational institutions AND in public employment, EXCLUSIVE of existing SC/ST/OBC reservations. The Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (Nov 2022, 3-2 majority) upheld the constitutional validity of the amendment. Articles 14 and 17 were untouched. Knowing 15(6) AND 16(6) both were inserted — not just one — is the high-ROI distinction.

cards.front:
A school in Delhi maintains separate entry gates for boys and girls. A parent challenges this as violating Article 15. Which of the following is the most legally accurate assessment?

(A) It certainly violates Article 15(1) because sex is an enumerated ground of prohibited discrimination
(B) It does not violate Article 15(1) if the classification is based on 'sex plus' (sex combined with a reasonable rationale) and does NOT subject either gender to disadvantage
(C) It violates Article 17
(D) It is covered by Article 18 — the State cannot confer gendered titles
cards.back:
(B) It does not violate Article 15(1) if the classification is based on 'sex plus' (sex combined with a reasonable rationale) and does NOT subject either gender to disadvantage

Fundamental Rights — Article 15(1) forbids discrimination ONLY when the prohibited ground is the SOLE operative reason and one party is disadvantaged. The Supreme Court has recognised 'sex plus' classifications — sex combined with another neutral factor that doesn't disadvantage either gender — as constitutionally permissible (compare Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association, 2008). Separate entry gates alone don't disadvantage either group, so they generally pass muster. Article 17 is untouchability — irrelevant. Article 18 deals with titles — also irrelevant. Option A oversimplifies.

cards.option3: It is covered by Article 18 — the State cannot confer gendered titles

The Supreme Court has recognised 'sex plus' classifications — sex combined with another neutral factor that doesn't disadvantage either gender — as constitutionally permissible (compare Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association, 2008). Separate entry gates alone don't disadvantage either group, so they generally pass muster. Article 17 is untouchability — irrelevant. cards.front:
Which of the following is an enabling provision that PERMITS the State to make special provisions for women and children, despite the general non-discrimination rule of Article 15?

(A) Article 15(2)
(B) Article 15(3)
(C) Article 15(4)
(D) Article 15(5)
cards.back:
(B) Article 15(3)

Fundamental Rights — Article 15(3) is the specific carve-out: 'Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children.' This is the basis for laws like reservations for women in local bodies, maternity benefits, child-protection legislation. 15(2) prohibits discrimination by private actors in access to shops/restaurants/wells. 15(4) enables special provisions for SEBCs/SC/ST (added by the 1st Amendment 1951 after the Champakam Dorairajan judgment). 15(5) enables reservations in educational institutions (added by the 93rd Amendment 2005).

This is the basis for laws like reservations for women in local bodies, maternity benefits, child-protection legislation. 15(2) prohibits discrimination by private actors in access to shops/restaurants/wells. 15(4) enables special provisions for SEBCs/SC/ST (added by the 1st Amendment 1951 after the Champakam Dorairajan judgment). 15(5) enables reservations in educational institutions (added by the 93rd Amendment 2005).

cards.front:
Article 19 of the Constitution originally enumerated SEVEN freedoms. The 'right to acquire, hold and dispose of property' [Article 19(1)(f)] was DELETED by which Constitutional Amendment, thereby reducing the freedoms to the current SIX?

(A) 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
(B) 44th Amendment Act, 1978
(C) 61st Amendment Act, 1988
(D) 73rd Amendment Act, 1992
cards.back:
(B) 44th Amendment Act, 1978

Fundamental Rights — The 44th Amendment Act 1978 — passed by the Janata Government after the 1977 elections — deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 (right to property). Property is now only a LEGAL right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right. The 42nd Amendment (1976, 'mini-Constitution') added Fundamental Duties and expanded DPSP — but it was actually the 44th that corrected several of its excesses and made this specific property change. 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. 73rd added Panchayati Raj (Part IX).

cards.front:
The doctrine of 'due process of law' was imported into Indian jurisprudence — via a creative reading of Article 21 — in which landmark judgment?

(A) A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
(B) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
(C) Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
(D) Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
cards.back:
(B) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)

Fundamental Rights — A.K. Gopalan (1950) read Article 21 narrowly — 'procedure established by law' meant ANY procedure Parliament laid down, however arbitrary. MANEKA GANDHI (1978) overruled this: 'procedure established by law' now means fair, just, and reasonable procedure — effectively importing American-style 'due process'. It also linked Articles 14-19-21 into the 'golden triangle' — any law restricting personal liberty must pass all three tests simultaneously. Kesavananda is the basic-structure case (Fundamental Rights vs amendment power). Minerva Mills protected basic structure against 42nd Amendment's over-reach.
cards.option1: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
cards.option2: Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
cards.option3: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)

cards.front:
The Right to Privacy was finally declared a Fundamental Right in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). Under which Article(s) does the Supreme Court primarily anchor this right?

(A) Article 14 alone
(B) Article 19 alone
(C) Article 21 read with the freedoms under Article 19 and equality under Article 14
(D) Article 25 (freedom of religion)
cards.back:
(C) Article 21 read with the freedoms under Article 19 and equality under Article 14

Fundamental Rights — The 9-judge bench in Puttaswamy (24 Aug 2017) unanimously held that the right to privacy is intrinsic to Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty), necessarily linked to Article 19's freedoms, and informed by Article 14's equality principle. The judgment explicitly overruled earlier precedents (M.P. Sharma 1954, Kharak Singh 1962) that had denied privacy as an FR. The 'golden triangle' (Arts 14-19-21) framework — from Maneka Gandhi — was applied here. Note: while the DEFAULT anchor is Article 21, the multi-Article framing in option C captures the complete doctrinal basis.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT one of the six freedoms currently guaranteed under Article 19(1)?

(A) Freedom of speech and expression
(B) Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms
(C) Freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
(D) Freedom to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business
cards.back:
(C) Freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property

Fundamental Rights — The six CURRENT freedoms under Article 19(1): (a) speech and expression, (b) peaceable assembly, (c) form associations/unions, (d) move freely throughout the territory of India, (e) reside and settle in any part of India, (g) practise any profession/occupation/trade/business. Note: 19(1)(f) — the right to acquire/hold/dispose of property — was DELETED by the 44th Amendment 1978 and sub-clause (g) now follows directly after (e). So option C is NOT a current FR (though it was pre-1978).

cards.front:
Article 20(3) guarantees protection against SELF-INCRIMINATION — 'no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself'. Which of the following is NOT protected under this provision, as interpreted by the Supreme Court?

(A) Giving oral statements under duress to the police
(B) Giving fingerprints, handwriting samples, or voice samples
(C) Being forced to decrypt a personal mobile-phone passcode
(D) Subjecting the accused to narco-analysis, polygraph, or brain-mapping tests without consent
cards.back:
(B) Giving fingerprints, handwriting samples, or voice samples

Fundamental Rights — In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), the Supreme Court clarified that Article 20(3) protects against compelled TESTIMONIAL evidence — NOT against the giving of PHYSICAL evidence. Fingerprints, handwriting samples, blood samples, voice samples, specimen signatures etc. are physical/objective evidence and CAN be legally compelled (e.g. under Section 73 of the Evidence Act or Section 311A CrPC). Options A, C, and D are protected: oral statements under coercion (Kartar Singh, Selvi), forced decryption (emerging doctrine), narco/polygraph without consent (Selvi v. Karnataka 2010) all violate 20(3).

cards.option2: Being forced to decrypt a personal mobile-phone passcode
cards.option3: Subjecting the accused to narco-analysis, polygraph, or brain-mapping tests without consent
