The Right to Education (Article 21A) was inserted into the Constitution by which Amendment Act, and for which age group?

(A) 73rd Amendment (1992), ages 0-14
(B) 86th Amendment (2002), ages 6-14
(C) 93rd Amendment (2005), ages 3-18
(D) 101st Amendment (2016), ages 5-16

The enabling legislation is the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act 2009. The 73rd Amendment (1992) dealt with Panchayati Raj, NOT education. cards.front:
Under Article 22(4), a person can be detained under a preventive detention law for more than THREE MONTHS only if:

(A) The Prime Minister personally reviews the case
(B) An Advisory Board — consisting of persons qualified to be High Court judges — has reported sufficient cause for such detention
(C) Parliament passes a special resolution
(D) The President approves the extension under emergency powers
cards.back:
(B) An Advisory Board — consisting of persons qualified to be High Court judges — has reported sufficient cause for such detention

Fundamental Rights — Article 22(4)(a) specifies that preventive detention beyond THREE MONTHS requires a report from an Advisory Board (members: persons who are, have been, or are qualified to be High Court judges) finding sufficient cause. Alternatively, 22(4)(b) permits longer detention without Board review IF Parliament prescribes it by law (e.g. under the original 1950 Preventive Detention Act). The Advisory Board mechanism is the key procedural safeguard — weakening it undermines preventive-detention accountability. Options A, C, and D invent mechanisms that don't exist in 22(4).

cards.option3: The President approves the extension under emergency powers

cards.front:
Which of the following rights has the Supreme Court explicitly READ INTO Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty)?

(A) Right to shelter
(B) Right to speedy trial
(C) Right to a clean environment
(D) All of the above
cards.back:
(D) All of the above

Fundamental Rights — Post-Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Court has expansively read Article 21 to include: right to shelter (Chameli Singh 1995); right to speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon 1979); right to clean environment (MC Mehta, Rural Litigation & Entitlement Kendra 1985); right to privacy (Puttaswamy 2017); right to livelihood (Olga Tellis 1985); right to health; right to education (Mohini Jain 1992, later codified as 21A); right to die with dignity (Common Cause 2018 on passive euthanasia); right to food; right against sexual harassment at workplace (Vishaka 1997). This expansionist jurisprudence is called the 'golden thread' of Article 21.

cards.front:
Article 20(1) prohibits EX POST FACTO criminal laws. Which of the following falls OUTSIDE the protection of this clause?

(A) Conviction for an act that was not an offence at the time it was committed
(B) Imposing a penalty greater than what was prescribed at the time the act was committed
(C) Applying a PROCEDURAL change retroactively
(D) Imposing a BRAND-NEW retroactive criminal liability on conduct that was previously legal
cards.back:
(C) Applying a PROCEDURAL change retroactively

Fundamental Rights — Article 20(1) protects against retroactive SUBSTANTIVE criminal law — creating offences or increasing penalties after the act. It does NOT protect against retroactive procedural changes. Courts routinely apply new procedural rules (evidence, trial procedure, sentencing guidelines) to ongoing cases. A classic 2010 Supreme Court case reiterated this: the accused has no right to be tried under the specific procedural law that existed at the moment of the offence. Options A, B, and D are all within the protection. e.g. rules of evidence, trial procedure.
cards.option1: Conviction for an act that was not an offence at the time it was committed
cards.option2: Imposing a penalty greater than what was prescribed at the time the act was committed
cards.option3: Imposing a BRAND-NEW retroactive criminal liability on conduct that was previously legal
cards.storedExplanation: Article 20(1) protects against retroactive SUBSTANTIVE criminal law — creating offences or increasing penalties after the act. It does NOT protect against retroactive procedural changes. Courts routinely apply new procedural rules (evidence, trial procedure, sentencing guidelines) to ongoing cases. A classic 2010 Supreme Court case reiterated this: the accused has no right to be tried under the specific procedural law that existed at the moment of the offence. Options A, B, and D are all within the protection. e.g. rules of evidence, trial procedure.

cards.front:
Article 19(2) permits 'reasonable restrictions' on the freedom of speech and expression. Which of the following grounds is NOT enumerated in Article 19(2)?

(A) Security of the State
(B) Contempt of court
(C) Scientific accuracy
(D) Defamation
cards.back:
(C) Scientific accuracy

Fundamental Rights — Article 19(2) enumerates EIGHT grounds for reasonable restrictions on speech: (1) sovereignty and integrity of India, (2) security of the State, (3) friendly relations with foreign States, (4) public order, (5) decency or morality, (6) contempt of court, (7) defamation, (8) incitement to an offence. 'Scientific accuracy' is NOT among them — and has never been a constitutional ground to restrict speech. The 'sovereignty and integrity' ground was added by the 16th Amendment 1963 in the wake of the China war and secessionist movements.

The 'sovereignty and integrity' ground was added by the 16th Amendment 1963 in the wake of the China war and secessionist movements.

cards.front:
The safeguards in Article 22 distinguish between 'punitive' and 'preventive' detention. Which of the following safeguards applies to PUNITIVE detention (arrest under ordinary criminal law) but NOT to preventive detention?

(A) Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
(B) Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
(C) Right against double jeopardy
(D) Right to freedom of movement
cards.back:
(B) Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours

Fundamental Rights — Article 22(1)-(2) lays safeguards for PUNITIVE (criminal) arrests: right to be informed of grounds of arrest, right to consult a lawyer of one's choice, AND right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time). These do NOT apply to preventive detention — Article 22(3) explicitly excludes preventive detention from 22(1)-(2). Preventive detention gets its own safeguards under 22(4)-(7): Advisory Board for detention beyond 3 months, maximum period fixed by Parliament, grounds to be communicated (but confidential grounds may be withheld in the public interest).
cards.option1: Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
cards.storedExplanation: Article 22(1)-(2) lays safeguards for PUNITIVE (criminal) arrests: right to be informed of grounds of arrest, right to consult a lawyer of one's choice, AND right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time). These do NOT apply to preventive detention — Article 22(3) explicitly excludes preventive detention from 22(1)-(2). Preventive detention gets its own safeguards under 22(4)-(7): Advisory Board for detention beyond 3 months, maximum period fixed by Parliament, grounds to be communicated (but confidential grounds may be withheld in the public interest).

cards.front:
The 'double jeopardy' clause under Article 20(2) — 'no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once' — is NARROWER than the American Fifth Amendment version. The key narrowness is that Article 20(2) applies ONLY when:

(A) The previous proceeding was before a competent court AND resulted in either conviction OR acquittal with punishment
(B) Even a mere departmental enquiry has concluded, regardless of outcome
(C) The previous proceeding was only civil in nature
(D) The accused was merely summoned without trial
cards.back:
(A) The previous proceeding was before a competent court AND resulted in either conviction OR acquittal with punishment

Fundamental Rights — Article 20(2) requires BOTH: (i) the earlier proceeding was before a court of competent jurisdiction (quasi-judicial bodies, departmental enquiries don't count); and (ii) the earlier proceeding resulted in conviction AND punishment — a mere acquittal (without the accused having been 'punished') does NOT trigger the bar. Contrast with the US Fifth Amendment which bars RE-TRIAL after acquittal too. The Supreme Court confirmed this narrow reading in Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay (1953) — customs confiscation followed by criminal trial was permissible since customs was administrative, not judicial.
cards.option1: Even a mere departmental enquiry has concluded, regardless of outcome
cards.option2: The previous proceeding was only civil in nature
cards.option3: The accused was merely summoned without trial

Contrast with the US Fifth Amendment which bars RE-TRIAL after acquittal too. The Supreme Court confirmed this narrow reading in Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay (1953) — customs confiscation followed by criminal trial was permissible since customs was administrative, not judicial.

cards.front:
Which Article of the Constitution protects a person against the law that makes an act punishable that was legal at the time it was committed?

(A) Article 20(1)
(B) Article 20(2)
(C) Article 21
(D) Article 22
cards.back:
(A) Article 20(1)

Fundamental Rights — Article 20(1): 'No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law IN FORCE at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.' This is the ex-post-facto protection. 20(2) is double jeopardy; 21 is life/liberty; 22 deals with arrest/detention. All four articles fall in the same constitutional neighbourhood — hence the common exam trap of confusing them.

This is the ex-post-facto protection. 20(2) is double jeopardy; 21 is life/liberty; 22 deals with arrest/detention. All four articles fall in the same constitutional neighbourhood — hence the common exam trap of confusing them.

cards.front:
Article 19(1)(g) grants the freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business. The 'reasonable restrictions' permitted under Article 19(6) include:

(A) Only restrictions imposed in the interest of public order
(B) Prescribing professional/technical qualifications AND carrying on business by the State to the exclusion of citizens
(C) Restrictions only against non-citizens
(D) Complete nationalisation of private property without compensation
cards.back:
(B) Prescribing professional/technical qualifications AND carrying on business by the State to the exclusion of citizens

Fundamental Rights — Article 19(6) explicitly permits TWO categories of restriction: (i) laws requiring professional or technical qualifications for carrying on an occupation/trade (e.g. Medical Council requirements, Bar Council rules, Chartered Accountant regulations); (ii) laws allowing the State to carry on any trade, business, industry, or service — wholly or partly — TO THE EXCLUSION of citizens (this is the 'State monopoly' provision, used for things like the Indian Posts, certain nationalised industries). Public order is a 19(2) ground for speech restrictions, not a dominant 19(6) ground. Option D would violate Article 300A (right to property as a legal right).
cards.option1: Only restrictions imposed in the interest of public order
cards.option3: Complete nationalisation of private property without compensation
cards.storedExplanation: Article 19(6) explicitly permits TWO categories of restriction: (i) laws requiring professional or technical qualifications for carrying on an occupation/trade (e.g. Medical Council requirements, Bar Council rules, Chartered Accountant regulations); (ii) laws allowing the State to carry on any trade, business, industry, or service — wholly or partly — TO THE EXCLUSION of citizens (this is the 'State monopoly' provision, used for things like the Indian Posts, certain nationalised industries). Public order is a 19(2) ground for speech restrictions, not a dominant 19(6) ground. Option D would violate Article 300A (right to property as a legal right).

cards.front:
The Supreme Court in SELVI v. State of Karnataka (2010) ruled that which investigative techniques — when administered WITHOUT consent of the accused — violate Article 20(3) and Article 21?

(A) Fingerprinting and DNA sampling
(B) Narco-analysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping (BEAP) tests
(C) Interrogation by a magistrate after arrest
(D) Search of personal belongings with a warrant
cards.back:
(B) Narco-analysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping (BEAP) tests

Fundamental Rights — In Selvi (2010), a 3-judge bench of the Supreme Court (Balakrishnan CJ, Ganguly, Kapadia JJ) held that INVOLUNTARY administration of narco-analysis, polygraph, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP/brain-mapping) tests violates Article 20(3) (self-incrimination), Article 21 (personal liberty, mental privacy), and general standards of 'substantive due process'. HOWEVER, with free and voluntary informed consent, these tests may be used — the RESULTS aren't admissible as direct evidence but may be used for investigation leads. Fingerprinting (option A) is permissible (physical evidence per Kathi Kalu Oghad). Options C and D describe ordinary criminal procedure — unrelated.
cards.option2: Interrogation by a magistrate after arrest
cards.option3: Search of personal belongings with a warrant
cards.storedExplanation: In Selvi (2010), a 3-judge bench of the Supreme Court (Balakrishnan CJ, Ganguly, Kapadia JJ) held that INVOLUNTARY administration of narco-analysis, polygraph, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP/brain-mapping) tests violates Article 20(3) (self-incrimination), Article 21 (personal liberty, mental privacy), and general standards of 'substantive due process'. HOWEVER, with free and voluntary informed consent, these tests may be used — the RESULTS aren't admissible as direct evidence but may be used for investigation leads. Fingerprinting (option A) is permissible (physical evidence per Kathi Kalu Oghad). Options C and D describe ordinary criminal procedure — unrelated.

cards.front:
The right to equality before the law is guaranteed by which Article of the Indian Constitution?

(A) Article 12
(B) Article 14
(C) Article 19
(D) Article 21
cards.back:
(B) Article 14

Fundamental Rights — Art 14 — 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' 'Equality before the law' is a British concept from Dicey's rule of law; 'equal protection of laws' is from the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution. Art 12 defines the 'State' for Part III purposes.

'Equality before the law' is a British concept from Dicey's rule of law; 'equal protection of laws' is from the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution. Art 12 defines the 'State' for Part III purposes.

cards.front:
Article 19 guarantees citizens how many freedoms (in the current Constitution)?

(A) Seven
(B) Six
(C) Five
(D) Eight
cards.back:
(B) Six

Fundamental Rights — Six freedoms after the 44th Amendment (1978): speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession. The 'right to property' was originally the seventh freedom under Art 19(1)(f) but was removed and converted into an ordinary legal right under Art 300A. All six freedoms apply only to citizens, not foreigners.

The 'right to property' was originally the seventh freedom under Art 19(1)(f) but was removed and converted into an ordinary legal right under Art 300A. All six freedoms apply only to citizens, not foreigners.

cards.front:
Article 21 protects the right to:

(A) Property
(B) Life and personal liberty
(C) Freedom of religion
(D) Elementary education
cards.back:
(B) Life and personal liberty

Fundamental Rights — Art 21 — 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' Expanded by the Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi (1978) to require the procedure to be fair, just and reasonable. Later readings have recognised the right to privacy (2017 Puttaswamy), clean environment, shelter, livelihood, dignity, and education. Art 21A (86th Amendment) separately guarantees free compulsory education for children aged 6-14.

Art 21A (86th Amendment) separately guarantees free compulsory education for children aged 6-14.

cards.front:
Which Article gives the right to constitutional remedies, described by Dr Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?

(A) Article 14
(B) Article 32
(C) Article 226
(D) Article 136
cards.back:
(B) Article 32

Fundamental Rights — Art 32 allows any person to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and empowers the Court to issue writs for that purpose. Art 226 gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction (FRs + any other legal right) but the remedy itself is not a fundamental right. Art 136 is the SC's special leave jurisdiction. Art 32 cannot be suspended except during a National Emergency.

Art 226 gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction (FRs + any other legal right) but the remedy itself is not a fundamental right. Art 136 is the SC's special leave jurisdiction. Art 32 cannot be suspended except during a National Emergency.

cards.front:
The five 'writs' available under Article 32 are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and:

(A) Injunction
(B) Quo Warranto
(C) Subpoena
(D) Stay
cards.back:
(B) Quo Warranto

Fundamental Rights — Five writs: Habeas Corpus ('produce the body' — against unlawful detention), Mandamus (order a public official to do his duty), Prohibition (stop a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction), Certiorari (quash an illegal order of a lower court), Quo Warranto (by what authority — question a person's right to a public office). Injunctions, subpoenas and stays are ordinary civil remedies, not constitutional writs.

Injunctions, subpoenas and stays are ordinary civil remedies, not constitutional writs.

cards.front:
The Right to Education was added as Article 21A by which Constitutional Amendment?

(A) 42nd Amendment
(B) 86th Amendment
(C) 73rd Amendment
(D) 44th Amendment
cards.back:
(B) 86th Amendment

Fundamental Rights — 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Art 21A — free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 as a Fundamental Right. It was operationalised by the Right to Education Act, 2009. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A); 73rd (1992) added Panchayati Raj (Part IX); 44th (1978) tightened the Emergency provisions.

cards.front:
In the landmark Puttaswamy case (2017) the Supreme Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right, flowing primarily from:

(A) Article 14 only
(B) Article 21 and other freedoms in Part III
(C) Article 32 alone
(D) The Preamble
cards.back:
(B) Article 21 and other freedoms in Part III

Fundamental Rights — K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — a nine-judge bench held, unanimously, that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Art 21, and forms part of the freedoms guaranteed in Part III. It overruled earlier contrary precedents (M.P. Sharma 1954, Kharak Singh 1962). The case arose out of challenges to the mandatory linking of Aadhaar.

Union of India (2017) — a nine-judge bench held, unanimously, that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Art 21, and forms part of the freedoms guaranteed in Part III. It overruled earlier contrary precedents (M.P. Sharma 1954, Kharak Singh 1962). The case arose out of challenges to the mandatory linking of Aadhaar.

cards.front:
Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are enshrined in:

(A) Part II (Articles 5-11)
(B) Part III (Articles 12-35)
(C) Part IV (Articles 36-51)
(D) Part IV-A (Article 51A)
cards.back:
(B) Part III (Articles 12-35)

Fundamental Rights — Part III — Fundamental Rights (Arts 12-35). Part II — Citizenship (5-11). Part IV — DPSP (36-51). Part IV-A — Fundamental Duties (51A). Inspired by the US Bill of Rights.
cards.storedExplanation: Part III — Fundamental Rights (Arts 12-35). Part II — Citizenship (5-11). Part IV — DPSP (36-51). Part IV-A — Fundamental Duties (51A). Inspired by the US Bill of Rights.

cards.front:
Currently, how many CATEGORIES of Fundamental Rights are there in the Indian Constitution?

(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 4
cards.back:
(B) 6

Fundamental Rights — Six Fundamental Rights: (1) Right to Equality (14-18), (2) Right to Freedom (19-22), (3) Right against Exploitation (23-24), (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), (5) Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). The Right to Property was demoted from FR to legal right under Article 300A by the 44th Amendment, 1978.

The Right to Property was demoted from FR to legal right under Article 300A by the 44th Amendment, 1978.

cards.front:
Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees:

(A) Right to life
(B) Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws
(C) Freedom of expression
(D) Abolition of untouchability
cards.back:
(B) Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws

Fundamental Rights — Article 14 — 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' Applies to all persons (not just citizens). Article 15 — prohibition of discrimination; Article 17 — abolition of untouchability; Article 19 — six freedoms; Article 21 — right to life and personal liberty.
cards.storedExplanation: Article 14 — 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' Applies to all persons (not just citizens). Article 15 — prohibition of discrimination; Article 17 — abolition of untouchability; Article 19 — six freedoms; Article 21 — right to life and personal liberty.

cards.front:
Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) was expanded by the SC in MANEKA GANDHI v. UNION OF INDIA (1978) to include:

(A) Only physical life
(B) The right to live with dignity
(C) Right to vote only
(D) Right to property
cards.back:
(B) The right to live with dignity

Fundamental Rights — Maneka Gandhi (1978) — the SC held that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must also be fair, just, reasonable. Subsequent cases have unfolded 'the right to life' into right to privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), education (UC Hyderabad), dignity, clean environment, speedy trial, livelihood, shelter etc. including many 'implicit' rights (clean environment, livelihood, education etc.).

Subsequent cases have unfolded 'the right to life' into right to privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), education (UC Hyderabad), dignity, clean environment, speedy trial, livelihood, shelter etc. including many 'implicit' rights (clean environment, livelihood, education etc.).

cards.front:
Match the ARTICLE with its SUBJECT. A. Article 17.  B. Article 19.  C. Article 23.  D. Article 25. List-II: 1. Abolition of untouchability.  2. Six freedoms (speech, assembly, etc.).  3. Prohibition of human trafficking and forced labour.  4. Freedom of religion.

(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(B) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4
(C) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(D) A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3
cards.back:
(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4

Fundamental Rights — Art 17 — untouchability abolished, its practice forbidden. Art 19(1) — six freedoms: speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession. Art 23 — prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour. Art 25 — freedom of conscience and free profession/propagation of religion.
cards.storedExplanation: Art 17 — untouchability abolished, its practice forbidden. Art 19(1) — six freedoms: speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession. Art 23 — prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour. Art 25 — freedom of conscience and free profession/propagation of religion.

cards.front:
Which FR is available only to INDIAN CITIZENS (not to aliens)?

(A) Article 14
(B) Article 19
(C) Article 21
(D) Article 20
cards.back:
(B) Article 19

Fundamental Rights — Arts 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 — only citizens. Art 14 (equality), 20 (protection against ex-post-facto laws etc.), 21 (life & liberty), 22 (protection from arrest/detention), 25-28 (religion) — available to 'ANY PERSON', including foreigners. six freedoms.

cards.front:
Which Fundamental Right did Dr. Ambedkar call 'the heart and soul of the Constitution'?

(A) Right to Equality (Art 14)
(B) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32)
(C) Right to Life (Art 21)
(D) Right against Exploitation (Art 23)
cards.back:
(B) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32)

Fundamental Rights — Art 32 — the right to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Ambedkar: 'If I was asked to name any particular article in this Constitution as the most important — an article without which this Constitution would be a nullity — I could not refer to any other article except this one. It is the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.'

Ambedkar: 'If I was asked to name any particular article in this Constitution as the most important — an article without which this Constitution would be a nullity — I could not refer to any other article except this one. It is the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.'

cards.front:
FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS in the Indian Constitution are guaranteed under which Part?

(A) Part II — citizenship of India
(B) Part III — Articles 12 to 35
(C) Part IV — Directive Principles
(D) Part IV-A — Fundamental Duties
cards.back:
(B) Part III — Articles 12 to 35

Fundamental Rights — Part III of the Constitution = Fundamental Rights, Articles 12-35. Originally 7 categories; right to property removed by 44th Amendment (1978) → now 6 categories: (1) RIGHT TO EQUALITY (14-18); (2) RIGHT TO FREEDOM (19-22); (3) RIGHT AGAINST EXPLOITATION (23-24); (4) FREEDOM OF RELIGION (25-28); (5) CULTURAL + EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS (29-30); (6) RIGHT TO CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES (32) — Ambedkar called this 'heart and soul'.

cards.front:
Right to LIFE + Personal Liberty is enshrined in which Article?

(A) Article 14, the equality clause
(B) Article 21, with widest interpretation
(C) Article 19, the six freedoms list
(D) Article 32, the writ-jurisdiction one
cards.back:
(B) Article 21, with widest interpretation

Fundamental Rights — Article 21 — 'No person shall be deprived of his LIFE or PERSONAL LIBERTY except according to procedure established by law.' Most expanded right: Maneka Gandhi (1978) — procedure must be just, fair, reasonable, not arbitrary; Sunil Batra; Olga Tellis (right to livelihood); Vishaka (sexual harassment guidelines); Right to PRIVACY (Puttaswamy 2017, 9-judge bench); Right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia, 2018); right to clean environment, food, shelter, health, education (Mohini Jain, Unni Krishnan), speedy trial, legal aid — all read into Article 21. India's most powerful right.

cards.front:
Article 19(1) gives 6 freedoms. Which one was REMOVED by the 44th Amendment in 1978?

(A) Freedom of speech and expression remained
(B) Freedom to acquire and hold private property
(C) Freedom of profession, trade and occupation
(D) Freedom to assemble peacefully without arms
cards.back:
(B) Freedom to acquire and hold private property

Fundamental Rights — Article 19(1) originally had 7 freedoms: (a) speech + expression; (b) assembly peaceably without arms; (c) form associations; (d) move freely throughout India; (e) reside + settle anywhere in India; (f) ACQUIRE, HOLD, DISPOSE OF PROPERTY — DELETED by 44th Amendment (1978); (g) practise any profession / carry on trade. Right to property was made a LEGAL right (Article 300A) instead of fundamental — to enable land reforms + nationalisation without constitutional challenges. So now 6 freedoms in 19(1).
cards.option1: Freedom of speech and expression remained
cards.option2: Freedom of profession, trade and occupation
cards.option3: Freedom to assemble peacefully without arms
cards.storedExplanation: Article 19(1) originally had 7 freedoms: (a) speech + expression; (b) assembly peaceably without arms; (c) form associations; (d) move freely throughout India; (e) reside + settle anywhere in India; (f) ACQUIRE, HOLD, DISPOSE OF PROPERTY — DELETED by 44th Amendment (1978); (g) practise any profession / carry on trade. Right to property was made a LEGAL right (Article 300A) instead of fundamental — to enable land reforms + nationalisation without constitutional challenges. So now 6 freedoms in 19(1).

cards.front:
Article 14 ensures EQUALITY before LAW. It applies to:

(A) Indian citizens only, not foreigners
(B) All persons (citizens + non-citizens)
(C) Only adult citizens above age 18
(D) Only Indian citizens, with residency
cards.back:
(B) All persons (citizens + non-citizens)

Fundamental Rights — Article 14: 'The State shall not deny to any PERSON equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' Note 'PERSON' (not 'citizen') — applies to ALL HUMAN BEINGS in India, including foreigners. Even legal persons (companies). Other rights for citizens-only: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29. Rights for all: 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28. Concept of equality = (1) Equality BEFORE law (negative, British); (2) Equal PROTECTION of laws (positive, US-influenced).

cards.front:
Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) allows a citizen to move directly to the:

(A) High Court of the relevant state
(B) Supreme Court for FR enforcement
(C) Tribunal of Constitution as first step
(D) President of India for redressal
cards.back:
(B) Supreme Court for FR enforcement

Fundamental Rights — Article 32 — guarantees the right to MOVE THE SUPREME COURT directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. AMBEDKAR called Article 32 the 'HEART AND SOUL of the Constitution'. SC can issue 5 WRITS: HABEAS CORPUS (produce body — illegal detention); MANDAMUS (we command — order to a public official); PROHIBITION (don't act — to lower court); CERTIORARI (be informed — quash a lower court's order); QUO WARRANTO (by what authority — challenge official's right to public office). Article 226 — gives HIGH COURTS the same writ jurisdiction (broader: not limited to FRs). Article 32 itself is a FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT — cannot be removed except by constitutional amendment.

cards.front:
Right to Education (RTE) was added as a Fundamental Right by the 86th Amendment as Article:

(A) Article 19A, on free expression too
(B) Article 21A, with free education ages 6-14
(C) Article 14A, on equality protection
(D) Article 32A, on writs jurisdiction
cards.back:
(B) Article 21A, with free education ages 6-14

Fundamental Rights — Article 21A — added by 86th Amendment (2002): 'The State shall provide FREE AND COMPULSORY EDUCATION to all children of the age of 6 to 14 years.' Operationalised by RTE ACT (2009), in force from 1 April 2010. Mandates: free seats up to ~25% in private schools for disadvantaged sections; minimum standards for schools; teacher-pupil ratios; no detention up to Class 8 (later relaxed). Same Amendment also: (a) made education 11th Fundamental Duty for parents (Article 51A(k)); (b) modified DPSP (Article 45 — early childhood education for under-6s).

cards.front:
Article 25 grants FREEDOM OF RELIGION. Which religious activity does it NOT directly protect?

(A) Profess (declare faith openly)
(B) Forced conversion of others by inducement
(C) Practise any religion personally
(D) Propagate one's religious teachings
cards.back:
(B) Forced conversion of others by inducement

Fundamental Rights — Article 25(1) — freedom to PROFESS, PRACTISE + PROPAGATE religion (subject to public order, morality, health). 'Propagate' includes the right to spread one's faith, but does NOT include the right to CONVERT OTHERS by force, inducement, or fraud (Stanislaus case 1977). Many states have passed ANTI-CONVERSION laws (Odisha 1967, MP 1968, recently UP 2021, MP 2021, Karnataka 2022 etc.) — controversial. Other sub-clauses: 25(2) — state can regulate non-religious activities, social welfare reform (e.g., temple entry for all). Religious-freedom rights apply to all PERSONS (citizens + non-citizens).

cards.front:
The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in which Part of the Indian Constitution?

(A) Part III (Articles 12-35)
(B) Part IV (Articles 36-51)
(C) Part IV-A (Articles 51-A)
(D) Part V (Articles 52-151)
cards.back:
(B) Part IV (Articles 36-51)

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP = Part IV (Articles 36-51), borrowed from the IRISH CONSTITUTION (which borrowed from Spain). Part III = Fundamental Rights (justiciable, enforceable). Part IV-A = Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment 1976, non-justiciable). DPSPs are NON-JUSTICIABLE — cannot be enforced by courts — but 'FUNDAMENTAL IN THE GOVERNANCE OF THE COUNTRY' (Article 37). Aim: build a WELFARE STATE. Classification into 3 groups by the nature of principles: (1) SOCIALIST — aimed at economic + social democracy (Arts 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 47); (2) GANDHIAN — based on Gandhi's ideals (Arts 40, 43, 46, 47, 48); (3) LIBERAL-INTELLECTUAL — liberal democratic ideals (Arts 44, 45, 48, 49, 50, 51). DPSP + FR + FD together = Conscience of the Constitution (Granville Austin).

cards.front:
Article 44 of the DPSP directs the State to endeavour to secure:

(A) Village Panchayats (Art 40)
(B) UNIFORM CIVIL CODE for all citizens throughout India
(C) Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs (Art 47)
(D) Separation of judiciary from executive (Art 50)
cards.back:
(B) UNIFORM CIVIL CODE for all citizens throughout India

Directive Principles & Duties — ARTICLE 44 — directs the State to endeavour to secure a UNIFORM CIVIL CODE (UCC) for all citizens throughout India. A UCC would replace personal laws (based on religion — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi, etc.) with a common set of laws governing every citizen — on matters of marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption, etc. Currently only GOA has a UCC (Portuguese legacy). UTTARAKHAND became the first state to enact a UCC bill in Feb 2024 (now law). Controversial — seen by supporters as essential for equality, secularism; by opponents as threat to religious/cultural diversity. LANDMARK CASES: Shah Bano (1985 — SC ruled Muslim woman entitled to alimony under CrPC 125, Parliament overturned via Muslim Women Act 1986); Sarla Mudgal (1995); Shayara Bano (2017 — triple talaq unconstitutional). Other famous DPSPs: ART 40 — Village Panchayats (implemented via 73rd Amendment 1992); ART 45 — early childhood care + free compulsory education for all under 14 (became FR via 86th Amendment 2002 → Art 21-A); ART 50 — separation of judiciary from executive.

(A) USA
(B) Ireland
(C) UK

cards.back:

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP was borrowed from the IRISH CONSTITUTION of 1937 (Ireland itself borrowed from the Spanish Constitution of 1931). Major sources of different Indian constitutional provisions: (1) IRELAND: DPSP, method of election of President, nomination of RS members. (2) UK: Parliamentary government, single citizenship, PM + CoM, bicameralism, rule of law, writs. (3) USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment of Judges + President, VP role, SC (original + appellate jurisdiction). (4) CANADA: Federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, appointment of Governors by Centre, advisory SC jurisdiction. (5) AUSTRALIA: Concurrent List, trade + commerce provisions, Joint Sitting of Parliament. (6) USSR: Fundamental Duties, Five-Year Plans, Ideals of Justice (social/economic/political) in Preamble. (7) FRANCE: 'Republic' + Liberty/Equality/Fraternity in Preamble. (8) SOUTH AFRICA: Amendment procedure, RS elections by proportional representation. (9) GERMANY (WEIMAR): Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency. (10) JAPAN: 'Procedure established by law' phrase (Art 21).

cards.front:
Are DPSPs JUSTICIABLE (enforceable through courts)?

(A) Yes, like Fundamental Rights
(B) NO — they are non-justiciable per Article 37, but fundamental in governance
(C) Yes, only for economic directives
(D) Only after Parliament passes enabling legislation
cards.back:
(B) NO — they are non-justiciable per Article 37, but fundamental in governance

Directive Principles & Duties — ARTICLE 37 — DPSPs are NOT enforceable by any court. Cannot be enforced by a court of law in case of violation. However, they are 'FUNDAMENTAL IN THE GOVERNANCE OF THE COUNTRY' and 'IT SHALL BE THE DUTY OF THE STATE TO APPLY THESE PRINCIPLES in making laws'. In short, DPSPs are MORAL MANDATES, not legal obligations. Philosophy: DPSP = positive direction to State; FR = negative restriction on State. DPSP harmonisation with FR: (1) SHANKARI PRASAD v UNION (1951) — DPSP cannot override FR. (2) CHAMPAKAM DORAIRAJAN (1951) — FR prevails over DPSP (led to 1st Amendment). (3) GOLAKNATH (1967) — FR untouchable even via amendment. (4) KESAVANANDA BHARATI (1973) — Basic Structure doctrine; certain FR + DPSP both part of basic structure. (5) MINERVA MILLS (1980) — 'HARMONIOUS CONSTRUCTION' between FR + DPSP; both are equally important. Parliament tried to give DPSP supremacy (42nd Amendment, Arts 31-C), largely struck down in Minerva Mills. Today: DPSP guides policy; FR guarantees rights.
cards.option3: Only after Parliament passes enabling legislation

cards.front:
Which article of the DPSP deals with 'PROMOTION OF INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY'?

(A) Article 48
(B) Article 51
(C) Article 40
(D) Article 44
cards.back:
(B) Article 51

Directive Principles & Duties — ARTICLE 51 — directs the State to endeavour to: (a) promote INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY; (b) maintain JUST AND HONOURABLE RELATIONS between nations; (c) foster respect for INTERNATIONAL LAW + treaty obligations; (d) encourage settlement of INTERNATIONAL DISPUTES BY ARBITRATION. This reflects Nehru's vision of Panchsheel + Non-Aligned Movement. India has been an active UN member, UNPKF contributor, G20 presidency 2023, etc. IMPORTANT DPSPs by Article number: Art 38 — welfare state; Art 39 — equitable distribution of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protection of children; Art 39-A (added 42nd) — free legal aid; Art 40 — organise village panchayats; Art 41 — right to work, education, public assistance; Art 42 — just + humane working conditions + maternity relief; Art 43 — living wages; Art 43-A (42nd) — workers' participation in management; Art 43-B (97th, 2011) — co-operative societies; Art 44 — UCC; Art 45 — early childhood education (originally up to 14, now with Art 21-A); Art 46 — promote SC/ST/BC interests; Art 47 — prohibition of liquor, narcotic drugs; Art 48 — agriculture + husbandry + cow protection; Art 48-A (42nd) — protect environment; Art 49 — protect monuments; Art 50 — separate judiciary from executive; Art 51 — international peace.

cards.front:
Article 47 of DPSP directs the State to raise the level of nutrition + standard of living and specifically to:

(A) Promote private healthcare
(B) Bring about PROHIBITION of consumption of INTOXICATING DRINKS and DRUGS injurious to health
(C) Enforce yoga as compulsory
(D) Mandate vegetarianism
cards.back:
(B) Bring about PROHIBITION of consumption of INTOXICATING DRINKS and DRUGS injurious to health

Directive Principles & Duties — ARTICLE 47 — 'The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition + the standard of living + the improvement of public health as among its primary duties and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about PROHIBITION of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of INTOXICATING DRINKS AND DRUGS which are injurious to health.' GANDHIAN principle. Implementation: Some Indian STATES have imposed prohibition (wholly or partly) — GUJARAT (since 1960), BIHAR (since 2016 under Nitish Kumar), MIZORAM, NAGALAND, LAKSHADWEEP. Most states follow partial regulations (dry days, age limits). Kerala had a brief prohibition attempt (2014-17, rolled back). Other Gandhian DPSPs: Art 40 (Panchayati Raj), Art 43 (cottage industries), Art 46 (SC/ST/weaker section welfare), Art 48 (COW PROTECTION ban on cow slaughter — implemented via state laws; cow slaughter banned in many states but varies), Art 43-B (cooperatives). The Constitution's Gandhian flavor — especially Parts III and IV — reflects the values central to India's freedom struggle.

cards.front:
Article 39(b) + 39(c) of DPSP — directing equitable distribution of material resources for the common good — were given PRIMACY over certain FRs by the 25th Amendment (1971) via:

(A) Article 368
(B) Article 31-C (inserted)
(C) Article 32
(D) Article 14
cards.back:
(B) Article 31-C (inserted)

Directive Principles & Duties — ARTICLE 31-C — inserted by 25th AMENDMENT (1971) under Indira Gandhi. Originally said: any law enacted to give effect to the DPSPs contained in Articles 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be challenged on grounds of violating Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms), 31 (property). The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended this protection to ALL DPSPs (not just 39b/c). MINERVA MILLS v UNION (1980) — SC STRUCK DOWN the 42nd Amendment's extension (saying it violated the Basic Structure by making DPSP supreme over FR without balance). So TODAY, Art 31-C's original scope — protection ONLY for laws under Art 39(b) and 39(c) — survives. 39(b) — 'ownership and control of material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good'; 39(c) — 'operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment'. These were the key enabling provisions for NATIONALISATION drives + LAND REFORMS. LIC nationalisation (1956), Bank nationalisation (1969, 1980), Coal nationalisation (1973) — all grounded in Art 39.

OPERATIONALISED by 73rd Amendment (1992) — added Part IX + 11th Schedule (29 subjects); created mandatory 3-tier panchayati raj (Village, Block, District); reservations for SC/ST + women; Panchayat elections every 5 yrs. Similarly 74th Amendment (1992) — for URBAN local bodies (municipalities, municipal corps). Other GANDHIAN DPSPs: Article 43 (cottage industries), 46 (welfare of SC/ST/weaker sections), 47 (prohibition of intoxicants — operationalised in Bihar, Gujarat, Nagaland), 48 (cow protection), 48A (forest + wildlife). INSIGHT — Gandhi originally wanted Constitution to be more decentralised; partly addressed by these DPSPs + later Panchayati Raj amendments.

cards.front:
When DPSP CONFLICTS with FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS, which prevails?

(A) Fundamental Rights generally prevail
(B) DPSP always prevail over rights
(C) President decides on each case
(D) States decide their own choice
cards.back:
(A) Fundamental Rights generally prevail

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP vs FR conflict: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS PREVAIL because they're justiciable (FRs enforceable via courts; DPSPs not). KEY CASES: STATE OF MADRAS vs CHAMPAKAM DORAIRAJAN (1951) — court held FR prevails; led to 1st Amendment. CHAMPAKAM CASE: Madras govt's caste-based reservation in college admission (DPSP-aligned, helping backward classes) struck down for violating Article 15 + 29 (FR). 1st Amendment → added Article 15(4) authorising reservation. KESAVANANDA BHARATI (1973) — articulated 'BASIC STRUCTURE'. MINERVA MILLS (1980) → SC struck parts of 42nd Amendment that gave DPSP overriding power (Article 31C). NOW (settled): both FR + DPSP balance — neither absolutely supreme; courts harmonise. RECENT trend: SC reads DPSPs INTO Article 21 (right to life) — environment, education, livelihood, health, food = derived rights.

cards.front:
Which Article of DPSP relates to PROHIBITION OF INTOXICATING DRINKS?

(A) Article 47 (also nutrition + public health)
(B) Article 21 (Fundamental Right - life)
(C) Article 48 (cow protection only)
(D) Article 39 (livelihood + work) too
cards.back:
(A) Article 47 (also nutrition + public health)

Directive Principles & Duties — Article 47: 'Duty of the state to raise the level of NUTRITION + standard of living + IMPROVE PUBLIC HEALTH; specifically, the state shall endeavour to bring about PROHIBITION of intoxicating drinks + drugs which are injurious to health.' GANDHI strongly favoured prohibition. STATES that have implemented (full or partial alcohol prohibition): GUJARAT (since 1960, fully dry), BIHAR (since 2016), NAGALAND, MIZORAM, LAKSHADWEEP. Many other states tried + reversed (Andhra under YSRCP relaxed earlier prohibition; Kerala reversed). PYQ: prohibition is in DPSP → state's CHOICE; not nationwide. ALCOHOL-RELATED state revenue is huge (~25% of state taxes for some states like UP, Maharashtra) — disincentive to prohibition.

cards.front:
Are DPSPs JUSTICIABLE (enforceable in court)?

(A) NO — non-justiciable but fundamental in governance
(B) Yes — fully enforceable through writs
(C) Some are; depends on amendment status
(D) Only post-1976 (after 42nd Amendment)
cards.back:
(A) NO — non-justiciable but fundamental in governance

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP — NON-JUSTICIABLE (Article 37: 'shall not be enforceable by any court'). BUT 'FUNDAMENTAL in the governance of the country' → state's MORAL OBLIGATION; courts CONSIDER them while interpreting laws + rights. INSIGHT — courts INDIRECTLY enforce DPSPs by reading them into Article 21 (right to life): right to LIVELIHOOD (Olga Tellis, 1985), CLEAN ENVIRONMENT (MC Mehta cases), EDUCATION (Mohini Jain, 1992 — later FR by 86th Amendment), HEALTH, FOOD, SHELTER. AMBEDKAR explanation: DPSPs are 'novel features' of Constitution; while not enforceable now, they should serve as standards courts + governments aspire to. KEY DIFFERENCE: FR are 'Negative obligations' (state shall NOT do X to citizen); DPSP are 'Positive obligations' (state SHALL do Y for citizen).
cards.option2: Some are; depends on amendment status

cards.front:
Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are contained in which Part of the Constitution?

(A) Part III (Articles 12-35)
(B) Part IV (Articles 36-51)
(C) Part V (Articles 52-151)
(D) Part IVA (Article 51A)
cards.back:
(B) Part IV (Articles 36-51)

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP — Part IV, Articles 36-51. Part III (12-35) — Fundamental Rights. Part IVA (Article 51A) — Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment, 1976; 11 duties after 86th Amendment added the right to education-linked duty in 2002). DPSP are non-justiciable (Article 37 — not enforceable by any court), but 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and the State has a duty to apply them while making laws.

DPSP are non-justiciable (Article 37 — not enforceable by any court), but 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and the State has a duty to apply them while making laws.

cards.front:
DPSP in the Indian Constitution is BORROWED FROM the constitution of:

(A) United Kingdom
(B) Ireland (which itself borrowed it from the Spanish Constitution)
(C) United States
(D) Canada
cards.back:
(B) Ireland (which itself borrowed it from the Spanish Constitution)

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP — borrowed from Ireland (Irish Constitution of 1937). Other borrowings: Parliamentary system + rule of law (UK); FRs + judicial review + Preamble structure (US); Federal scheme + residuary powers with centre (Canada); Concurrent List (Australia); Emergency provisions (Germany — Weimar); Procedure for amendment (South Africa); Five-Year Plans (USSR); Fundamental Duties (USSR). Ireland adopted the concept from the Spanish Constitution, originally a Spanish innovation.

cards.front:
Article 44 of the Constitution directs the State to secure for citizens a:

(A) Right to free legal aid
(B) Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India
(C) Right to work
(D) Living wage for workers
cards.back:
(B) Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India

Directive Principles & Duties — Article 44 — Uniform Civil Code (UCC). Currently civil matters (marriage, divorce, succession, adoption) follow personal laws by religion. Goa is the only state with a UCC (inherited from Portuguese colonial code). Uttarakhand became the first state to legislate a UCC in 2024. Article 39A — equal justice + free legal aid. Article 41 — right to work, education, public assistance. Article 43 — living wage. Shah Bano case (1985) and Shayara Bano case (2017, triple talaq) revived UCC debate.

Articles 39(b) and 39(c), which direct ownership and control of material resources to subserve the common good, are classified as:

(A) Gandhian principles
(B) Socialist principles
(C) Liberal-intellectual principles
(D) Fundamental Duties
cards.back:
(B) Socialist principles

Directive Principles & Duties — DPSP classification (academic, not constitutional): SOCIALIST — Articles 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47 (welfare state, equitable distribution). GANDHIAN — Articles 40 (village panchayats), 43 (cottage industries), 43B (cooperatives), 46 (SC/ST/weaker sections), 47 (prohibition), 48 (cow protection). cards.front:
Article 48A — protection and improvement of environment, forests and wildlife — was added to the Constitution by the:

(A) 1st Amendment, 1951
(B) 42nd Amendment, 1976
(C) 44th Amendment, 1978
(D) 73rd Amendment, 1992
cards.back:
(B) 42nd Amendment, 1976

Directive Principles & Duties — 42nd Amendment, 1976 ('Mini-Constitution', Indira Gandhi's emergency-era amendment) — added FOUR new DPSP: Article 39A (equal justice + free legal aid); 43A (workers' participation in management); 48A (environment, forests, wildlife); also created Part IVA (Fundamental Duties — Article 51A, 10 duties). 86th Amendment, 2002 — modified Article 45 (childhood care below 6) and added Article 21A (Right to Education as FR). 97th Amendment, 2011 — added 'cooperative societies' (43B) and Part IXB. Note — DPSP have grown over time.

Which DPSP article directs the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government?

(A) Article 39
(B) Article 40
(C) Article 45
(D) Article 50
cards.back:
(B) Article 40

Directive Principles & Duties — Article 40 — village panchayats as units of self-government (Gandhian principle). Translated into reality by 73rd Amendment (1992) — added Part IX + Schedule 11; mandated panchayati raj institutions, gram sabhas, reservations for SC/ST/women (1/3, raised to 1/2 in many states). Article 50 — separation of judiciary from executive (achieved by Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Article 45 — early childhood care (originally free + compulsory primary education, now covered by Article 21A). Article 39 — distribution of material resources.

cards.front:
Regarding the relationship between Fundamental Rights (FRs) and DPSP, which is CORRECT?

(A) FRs always override DPSP
(B) DPSP are subordinate to FRs but Article 31C (since 1971) gives some DPSP precedence over Articles 14, 19
(C) DPSP always override FRs
(D) DPSP are enforceable in court like FRs
cards.back:
(B) DPSP are subordinate to FRs but Article 31C (since 1971) gives some DPSP precedence over Articles 14, 19

Directive Principles & Duties — Champakam Dorairajan (1951) — FRs prevail over DPSP. State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas — courts try to harmonise. 25th Amendment (1971) added Article 31C — laws giving effect to 39(b)/39(c) cannot be challenged on grounds of Article 14 or 19. 42nd Amendment tried to extend this to ALL DPSP, but Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension — basic-structure doctrine: harmony between FRs and DPSP is part of the basic structure. So FRs and DPSP are now read complementarily; courts interpret FRs in light of DPSP (e.g., environmental rights derived from Article 21 + 48A).
cards.option3: DPSP are enforceable in court like FRs

cards.front:
Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the:

(A) 44th Amendment, 1978
(B) 42nd Amendment, 1976 (on Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation)
(C) 73rd Amendment, 1992
(D) 1st Amendment, 1951
cards.back:
(B) 42nd Amendment, 1976 (on Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation)

Directive Principles & Duties — Fundamental Duties added by 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — based on Sardar Swaran Singh Committee's recommendations during the Emergency. Inserted Part IV-A (Article 51A). Inspired by USSR Constitution. Originally 10 duties; an 11th was added by 86th Amendment, 2002 (parents to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6-14). Total: 11 Fundamental Duties as of today.

(A) 10
(B) 11

cards.front:
Fundamental Duties in India are:

(A) Justiciable — directly enforceable in courts
(B) Non-justiciable but courts can refer to them when interpreting laws
(C) Enforceable only against citizens, not state
(D) Same as Fundamental Rights
cards.back:
(B) Non-justiciable but courts can refer to them when interpreting laws

Directive Principles & Duties — Fundamental Duties are NON-justiciable — no direct legal remedy if not performed. Like DPSPs, they are moral obligations. However, courts have used FDs to interpret existing laws (AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS, 2002 — gave them weight equal to DPSPs in constitutional interpretation). Some duties have legislative backing — Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955. Punjab and Haryana HC ruled (2003) that protecting environment is enforceable.
cards.option2: Enforceable only against citizens, not state

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT among the 11 Fundamental Duties under Article 51A?

(A) To safeguard public property and abjure violence
(B) To protect and improve the natural environment
(C) To pay income tax honestly
(D) To develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry
cards.back:
(C) To pay income tax honestly

Directive Principles & Duties — Paying tax is a LEGAL duty (under Income Tax Act) but NOT a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A. The 11 FDs cover: respect Constitution, anthem, flag, abide by ideals; cherish freedom-struggle ideals; protect sovereignty, integrity, unity; defend country & render national service; promote harmony & brotherhood, renounce derogatory practices to women's dignity; preserve culture; protect environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property + abjure violence; strive towards excellence; provide education to one's child (added 2002).

cards.option2: To protect and improve the natural environment
cards.option3: To develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry

Which committee, in 1999, recommended introducing Fundamental Duties into the school curriculum and operationalising them?

(A) Sarkaria Commission
(B) Justice J.S. Verma Committee
(C) Punchhi Commission
(D) Liberhan Commission
cards.back:
(B) Justice J.S. Verma Committee

Directive Principles & Duties — Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) — appointed by the Centre — recommended teaching Fundamental Duties through education + enforcement via existing laws + identifying laws connected to each duty. Found that 11 of the 11 FDs are reflected in some existing law. Recommended a 'National Foundation for Fundamental Rights and Duties'. cards.front:
The Fundamental Duty to 'develop scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry' was inspired by:

(A) Mahatma Gandhi's writings
(B) Jawaharlal Nehru's vision (Discovery of India)
(C) B.R. Ambedkar's speeches
(D) American Bill of Rights
cards.back:
(B) Jawaharlal Nehru's vision (Discovery of India)

Directive Principles & Duties — Article 51A(h) — 'to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.' Reflects Nehru's vision articulated in 'Discovery of India' (1946). Term 'scientific temper' was coined by Nehru himself. Nehru wanted India to embrace rational thinking, evidence-based reasoning. The phrase is invoked frequently in court judgements opposing superstition (e.g., banning of dolphin shows, witch-hunting laws). Maharashtra Anti-Superstition Act (2013) draws from this duty.

cards.front:
Among major democracies, only one country alongside India explicitly enshrines a list of citizen duties. That country is:

(A) USA
(B) USSR (now Russian Federation; the original FD-list inspiration)
(C) United Kingdom
(D) Australia
cards.back:
(B) USSR (now Russian Federation; the original FD-list inspiration)

Directive Principles & Duties — Soviet Constitution (1977) had Articles 60-69 listing duties of Soviet citizens. India's Swaran Singh Committee (1976) drew inspiration from it. After USSR dissolution, the Russian Federation Constitution (1993) retained some duties. Other democracies — US, UK, Australia, Canada — do not have explicit constitutional duty lists; civic obligations exist via ordinary laws. Japan, China, Vietnam, Cuba have constitutional duties. India is one of the few major democracies with this feature.

cards.front:
A 'Money Bill' is defined under which Article of the Indian Constitution?

(A) Article 109
(B) Article 110
(C) Article 117
(D) Article 368
cards.back:
(B) Article 110

Parliament — Money Bill — defined in Article 110(1). Must contain ONLY provisions dealing with: (a) imposition / abolition / remission / variation of tax; (b) regulation of borrowing by Government of India; (c) custody / withdrawal from Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund; (d) appropriation from Consolidated Fund; (e) declaring expenditure as 'charged' on Consolidated Fund; (f) receipts on/issue from Consolidated Fund or audit of Centre/State; (g) any matter incidental to (a)-(f). The SPEAKER of Lok Sabha decides whether a bill is a Money Bill — and her decision is FINAL (not justiciable in earlier rulings; recent SC questioning in Aadhaar / RTI cases). Article 109 — procedure for Money Bills. Article 117 — Financial Bills.

cards.front:
Regarding the procedure for a Money Bill, which is INCORRECT?

(A) It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (not Rajya Sabha)
(B) It can be introduced only on the recommendation of the President
(C) Rajya Sabha can amend / reject it like any other bill
(D) Rajya Sabha must return the Money Bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations; Lok Sabha may accept or reject
cards.back:
(C) Rajya Sabha can amend / reject it like any other bill

Parliament — Money Bill procedure (Articles 109 + 110): (1) Introduced ONLY in Lok Sabha; (2) ONLY on Presidential recommendation; (3) Once passed by Lok Sabha, sent to Rajya Sabha; (4) Rajya Sabha can ONLY make recommendations (not amend or reject); must return within 14 DAYS; (5) Lok Sabha may ACCEPT or REJECT Rajya Sabha's recommendations — its decision is final; (6) If Rajya Sabha doesn't return within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed in the original form. (7) Goes to President — who can ASSENT or WITHHOLD assent (no return for reconsideration, unlike ordinary bills under Article 111). This power asymmetry between LS and RS is a deliberate constitutional design — Lok Sabha (directly elected) controls public finance.

cards.option2: It can be introduced only on the recommendation of the President
cards.option3: Rajya Sabha must return the Money Bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations; Lok Sabha may accept or reject

cards.front:
The Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) is presented to Parliament under which Article?

(A) Article 110
(B) Article 112
(C) Article 124
(D) Article 245
cards.back:
(B) Article 112

Parliament — Article 112 — 'Annual Financial Statement' (popularly the Union Budget). Statement of estimated receipts + expenditure of the Govt of India for the financial year. Two parts: (1) RECEIPTS — Tax revenue, non-tax revenue, capital receipts (loans, disinvestment, recoveries); (2) EXPENDITURE — Revenue expenditure (recurring) + Capital expenditure (asset-creating). Charged Expenditure (President's salary, judges' salaries, debt obligations) — non-votable. Voted Expenditure — needs Parliament's approval. Consolidated Fund of India (Art 266) — into which all Govt receipts go. Contingency Fund (Art 267) — at the disposal of the President for unforeseen expenses. Public Account (Art 266) — Provident Fund, small savings, judicial deposits. Union Budget is presented on FEBRUARY 1 (since FY 2017-18 — earlier was last working day of Feb).

cards.front:
What is the difference between a 'Finance Bill' and a 'Money Bill'?

(A) They are the same thing
(B) Every Money Bill is a Finance Bill, but every Finance Bill is NOT a Money Bill (a Finance Bill may include matters beyond the Article 110 list)
(C) A Finance Bill cannot deal with taxation
(D) A Money Bill needs Rajya Sabha approval
cards.back:
(B) Every Money Bill is a Finance Bill, but every Finance Bill is NOT a Money Bill (a Finance Bill may include matters beyond the Article 110 list)

Parliament — Categories of Financial Bills: (1) MONEY BILL (Art 110) — strictly dealing only with Art 110(1)(a-g) matters. (2) FINANCIAL BILL CATEGORY-I (Art 117(1)) — contains Art 110 matters PLUS other matters (e.g., bill that has tax clauses + general administration). Procedure as Money Bill for introduction (LS only, President recommendation), but Rajya Sabha can amend or reject like an ordinary bill. (3) FINANCIAL BILL CATEGORY-II (Art 117(3)) — does NOT contain Art 110 matters but involves expenditure from Consolidated Fund. Like an ordinary bill except needs President's recommendation for consideration (not for introduction). The annual Finance Bill that gives effect to budget proposals (taxes, etc.) is typically a FINANCIAL BILL CATEGORY-I or sometimes a MONEY BILL depending on its content. Speaker certifies which.
cards.option2: A Finance Bill cannot deal with taxation
cards.option3: A Money Bill needs Rajya Sabha approval

cards.front:
An 'Appropriation Bill' is required because, under the Constitution:

(A) Money cannot be spent without the President's signature
(B) No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except by appropriation made by law (Article 114)
(C) It is required for income tax
(D) Only Rajya Sabha can authorise spending
cards.back:
(B) No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except by appropriation made by law (Article 114)

Parliament — Article 114 — Appropriation Bill. After Demands for Grants are voted on by Lok Sabha (within the Parliamentary Budget process), the Appropriation Bill is introduced — providing legal authority for withdrawal from Consolidated Fund. NO AMENDMENTS that vary the amount or change destination of grants are admissible. Once passed, becomes the Appropriation Act. The Finance Bill is separate — it gives effect to taxation proposals. Order of major budget steps: (1) Budget speech; (2) Discussion on the Budget; (3) Vote on Account (interim approval to allow government to function until full appropriation passes); (4) Demands for Grants; (5) APPROPRIATION BILL; (6) FINANCE BILL. CUT MOTIONS — Policy cut (token ₹1, expressing disapproval); Economy cut (specific reduction); Token cut (₹100 reduction, raising specific grievance).

cards.option2: It is required for income tax
cards.option3: Only Rajya Sabha can authorise spending

cards.front:
Which of these CONSTITUTIONAL OFFICES has its salary CHARGED on the Consolidated Fund of India (i.e., not subject to a vote)?

(A) Salary of MPs
(B) Salaries of the President, Vice-President, Speaker, Judges of the Supreme Court / High Courts, CAG, etc.
(C) Salary of cabinet ministers
(D) Defence personnel salaries
cards.back:
(B) Salaries of the President, Vice-President, Speaker, Judges of the Supreme Court / High Courts, CAG, etc.

Parliament — CHARGED Expenditure (non-votable; cannot be discussed in voting context but can be discussed): (1) Emoluments + allowances of the President; (2) Salaries + allowances of Chairman / Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha + Speaker / Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha; (3) Debt charges of GoI; (4) Salaries of SC + HC judges, CAG, UPSC chairman; (5) Pensions of judges; (6) any sum required to satisfy a court judgment. Reason for being 'charged': to insulate independent constitutional functionaries from political pressure (their salary cannot be reduced or held hostage by Parliament voting). VOTED Expenditure (rest, including ministers' salaries, defence, MGNREGA, etc.) — Lok Sabha votes on Demands for Grants, headed by ministry.

cards.front:
Who, as per the Constitution, decides whether a bill is a 'Money Bill' or not?

(A) President of India
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha
(C) Finance Minister
(D) Supreme Court
cards.back:
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha

Parliament — Article 110(3) — 'If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People [Lok Sabha] thereon shall be final.' SPEAKER's certificate accompanies the bill. Controversies — Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill (despite covering broad provisions), bypassing Rajya Sabha. SC in K.S. Puttaswamy II (2018) upheld it but a dissent (Justice Chandrachud) called the certification a 'fraud on the Constitution'. Subsequent challenge — 7-judge bench in Rojer Mathew (2019) referred the question of whether Aadhaar was correctly classified as a Money Bill to a LARGER bench (still pending as of 2026). The decision is constitutionally final but increasingly seen as judicially reviewable on procedural grounds.

cards.front:
The MAXIMUM strength of the LOK SABHA, as per the Constitution, is:

(A) 552 members in total
(B) 545 members in total
(C) 543 members in total
(D) 560 members in total
cards.back:
(A) 552 members in total

Parliament — Article 81 — Maximum LS strength = 552: 530 from STATES + 20 from UTs + 2 ANGLO-INDIAN nominees (originally; REMOVED by 104th Amendment, 2019). NOW = 543 actual elected members (530 from states + 13 from UTs). India is currently in 18th Lok Sabha (June 2024). Term = 5 years (Article 83) unless dissolved sooner; can be extended by 1 year during emergency.

The MINIMUM AGE to contest as a Lok Sabha candidate is:

(A) 21 years for the candidate
(B) 25 years for the candidate
(C) 30 years for the candidate
(D) 35 years for the candidate

(B) 25 years for the candidate

Voter (electorate) age = 18 (lowered from 21 by 61st Amendment, 1989). LS member must also: be Indian citizen, registered voter in any constituency, not hold office of profit (Article 102 — disqualifications). 'Anti-defection' (10th Schedule) — defection grounds for disqualification.

cards.front:
The QUORUM (minimum members for LS sitting) is what fraction of total membership?

(A) 1/4 of total LS membership
(B) 1/10 of total LS membership
(C) 1/3 of total LS membership
(D) 1/2 of total LS membership
cards.back:
(B) 1/10 of total LS membership

Parliament — Article 100(3) — Quorum for either House = 1/10 of total membership (Speaker / Chairman included). LS quorum = 543/10 ≈ 55. RS quorum = 245/10 ≈ 25. If quorum not met during a sitting, Speaker / Chairman ADJOURNS the House. The threshold is intentionally low — to allow business when many MPs are away. 1/10 was chosen by Constituent Assembly (Ambedkar's recommendation).

cards.front:
The Lok Sabha can be DISSOLVED by:

(A) Speaker of the Lok Sabha by motion
(B) President on PM's advice (or expiry of 5 yrs)
(C) Supreme Court when needed urgently
(D) Vote of all state legislative assemblies
cards.back:
(B) President on PM's advice (or expiry of 5 yrs)

Parliament — Article 85 — President SUMMONS, prorogues, dissolves Parliament. PRESIDENT dissolves LS — typically on PRIME MINISTER's advice. Or LS dissolves automatically at end of its 5-year term. AFTER dissolution → general elections must be held (within 6 months — though practically faster). Speaker continues until day before new LS first sitting. Note: Rajya Sabha is PERMANENT — never dissolved (1/3 retire every 2 years). Distractor 1 — Speaker can't dissolve (he/she only presides). Distractor 3 — SC can't dissolve.

(A) Council of States, in upper house terms
(B) House of the People (popular house)
(C) Constituent Assembly (1946-50 body)

(A) 3 months between Parliament sessions
(B) 6 months between Parliament sessions
(C) 9 months between Parliament sessions
(D) 12 months between Parliament sessions

FIRST HOUR of every working day in the Lok Sabha is called:

(B) Question Hour, devoted to questions
(C) Cabinet Hour, the ministers' Q&A

Parliament — QUESTION HOUR (11 AM-12 PM) — first hour of every parliamentary working day. MPs ask QUESTIONS to ministers; ministers answer + are held accountable. ZERO HOUR (12 noon-1 PM) — Indian innovation (1962); MPs raise urgent matters without prior notice. Most TV-attention-grabbing time. Parliament — Art 83(2) — during National Emergency (Art 352), Parliament may extend Lok Sabha by up to 1 year at a time (but not more than 6 months past the end of the Emergency). Used once — 1975-77 Emergency: Lok Sabha extended twice beyond its normal 5-year term.

cards.front:
QUESTION HOUR in Lok Sabha is held during the:

(A) First hour of every sitting (11 AM-12 noon)
(B) Last hour of any sitting (5-6 PM)
(C) Lunch hour daily for one hour (option here)
(D) Once a week on Mondays only (option here)
cards.back:
(A) First hour of every sitting (11 AM-12 noon)

Parliament — QUESTION HOUR — first hour of LOK SABHA sittings (11:00 AM to 12:00 noon usually). Members ask QUESTIONS to MINISTERS regarding their portfolios; ministers (or junior ministers) provide answers. THREE TYPES OF QUESTIONS: (1) STARRED — receive ORAL answer; supplementary questions allowed; marked with asterisk (*). (2) UNSTARRED — receive WRITTEN answer; no supplementary questions. (3) SHORT-NOTICE — for matter of urgent public importance; must give 10 days' notice; rules at Speaker's discretion. PROCEDURE: notice must be given 21 DAYS in advance; Speaker decides admissibility. PURPOSE: a fundamental tool of executive ACCOUNTABILITY — ministers face direct questioning by elected MPs. RECENT TRENDS: in last few years, Question Hour has been DISRUPTED frequently due to opposition protests; ~50% loss of question hour during turbulent sessions. ZERO HOUR follows immediately AFTER Question Hour (noon to 1 PM); not constitutionally provided but a parliamentary CONVENTION since 1962. NOT FOUND IN CONSTITUTION: Question Hour is governed by the RULES OF PROCEDURE of LOK SABHA, NOT the Constitution itself. SPEAKER's role: presides over Question Hour, decides admissibility, expunges objectionable language. PYQ FREQUENCY: Question Hour basics in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC polity 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
ZERO HOUR in Indian Parliament is:

(A) Time after Question Hour for urgent matters
(B) Time when no work is conducted
(C) Period when Parliament is dissolved
(D) First hour of monsoon session there
cards.back:
(A) Time after Question Hour for urgent matters

Parliament — ZERO HOUR — informal parliamentary convention; immediately follows QUESTION HOUR — runs typically from 12 NOON to 1 PM (in Lok Sabha) — used by MPs to RAISE MATTERS OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE. ORIGIN: started in 1962 (an Indian innovation; not in any other Parliament's procedure). NOT MENTIONED in Rules of Procedure or Constitution; purely a CONVENTION. NAME 'ZERO HOUR': because it begins at the 'zeroth hour' (12:00 noon, between session segments). PROCEDURE: MPs give NOTICE to Speaker (between 10 AM and 12 PM same day) about issues they want to raise; Speaker selects which to permit; each issue limited to ~3 minutes typically. TYPICAL ISSUES: local emergencies, accidents, prices, controversies, drought, floods, regional concerns. CRITICISM: often becomes a platform for grandstanding; serious legislation suffers when much of session is consumed by Zero Hour drama. CONTRAST WITH OTHER MOTIONS: (1) ADJOURNMENT MOTION — formal, demands suspension of business; needs 50 MP support; usually rejected by Speaker. (2) HALF-AN-HOUR DISCUSSION — pre-arranged; held after the day's business concludes. (3) PRIVILEGE MOTION — about breach of privilege. (4) CALLING-ATTENTION MOTION — shorter version of half-hour, called by Speaker. PYQ FREQUENCY: Zero Hour in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.option3: First hour of monsoon session there

cards.front:
A NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION can be moved against:

(A) Council of Ministers (CoM, govt as whole)
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha alone (option here)
(C) President of India directly (option here)
(D) Individual MP for any reason (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Council of Ministers (CoM, govt as whole)

Parliament — NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION — moved against the COUNCIL OF MINISTERS (i.e., the government as a whole, headed by the PRIME MINISTER) under Article 75(3) read with Rules. RULES: (1) Notice in writing by MP. (2) ADMISSIBLE only if 50 MEMBERS support (in 543-member House). (3) Speaker decides admissibility. (4) DEBATE typically 2-3 days; PM must speak. (5) DIVISION (vote) at end. PASSAGE: if motion gets MAJORITY of MEMBERS PRESENT AND VOTING → government LOSES confidence → must RESIGN (PM submits resignation to President). KEY: a successful no-confidence motion automatically dismisses the entire government, NOT just one minister. NUMBER of NO-CONFIDENCE MOTIONS in INDIA: ~28 since 1947 (in Lok Sabha); only a HANDFUL successful — most famous is the FALL OF VAJPAYEE'S 13-DAY GOVERNMENT (1996, lost by 1 vote — 269 to 270). RECENT: Modi government faced no-confidence motions July 2018 and August 2023 — both DEFEATED easily (BJP majority). DIFFERENT MOTIONS: (1) NO-CONFIDENCE — against entire CoM. (2) CENSURE MOTION — against entire CoM or individual minister; doesn't bring down govt; expresses disapproval; requires reason. (3) ADJOURNMENT MOTION — to discuss urgent matter; doesn't bring down govt. (4) MOTION OF THANKS — on President's address; convention. PYQ FREQUENCY: no-confidence motion in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Who decides whether a Bill is a MONEY BILL or not?

(A) Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Art 110)
(B) Vice President of India here
(C) Supreme Court of India only
(D) Finance Minister (just suggests)
cards.back:
(A) Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Art 110)

Parliament — ARTICLE 110 — SPEAKER OF THE LOK SABHA decides whether a bill is a MONEY BILL. The Speaker's CERTIFICATION is FINAL — Article 110(3) explicitly states this; the decision cannot be questioned in courts (a contentious area). MONEY BILL CHARACTERISTICS: deals exclusively with: (a) Imposition, abolition, alteration of TAXES. (b) Borrowing/lending of money by GoI. (c) Custody of Consolidated Fund / Contingency Fund. (d) Appropriation of money from Consolidated Fund. (e) Any matter incidental to above. NOT covered (mere fee for service, fine, etc.) → not a money bill. KEY PROCEDURE for MONEY BILL: (1) Introduced ONLY in LOK SABHA (not Rajya Sabha) — Article 109. (2) Cannot be amended by Rajya Sabha; only RECOMMENDATIONS allowed. (3) Lok Sabha may accept or reject Rajya Sabha's recommendations; if rejected, bill becomes law as Lok Sabha passed it. (4) Rajya Sabha must return within 14 days; else deemed passed. (5) President can ONLY ASSENT or WITHHOLD assent (cannot return for reconsideration). CONTROVERSY: ADHAAR ACT 2016 was certified as Money Bill — challenged in SC (Puttaswamy case 2018, K.S. Puttaswamy v. UoI on Adhaar). SC upheld certification (4-1) but warned against overuse of Money Bill route. RECENT (2023): Speaker has certified some controversial bills as Money Bills, drawing criticism. PYQ FREQUENCY: money bill rules in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which official in Lok Sabha presides when both Speaker AND Deputy Speaker are absent?

(A) Member from Panel of Chairpersons
(B) Senior-most member by experience
(C) Vice President of India directly
(D) Pro tem Speaker (only at start)
cards.back:
(A) Member from Panel of Chairpersons

Parliament — PANEL OF CHAIRPERSONS — Article 95(1): when both SPEAKER and DEPUTY SPEAKER are absent, a member from the PANEL OF CHAIRPERSONS (nominated by Speaker, normally a list of ~10 senior MPs) presides over the Lok Sabha. ARTICLE 95: 'In the absence of both Speaker and Deputy Speaker, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the House, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the House.' PRO TEM SPEAKER (Article 99): different role — appointed at the START of a NEW Lok Sabha (after general elections) by the President; presides only over the first sitting until a new SPEAKER is elected from members. SPEAKER's election: in the first sitting of newly-elected Lok Sabha; pro tem Speaker (usually senior-most MP) presides. SPEAKER'S TENURE: continues until dissolution of Lok Sabha or his/her resignation/removal. RAJYA SABHA equivalent — VICE PRESIDENT is ex-officio CHAIRMAN (Art 89); DEPUTY CHAIRMAN is elected by RS members. When both VP and Deputy Chairman absent, panel of vice-chairmen presides. CURRENT (2026): LS Speaker = Om Birla (2nd term, 2024-29); Deputy Speaker = vacant since 2019 (controversial). PYQ FREQUENCY: presiding officers procedure in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
What is the QUORUM required for Lok Sabha sittings?

(A) 1/10 of members present (~55 of 543)
(B) 1/3 of total members always
(C) Simple majority (272 members)
(D) 100 members minimum required
cards.back:
(A) 1/10 of members present (~55 of 543)

Parliament — ARTICLE 100(3) — QUORUM (minimum members required) for Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha = 1/10th of TOTAL membership of the House. For LOK SABHA (543 members) → quorum = 55 (1/10 = 54.3, rounded up). For RAJYA SABHA (245 members) → quorum = 25 (245/10 = 24.5, rounded up). IF QUORUM IS NOT MET: presiding officer SUSPENDS the sitting until quorum is restored. CRITICISM: low quorum requirement means most decisions are taken by less than 10% of MPs in attendance — concerns about democratic legitimacy. PRACTICAL OBSERVATION: actual attendance often LOW; some bills passed with attendance ~50-60 MPs. SPEAKER'S RESPONSE: usually doesn't suspend sitting unless someone formally raises 'point of quorum'. CONSTITUTIONAL VS LEGISLATIVE quorum: (1) FOR PASSING ORDINARY LEGISLATION: quorum (1/10) + simple majority of those present. (2) FOR CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS (Art 368): special majority — 2/3 of present + 50% of total membership. (3) FOR REMOVAL OF JUDGES, etc.: also special majority. PYQ FREQUENCY: quorum + voting requirements in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC polity — 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests precise constitutional numbers + procedural details.
