cards.front:
An ADJOURNMENT MOTION in Lok Sabha is moved to:

(A) Discuss matter of urgent public importance
(B) Postpone all parliament sessions
(C) Dismiss the government immediately
(D) End the Question Hour early
cards.back:
(A) Discuss matter of urgent public importance

Parliament — ADJOURNMENT MOTION — extraordinary procedure that, if PASSED, suspends the day's business to discuss a SPECIFIC MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE. Used to bring govt's attention to a serious issue (riots, accidents, financial scams, security failures). PROCEDURE: (1) Notice in writing to Speaker before 10 AM. (2) Topic must be DEFINITE, RECENT, of URGENT public importance, requiring URGENT discussion (not subject of pending judicial proceedings). (3) Speaker decides admissibility. (4) Requires SUPPORT of 50 MPs. (5) Discussion can last for max 2.5 hours. (6) MOTION USUALLY DEFEATED — symbolic value rather than legal effect. ELEMENT OF CENSURE: passing of the motion implies CRITICISM of govt — strong political weapon. SAMPLE INSTANCES: 1947-2024 — many adjournment motions on partition violence (1947), Indo-China war (1962), Chinese aggression (2020), Pulwama (2019), railway accidents, Delhi riots, etc. CRITICISM: in BJP-majority Lok Sabha, recent admissibility of opposition's adjournment motions has been low; opposition resorts to Zero Hour or media. CONTRAST: NO-CONFIDENCE motion brings DOWN govt; ADJOURNMENT motion is a censure-like tool that doesn't directly affect govt's continuation. ADJOURNMENT-SINE-DIE: ending of a session indefinitely — different concept; done by Speaker. PYQ FREQUENCY: adjournment motion in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by:

(A) All MPs of both Houses by single transferable vote
(B) Members of the Lok Sabha from amongst themselves
(C) President on advice of the Prime Minister
(D) Council of Ministers by absolute majority vote
cards.back:
(B) Members of the Lok Sabha from amongst themselves

Parliament — Article 93 — Lok Sabha shall elect a Speaker + Deputy Speaker from amongst its members. Elected by simple majority. Conventionally — Speaker from ruling party, Deputy Speaker from opposition (since 6th LS). Speaker continues even if LS is dissolved, until the new Speaker is elected. Salary + allowances charged on Consolidated Fund of India (Article 112). Distractor 1 — that's how President is elected (with weighted formulae). Distractor 3 — President doesn't appoint. Distractor 4 — Council doesn't elect.

cards.option2: President on advice of the Prime Minister
cards.option3: Council of Ministers by absolute majority vote

cards.front:
The CASTING VOTE in the Lok Sabha is exercised by:

(A) The Prime Minister, in case of any tie vote
(B) The Speaker, only when there is a tie
(C) The Leader of Opposition, on a tie vote
(D) The President of India in deadlock cases
cards.back:
(B) The Speaker, only when there is a tie

Parliament — Article 100 — Speaker does NOT vote in the first instance. But in case of a TIE (equal votes for and against), Speaker has the CASTING VOTE — the second, deciding vote. This preserves Speaker's appearance of impartiality during normal voting. Same convention in Westminster + most parliaments. Notable use: Vajpayee government fell by 1 vote in 1999 (no-confidence; 269 vs 270, did not require Speaker's casting vote). Distractor 1 — PM is an MP, votes normally. Distractor 3 — LoP has no special vote. Distractor 4 — President doesn't vote in Parliament.

cards.option2: The Leader of Opposition, on a tie vote
cards.option3: The President of India in deadlock cases

cards.front:
The Speaker is REMOVED from office by:

(A) Resolution passed by majority of all members of LS
(B) Direct order of the Prime Minister with cabinet
(C) Joint sitting of both Houses with 2/3 majority
(D) Two-thirds vote of the Supreme Court only
cards.back:
(A) Resolution passed by majority of all members of LS

Parliament — Article 94 — Speaker can be removed by a RESOLUTION passed by a MAJORITY OF ALL THE THEN MEMBERS of Lok Sabha (effective majority — more than half of total membership, NOT just present + voting). Requires 14-day prior notice. While the resolution is being considered, Deputy Speaker presides. Speaker can speak + vote in such resolution. Other grounds for vacancy: cease to be MP; resignation (to Deputy Speaker). Distractor 2 — PM can't remove. Distractor 3 — joint sitting not the procedure. Distractor 4 — SC doesn't remove the Speaker.

cards.option3: Two-thirds vote of the Supreme Court only

MONEY BILL certification (whether a bill IS or IS NOT a Money Bill) is done by:

(A) Finance Minister of the central government
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha (final decision)
(C) Chairman (Vice-President) of Rajya Sabha
(D) President in consultation with the cabinet
cards.back:
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha (final decision)

Parliament — Article 110(3) — 'If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill, the decision of the SPEAKER of the House of the People shall be final.' Hugely consequential power: Money Bills bypass Rajya Sabha (RS can only recommend; LS can override). Aadhaar Act 2016 was certified as Money Bill by Speaker — controversially, leading to SC rulings. SC has held the Speaker's decision is justiciable on the basis of constitutional interpretation (Rojer Mathew, 2019, referred to larger bench, pending). Distractors are not the certifying authority.

The FIRST Speaker of the Lok Sabha (post-Constitution) was:

(A) G.V. Mavlankar, the 'Father of Lok Sabha'
(B) M.A. Ayyangar, who succeeded Mavlankar later
(C) Sumitra Mahajan, the second woman Speaker
(D) Meira Kumar, the first woman LS Speaker
cards.back:
(A) G.V. Mavlankar, the 'Father of Lok Sabha'

Parliament — G.V. MAVLANKAR — first Speaker of Lok Sabha (15 May 1952 - 27 Feb 1956); died in office. Earlier presided over the Constituent Assembly (Legislative). Called 'FATHER OF LOK SABHA'. Successors: M.A. AYYANGAR (1956-62), Hukam Singh, N. Sanjiva Reddy (later President), G.S. Dhillon, Bali Ram Bhagat. First WOMAN speaker — MEIRA KUMAR (2009-14, daughter of Jagjivan Ram). SUMITRA MAHAJAN was the second woman speaker (2014-19). Current Speaker (Jun 2024-): Om Birla.

cards.front:
When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker:

(A) Vacates office immediately on dissolution
(B) Continues in office till the new LS is constituted
(C) Becomes acting Prime Minister till elections
(D) Joins the Rajya Sabha as a nominated member
cards.back:
(B) Continues in office till the new LS is constituted

Parliament — Speaker continues in office EVEN AFTER dissolution of the Lok Sabha — until the day immediately before the first sitting of the next Lok Sabha. This ensures continuity and that someone can preside if a special session is called between dissolution and the new LS. Speaker's ROLE: presides over LS; maintains discipline; decides points of order; certifies Money Bills; chairs the Joint Sitting of both Houses (Article 108).
cards.option2: Becomes acting Prime Minister till elections
cards.option3: Joins the Rajya Sabha as a nominated member

cards.front:
The Speaker's role under the 10th SCHEDULE (Anti-Defection Law) is to:

(A) Enforce party whip on every parliamentary vote
(B) Decide cases of disqualification of MPs for defection
(C) Suspend defecting members for one full session
(D) Refer defection cases to the Election Commission
cards.back:
(B) Decide cases of disqualification of MPs for defection

Parliament — Under 10th Schedule, Speaker (LS) / Chairman (RS) decides disqualification cases for defection. Earlier rulings — Speaker's decision was 'final and not subject to judicial review'. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1993) — SC held that Speaker's decision IS subject to judicial review (under Articles 136, 226, 227) — but COURT cannot intervene BEFORE the Speaker decides. SC has criticised Speakers for delaying decisions on convenience (Maharashtra 2022, Manipur 2020 — recommended Parliament consider an INDEPENDENT TRIBUNAL).

cards.front:
A Money Bill is defined in which Article of the Indian Constitution?

(A) Article 108
(B) Article 110
(C) Article 112
(D) Article 117
cards.back:
(B) Article 110

Parliament — Article 110 — exhaustive definition. A bill is a Money Bill only if it contains provisions dealing exclusively with any of seven specified matters — imposition/abolition of a tax, borrowing of money, Consolidated Fund / Contingency Fund, appropriation from Consolidated Fund, declaring an expenditure 'charged' on CFI, receipts/audit of public accounts, or any matter incidental to these. Article 108 is joint sitting; Article 112 is Annual Financial Statement; Article 117 is Financial Bills.

Article 108 is joint sitting; Article 112 is Annual Financial Statement; Article 117 is Financial Bills.

cards.front:
The final authority to certify whether a bill is a Money Bill rests with the:

(A) President of India
(B) Speaker of Lok Sabha
(C) Prime Minister
(D) Chairman of Rajya Sabha
cards.back:
(B) Speaker of Lok Sabha

Parliament — Article 110(3) — 'the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People thereon shall be final.' The Speaker's endorsement on every Money Bill certifies its status; Rajya Sabha cannot question the certificate. The Supreme Court in Rojer Mathew (2019) held that judicial review of the Speaker's certification is possible but has never overturned one. A Money Bill originates only in Lok Sabha with prior recommendation of the President.

cards.front:
Under Article 109, Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill with or without its recommendations within how many days from receipt?

(A) 7 days
(B) 14 days
(C) 21 days
(D) 30 days
cards.back:
(B) 14 days

Parliament — Article 109(4) — if Rajya Sabha does not return the Money Bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses at the end of the 14-day period in the form passed by Lok Sabha. Lok Sabha can accept or reject any of Rajya Sabha's recommendations — there is no joint-sitting provision for Money Bills. The 14-day clock is constitutionally fixed; it cannot be extended.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a feature that distinguishes a Money Bill from an ordinary bill?

(A) Originates only in Lok Sabha
(B) Requires prior recommendation of the President
(C) Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations, not amendments
(D) Joint sitting can be convened if disagreement arises
cards.back:
(D) Joint sitting can be convened if disagreement arises

Parliament — Article 108 (joint sitting) does NOT apply to Money Bills — because there can be no disagreement. If Rajya Sabha rejects or delays, the bill is deemed passed after 14 days anyway. Joint sittings have happened only 3 times in Indian history (Dowry Prohibition 1961, Banking Services Commission 1978, POTA 2002) — all ordinary bills. A, B and C are all distinguishing features of Money Bills.

cards.front:
A 'Financial Bill' under Article 117(1) differs from a Money Bill because a Financial Bill:

(A) Does not need President's recommendation
(B) Contains matters beyond Article 110 but also includes matters under Article 110
(C) Can only be introduced in Rajya Sabha
(D) Requires Supreme Court clearance
cards.back:
(B) Contains matters beyond Article 110 but also includes matters under Article 110

Parliament — Three-fold classification: Money Bill (Art 110) — exclusively A110 matters; Financial Bill Category I (Art 117(1)) — contains A110 matters plus other provisions; Financial Bill Category II (Art 117(3)) — involves expenditure from CFI but no A110 matters. A and B require President's recommendation to introduce; only C does not. Rajya Sabha has full powers over Financial Bills (including joint sitting possible) — unlike Money Bills.

cards.front:
The Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill. The Supreme Court's majority view in Puttaswamy (2018) / K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) was:

(A) Certification as Money Bill was unconstitutional
(B) Certification was valid; the Aadhaar scheme was constitutional
(C) Aadhaar itself was struck down entirely
(D) The Speaker must always consult President
cards.back:
(B) Certification was valid; the Aadhaar scheme was constitutional

Parliament — In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (26 Sep 2018), the 5-judge bench by 4:1 upheld Aadhaar Act's passage as a Money Bill — Section 7 (targeted delivery of subsidies from Consolidated Fund) was held to be the bill's core purpose. Justice Chandrachud dissented. In Rojer Mathew (2019) a 5-judge bench referred the Money Bill question to a 7-judge bench; decision still pending. Aadhaar scheme itself was upheld except Sections 33(2), 47, 57.

cards.front:
The Union Budget, placed before Parliament each year, is technically called the:

(A) Fiscal Responsibility Statement
(B) Annual Financial Statement
(C) Consolidated Budget Memorandum
(D) Appropriation Account
cards.back:
(B) Annual Financial Statement

Parliament — Article 112 — the 'Annual Financial Statement' (AFS) is the document of estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for a financial year. Popularly called 'the Budget'. The Finance Bill (Art 117) implements taxation proposals; the Appropriation Bill (Art 114) authorises withdrawal from CFI. Both are typically certified as Money Bills. Railway Budget was merged with the Union Budget from 2017-18.

cards.front:
The INDIAN PARLIAMENT is BICAMERAL, consisting of:

(A) Lok Sabha only
(B) PRESIDENT + LOK SABHA (House of the People) + RAJYA SABHA (Council of States) — Art 79
(C) Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha only
(D) President + Lok Sabha only
cards.back:
(B) PRESIDENT + LOK SABHA (House of the People) + RAJYA SABHA (Council of States) — Art 79

Parliament — ARTICLE 79 — 'There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the PRESIDENT and TWO HOUSES to be known respectively as the Council of States (RAJYA SABHA) and the House of the People (LOK SABHA)'. So Indian Parliament has 3 components: (1) PRESIDENT — NOT a member of either House but integral to Parliament; bills need his assent; summons + prorogues both Houses; dissolves LS. (2) RAJYA SABHA (COUNCIL of STATES) — Upper House; MAX STRENGTH 250 (238 elected from states/UTs + 12 NOMINATED by President from fields of Literature, Science, Art, Social Service). Currently 245 seats (233 + 12). Permanent body, NOT SUBJECT TO DISSOLUTION; 1/3 members retire every 2 years → 6-year term. Indirect election by ELECTED members of STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES (MLAs) via proportional representation by single transferable vote. Chairman = VICE-PRESIDENT of India (ex-officio). First sitting 13 May 1952. (3) LOK SABHA (HOUSE of the PEOPLE) — Lower House; MAX STRENGTH 552 (530 states + 20 UTs + 2 Anglo-Indians, but 2 Anglo-Indians removed by 104th CAA 2020); current 543 (with 2020 amendment — 2 Anglo-Indian seats lapsed). Members DIRECTLY elected from single-member constituencies (first-past-the-post); 5-year term (can be dissolved earlier). Age 25+. Speaker elected from among members. Quorum 1/10 of House (~55 for LS, ~25 for RS). PARLIAMENT SESSIONS: min 3 per year — (a) BUDGET (Feb-May); (b) MONSOON (Jul-Sep); (c) WINTER (Nov-Dec). MAX gap between sessions = 6 months (Art 85). New PARLIAMENT BUILDING inaugurated 28 May 2023 — triangular shape, designed by HCP (Bimal Patel of Gujarat). REFERENCES: President's address (Art 87, at start of every general election LS session + each year's first session), Question Hour, Zero Hour, Calling Attention, Adjournment Motions, No-Confidence Motion, Ordinance-making power (Art 123).

cards.front:
The MAXIMUM gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed:

(A) 3 months
(B) 6 MONTHS
(C) 1 year
(D) 9 months
cards.back:
(B) 6 MONTHS

Parliament — ARTICLE 85(1) — 'The President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but SIX MONTHS shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.' PRACTICAL RESULT: at least 3 sessions every year. 3 REGULAR sessions: (1) BUDGET SESSION (Feb-May) — longest; Presidential address (joint sitting at start); Budget presentation; 2 PARTS — Part 1 (Budget presentation + general discussion), then 3-4 week gap for Standing Committees to scrutinise, Part 2 (voting on demands for grants + passing Finance Bill + Appropriation Bill). (2) MONSOON SESSION (Jul-Aug). (3) WINTER SESSION (Nov-Dec). GENERAL PROVISIONS: (a) SUMMONED by President (on advice of CoM); (b) PROROGUED by President (ends a session); (c) DISSOLUTION applies only to LS (Art 85(2)(b)); RS NOT dissolved (permanent body). (d) JOINT SITTING (Art 108) called by President when houses disagree on a Bill (except Money Bills + Constitutional Amendments). Only 3 joint sittings in Indian history — (1) 1961 Dowry Prohibition Bill; (2) 1978 Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill; (3) 2002 POTA (Prevention of Terrorism Act). Speaker presides. (e) Sessions can extend beyond 6 months with Presidential + Speaker's approval. (f) PARLIAMENT'S SITTINGS: LOK SABHA ~60-80 days/year recent, historically ~130+; RS ~50-70 days. Declining sitting days a concern. QUORUM: 1/10 of total strength each House (Art 100). ZERO HOUR: first hour after Question Hour (12 noon in LS), MP raises issue without notice; flexible. QUESTION HOUR: first hour (11 AM-12 noon). LAME DUCK session — last session of an outgoing LS after general election; members who lost election still attend (rare). No MP CAN be absent for 60 consecutive days without permission or seat vacates (Art 101). Article 85(1); at least 3 sessions every year; President summons each house.

cards.front:
A MONEY BILL (Article 110) can be introduced:

(A) In either House
(B) ONLY in the LOK SABHA, on PRESIDENT's recommendation
(C) Only in the Rajya Sabha
(D) By Finance Minister in joint session
cards.back:
(B) ONLY in the LOK SABHA, on PRESIDENT's recommendation

Parliament — MONEY BILL — specially defined in Art 110. DEFINITION (7 specific matters exclusively): (a) Imposition/abolition/remission/alteration/regulation of ANY TAX; (b) regulation of Union borrowing; (c) Consolidated Fund custody/appropriation/withdrawal; (d) declaration of any expenditure as charged on CFI; (e) appropriation of CFI moneys; (f) CF-linked audit/payment; (g) ANY matter incidental to (a)-(f). NOT incidental taxes/cesses for local or special purposes. PROCEDURE: (1) Introduced ONLY in LOK SABHA (not RS); (2) only on PRESIDENT's prior RECOMMENDATION; (3) after LS passage, sent to RS; (4) RS has only 14 DAYS to return with RECOMMENDATIONS; LS may ACCEPT or REJECT them — not binding; (5) Deemed passed by both Houses after 14 days; sent to President for assent; (6) PRESIDENT can either ASSENT or WITHHOLD — CANNOT RETURN (unlike ordinary Bill). RS HAS NO VETO over Money Bills — LS supreme. SPEAKER's CERTIFICATE: Speaker of LS DECIDES if a Bill is Money Bill; decision FINAL + NOT REVIEWABLE by any court (per Art 110(3)). HOWEVER, SC has in recent cases (Roger Matthew, 2019; Aadhaar Puttaswamy-II 2018 — split view) said Speaker's decision IS subject to judicial review if it's manifestly wrong. FINANCE BILL (broader) vs MONEY BILL: (a) ALL Money Bills are Finance Bills, NOT vice versa. (b) Finance Bills Category A (Art 117(1)) — involve any Art 110 matter; require Presidential recommendation; only in LS. Category B (Art 117(3)) — involve expenditure from CFI; can be in either House but need Presidential recommendation. Ordinary Finance Bill (non-110 matters) — RS has full powers. RECENT CONTROVERSIES: (1) AADHAAR ACT 2016 passed as Money Bill (bypassing RS where NDA lacked majority); challenged — SC upheld in Puttaswamy-II (2018) 4-1 with Chandrachud's dissenting that it was NOT a Money Bill (hence misuse of Art 110). (2) 2017 Finance Bill amended several non-financial laws (PMLA, Companies Act, Tribunals) as Money Bill — challenged in Roger Matthew case; SC referred to 7-judge bench (still pending). MONEY BILL mechanism is a KEY CENTRE of power-imbalance debate between LS + RS. not binding; RAJYA SABHA can only RECOMMEND changes within 14 days.

cards.front:
The SPEAKER of LOK SABHA:

(A) Is appointed by the President
(B) Is ELECTED by LS members FROM AMONG themselves at first meeting; presides over LS; has CASTING VOTE in case of tie; remains in office until new LS meets
(C) Is nominated by the ruling party
(D) Must be the senior-most MP
cards.back:
(B) Is ELECTED by LS members FROM AMONG themselves at first meeting; presides over LS; has CASTING VOTE in case of tie; remains in office until new LS meets

Parliament — SPEAKER OF LOK SABHA — Art 93. ELECTED by LS members from among themselves at the FIRST MEETING of a new Lok Sabha, presided over by PRO TEM Speaker (senior-most MP nominated by President, administers oath to new MPs; first task = Speaker election). POWERS + FUNCTIONS: (1) PRESIDES over LS sittings; (2) INTERPRETS Rules of Procedure (rulings not subject to judicial review per Art 122 on internal Parliament matters — with narrow exceptions); (3) maintains ORDER + decorum (suspension of members); (4) decides WHO SPEAKS (order of precedence); (5) CERTIFICATION of MONEY BILLS (Art 110(3)) — final; (6) presides over JOINT SITTING of two Houses (Art 108); (7) ADMITS motions, questions, resolutions per rules; (8) DECIDES on POINT OF ORDER; (9) only CASTING VOTE when tie; no vote otherwise; (10) decides DISQUALIFICATION on grounds of defection (10th Schedule — since Kihoto Hollohan 1993, subject to judicial review). TENURE: until the NEXT LS meets + elects a new Speaker — so continues through general election, unlike other MPs (who cease with LS dissolution). Thus when LS is dissolved, Speaker continues until just before first sitting of next LS. CAN BE REMOVED by RESOLUTION passed by effective majority (> 50% of total then-existing LS members) per Art 94(c); 14-day notice. Has VOLUNTARILY RESIGNED in past (Balram Jakhar 1989, Somnath Chatterjee 2009 out of CPI(M) expulsion row). DEPUTY SPEAKER — Art 93; also elected by LS; usually by OPPOSITION (convention, not mandatory). Currently (as of 2024-25) NO Deputy Speaker — this post was VACANT throughout 17th LS (2019-24), controversially. NOTABLE SPEAKERS: (1) G.V. MAVALANKAR (1952-56) — 'Father of Lok Sabha'; set conventions. (2) BALRAM JAKHAR (1980-89) — longest tenure (nearly 2 full terms). (3) RABI RAY, Shivraj Patil, Manohar Joshi. (4) SOMNATH CHATTERJEE (2004-09) — commanded respect across spectrum. (5) MEIRA KUMAR (2009-14) — FIRST WOMAN Speaker; daughter of Jagjivan Ram. (6) SUMITRA MAHAJAN (2014-19) — second woman. (7) OM BIRLA (2019-2024, 2024- current) — first Speaker re-elected to post. RS PRESIDING: Chairman = VP (ex-officio); Deputy Chairman = elected member.

MAVALANKAR (1952-56) — 'Father of Lok Sabha'; set conventions. (2) BALRAM JAKHAR (1980-89) — longest tenure (nearly 2 full terms). (3) RABI RAY, Shivraj Patil, Manohar Joshi. (4) SOMNATH CHATTERJEE (2004-09) — commanded respect across spectrum. (5) MEIRA KUMAR (2009-14) — FIRST WOMAN Speaker; daughter of Jagjivan Ram. (6) SUMITRA MAHAJAN (2014-19) — second woman. (7) OM BIRLA (2019-2024, 2024- current) — first Speaker re-elected to post. RS PRESIDING: Chairman = VP (ex-officio); Deputy Chairman = elected member.

cards.front:
A NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION against the Council of Ministers can be moved:

(A) In either House
(B) ONLY in LOK SABHA, by any MP with 50-MP support, under Rule 198
(C) Only in Rajya Sabha
(D) In joint sitting
cards.back:
(B) ONLY in LOK SABHA, by any MP with 50-MP support, under Rule 198

Parliament — NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION — procedure under RULE 198 of Rules of Procedure + Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha. KEY FEATURES: (1) MOVED ONLY IN LOK SABHA (not Rajya Sabha) — because CoM is COLLECTIVELY RESPONSIBLE only to LS (Art 75(3)). (2) Any MP can give notice; SPEAKER admits if has support of AT LEAST 50 MEMBERS; discussion then scheduled. (3) 10 days notice + discussion scheduled by BAC (Business Advisory Committee). (4) No specific reasons required; just loss of confidence in CoM asserted. (5) If motion PASSES by SIMPLE MAJORITY of members PRESENT + voting, entire CoM must RESIGN. (6) PM has option of advising dissolution instead; but no CoM can continue without LS confidence. HISTORY: First NC motion was moved in Aug 1963 by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru (defeated). ~27+ NC motions moved so far (till 2024); only 3 SUCCEEDED leading to government fall: (1) 1979 — Morarji Desai resigned before vote; Charan Singh-led minority JP(S) govt briefly; (2) 1990 — V.P. Singh lost NC motion + resigned; (3) 1997 — Deve Gowda lost NC (Cong withdrew support); (4) 1999 — ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE's NDA-1 (1998-99) LOST by just 1 VOTE — 269 to 270 — due to absence of Saifuddin Soz (who broke party whip) + Odisha CM Giridhar Gamang (who was Odisha CM but still voted as MP). MOST FAMOUS VOTE. SUBSEQUENTLY defeated: (5) 2003 — Sonia Gandhi's NC against Vajpayee (defeated). (6) 2008 — UPA-I faced TRUST VOTE after Left withdrew support over Indo-US nuclear deal; UPA won 275-256 amid chaotic scenes + 'cash-for-votes' scandal (SP + JD(U) defectors helped). (7) 2018 — NDA-I v. Modi NC (lost 126-325). RELATED MOTIONS: (a) CONFIDENCE MOTION — moved by PM/Govt to prove majority; rare. (b) CUT MOTIONS — disapproval of government policy; rejects demand for grant (by symbolic ₹100, or actual amount, etc.); if passed = govt has to resign (treated like NC). (c) CENSURE MOTION — disapproval of specific policy / minister; does not require govt to resign. (d) ADJOURNMENT MOTION — brings LS business to halt to discuss urgent matter; needs 50 MPs; censure implicit. (e) PRIVILEGE MOTION. Govt resigns if motion PASSES by simple majority.

cards.front:
The ANTI-DEFECTION LAW is in which SCHEDULE of the Constitution?

(A) 8th Schedule
(B) 10th SCHEDULE
(C) 11th Schedule
(D) 9th Schedule
cards.back:
(B) 10th SCHEDULE

Parliament — ANTI-DEFECTION LAW (Aaya Ram Gaya Ram Act) — added as 10th SCHEDULE to Constitution via 52nd CAA 1985 (Rajiv Gandhi era). Named after Haryana MLA GAYA LAL who changed parties 3 times in 1 day in 1967 — 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' phrase born. DISQUALIFICATION GROUNDS under 10th Schedule: (1) VOLUNTARILY GIVING UP membership of his ORIGINAL party; (2) VOTING OR ABSTAINING contrary to party WHIP (directive) WITHOUT prior permission — within 15 days; (3) If INDEPENDENT MEMBER joins a party after election; (4) If NOMINATED MEMBER joins a party after 6 months of taking seat. EXCEPTIONS (original 1985): (a) 'SPLIT' if 1/3 or more members broke off — protected (allowed new group formation without disqualification). (b) 'MERGER' if 2/3 of legislature party agreed to merge with another — not defection. 91st CAA 2003 REMOVED the 1/3 SPLIT exemption (misused for profiteering); now only MERGERS with 2/3 support protected. ADJUDICATION: presiding officer of House (Speaker in LS, Chairman in RS, Speaker in Assembly) decides on disqualification. KIHOTO HOLLOHAN v. ZACHILLHU (1992) — SC held Speaker's decision is JUDICIALLY REVIEWABLE. NOTABLE cases: (1) Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007). (2) Madhya Pradesh Assembly crisis 2020 — 22 Cong MLAs resigned, Speaker accepted; Kamal Nath govt fell; Chouhan took over. (3) Maharashtra 2022 — Shinde faction split Shiv Sena; delayed Speaker's ruling; SC Subhash Desai 2023 remanded. (4) Telangana + Karnataka defections in 2019-2024 — multiple disqualification cases. CRITIQUES: (1) party-centric democracy — diminishes MP's individual judgment; (2) Speaker bias — ruling party's choice often sympathetic; (3) DELAYS by Speaker = de facto impunity; (4) merger threshold 2/3 too low — horse-trading still happens (just wholesale instead of retail). RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) NCRWC 2002 — decide anti-defection cases within 3 months. (b) Goswami Committee, Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Law Commission. (c) 2020 SC Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil case suggested TIME-BOUND decision (3 months). NO LEGAL TEETH yet added. STRENGTHENING the anti-defection law is a long-pending reform. added by 52nd CAA (1985); further amended by 91st CAA (2003) to remove 1/3 split exemption.

cards.front:
A constitutional AMENDMENT BILL under Article 368 requires:

(A) Simple majority in both Houses
(B) SPECIAL MAJORITY
(C) Only LS approval
(D) Presidential ordinance
cards.back:
(B) SPECIAL MAJORITY

Parliament — ARTICLE 368 — power of Parliament to AMEND the Constitution. 3 TYPES of amendments: (1) SIMPLE MAJORITY (not under Art 368 technically, but common) — for certain matters NOT covered by Art 368: e.g., admission/creation of new states, alteration of state boundaries (Art 2-4), citizenship provisions (Art 5-11 of Part II but NOT FRs), abolition/creation of Legislative Councils (Art 169), salaries of judges, etc. Only simple majority in both Houses. (2) SPECIAL MAJORITY — required for MOST constitutional amendments under Art 368 (including FRs, DPSPs, basic framework). Requires: (a) majority of TOTAL membership of each House (>50% of house's total strength, not just present); (b) 2/3 of MEMBERS PRESENT + VOTING in each House. Both conditions must be satisfied in each House. NO joint sitting available for constitutional amendments. (3) SPECIAL MAJORITY + STATE RATIFICATION — required for 'federal provisions' that affect Centre-State balance. Same special majority + RATIFICATION by at least HALF the state legislatures (not 2/3 states — that's a common misconception). Matters requiring state ratification: (a) Art 54 + Art 55 — Election of President; (b) Art 73 + 162 — extent of executive power of Union + States; (c) SC + HC provisions (Art 124-147, 214-231); (d) Art 245-255 — legislative relations; (e) Art 368 itself; (f) representation of states in Parliament; (g) any item in Union List/State List/Concurrent List of 7th Schedule. IN Total ~106 CAAs passed so far (as of 2024). STATES' RATIFICATION recent — 101st CAA (GST 2016) required state ratification; done. IMPORTANT CAAs: (1) 1st (1951) — 9th Schedule introduced for land reforms. (2) 24th (1971) — Parliament's power to amend FRs (overturned Golaknath). (3) 42nd ('mini-Constitution' Mar 1976) — most sweeping; 59 changes; curbed judicial review; FDs added; Socialist + Secular + Integrity added to Preamble; extended LS term 5→6 yrs; DPSP primacy over FRs (struck down by Minerva Mills 1980). (4) 44th (1978, Janata) — reversed many 42nd changes; LS term back to 5 yrs; abolished property right as FR. (5) 52nd (1985) — 10th Schedule anti-defection. (6) 61st (1989) — voting age 21→18. (7) 73rd + 74th (1992) — Panchayati Raj + ULG. (8) 86th (2002) — Art 21A, RTE. (9) 91st (2003) — CoM cap 15%. (10) 101st (2016) — GST. (11) 102nd (2018) — NCBC constitutional. (12) 103rd (2019) — EWS reservation 10%. (13) 105th (2021) — states' identify OBC. (14) 106th (2023) — Women's Reservation in LS + Assemblies (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, post-delimitation implementation). majority of TOTAL membership + 2/3 of members PRESENT + VOTING in EACH House; some amendments additionally need ratification by 1/2 of states.

cards.front:
The FIRST HOUR of every Parliament sitting is reserved for:

(A) Zero Hour
(B) QUESTION HOUR
(C) Introduction of Bills
(D) Prime Minister's Address
cards.back:
(B) QUESTION HOUR

Parliament — QUESTION HOUR — FIRST HOUR of every Parliamentary sitting (11:00 AM – 12:00 NOON). Key feature of parliamentary accountability — MPs can ask questions to Ministers. 3 TYPES of Questions: (1) STARRED QUESTIONS — oral answer sought, identified by ASTERISK (*); 20 permitted per day in LS; Minister answers orally; SUPPLEMENTARY questions allowed. (2) UNSTARRED QUESTIONS — written answer; up to 230 per day LS; no supplementaries. (3) SHORT NOTICE QUESTIONS — urgent matter of public importance; less than 10 days notice; ORAL answer; Speaker's permission. ROSTER: each day's Qs directed to specific ministries (fixed rotation — Monday = certain ministries, Tuesday = others, etc.). Notice period: 15 DAYS ordinary; 10 for short notice. MINISTER FREEDOM: can decline to answer if national security, judicial proceedings sub-judice, or too onerous (answer). PARLIAMENTARY STANDING COMMITTEE for each Q — Railways, Transport, Health, Defence, Finance etc. ZERO HOUR (12 NOON-1 PM) — INFORMAL; unique to Indian parliamentary practice (NOT mentioned in Rules, started 1962). MPs raise urgent issues WITHOUT notice; flexible; Minister may or may not respond. Chaotic sometimes. Speaker's discretion to permit. OTHER KEY TIMES: (1) LUNCH BREAK (1-2 PM). (2) AFTERNOON SESSION (2-6 PM) — Bills, motions, discussions. (3) PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS: FRIDAY afternoons (2:30-6 PM) — Private Member's Bills + Resolutions. In practice, barely any Private Member Bill has passed (only 14 in Indian history; last in 1970). DEVICES to raise issues: (a) Calling Attention; (b) Adjournment Motion; (c) No-day-yet-named motion; (d) Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193); (e) Half-hour discussion; (f) Rule 377 mention. LOK SABHA daily business order: (1) Oath by new MP / VP (if any); (2) Obituary references; (3) Question Hour (11-12); (4) Zero Hour (~12-1); (5) Lunch; (6) Legislative business (Bills, discussions); (7) Resolutions. STANDING COMMITTEES: Parliament forms ~24 Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) + Financial Committees (PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings) + Department Committees (Business Advisory, Rules, Privileges, Govt Assurances etc.) — scrutinise Bills + budgets + reports. Members ask questions to Ministers for oral (Starred) or written (Unstarred) answers; also Short-Notice Questions; 11 AM-12 noon.

cards.front:
The PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE (PAC), which examines CAG reports, is:

(A) Chaired by Finance Minister
(B) A 22-member joint LS+RS committee
(C) Chaired by Speaker
(D) An executive body
cards.back:
(B) A 22-member joint LS+RS committee

Parliament — PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE (PAC) — FINANCIAL COMMITTEE of Indian Parliament; examines CAG's reports on GOVT expenditure + audit. Est. 1921 (under Govt of India Act 1919). FORMATION: 22 MEMBERS (15 from Lok Sabha + 7 from Rajya Sabha); elected by Parliament ANNUALLY by proportional representation (single transferable vote) ensuring all parties + independents proportional representation. CHAIRMAN: appointed by SPEAKER of LS; by CONVENTION (not legal requirement) = a SENIOR MP from OPPOSITION party. This convention: (a) intended by M.N. Kaul, first Secretary-General of LS; (b) since 1967 regularly followed; (c) strengthens oversight — opposition MP chairs ≠ rubber-stamp. FUNCTIONS: (1) EXAMINE CAG REPORTS (audit on Consolidated Fund, Contingency, Public Account; appropriation accounts; finance accounts; audit of PSUs). Reports post-audit deviations, misappropriations, improper expenditure, systemic issues. (2) Scrutinise actual expenditure vs GRANTS passed by Parliament; flag excess, diversion, 'irregularities, losses, fraudulent' transactions. (3) Ensures ACCOUNTABILITY of executive for public money. (4) Reports SUBMITTED to Parliament annually (PAC typically produces ~20 reports each year). LIMITATIONS: (a) POST-FACTO examination only; (b) no direct power to punish; (c) recommendations TABLED; govt can reject (though rare); (d) scrutinises CAG reports only — cannot initiate suo-moto inquiries. FAMOUS PAC DISCOVERIES / cases: (1) BOFORS scandal (1987, chaired by V.K. Krishna Menon; reports controversial); (2) 2G SPECTRUM report (2011, chaired by Murli Manohar Joshi, BJP); (3) Coalgate, Commonwealth Games. RECENT CHAIRS: (a) BJP's Murli Manohar Joshi (2009-14 UPA-II); (b) Cong's K.V. Thomas, Mallikarjun Kharge (2014-19 NDA); (c) Cong's Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury (2019-24); (d) K.C. Venugopal (2024-). OTHER FINANCIAL COMMITTEES: (1) ESTIMATES COMMITTEE — 30 LS members; examines BUDGET ESTIMATES + efficiency; chaired by ruling party MP. (2) COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC UNDERTAKINGS (COPU) — 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS); examines CPSE performance + reports. DEPARTMENTAL STANDING COMMITTEES are SEPARATE (introduced 1993); examine ministry-wise demands for grants + Bills. BY CONVENTION, chaired by a SENIOR OPPOSITION MP; scrutinises CAG audit reports of Govt expenditure.

cards.front:
The WOMEN'S RESERVATION ACT (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), 2023 reserves:

(A) 50% seats in LS
(B) 33% of seats (1/3) in LOK SABHA + STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES for WOMEN
(C) 25% in Rajya Sabha
(D) 50% in Panchayats only
cards.back:
(B) 33% of seats (1/3) in LOK SABHA + STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES for WOMEN

Parliament — 106TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 2023 / NARI SHAKTI VANDAN ADHINIYAM ('Women's Empowerment Law') — landmark legislation reserving 33% (1/3) of seats for WOMEN in LOK SABHA + STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES + Delhi LA. PASSAGE: passed Sept 2023 during the SPECIAL SESSION (new Parliament building inauguration), in both LS + RS with near-unanimity. Signed by President Droupadi Murmu 28 Sep 2023. HISTORY OF DEMAND: (1) First Private Member Bill introduced 1996; failed several times thereafter — RS passed 2010 but never in LS. (2) 81st CAA Bill (2008), re-introduced as 108th CAA Bill (2010) — passed RS, lapsed in LS. (3) Finally in 2023 (17th LS) passed as 128th CAB → 106th CAA. KEY FEATURES: (1) 1/3 seats in LS + State Assemblies + Delhi LA. (2) RESERVATION ROTATION — constituencies reserved for women to ROTATE every election/delimitation. (3) HORIZONTAL RESERVATION — 1/3 of SC + ST seats also reserved for women from those groups. (4) ANGLO-INDIAN SEATS (now abolished) were excluded from scope. (5) DURATION — 15 YEARS initially; can be extended. cards.front:
The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Indian Parliament has how many members at present?

(A) 15 (all from Lok Sabha)
(B) 22 — 15 from Lok Sabha + 7 from Rajya Sabha
(C) 30 (all from Lok Sabha)
(D) 45
cards.back:
(B) 22 — 15 from Lok Sabha + 7 from Rajya Sabha

Parliament — PAC — total 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS) elected for 1 year. Tradition since 1967: Chair from the Opposition (a courtesy, not constitutional). Set up first in 1921 under Government of India Act 1919. Examines Audit Reports of CAG laid before Parliament — finds whether public money was spent for the authorised purpose. PAC cannot question policy; only review accounts. Often called the 'twin' of Estimates Committee + Committee on Public Undertakings.

cards.front:
The Estimates Committee — the largest financial committee in Parliament — consists of:

(A) 15 members from Lok Sabha only
(B) 30 members all from Lok Sabha (no Rajya Sabha members)
(C) 45 members combined
(D) 60 members combined
cards.back:
(B) 30 members all from Lok Sabha (no Rajya Sabha members)

Parliament — Estimates Committee — 30 members ALL from Lok Sabha (no Rajya Sabha representation). Originally 25 (1950), increased to 30 in 1956. Constituted annually. Sometimes called 'Continuous Economy Committee' — examines budget estimates of ministries and suggests economies. Cannot examine matters relating to the Defence Department's secret operations. Chair is appointed by Speaker from among members. PAC and Estimates Committee together oversee 'before' and 'after' aspects of public expenditure.

cards.front:
Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) were established in 1993 (initially 17, now 24). Each committee has:

(A) 21 members - all from Lok Sabha
(B) 31 members — 21 LS + 10 RS, term 1 year
(C) 45 members combined
(D) 20 LS + 10 RS, term 5 years
cards.back:
(B) 31 members — 21 LS + 10 RS, term 1 year

Parliament — DRSCs — 24 standing committees, each with 31 members (21 LS + 10 RS), 1-year term. Each examines bills + budget demands + annual reports of one or more allied ministries. Chair drawn from majority OR opposition (rotates). Major reform in legislative scrutiny — ministers can't be members. 8 DRSCs serviced by Rajya Sabha Secretariat (chaired by RS members), 16 by Lok Sabha Secretariat. Bills are referred for clause-by-clause examination before passage.

cards.front:
The 'Business Advisory Committee' (BAC) of Lok Sabha is chaired by:

(A) Prime Minister
(B) Speaker of Lok Sabha
(C) Leader of Opposition
(D) Senior-most member of Lok Sabha
cards.back:
(B) Speaker of Lok Sabha

Parliament — Business Advisory Committee — 15 members in Lok Sabha (chaired by Speaker), 11 in Rajya Sabha (chaired by Chairman). Recommends time allocation for legislative and other business. Effectively decides the parliamentary calendar. The Speaker / Chairman is the binding authority — committee functions advisorily. Decisions usually reached by consensus among parties' representatives. Other key Lok Sabha committees: Rules Committee (chaired by Speaker), Committee on Privileges, Ethics Committee, Committee on Government Assurances.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a financial committee of Indian Parliament?

(A) Public Accounts Committee
(B) Estimates Committee
(C) Committee on Public Undertakings (CoPU)
(D) Committee on Subordinate Legislation
cards.back:
(D) Committee on Subordinate Legislation

Committee on Subordinate Legislation is a SCRUTINY committee (15 LS members) — examines whether powers to make rules/regulations conferred by Parliament are being properly exercised. Other scrutiny committees: Committee on Government Assurances, Committee on Petitions.

Which kind of parliamentary committee is constituted to examine a particular bill / matter and ceases to exist on submission of its report?

(A) Standing Committee
(B) Ad-hoc Committee (e.g. Select Committee, Joint Parliamentary Committee)
(C) Committee of the Whole House
(D) Departmentally Related Standing Committee
cards.back:
(B) Ad-hoc Committee (e.g. Select Committee, Joint Parliamentary Committee)

Sub-types: Select Committee (one House), Joint Committee (both Houses), JPC (Joint Parliamentary Committee — has investigative powers, e.g. JPC on Bofors 1987, 2G 2011, NRC). Standing committees are permanent / annually reconstituted (PAC, Estimates, CoPU, DRSCs, BAC). 'Committee of the Whole House' = the entire House sitting as a committee, usually for the Finance Bill or Appropriation Bill clause-by-clause discussion.

cards.front:
Tradition since 1967: the Chairmanship of the Public Accounts Committee is given to:

(A) The senior-most member of the ruling party
(B) A member from the Opposition (usually the Leader of the Opposition or a senior Opposition MP)
(C) The Finance Minister
(D) The Speaker of Lok Sabha
cards.back:

This is a CONVENTION (not constitutional / statutory) — the only similar convention is for the Estimates Committee NOT to be chaired by an Opposition member (it remains with the ruling side). The first PAC Chairman was K.M. Munshi (1949-50), 1st Opposition PAC Chair was M.R. Masani (1967-69).

The SPEAKER of the Lok Sabha is elected:

(A) By the President
(B) By members of the Lok Sabha from amongst themselves

cards.front:
A MONEY BILL can be introduced in:

(A) Either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha

cards.front:
Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGES of MPs?

(A) Article 105 (privileges of Parliament)
(B) Article 14 (right to equality matters)
(C) Article 19 (freedom of speech rights)
(D) Article 32 (writs to enforce rights)
cards.back:
(A) Article 105 (privileges of Parliament)

Parliament — ARTICLE 105 of the Constitution — PRIVILEGES OF the HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT and THEIR MEMBERS. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) FREEDOM OF SPEECH in Parliament: MPs CANNOT be sued in any court for anything they say in Parliament or its committees (Art 105(2)). (2) IMMUNITY for VOTES — MPs aren't liable for any vote cast in Parliament or committees. (3) RIGHT TO PUBLISH proceedings — under authority of either House, no one can be sued. (4) Other privileges 'as may from time to time be defined by Parliament by law' — Parliament hasn't enacted a comprehensive law, so privileges remain those of UK House of Commons (1950) + judicial decisions. ARTICLE 194 — CORRESPONDING privileges for STATE LEGISLATURES. TYPES: (1) COLLECTIVE PRIVILEGES — of the House: right to publish proceedings, exclude strangers, regulate own procedures, punish for contempt. (2) INDIVIDUAL PRIVILEGES — of MPs: freedom of speech, freedom from arrest in CIVIL cases (NOT criminal) during 40 days before/after session + during session. CONFLICT: parliamentary privileges + judicial review have led to DEBATES (e.g., Karnataka MLAs disqualification 2019). PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 105 in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC.

cards.front:
Members of Parliament have FREEDOM FROM ARREST in:

(A) Civil cases during sessions only
(B) All criminal cases at all times
(C) All cases unconditionally always
(D) Tax-related matters only here
cards.back:
(A) Civil cases during sessions only

Parliament — MPs have FREEDOM FROM ARREST ONLY IN CIVIL CASES — and only DURING the 40 DAYS BEFORE the session, the SESSION itself, and 40 DAYS AFTER it ends. CRIMINAL CASES — NO IMMUNITY: MPs CAN be arrested for criminal offences at ANY time (e.g., murder, corruption, bribery). ALSO NO IMMUNITY for: (1) Preventive detention. (2) Civil proceedings other than arrest (e.g., service of summons). (3) Cases under the Indian Penal Code. NOTABLE CASE — JMM BRIBERY CASE (1998): SC held that MPs accepting bribes for VOTES IN PARLIAMENT were NOT immune from prosecution under Art 105. RECENT 2024 — MP Sita Soren CASE: SC OVERTURNED the JMM case via a 7-judge bench (Sita Soren v. Union of India, March 2024) — held that NO IMMUNITY for MPs/MLAs against bribery prosecution, even if related to votes/speeches in House. This was a major judicial pivot. ENTERING & SEARCHING PARLIAMENT: police cannot enter parliament premises without speaker's consent. ATTACHED PRIVILEGE: MPs cannot be summoned by court when Parliament is in session (must seek leave of House). PYQ FREQUENCY: arrest immunity is a top UPSC, MPSC MCQ — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
BREACH OF PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGE refers to:

(A) Disrespect or obstruction to Parliament
(B) Voting against the party whip
(C) Making a personal attack speech
(D) Not attending Parliament sessions
cards.back:
(A) Disrespect or obstruction to Parliament

Parliament — BREACH OF PRIVILEGE — any ACT that DISREGARDS or VIOLATES privileges of the House or its Members. Parliament can punish such breaches as 'CONTEMPT OF THE HOUSE'. EXAMPLES: (1) Publishing FALSE/MISLEADING reports of proceedings. (2) Insulting/intimidating MPs in connection with their parliamentary duties. (3) Disturbing parliamentary proceedings (e.g., shouting from gallery). (4) Refusing to appear before a committee when summoned. (5) Misleading a parliamentary committee with false testimony. (6) Bribery of MPs (now NO immunity per Sita Soren 2024). PROCEDURE for breach allegations: (1) MP raises issue in House; presiding officer (Speaker/Chairman) decides if it should go to PRIVILEGES COMMITTEE. (2) Committee investigates, calls evidence. (3) Recommends action. (4) House takes final decision — admonishment, reprimand, suspension, EVEN IMPRISONMENT (rare). NOTABLE CASE: 2005 'CASH FOR QUESTIONS' SCANDAL — 11 MPs caught taking bribes for questions; expelled from Parliament. PARLIAMENTARY ETHICS COMMITTEE handles ethical lapses (different from privileges committee). PYQ FREQUENCY: breach-of-privilege concept in UPSC, state PSC polity 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
An MP's IMMUNITY for SPEECH in the House extends to:

(A) Anything said inside Parliament/committees
(B) Speeches given outside in public rallies
(C) All public statements made by MPs
(D) Comments on social media platforms
cards.back:
(A) Anything said inside Parliament/committees

Parliament — FREEDOM OF SPEECH (Art 105(2)) — MPs CANNOT be sued in any court for ANYTHING they say in Parliament or its committees. This is BROAD: covers debates, questions, speeches, comments — even if they are FALSE, DEFAMATORY, or INFLAMMATORY. RATIONALE: ensures fearless representation; MPs need not censor themselves for fear of litigation. KEY LIMITS: (1) Outside Parliament — NO IMMUNITY: speeches at public rallies, social media posts, press interviews ARE subject to defamation laws. (2) Within Parliament, subject to Rules of Procedure: presiding officer can call MPs to order, expunge unparliamentary words, suspend the speaker. (3) Bribery for speeches: SC's 2024 Sita Soren judgment — bribery prosecutable (no immunity). HISTORICAL EXAMPLES: (1) Derogatory statements in Parliament that would be defamation outside — fully protected. (2) JNU 'tukde-tukde' debates — speech inside Parliament safe; speeches at JNU campus are not. UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE LIST (LS Secretariat) — Speaker maintains a registry of words to be expunged: 'I will not say' lists in past included 'turncoat', 'jumla', etc. PYQ ANGLE: speech immunity tested in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests boundaries of constitutional protection.

cards.option2: All public statements made by MPs

cards.front:
The Sita Soren case (2024) is a landmark judgment regarding:

(A) Bribery for parliamentary votes/speeches not immune
(B) MP salary increases (revising old rules)
(C) Election expenses limits in campaigns
(D) Anti-defection law applicability rules

(A) Bribery for parliamentary votes/speeches not immune

Parliament — SITA SOREN v. UNION OF INDIA (March 2024) — a 7-judge SC Constitution Bench unanimously OVERTURNED the 1998 JMM Bribery Case ruling. NEW POSITION: PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGE under Art 105 does NOT extend to BRIBERY for VOTES OR SPEECHES — MPs/MLAs CAN be prosecuted criminally for accepting illegal gratification. KEY REASONING: (a) Privilege under Art 105(2) is for 'speech and votes' — not for ACCEPTING BRIBES related to them. (b) Bribery is COMPLETED at the moment of taking money, BEFORE the speech/vote happens — so the act of bribery itself is OUTSIDE the protected zone. (c) Any other reading would create a 'license to corruption' for legislators. CASE BACKGROUND: Sita Soren (Hemant Soren's sister-in-law, JMM legislator) was alleged to have accepted bribe to vote for a particular Rajya Sabha candidate from Jharkhand in 2012 — but voted differently. Initial ruling (per JMM 1998) gave her immunity. Now overturned. IMPLICATIONS: (1) Future legislator bribery cases will proceed in court. (2) ED/CBI cases on MPs become more enforceable. (3) Senior counsel debates have flagged need for clearer law of legislative privileges. PYQ FREQUENCY: 2024-26 papers will likely include this case in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC.

cards.front:
Which Article of the Constitution provides PRIVILEGES for STATE LEGISLATURES (similar to Art 105 for Parliament)?

(A) Article 194 (state-level mirror)
(B) Article 200 (assent to bills)
(C) Article 213 (Governor's ordinance)
(D) Article 226 (HC writ jurisdiction)
cards.back:
(A) Article 194 (state-level mirror)

Parliament — ARTICLE 194 — PRIVILEGES of STATE LEGISLATURES and their members. Mirror of Article 105 (which applies to Parliament). KEY PROVISIONS: (1) Freedom of speech in state legislature. (2) Right to publish proceedings. (3) Other privileges as defined by state legislature (or as enjoyed by UK House of Commons in 1950). PARALLEL STRUCTURE: Art 105 (Centre) ↔ Art 194 (States); Art 79 (Parliament constitution) ↔ Art 168 (state legislature constitution); Art 99 (oath/affirmation) ↔ Art 188 (state); Art 100 (voting + quorum) ↔ Art 189 (state). POWERS of STATE LEGISLATURES: (a) Pass state laws (List II, III subjects). (b) Approve state budget. (c) Hold executive accountable. (d) Initiate impeachment-related processes (HC judges). NOTABLE CASE: 1964 KESHAV SINGH CASE — clash between UP Vidhan Sabha and Allahabad HC over the Vidhan Sabha's privilege to send a person to jail. SC held that PRIVILEGES + Fundamental Rights must be HARMONIZED; courts can review whether a privilege violated FRs. PRIVILEGES vs. FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS: ongoing tension; constitution amendment proposed but never enacted to clarify. PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 194 mirror in UPSC, state PSC polity — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
An MP CANNOT be served a court summons:

(A) Within Parliament premises during session
(B) At any place at any time freely
(C) Even at home for criminal cases
(D) While not in actual session ever
cards.back:
(A) Within Parliament premises during session

Parliament — MPs are protected from being SERVED with court PROCESSES (summons, warrants, etc.) WITHIN the precincts of Parliament during sessions WITHOUT prior permission of the SPEAKER (LS) or CHAIRMAN (RS). This is a COLLECTIVE PRIVILEGE of the House — to PROTECT its dignity and prevent disruption of proceedings. KEY POINTS: (1) Outside Parliament premises: MP can be served normally (at home, office). (2) Inside Parliament: requires Speaker's prior nod. (3) Police can't enter Parliament without Speaker's consent for arrest, search, seizure. PRECEDENTS: (a) An arrest warrant for an MP — police must inform Speaker first; Speaker decides whether/how it'll be served. (b) Civil summons — same protocol. RECENT EVENTS: 2008 'cash-for-vote' scandal — speaker permitted CBI access to certain documents but limited interference. RELATED PRIVILEGES: (1) Right to EXCLUDE STRANGERS from House (e.g., gallery passes are revocable). (2) Right to REGULATE OWN PROCEDURES (per Articles 118 and 208 — Parliament/legislature makes its own Rules). (3) Right to PUNISH CONTEMPT (rarely used; in 2007 the LS suspended MP Suresh Kalmadi for misconduct). PYQ ANGLE: parliamentary precincts privilege in UPSC, MPSC 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
Which of the following motions, if passed by the Lok Sabha, compels the Council of Ministers to resign immediately?

(A) Adjournment motion
(B) No-confidence motion
(C) Censure motion
(D) Call-attention motion
cards.back:
(B) No-confidence motion

Parliament — A no-confidence motion — requires 50 members to support its introduction (Rule 198) — if passed, the Council of Ministers must resign (Art 75(3)). A censure motion expresses disapproval of a specific policy / action but does not compel resignation. Adjournment motion — discussion on a matter of urgent public importance, involves censure of the government but is not a no-confidence vote. Call-attention motion draws the government's notice to an urgent issue.

cards.front:
The first hour of every parliamentary sitting, devoted to oral questions to Ministers, is known as:

(A) Zero Hour
(B) Question Hour
(C) Adjournment Hour
(D) Session Hour
cards.back:
(B) Question Hour

Parliament — Question Hour (11 AM to 12 noon) — questions to Ministers on matters of administration. Three kinds: starred (oral, green slip), unstarred (written, white slip), short-notice (pink slip). Zero Hour (12 noon to 1 PM) — an informal Indian innovation from 1962 — members raise matters of urgent public importance without prior notice (hence 'zero hour', the hour before lunch).

cards.front:
A 'Money Bill' in Indian Parliament can be introduced only in the:

(A) Rajya Sabha
(B) Lok Sabha
(C) Either House
(D) Joint sitting of both Houses
cards.back:
(B) Lok Sabha

Parliament — Art 109 — a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and with the prior recommendation of the President (Art 117). The Rajya Sabha has only a recommending role and must return the Bill within 14 days; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject its recommendations. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill — and that decision is final (subject to judicial review since the 2023 Rojer Mathew judgment).

cards.front:
The quorum required for a sitting of either House of Parliament is:

(A) One-fourth of total membership
(B) One-tenth of total membership
(C) One-third of total membership
(D) One-half of total membership
cards.back:
(B) One-tenth of total membership

Parliament — Art 100 — quorum for either House is 10 % of its total membership (including the Presiding Officer). So for Lok Sabha (545 members) quorum = 55; for Rajya Sabha (250 members maximum) quorum = 25. Below quorum, the Chair adjourns the House. The requirement has prevented rushed business in thinly-attended sittings.

cards.front:
A joint sitting of both Houses (Art 108) to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary Bill is presided over by the:

(A) President
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha
(C) Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice-President)
(D) The Prime Minister
cards.back:
(B) Speaker of the Lok Sabha

Parliament — Art 118 — the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over joint sittings of the two Houses. Joint sittings have been held only three times in India — Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill (1978), and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill / POTA (2002). Joint sittings are NOT held for Money Bills (the Rajya Sabha cannot block them anyway) or for Constitutional Amendment Bills (special majority required in both Houses separately).

cards.front:
The minimum age to be elected a member of the Rajya Sabha is:

(A) 25 years
(B) 30 years
(C) 35 years
(D) 21 years
cards.back:
(B) 30 years

Parliament — Art 84(b) — Rajya Sabha / Vidhan Parishad (Council of States / Legislative Council) members must be at least 30 years old. Lok Sabha / Vidhan Sabha — 25 years (Art 84(a) / 173). President / Vice-President / Governor — 35 years. Voter — 18 years.

cards.front:
If a member of Parliament remains absent from all sittings of the House for a period exceeding how many days, without permission, their seat becomes vacant?

(A) 30 days
(B) 60 days
(C) 90 days
(D) 180 days
cards.back:
(B) 60 days

Parliament — Art 101(4) — the seat of an MP becomes vacant if they are absent from all sittings of the House for 60 days without permission. The 60-day count excludes any period when the House is prorogued, adjourned for more than 4 days, or under recess. This provision ensures a minimum level of active participation.

cards.front:
The THREE regular sessions of Indian Parliament each year are:

(A) Budget, Monsoon, Winter sessions yearly
(B) Spring, Summer, Autumn sessions yearly
(C) January, May, October sessions yearly
(D) Pre-Budget, Budget, Post-Budget sessions yearly
cards.back:
(A) Budget, Monsoon, Winter sessions yearly

Parliament — Indian Parliament typically has 3 sessions: BUDGET (Jan/Feb to May, longest), MONSOON (July-August/September), WINTER (Nov-Dec). Total ~70-90 sittings per year (declining trend; 1950s used to see ~120). Article 85: gap between two sessions of the same House should not exceed 6 MONTHS. President SUMMONS sessions; PROROGUES (ends) sessions. PARLIAMENT may have a SPECIAL session at any time (e.g., 5-day session Sep 2023 for women's reservation bill).

cards.front:
The QUORUM required for a sitting of either House of Parliament is:

(A) One-fourth of the total membership of the House
(B) One-tenth of the total membership of the House
(C) Half of the total membership of the House
(D) Two-thirds of the total membership of the House
cards.back:
(B) One-tenth of the total membership of the House

Parliament — Article 100(3) — quorum = 1/10 of total membership of a House. Lok Sabha (545 max) → 55. Rajya Sabha (245 max) → 25. If quorum not present, Speaker/Chairman adjourns or suspends sitting. Quorum is NEEDED to conduct any business (debate, vote). For a CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT BILL passage, additional requirements: 2/3 of present + voting, AND majority of total membership.

cards.front:
A JOINT SITTING of the two Houses of Parliament is called under which Article and presided by whom?

(A) Article 108, presided by the Speaker of Lok Sabha
(B) Article 107, presided by the President of India
(C) Article 110, presided by the Vice-President
(D) Article 75, presided by the Prime Minister of India
cards.back:
(A) Article 108, presided by the Speaker of Lok Sabha

Parliament — Article 108 — JOINT SITTING. Called by President when there's a deadlock between LS and RS on an ordinary bill. Presided by SPEAKER of Lok Sabha (Deputy Speaker if Speaker absent). Decision by simple majority of present + voting. NOT applicable to Money Bills (LS supreme) or Constitutional Amendment Bills (need separate 2/3 in each House). Held only THREE times in Indian history: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Bill (1978), POTA Bill (2002). Article 110 = Money Bill definition. Article 107 = ordinary bills.

cards.front:
Which of these is a MOTION OF NO CONFIDENCE in the government?

(A) Adjournment motion, to discuss an urgent public matter
(B) No-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
(C) Privilege motion, against a member for breach of privilege
(D) Censure motion, against a single minister for misconduct
cards.back:
(B) No-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers

Parliament — NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION — moved in Lok Sabha (not Rajya Sabha). If passed, the Council of Ministers MUST resign (Article 75: cabinet collectively responsible to LS). Needs 50 MPs to support introduction; full debate; voted upon. Government has fallen 4 times via no-confidence: VP Singh (1990), Deve Gowda (1997), Vajpayee (1999, by 1 vote), and the most recent successful one. CENSURE motion — against a specific minister or government for specific policy/action; less serious; doesn't bring down govt. PRIVILEGE motion — against an MP for breach of parliamentary privilege.

cards.option3: Censure motion, against a single minister for misconduct

The QUESTION HOUR in Parliament is generally held during:

(A) The last hour of the parliamentary working day
(B) The first hour of every parliamentary sitting
(C) Every Friday afternoon, only as a fixed slot
(D) Once a fortnight, on alternate Mondays only
cards.back:
(B) The first hour of every parliamentary sitting

Parliament — QUESTION HOUR — first hour of each sitting (11:00 am to 12:00 noon usually) where ministers respond to questions from MPs. Three types of questions: STARRED (oral, marked with asterisk; ministers reply orally; supplementary questions allowed); UNSTARRED (written reply); SHORT NOTICE (urgent matters, less than 10 days notice). ZERO HOUR — the period AFTER Question Hour and BEFORE the agenda begins; informal time for raising urgent issues; an Indian innovation, not in the original Constitution. Very valuable mechanism of executive accountability.

cards.front:
The DIFFERENCE between PROROGATION and DISSOLUTION of a House of Parliament is that:

(A) Both terms mean the same thing in Indian polity
(B) Prorogation ends a session; dissolution ends the House's term
(C) Prorogation requires 2/3 majority; dissolution simple majority
(D) Prorogation done by Speaker; dissolution by President
cards.back:
(B) Prorogation ends a session; dissolution ends the House's term

Parliament — ADJOURNMENT — short suspension by Speaker/Chairperson within a session; House meets again on the appointed day. PROROGATION — formal end of a session by the President (Article 85); the House CONTINUES to exist (members + Speaker continue in office). DISSOLUTION — Lok Sabha is DISSOLVED by the President; ends the House's term and triggers fresh general elections. Rajya Sabha is a PERMANENT BODY; never dissolved (1/3 retire every 2 years). Distractor 1 — they're different. Distractor 3, 4 wrong specifics.

cards.option3: Prorogation done by Speaker; dissolution by President

The presiding officer of the RAJYA SABHA (the Upper House) is the:

(A) Speaker, who also presides over Lok Sabha
(B) Vice-President of India, ex-officio Chairman
(C) President of India, the head of the state
(D) Senior-most member of the House by age only

(B) Vice-President of India, ex-officio Chairman

Parliament — Article 64: Vice-President of India is the EX-OFFICIO Chairman of Rajya Sabha. Presides over RS sittings. (NB: VP is NOT a member of RS.) Lok Sabha — has its own Speaker, elected from amongst MPs. DEPUTY CHAIRPERSON of Rajya Sabha — elected from amongst RS members. President doesn't preside over either House (separation of executive + legislature). Distractor 1 — Speaker is for LS only. Distractor 3, 4 wrong.

A MONEY BILL can be introduced ONLY in:

(A) Either House (LS or RS) freely
(B) Lok Sabha only (per Article 110 rule)
(C) Rajya Sabha only (the upper house)
(D) Joint sitting of both Houses together
cards.back:
(B) Lok Sabha only (per Article 110 rule)

Parliament — Article 110 — MONEY BILL can be introduced ONLY in LOK SABHA, on PRESIDENT's recommendation. Examples: imposition / abolition of taxes; borrowing by govt; consolidated fund expenditure. SPEAKER decides if a bill is a Money Bill (final decision — Article 110(3)). RAJYA SABHA can only RECOMMEND changes within 14 DAYS; LS can accept or reject these. After 14 days, bill DEEMED PASSED. Once passed by LS, sent to PRESIDENT for assent (cannot withhold or return — must give assent or hold).

(C) Only Speaker for ordinary bills
(D) Half the state legislatures' approval

(B) Both Houses, then President's assent

Parliament — ORDINARY BILL — passed by SIMPLE majority in BOTH HOUSES (LS + RS). If disagreement → JOINT SITTING (Article 108) called by President; LS Speaker presides; total ~788 members vote — LS usually dominates due to greater numbers (543 vs 245). cards.front:
CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT BILLS (Article 368) require:

(A) Simple majority of those present + voting
(B) Special majority (2/3 P+V plus >50% total)
(C) Majority of state legislatures only ratify
(D) Half of population's vote in referendum
cards.back:
(B) Special majority (2/3 P+V plus >50% total)

Parliament — Article 368 — Constitutional amendments require SPECIAL MAJORITY: (1) Majority of TOTAL MEMBERSHIP of each House; (2) AND 2/3 of MEMBERS PRESENT + VOTING. Some amendments ALSO require RATIFICATION by HALF OF STATE LEGISLATURES — esp. amendments affecting: federal structure, election of President, distribution of powers, representation in parliament. NO JOINT SITTING for constitutional amendments. PRESIDENT must give ASSENT — cannot withhold or return. KESHAVANANDA BHARATI (1973) — SC held BASIC STRUCTURE doctrine: Parliament cannot amend basic features (democracy, federalism, secularism, judicial review, etc.).

cards.option2: Majority of state legislatures only ratify

cards.front:
DIFFERENCE between MONEY BILL and FINANCE BILL is that:

(A) Money bill is broader; finance bill is narrower in scope
(B) Money bill = Article 110 strict; finance bill = broader fiscal
(C) Both terms refer to exactly the same concept always
(D) Finance bill needs SC's approval before any passing
cards.back:
(B) Money bill = Article 110 strict; finance bill = broader fiscal

Parliament — MONEY BILL (Art 110) — strictly defined: only matters listed in Art 110(1). Speaker certifies. RS has limited say (14-day recommend only). FINANCE BILL (Art 117) — broader scope; deals with general fiscal matters but may include non-Money-Bill provisions too. Three categories: (a) FINANCE BILL THAT IS A MONEY BILL — = Money Bill; (b) FINANCE BILL CATEGORY I — Money Bill matters + other matters; introduced only in LS, on Pres recommendation; RS gets full role; (c) FINANCE BILL CATEGORY II — only other taxation/finance matters not in Art 110; treated like ordinary bill (can be introduced in either House). The annual BUDGET'S 'Finance Bill' (giving effect to taxation proposals) is usually a Money Bill.

cards.front:
PRIVATE MEMBER's BILL means a bill introduced by:

(A) Prime Minister only as private member
(B) Any MP who is not a Minister
(C) Members of the Cabinet only
(D) Member of state legislatures (Vidhan Sabha)
cards.back:
(B) Any MP who is not a Minister

Parliament — PRIVATE MEMBER's BILL — introduced by an MP who is NOT a MINISTER (i.e., not part of the cabinet). Other side: GOVERNMENT BILL — by a Minister. Differences: introduction rules + scheduling vary. PMBs scheduled on FRIDAYS in LS. RARELY pass — only 14 PMBs have become law in Indian history; last was in 1970 (Supreme Court — Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction). Famous examples: Tiruchi Siva's Rights of Transgender Persons Bill (2014, RS — passed RS but lapsed); Dr. K. Subbarayan's NRI Voting Rights Bill 2018; recently Sudha Yadav, Bhatia (climate change). Even non-passing PMBs influence policy debate.

cards.front:
If a Bill passed by both Houses + sent to PRESIDENT, the President can:

(A) Only give assent without any other option there
(B) Assent, withhold, or return (once) for reconsideration
(C) Modify the bill himself with the changes wanted
(D) Send the bill directly to Supreme Court for review
cards.back:
(B) Assent, withhold, or return (once) for reconsideration

Parliament — Article 111 — Pres options for an ordinary bill: (1) ASSENT — bill becomes law; (2) WITHHOLD assent — 'POCKET VETO' (Indian Pres has no formal pocket veto, but indefinite delay possible — Zail Singh used this on Indian Post Office Amendment Bill 1986); (3) RETURN with message for reconsideration. If Parliament repasses (with or without changes), Pres MUST give assent (within reasonable time, though Constitution doesn't specify). For MONEY BILL: cannot return; only assent or withhold. For CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT: must assent. R Sankari Prasad / Golaknath cases earlier; Kesavananda 1973 affirmed President's role. State Bill (governor sends): Pres can also reserve for President (Articles 200-201).

cards.front:
JOINT SITTING of Parliament is summoned by President when:

(A) All Money Bills get rejected by RS
(B) Two Houses disagree on an Ordinary Bill
(C) President wishes to address Parliament
(D) Constitutional Amendment Bills get stalled
cards.back:
(B) Two Houses disagree on an Ordinary Bill

Parliament — JOINT SITTING (Article 108) — when LS + RS disagree on an ORDINARY BILL: (a) bill rejected by other House, OR (b) more than 6 months pass without action, OR (c) Houses don't agree on amendments — Pres can summon joint sitting. LS SPEAKER presides; absolute majority needed. Joint sitting NOT for: MONEY BILL (RS has limited 14-day role), CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT, BUDGET (treated separately). HISTORY: Only 3 joint sittings — Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978), POTA (2002). Distractor 3 — Pres can address joint sitting at start of session (Art 87) but that's an 'address', not a 'sitting' for legislation.

RATIONALE: federalism — RS represents STATE interests, so any encroachment on state powers needs RS's go-ahead.

cards.front:
On a MONEY BILL, the Rajya Sabha can:

(A) Reject it outright with no consequence
(B) Only RECOMMEND changes within 14 days
(C) Pass it into law without LS approval
(D) Demand a joint sitting on the bill

RS effectively has no veto on Money Bills — design choice to keep financial control with the directly elected House. JOINT SITTING is NOT used for money bills. Speaker decides whether bill is a Money Bill — final decision (Article 110(3)).

cards.front:
Rajya Sabha is a 'permanent' / 'continuous' chamber. The retirement pattern is:

(A) All members retire every 5 years
(B) 1/3 of members retire every 2 years; each member's term is 6 years
(C) Half retire every 3 years
(D) All members for life
cards.back:

Lok Sabha (Article 83(2)) — 5-year term unless dissolved earlier. Original 5-year term came down to 6 from the original constitutional vagueness — the current 1/3 every 2 years pattern was set by Representation of the People Act, 1951.

(A) Pass a Motion of No-Confidence against the Government
(B) Discuss budget
(C) Initiate impeachment of the President

(A) The Vice-President
(B) The Chief Justice of India
(C) The Prime Minister
(D) The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

cards.front:
Who was the first President of India, and for how many terms did he hold office?

(A) Dr. S. Radhakrishnan — 1 term
(B) Dr. Rajendra Prasad — 2 full terms
(C) Dr. Zakir Hussain — 1 term
(D) V. V. Giri — 2 terms
cards.back:
(B) Dr. Rajendra Prasad — 2 full terms

President & Vice President — Dr. Rajendra Prasad (26 Jan 1950 – 13 May 1962) was India's FIRST President and the ONLY one to serve TWO FULL TERMS (1950-57 and 1957-62). He was also the President of the Constituent Assembly (1946-50). Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (2nd, 1962-67). Dr. Zakir Hussain (3rd, 1967-69, died in office). V.V. Giri (4th, acting then elected, 1969-74). As of 2026 there have been 15 Presidents; Droupadi Murmu (15th, since 2022) is the first tribal & 2nd woman President.

cards.front:
The term of office of the President of India is:

(A) 4 years
(B) 5 years from the date he enters upon his office
(C) 6 years
(D) Co-terminus with the Lok Sabha
cards.back:
(B) 5 years from the date he enters upon his office

President & Vice President — Article 56: President holds office for 5 years from the date of entering office. Eligible for re-election any number of times (unlike the US 22nd Amendment limit). Tenure NOT tied to Lok Sabha. 6-year tenure is for the CAG, not the President (common trap).

cards.front:
The procedure for impeachment of the President of India is laid down in which Article?

(A) Article 56
(B) Article 60
(C) Article 61
(D) Article 63
cards.back:
(C) Article 61

President & Vice President — Article 61: President can be impeached for 'violation of the Constitution'. Procedure: (1) charge must be signed by ≥ 1/4 of total members of either House + 14-day prior notice; (2) passed by ≥ 2/3 of total membership of the moving House; (3) other House investigates (President can appear personally); (4) the 2nd House must also pass by ≥ 2/3 of total membership → removal. No Indian President has ever been impeached. Nominated members of RS/LS CAN participate in impeachment (they're part of Parliament), unlike in election.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a DISCRETIONARY power of the President of India (where he can act without cabinet advice)?

(A) Appointing a PM when no party has clear majority
(B) Dissolving Lok Sabha when CoM has lost majority
(C) Pocket veto (indefinitely withholding assent to a non-Money Bill)
(D) Declaring National Emergency under Article 352
cards.back:
(D) Declaring National Emergency under Article 352

President & Vice President — National Emergency under Article 352 requires WRITTEN recommendation from the Cabinet (not just PM) per the 44th Amendment, 1978 — NOT discretionary. Discretionary powers include: (a) appointing PM when no clear majority; (b) dismissal of CoM that loses confidence but doesn't resign; (c) dissolving LS when CoM has lost majority; (d) POCKET VETO — sitting on a non-Money bill indefinitely without signing or returning; (e) advice to CoM to reconsider a bill (suspensive veto) once. Essentially 'nominal' in most matters, discretionary in a few.

cards.front:
The pardoning power of the President of India is granted under which Article?

(A) Article 72
(B) Article 74
(C) Article 161
(D) Article 123
cards.back:
(A) Article 72

President & Vice President — Article 72: President's pardoning power includes PARDON (full forgiveness — removes conviction), COMMUTATION (substitution with a lighter form — e.g., death to life imprisonment), REMISSION (reduces period without changing character), RESPITE (lighter punishment due to special circumstances — e.g., pregnancy), REPRIEVE (temporary stay of execution). President's jurisdiction: death sentences (EXCLUSIVE), court-martial sentences (EXCLUSIVE), Union List offences. Governor's pardoning (Article 161) excludes death sentences. Difference: only President can pardon DEATH sentences.

cards.front:
The ORDINANCE-making power of the President is granted under which Article, and the ordinance ceases to operate within how many weeks of Parliament's reassembly?

(A) Article 123; 6 weeks
(B) Article 213; 6 months
(C) Article 123; 6 months
(D) Article 239; 12 weeks
cards.back:
(A) Article 123; 6 weeks

President & Vice President — Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is NOT in session. Maximum duration: must be laid before Parliament when it reassembles; ceases to operate 6 weeks after reassembly (unless approved by Parliament, it disappears). Equivalent for Governor: Article 213. Ordinances have the same force as an Act of Parliament during their life. Famous case: D.C. Wadhwa v State of Bihar (1987) — SC struck down re-promulgation of ordinances without parliamentary approval as a 'fraud on the Constitution'. Krishna Kumar Singh case (2017) reaffirmed this.

cards.front:
The President's VETO powers in India include all EXCEPT:

(A) Absolute veto (refuse assent; bill dies)
(B) Suspensive veto (return bill for reconsideration)
(C) Pocket veto (sit on bill indefinitely)
(D) Qualified veto (vetoed bill needs 2/3 to override)
cards.back:
(D) Qualified veto (vetoed bill needs 2/3 to override)

President & Vice President — Indian President has THREE veto powers: (1) ABSOLUTE — used for private member bills, bills passed by CoM that subsequently resigns; (2) SUSPENSIVE — return bill (except Money Bill) to Parliament for reconsideration; if Parliament repasses with or without amendments, President must assent (Article 111); (3) POCKET — sit on the bill indefinitely (no constitutional time limit). The USA Constitution has QUALIFIED veto (2/3 supermajority override needed); India does NOT. Famous pocket veto: PRESIDENT ZAIL SINGH on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill 1986.

cards.front:
The President of India is part of Parliament (Article 79). What are the two Houses?

(A) Lok Sabha (lower) + Rajya Sabha (upper)
(B) House of Representatives + Senate
(C) Lok Sabha + Vidhan Sabha
(D) State Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council
cards.back:
(A) Lok Sabha (lower) + Rajya Sabha (upper)

President & Vice President — Article 79: 'There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States [RAJYA SABHA] and the House of the People [LOK SABHA].' So Parliament includes the President as a constituent part. Important implication: a bill becomes law only after President's assent (Article 111). In the UK, similarly, the Monarch is part of Parliament ('King/Queen in Parliament'). In contrast, the US Constitution makes Congress and the President separate bodies.

cards.front:
If the office of both the President AND Vice-President is vacant, who performs the duties of the President?

(A) The Prime Minister
(B) The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
(C) The Chief Justice of India
(D) The senior-most Governor
cards.back:

If the CJI is unable to act, the senior-most SC judge available does so. This happened ONCE — in 1969, when President Dr. Zakir Hussain died in office (May 3, 1969) and then acting President V.V. Giri resigned (July 20, 1969) to contest; Justice M. HIDAYATULLAH (CJI) served as Acting President from 20 July to 24 August 1969. or in his absence, senior-most SC judge.

cards.front:
Article 111 deals with the President's power to:

(A) Assent to or withhold from bills
(B) Grant pardons (Article 72)
(C) Promulgate ordinances (Art 123)
(D) Address Parliament (Art 87)
cards.back:
(A) Assent to or withhold from bills

President & Vice President — ARTICLE 111 — President's role with respect to BILLS PASSED BY PARLIAMENT. The President can: (1) GIVE ASSENT — bill becomes law. (2) WITHHOLD ASSENT — bill dies (rare, controversial — 'absolute veto'). (3) RETURN bill (NOT money bill) for RECONSIDERATION — bill reconsidered by Parliament; if passed AGAIN with or without modification, President MUST give assent ('suspensive veto'). KEY: there is no explicit TIME LIMIT for President to act; this allows 'POCKET VETO' (President sits on the bill indefinitely without acting). TYPES OF VETO POWER (memorize): (1) ABSOLUTE VETO — President REFUSES assent; bill dies. Used very rarely; once by Dr. Rajendra Prasad against PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954. (2) SUSPENSIVE VETO — President RETURNS bill; Parliament can re-pass; President must then assent. Used by Zail Singh, R. Venkataraman, etc. (3) POCKET VETO — sit on bill, take no action. Famous case: ZAIL SINGH on Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill 1986 (kept it for 3 years; bill never became law). NOT MENTIONED in Constitution. (4) US has only suspensive veto; PRESIDENT signs in 10 days or vetoes; Congress can override 2/3 majority. INDIA's pocket veto is a unique Indian feature. PYQ FREQUENCY: presidential veto in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.
