cards.front:
Which type of VETO involves the President sitting on a bill INDEFINITELY without action?

(A) Pocket veto (no time limit)
(B) Absolute veto (refuses assent)
(C) Suspensive veto (returns once)
(D) Qualified veto (cannot override)
cards.back:
(A) Pocket veto (no time limit)

President & Vice President — POCKET VETO — President neither assents, withholds, nor returns a bill — simply DOES NOTHING. Bill cannot become law without action. Possible because Article 111 specifies NO TIME LIMIT for presidential action on bills. NOTABLE INSTANCE: PRESIDENT GIANI ZAIL SINGH used pocket veto on the INDIAN POST OFFICE (AMENDMENT) BILL 1986 — Rajiv Gandhi's bill that gave govt sweeping power to intercept private mail. Zail Singh sat on it for 3 YEARS; it lapsed. FAMOUS US POCKET VETO context: in USA, the President has 10 days to sign or veto; if Congress is OUT OF SESSION, President can pocket-veto by simply not signing. INDIA does NOT have a strict time-limit — President can hold bills longer (effective pocket veto). POSSIBLE TIME LIMIT: 2025-2026 SC review — Tamil Nadu and Kerala state governors sat on state bills for years; SC issued guidelines in Tamil Nadu Governor case (April 2025) suggesting REASONABLE time-limits (~30 days for veto, ~90 days for reservation). ABSOLUTE VETO: President refuses assent; bill dies (Dr. Rajendra Prasad, 1954, PEPSU bill). SUSPENSIVE VETO: President returns once; if Parliament re-passes (with/without amendments), President MUST assent. RECENT (2024-2025): PROPOSALS for 'PRESIDENT'S CONSULTATION' on suspended bills; SC stricter scrutiny. PYQ FREQUENCY: pocket veto in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
If Parliament re-passes a bill returned by the President under SUSPENSIVE VETO, the President MUST:

(A) Give assent (mandatory after re-pass)
(B) Veto again (return again)
(C) Refer to Supreme Court for review
(D) Dissolve Parliament immediately
cards.back:
(A) Give assent (mandatory after re-pass)

President & Vice President — SUSPENSIVE VETO process: when President returns a bill under Art 111 (NOT a money bill), Parliament reconsiders it; may pass it AGAIN with or without modifications. If RE-PASSED, the President MUST give assent — NO option to veto AGAIN, NO further return possible. So suspensive veto can DELAY but not BLOCK a bill in the long run. CONTRAST: (1) ABSOLUTE VETO — President's withholding ENDS the bill; can never be overridden (rare in practice, controversial). (2) POCKET VETO — President's INACTION blocks bill (no formal veto, just delay). (3) SUSPENSIVE — only one return; mandatory assent on re-pass. EXCEPTIONS to suspensive veto: (a) MONEY BILLS — President cannot RETURN them; only ASSENT or WITHHOLD. (b) CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT BILLS — President MUST assent; no return option (per 24th Amendment 1971). FAMOUS USE: in 1987, President R. Venkataraman returned the SALARY, ALLOWANCES, AND PENSION OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT (AMENDMENT) BILL — Parliament re-passed unchanged; President assented. In 2018 — President Kovind returned a bill once; re-pass → assent. KEY ARTICLE TIMELINE: 1949 (original) — Art 111 written. 1971 (24th Amendment) — clarified President must assent to constitution amendments. PYQ FREQUENCY: suspensive veto + override in UPSC, MPSC polity 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
On a MONEY BILL passed by Parliament, the President can:

(A) Assent or withhold (not return)
(B) Return for reconsideration also
(C) Amend the bill personally
(D) Refer to Lok Sabha Speaker for review
cards.back:
(A) Assent or withhold (not return)

President & Vice President — ON MONEY BILLS — President's options are LIMITED to: (1) ASSENT (bill becomes law). (2) WITHHOLD ASSENT (bill dies — rare). The President CANNOT RETURN money bill for reconsideration — Article 111 explicitly excludes this. WHY: Money bills are essentially the GOVERNMENT'S BUDGET; Parliament's exclusive domain. KEY: a money bill is INTRODUCED ONLY in LOK SABHA (Art 109); RAJYA SABHA can only RECOMMEND changes; President's role is similarly limited. PRACTICAL: Money bills are RARELY withheld — would create a constitutional crisis (govt can't function without budget approval). MONEY BILL DEFINITION (Art 110): bill dealing EXCLUSIVELY with: imposition/abolition/regulation of TAXES; borrowing; appropriation from Consolidated Fund; etc. CERTIFICATION: Speaker of LS certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill — DECISION FINAL, not questioned in courts (except for fundamental constitutional issues, e.g., Aadhaar Act 2016 was challenged). RECENT CONTROVERSY: 2016-2024 — opposition criticized that several substantive bills were 'misused' as money bills to avoid Rajya Sabha scrutiny (Aadhaar Act, Finance Acts include unrelated items). SC's PUTTASWAMY judgment (2018, K.S. Puttaswamy on Aadhaar) — upheld Aadhaar's money-bill certification 4-1; warned against overuse. PYQ FREQUENCY: money bill + president in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
President GIANI ZAIL SINGH famously used POCKET VETO on which bill (1986)?

(A) Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill
(B) Constitution (24th Amendment) Bill
(C) Anti-Defection Law (52nd Amendment)
(D) Bofors investigation bill amendments
cards.back:
(A) Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill

President & Vice President — INDIAN POST OFFICE (AMENDMENT) BILL 1986 — passed by Parliament in 1986 under PM RAJIV GANDHI; would have given the GOVERNMENT SWEEPING POWERS to INTERCEPT POSTAL MAIL on grounds of public emergency, security. President GIANI ZAIL SINGH (1982-1987) opposed it as a violation of citizens' privacy + RIGHT TO PRIVATE COMMUNICATION; pocket-vetoed it (held it without action). Bill never became law. After Zail Singh's term ended (July 1987), his successor R. VENKATARAMAN inherited the bill; the Rajiv Gandhi government chose NOT to push it through. Bill formally lapsed in 1989 with election of V.P. Singh govt. CONTEXT: tensions between Zail Singh and Rajiv Gandhi were high (Zail Singh felt Rajiv didn't consult him on matters of state; suspected scandals). The pocket veto was widely seen as a SIGNAL to Rajiv. ZAIL SINGH BIO: born 1916, Sikh, was Punjab CM, Home Minister; chosen by Indira Gandhi to be President; his term saw OPERATION BLUE STAR (June 1984), Indira Gandhi assassination (Oct 1984), 1984 anti-Sikh riots, Rajiv Gandhi's PM tenure starting Oct 1984. CONSTITUTIONAL LESSON: Zail Singh's veto established that pocket veto is a USABLE tool — though ethically debated. RECENT controversy: governors (state-level) using analogous pocket veto on state bills — SC rulings in 2025 placed time limits. PYQ FREQUENCY: Zail Singh-Post Office Bill in UPSC, MPSC 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
On a CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT BILL passed by Parliament under Article 368, the President MUST:

(A) Give assent (cannot return or withhold)
(B) Return for reconsideration always
(C) Refer to Supreme Court (review)
(D) Withhold assent if controversial
cards.back:
(A) Give assent (cannot return or withhold)

President & Vice President — ARTICLE 368 (Constitution Amendment): Parliament can amend constitution by SPECIAL MAJORITY (2/3 of those present + voting, plus 50% of total membership). For some matters, RATIFICATION by half of state legislatures also needed. PRESIDENT's ROLE: After Parliament passes amendment bill, the PRESIDENT MUST GIVE ASSENT — has NO OPTION to withhold or return. This was clarified by the 24TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1971) — passed during Indira Gandhi era to overcome the 'GOLAK NATH CASE' (1967) restrictions. Before 24th amendment: SC's Golak Nath ruling implied Parliament might not have power to amend FRs — president's role was unclear. After 24th amendment: Article 368 explicitly states 'President shall give assent' to constitutional amendment bills. KEY: 24th amendment ALSO clarified Parliament's wide amending power, leading to: (a) MINERVA MILLS CASE (1980) — SC reaffirmed BASIC STRUCTURE doctrine (which had emerged from Kesavananda Bharati 1973). (b) Parliament can amend any provision but cannot DESTROY basic structure. RECENT CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS notable: (1) 73rd & 74th (1992) — Panchayati Raj. (2) 86th (2002) — RTE. (3) 101st (2017) — GST. (4) 103rd (2019) — EWS reservation. (5) 104th (2020) — extended SC/ST reservation in legislatures by 10 years. PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 368 + president in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
The President of India is BOUND BY ADVICE of the Council of Ministers on most matters. This was clarified by which Constitutional Amendment?

(A) 42nd Amendment (1976) and 44th (1978)
(B) 24th Amendment (1971) only
(C) 73rd Amendment (1992) for panchayats
(D) Original Constitution (1950) only
cards.back:
(A) 42nd Amendment (1976) and 44th (1978)

President & Vice President — ARTICLE 74 — Council of Ministers headed by PM aids and ADVISES the President. ORIGINAL Constitution (1950) didn't make the advice BINDING. The 42ND CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1976), passed during EMERGENCY by Indira Gandhi, made the President's act on ADVICE BINDING (he 'shall act' on advice). After defeat of Indira (1977), Janata govt brought 44TH AMENDMENT (1978), MODIFIED Art 74 to allow President ONE return for reconsideration; but if Cabinet sends back the SAME advice, President must accept it. CURRENT POSITION: (a) Cabinet's advice is BINDING (after 1-back loop). (b) President is a NOMINAL HEAD; real executive power lies with PM + Cabinet. RAMESHWAR PRASAD CASE (2006) — SC clarified President's role; ruled the dissolution of Bihar assembly (2005) by President Kalam was UNCONSTITUTIONAL; Kalam acted on Cabinet advice but advice itself was malafide. CONTRAST WITH GOVERNORS (Art 163): Governor's discretion is SLIGHTLY more (states have more flexibility). RELATED ARTICLES: Art 75 — appointment of PM by President + ministers on PM's advice. Art 78 — PM's duties to communicate to President. KEY: the President's role is largely CEREMONIAL but constitutionally important — symbol of nation, executive head, supreme commander of armed forces. PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 74 + 42/44 amendments in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
President of India is elected by an ELECTORAL COLLEGE consisting of:

(A) Direct popular vote of all citizens here also too. option used
(B) Elected MPs of both Houses + elected MLAs of states + UTs (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K)
(C) Only Lok Sabha members directly here also too. option used option
(D) Council of Ministers + Chief Justices here also too. option used
cards.back:
(B) Elected MPs of both Houses + elected MLAs of states + UTs (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K)

President & Vice President — Article 54 — President elected INDIRECTLY by ELECTORAL COLLEGE: (1) ELECTED members of both LS + RS (no nominated members vote); (2) ELECTED members of state legislative assemblies; (3) ELECTED members of LAs of UTs of Delhi, Puducherry, + J&K (added per 70th Amendment, 1992). Voting by SECRET BALLOT, SINGLE TRANSFERABLE VOTE, PROPORTIONAL REPRESENTATION. Each MP/MLA's vote has WEIGHTED VALUE — MLAs based on state population (e.g., UP MLA's vote weight is more than Sikkim MLA's). MP value derived to ensure equal influence with all MLAs combined. INSIGHT: indirect election keeps Pres above partisan popular politics; designed by Constituent Assembly to mirror parliamentary (not presidential) system.

cards.front:
Minimum AGE qualification for President is:

(A) 30 years (RS member age)
(B) 35 years (Article 58)
(C) 40 years (often confused)
(D) 25 years (LS member age)
cards.back:
(B) 35 years (Article 58)

President & Vice President — Article 58 — qualifications: (1) Indian CITIZEN; (2) at least 35 YEARS old; (3) qualified to be a Lok Sabha member; (4) NOT hold any office of profit (under Govt of India / state / local authority — explicit exemptions: PM, ministers, governors, etc.). NOMINATION: 50 proposers + 50 seconders (high threshold to filter casual candidates; raised from 5 in 1997). DEPOSIT: ₹15,000 (forfeited if <1/6 of votes). INSIGHT — same min age (35) for VICE PRESIDENT + GOVERNOR, but: Pres → 5-year term, no formal upper age limit; can be re-elected (no limit on terms — only Rajendra Prasad served 2 full terms; J. Nehru wanted 1 term as norm).

cards.front:
TERM of the President is:

(A) 4 years (US-style limit)
(B) 5 years (re-election allowed)
(C) 6 years (RS member length)
(D) Until age 65 (no fixed limit)
cards.back:
(B) 5 years (re-election allowed)

President & Vice President — Article 56 — term = 5 YEARS from date of taking office. Eligible for RE-ELECTION (no fixed limit). RAJENDRA PRASAD = ONLY president to serve 2 full terms (1950-62). RESIGNATION = addressed to VICE PRESIDENT. REMOVAL: by IMPEACHMENT (Article 61) — for VIOLATION OF CONSTITUTION. Process: charge initiated by EITHER House (1/4 of total membership signature + 14-day notice + 2/3 majority of total membership of that House); other House investigates + must also pass with 2/3 majority. ALL members vote (incl. nominated, EXCLUDED from his ELECTION but INCLUDED in impeachment). India: NO president has ever been impeached. AMERICAN FOUNDING analog: Andrew Johnson (1868), Bill Clinton (1998), Trump (twice, 2019 + 2021) — all acquitted by Senate.

cards.front:
First PRESIDENT of India was:

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru (he was PM)
(B) Rajendra Prasad (1950-1962)
(C) Sardar Patel (he was Home Min)
(D) BR Ambedkar (Constitution drafter)
cards.back:
(B) Rajendra Prasad (1950-1962)

President & Vice President — DR. RAJENDRA PRASAD (1884-1963) — first President of India; took oath 26 Jan 1950 (Republic Day). Served 2 full terms (1950-62) — only Pres to do so. Earlier presided over CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY (1946-49). Bharat Ratna 1962. Born in Bihar (Ziradei, Siwan). Educated in Calcutta. Joined Gandhi's freedom movement. Wrote 'India Divided' (1946), 'At the Feet of Mahatma Gandhi' (autobiography). DEMOCRACY ICONS: NEHRU (PM, statesman); PATEL (Iron Man, integrated 565 princely states); AMBEDKAR (constitution architect, dalit rights); RAJAGOPALACHARI (last Governor-General, Bharat Ratna). Subsequent Presidents: Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V.V. Giri, F.A. Ahmed (died in office, 1977), N.S. Reddy, Zail Singh, Venkataraman, S.D. Sharma, K.R. Narayanan, A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Pratibha Patil (first woman, 2007-12), Pranab Mukherjee, Ram Nath Kovind, DROUPADI MURMU (current, 2022-, first tribal woman).

cards.front:
President is the SUPREME COMMANDER of:

(A) All police forces of all states
(B) Armed forces of India (Article 53)
(C) Para-military + civil defence forces only
(D) Just the elite security force (SPG)
cards.back:
(B) Armed forces of India (Article 53)

President & Vice President — Article 53(2) — Supreme Command of DEFENCE FORCES (Army, Navy, Air Force) vested in PRESIDENT; exercised IN ACCORDANCE WITH LAW (i.e., on advice of council of ministers led by PM, who acts via Defence Minister + military chiefs). Symbolic role — President doesn't direct military operations day-to-day. President APPOINTS service chiefs (CDS, COAS, CNS, CAS). DECLARES war + concludes peace (per advice of Cabinet). PARDONS courts-martial (Article 72). NOT supreme over police (state subject under STATE LIST except in UTs). PARA-MILITARY (CRPF, BSF, ITBP, CISF) under Home Ministry. Comparable: US President is C-in-C of US Armed Forces under their Constitution.

cards.front:
President can grant PARDONS, REPRIEVES, etc. under which Article?

(A) Article 32 (writ jurisdiction)
(B) Article 72 (presidential pardons)
(C) Article 14 (equality before law)
(D) Article 21 (right to life)
cards.back:
(B) Article 72 (presidential pardons)

President & Vice President — Article 72 — gives President the power to grant: PARDON (full forgiveness; person treated innocent); COMMUTATION (substitute milder sentence — e.g., death → life); REMISSION (reduce punishment without changing nature — e.g., 10 yrs → 7 yrs); RESPITE (lesser sentence due to special circumstances — e.g., pregnancy, age); REPRIEVE (temporary stay, esp. of execution, while a final decision is reached). Pres has WIDER powers than GOVERNOR (Article 161): Pres can pardon DEATH SENTENCES + COURT-MARTIAL cases too. Mercy petition reaches Pres after all judicial appeals exhausted. Pres is BOUND by Cabinet's advice (post 42nd Amendment); but can return for reconsideration (44th Amendment). FAMOUS CASES: Afzal Guru (rejected 2013); Yakub Memon (rejected 2015); Nirbhaya convicts (rejected 2020).

cards.front:
Who can act as President when both President + Vice President offices are VACANT?

(A) Prime Minister of India
(B) Chief Justice of India (CJI)
(C) Lok Sabha Speaker (presiding over LS)
(D) Senior-most cabinet minister
cards.back:
(B) Chief Justice of India (CJI)

President & Vice President — If both PRES + VP offices vacant simultaneously: CHIEF JUSTICE OF INDIA (CJI) acts as President. If CJI also vacant, NEXT senior-most SC judge acts. Until new Pres + VP elected within 6 months. ACTUAL CASE: 1969 — Pres ZAKIR HUSAIN died in office (3 May 1969). VP V.V. GIRI became acting Pres (24 hrs after Husain's death). Giri then RESIGNED VP to contest Pres election. M. HIDAYATULLAH (CJI) ACTED as President from 20 July to 24 Aug 1969 — only such instance. Got narrow resolution from Cabinet to assume the role. Subsequent: Giri won + became 4th President. INSIGHT: Constitution has a clear succession ladder — VP → CJI → next SC judge — to ensure continuity.

(C) Only the Lok Sabha

Value of each vote is weighted by state population (1971 census, frozen by 84th Amendment). elected MPs + elected MLAs of all States + Delhi & Puducherry.

cards.front:
A PRESIDENTIAL VETO where the President just SITS ON a bill (neither signing nor rejecting) is called:

(A) Absolute veto
(B) Pocket veto
(C) Suspensive veto
(D) Line-item veto
cards.back:
(B) Pocket veto

President & Vice President — Three types available to Indian President: (1) Absolute veto — not assenting (rare, 1991 used on salary bill by Zail Singh). (2) Suspensive veto — returning for reconsideration (Art 111 — only for non-money bills); if Parliament re-passes, must sign. (3) Pocket veto — no time limit, keeps indefinitely; Zail Singh used this on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986 — never signed.

(3) Pocket veto — no time limit, keeps indefinitely; Zail Singh used this on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986 — never signed.

cards.front:
The President is IMPEACHED under Article:

(A) Article 58
(B) Article 61
(C) Article 74
(D) Article 352
cards.back:
(B) Article 61

President & Vice President — Art 61 — impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution'. Procedure: charge by either house (2/3 special majority), investigation, then passage by other house (2/3 majority). Nominated MPs CAN participate (unique to this vote). No Indian President has been impeached. 58 — qualifications. 74 — Council of Ministers. 352 — National Emergency.

cards.front:
Under Article 72, the President has the power to grant PARDONS. Which of these is NOT a type of pardon?

(A) Pardon
(B) Commutation
(C) Remission
(D) Annulment
cards.back:
(D) Annulment

President & Vice President — Art 72 — 5 types: (1) Pardon (complete), (2) Commutation (lesser form, e.g., death to life), (3) Remission (reduction without change of kind), (4) Respite (reduced sentence due to special circumstances), (5) Reprieve (postponement). 'Annulment' is not a legal pardon category.

(A) Absolute veto — refusing assent to any bill

cards.front:
ORDINANCE-making power of the President is exercised under which Article?

(A) Article 72, dealing with pardon and clemency powers
(B) Article 123, when Parliament is not in session
(C) Article 356, related to state-level emergency provisions
(D) Article 368, dealing with constitutional amendments

Must be laid before both Houses when they reconvene; lapses 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved by both Houses. Cannot violate FRs / basic structure (justiciable). Re-promulgation of ordinances was held a fraud on the Constitution by SC (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017). Article 213 — analogous power for Governors at state level. Distractor 1 = pardon (Article 72). cards.front:
The President's PARDON / CLEMENCY power under Article 72 includes:

(A) Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation
(B) Pardon only, with no other clemency variant
(C) Reprieve and respite only, in capital cases
(D) Power to acquit during the trial proceedings
cards.back:
(A) Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation

President & Vice President — Article 72 — President's pardoning power. Five forms: (1) PARDON — completely absolves the convict (record + sentence); (2) COMMUTATION — substitutes lighter sentence (e.g., death → life); (3) REMISSION — reduces sentence duration without changing nature; (4) RESPITE — lighter sentence due to special circumstances (pregnancy, age); (5) REPRIEVE — temporary stay of execution. Article 161 — Governor's similar power at state level (NO power over death sentence; that's exclusively the President's). President EXERCISES on cabinet's advice (Maru Ram, 1981). Mercy petitions famously delayed (Ajmal Kasab, Afzal Guru cases).

cards.front:
Three types of EMERGENCY are provided in the Constitution. Which is the MOST commonly invoked?

(A) National emergency under Article 352 of the Constitution
(B) President's Rule (state emergency) under Article 356
(C) Financial emergency under Article 360 of the Constitution
(D) Federal emergency, requiring full Parliament approval
cards.back:

(2) PRESIDENT'S RULE / State emergency (Art 356) — invoked over 130 TIMES (most common). Triggered when state's constitutional machinery fails; central govt takes over state administration. SC's Bommai judgment (1994) restricted misuse — SR Bommai vs Union. (3) FINANCIAL EMERGENCY (Art 360) — NEVER invoked. Distractor 4 — invented term.

cards.front:
The President of India is CONSTITUTIONALLY BOUND to act on the advice of:

(A) Only the Prime Minister, in all routine matters
(B) The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
(C) The Cabinet Secretary as the senior bureaucrat
(D) Only the Speaker of the Lok Sabha alone
cards.back:
(B) The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister

President & Vice President — Article 74(1) — there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to AID AND ADVISE the President, who SHALL act in accordance with such advice. (Originally said 'shall'; 42nd Amendment 1976 made 'shall' explicit; 44th Amendment 1978 added that the President MAY require the Council to reconsider their advice ONCE, but must accept the second advice.) President is thus a CEREMONIAL HEAD; effective executive power lies with the PM + Cabinet. Article 75 — PM appointed by President; other ministers appointed on PM's advice. Distractor 1 — PM alone isn't the constitutional advisor; the Council is. Distractor 3 — bureaucratic, not constitutional. Distractor 4 — Speaker has no advisory role to President.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the SUPREME COMMANDER of the Indian Armed Forces?

(A) The Prime Minister, the head of government
(B) The President of India, by Article 53(2)
(C) The Defence Minister, in the Union Cabinet
(D) The Chief of Defence Staff, recently created post
cards.back:
(B) The President of India, by Article 53(2)

Largely ceremonial; operational command flows through the Defence Minister + Service Chiefs + (since 2020) the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). The Indian Armed Forces salute the President. President-as-supreme-commander tradition mirrors UK's monarch role. Distractor 1 = effective head of executive but not formal supreme commander. Distractor 3 = political-administrative head of MoD. cards.front:
The President of India is elected by an Electoral College consisting of:

(A) All members of Parliament only
(B) Elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies + elected members of UT Assemblies of Delhi & Puducherry
(C) All members of all State Legislatures
(D) MPs and the Cabinet
cards.back:
(B) Elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies + elected members of UT Assemblies of Delhi & Puducherry

President & Vice President — Article 54 — Electoral College for President: ELECTED members of (i) both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha), (ii) all State Legislative Assemblies, (iii) Legislative Assemblies of UTs of Delhi & Puducherry (added by 70th Amendment, 1992). Nominated members do NOT vote. Elected by single transferable vote, secret ballot, proportional representation. Value of MLA's vote = (state population / total elected MLAs in state) / 1000. cards.front:
The 'Pocket Veto' — never used by any President but is most associated with President Zail Singh in 1986 — refers to:

(A) Returning a bill within 14 days
(B) Indefinite withholding of assent — neither signing nor returning the bill
(C) Sending a bill to the Supreme Court
(D) Vetoing a Money Bill
cards.back:
(B) Indefinite withholding of assent — neither signing nor returning the bill

President & Vice President — Pocket Veto — President neither signs the bill, nor returns it, nor refuses assent. The Constitution sets no time-limit for the President to act on an ordinary bill, so it can be 'put in the pocket' indefinitely. Zail Singh used it on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986 — bill never became law. Other vetoes — Absolute Veto (refuse assent), Suspensive Veto (return for reconsideration; if Parliament passes again, must assent), Qualified Veto (does NOT exist in India — it's a US concept where a 2/3 majority over-rides).

Under Article 72, the President can grant pardon, reprieve, respite, remission of punishment OR suspension — including for which case-type that the Governor cannot pardon?

(A) Cases under State law
(B) Death sentence and Court Martial cases
(C) Bailable offences only
(D) Civil cases
cards.back:

(ii) President can pardon Court-Martial sentences; Governor cannot. The Governor's pardoning power is restricted to offences against State laws (matters in the State List). Both can grant Pardon, Commutation, Remission, Respite, Reprieve. President's pardoning is exercised on aid and advice of the Cabinet (Maru Ram, 1980; Kehar Singh, 1989; Epuru Sudhakar, 2006).

cards.front:
An ordinance issued by the President under Article 123 must be approved by Parliament within:

(A) 30 days from the start of the next session
(B) 6 weeks from the start of the next session — else it lapses
(C) 6 months from issue
(D) 12 months from issue

(B) 6 weeks from the start of the next session — else it lapses

So effective maximum life = 6 months (max recess) + 6 weeks ≈ 7.5 months. Ordinances can be made only when Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied immediate action is necessary. (B) A Money Bill
(C) A Constitution Amendment Bill

Ordinary bills under Art 111 can be returned once.

Pre-1976 it was implicit; the 42nd Amendment made it textually binding.

cards.front:

cards.back:
(B) By a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by an effective majority and agreed to by the Lok Sabha

A 14-day prior notice is required. This is LESS STRINGENT than Presidential impeachment (which requires a two-thirds majority in each House). The VP's removal has never been invoked in practice.

(D) The joint sitting of Parliament

Majority requirements are computed by quota, not by simple/two-thirds.

(2) Ministers hold office during the PLEASURE of the President (in reality, so long as they retain Lok Sabha confidence). (3) 91st CAA (2003) — size of CoM capped at 15% of Lok Sabha strength (so max = 81 in a 543-member LS after 91st — though 540-seat 2024 LS means cap is 81). (4) Minister must be a MEMBER of either House within 6 MONTHS of being sworn in (Art 75(5)); if not elected by then, must resign. (5) Ministers collectively responsible to LOK SABHA (Art 75(3)). cards.front:
As per the 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003), the size of the Union Council of Ministers cannot exceed:

(A) 10% of Lok Sabha strength
(B) 15% of the TOTAL STRENGTH of the LOK SABHA
(C) 25% of Lok Sabha strength
(D) No limit
cards.back:
(B) 15% of the TOTAL STRENGTH of the LOK SABHA

Prime Minister & Cabinet — 91st CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 2003 — inserted Art 75(1A) [Union] + Art 164(1A) [State] to cap the size of the Council of Ministers. PROVISIONS: (1) TOTAL number of Ministers INCLUDING the PM shall not exceed 15% of LOK SABHA's total strength. For the current 543-member LS (will rise post-delimitation), the cap = 81 ministers. (2) SIMILAR cap for STATES: 15% of Legislative Assembly; minimum 12 even in small states. (3) ALSO made DEFECTED legislators disqualified from holding a ministerial post (plugs a loophole that let defectors join ruling coalition as ministers). BACKGROUND: 'JUMBO MINISTRIES' — e.g., in some states pre-2003, a CM would appoint 40-80 ministers to hold coalitions together; the amendment was passed on all-party consensus (NCRWC recommendation, National Commission to Review Working of the Constitution, 2002). CURRENT: Modi Cabinet (post-2024 elections) has ~72 ministers (Cabinet + MoS), well within 81 cap. RANKS of Ministers: (a) CABINET MINISTERS (members of Cabinet — senior); (b) MINISTERS OF STATE with Independent Charge (head a ministry, not in Cabinet); (c) Ministers of State (assist Cabinet Ministers). DEPUTY PMs (not a constitutional post) — there have been 8 historically (Patel, Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, Jagjivan Ram, Y.B. Chavan, Devi Lal, L.K. Advani). to curb jumbo ministries; including PM.

cards.front:
Who was India's first PRIME MINISTER to come from Lok Sabha via a no-confidence motion win after initially being in a minority?

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru
(B) P.V. NARASIMHA RAO (1991-96)
(C) Morarji Desai
(D) V.P. Singh
cards.back:
(B) P.V. NARASIMHA RAO (1991-96)

Prime Minister & Cabinet — P.V. NARASIMHA RAO (1921-2004) — 9th PM of India (21 June 1991 – 16 May 1996). Significance: (1) First PM from SOUTH INDIA (born in Karimnagar, united Andhra, now Telangana); (2) First FULL-TERM MINORITY GOVERNMENT to complete 5 years; (3) Polyglot — knew ~17 languages; (4) Architect of LPG REFORMS (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation, 1991) along with FM MANMOHAN SINGH — rescued India from the 1991 BoP crisis (FOREX reserves ~2 weeks; 67 tonnes of gold pledged to BoE + UBS); (5) Started the LOOK EAST POLICY; (6) Opened up India to FDI + scrapped the License Raj. COALITION MANAGEMENT: Congress had 244/543 seats, short of majority; Rao ran a minority govt surviving multiple no-confidence motions — most controversially the 1993 NC motion he won through allegations of paying JMM MPs (later Supreme Court ruled MPs immune for votes even if bribed — V. Ashok Kumar Singh case). Also PM during demolition of BABRI MASJID (6 Dec 1992) — a blot on his tenure. BOOK: 'THE INSIDER' — his political novel. AFTERMATH: sidelined by the Gandhi family after loss in 1996; denied state funeral in Delhi (cremated in Hyderabad). BHARAT RATNA awarded POSTHUMOUSLY in 2024. led minority Congress govt that survived by attracting defectors + passing LPG reforms.

cards.front:
Article 74(1) of the Constitution provides that there SHALL BE a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. The advice is BINDING on the President because of the:

(A) 42nd Amendment 1976 (made it binding) + 44th Amendment 1978
(B) It has always been binding since 1950
(C) Supreme Court judgments only
(D) It is only a convention, not legally binding
cards.back:
(A) 42nd Amendment 1976 (made it binding) + 44th Amendment 1978

Prime Minister & Cabinet — ARTICLE 74(1) — CoM advice to the President: (a) ORIGINAL text (1950-1976): 'There shall be a Council of Ministers with the PM at the head to aid and advise the President' — ambiguity whether binding; (b) 42nd AMENDMENT (1976): inserted 'who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice' — made advice binding; (c) 44th AMENDMENT (1978 — post-Emergency corrective): added proviso allowing the President to RETURN the advice ONCE for reconsideration; but the President SHALL ACT in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration. RESULT: President is effectively a CEREMONIAL head bound by CoM advice, except for the 'pocket veto' or the one-time send-back. Article 74(2) — the question whether any advice was tendered + what advice was tendered CANNOT be inquired into in any court (protects secrecy of deliberations). DISCRETIONARY POWERS of the President that survive (SITUATIONAL DISCRETION): (1) appointing PM when no party has majority (hung LS); (2) dismissing Council when it loses majority + refuses to resign; (3) dissolving LS when CoM has lost confidence. SHAMSHER SINGH case (1974) + S.R. BOMMAI case (1994) reaffirmed the binding nature subject to these exceptions. allowed ONE return for reconsideration.
cards.option1: It has always been binding since 1950
cards.option3: It is only a convention, not legally binding

cards.front:
Who was India's YOUNGEST Prime Minister?

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru at 58
(B) RAJIV GANDHI
(C) Narendra Modi at 63
(D) Indira Gandhi at 48
cards.back:
(B) RAJIV GANDHI

Prime Minister & Cabinet — RAJIV GANDHI (20 Aug 1944 – 21 May 1991) — 6th PM of India (31 October 1984 – 2 December 1989). Sworn in at 40 YEARS + 72 days — the YOUNGEST PM in India's history. CIRCUMSTANCES: mother Indira Gandhi assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards (Beant Singh + Satwant Singh) on the morning of 31 Oct 1984 — Rajiv was a young politician (entered politics only after younger brother Sanjay's death in 1980 plane crash); was sworn in the same evening by President Zail Singh. 1984 ELECTION: Congress won 414/514 seats — LARGEST MAJORITY EVER in Indian political history (sympathy wave). KEY INITIATIVES: (1) ANTI-DEFECTION LAW (52nd CAA 1985 — Tenth Schedule); (2) lowered voting age from 21 to 18 (61st CAA 1989); (3) Panchayati Raj Bill (became 73rd CAA later, 1992); (4) TELECOM + COMPUTER revolution — founded MTNL (1986) + Sam Pitroda's C-DoT + brought PCs to Indian ministries; (5) Educational Technology Mission + Operation Blackboard. LOWS: BOFORS scandal (kickbacks in Swedish artillery deal — unproven legally but politically fatal); IPKF intervention in Sri Lanka (1987-90); handling of 1984 anti-Sikh riots + Shah Bano case U-turn. ASSASSINATION: 21 May 1991 at Sriperumbudur (TN) by a LTTE suicide-bomber Thenmozhi Rajaratnam during a campaign rally — at age 46. Posthumous Bharat Ratna 1991. Atal Bihari Vajpayee became PM at ~73; Narendra Modi at ~63 (oldest BJP PM). sworn in at 40 years, on 31 October 1984 after the assassination of his mother Indira Gandhi.

cards.front:
The principle of COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY of the Council of Ministers means:

(A) Each minister is responsible only for his own department
(B) The CoM as a whole is RESPONSIBLE TO THE LOK SABHA
(C) Ministers are responsible to the Rajya Sabha
(D) The PM alone is responsible
cards.back:
(B) The CoM as a whole is RESPONSIBLE TO THE LOK SABHA

Prime Minister & Cabinet — COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY (Article 75(3)) — the bedrock of Parliamentary democracy: the Council of Ministers is COLLECTIVELY responsible to the LOK SABHA (not Rajya Sabha). IMPLICATIONS: (1) CoM stays in office only as long as it commands Lok Sabha's CONFIDENCE. If a NO-CONFIDENCE motion passes, or a confidence motion fails, the ENTIRE CoM must resign (including non-LS ministers). (2) CABINET DECISIONS are binding on ALL ministers — a minister who disagrees publicly must resign (e.g., Arun Shourie-Yashwant Sinha disagreements in Vajpayee Cabinet; more recently, Jaitley's disagreements). (3) CONFIDENTIALITY — ministers bound by an OATH OF SECRECY; Cabinet deliberations not to be disclosed. INDIVIDUAL RESPONSIBILITY (Art 75(2)): 'Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President' — but in practice, only the PM can recommend dismissal. INDIAN PRACTICE: PM often removes underperforming ministers (reshuffle) — e.g., Vajpayee removed Babulal Marandi; Modi dropped many in 2021 reshuffle + 2024 rejig. NO-CONFIDENCE MOTIONS THAT SUCCEEDED: VP Singh 1990, Deve Gowda 1997, Gujral 1998, Vajpayee 1999 (lost by 1 vote — 269-270 — Giridhar Gomango voted despite being Odisha CM). Most no-confidence motions FAIL (2003 Sonia against Vajpayee; 2018 against Modi). they swim + sink together; losing LS confidence compels resignation of the entire CoM.
cards.option1: Each minister is responsible only for his own department
cards.option2: Ministers are responsible to the Rajya Sabha

cards.front:
The ONLY Prime Minister of India who NEVER faced the Parliament as Prime Minister (resigned before addressing Lok Sabha) was:

(A) H.D. Deve Gowda
(B) CHOUDHARY CHARAN SINGH (1979-80)
(C) Chandra Shekhar
(D) Morarji Desai
cards.back:
(B) CHOUDHARY CHARAN SINGH (1979-80)

Prime Minister & Cabinet — CHAUDHARY CHARAN SINGH (1902-1987) — 5th PM of India, 28 July 1979 – 14 January 1980. ONLY PM to have NEVER addressed the Lok Sabha as PM (resigned before he could face the confidence vote — 170 days in office). CIRCUMSTANCES: (a) Janata Party government led by Morarji Desai collapsed in July 1979 over internal dissensions (Dual membership issue — Jana Sangh members continuing with RSS); (b) Charan Singh split with 'Janata (S)' + was invited by President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy to form government with OUTSIDE SUPPORT from Indira Gandhi's INC(I) + CPI. (c) Indira WITHDREW support just before the confidence vote; Charan Singh resigned on 20 Aug 1979 — but continued as CARETAKER PM until Jan 1980 elections. 1980 ELECTION: Indira Gandhi's Congress(I) swept back; Charan Singh never returned to power. BACKGROUND: Charan Singh — farmer-leader from UP, champion of the kulak (rich peasant) lobby; advocated for small-scale agrarian economy; as UP CM (1967, 1970), key architect of land reforms. Birthday (23 DECEMBER) celebrated as KISAN DIWAS (Farmers' Day). BHARAT RATNA 2024 (posthumous, along with PV Narasimha Rao + MS Swaminathan + Advani + Karpoori Thakur). Other short-tenure PMs: Gulzarilal Nanda (2 stints as acting PM, 13 days each); Chandrashekhar (7 months); I.K. Gujral (11 months); H.D. Deve Gowda (10 months). resigned before facing the House when INC(I) withdrew support; acted as caretaker till Jan 1980.

cards.front:
According to Article 75(5), if a person is appointed as a Minister and is not a member of either House of Parliament, he must become a member within:

(A) 3 months
(B) SIX (6) MONTHS
(C) 1 year
(D) No time limit
cards.back:
(B) SIX (6) MONTHS

Prime Minister & Cabinet — ARTICLE 75(5) — six-month rule for non-member ministers. A person can be sworn in as a MINISTER (including PM) WITHOUT being a current MP, but MUST be elected/nominated to either House within 6 MONTHS. If they fail, they MUST CEASE to be a Minister. RATIONALE: allows talented outsiders to be brought in, but requires democratic sanction. CLASSIC EXAMPLES: (1) MANMOHAN SINGH — an economist + former RBI Governor, made FM in 1991 Rao Cabinet while not an MP; elected to Rajya Sabha (from Assam) within 6 months; became PM (2004, 2009) — only PM to have NEVER won a Lok Sabha election; Rajya Sabha 5 times. (2) HD DEVE GOWDA — became PM in 1996 before being an MP. (3) P.V. NARASIMHA RAO — was not an MP when chosen PM in 1991; won by-election in Nandyal (AP) with record margin. SC JUDGMENT: S.R. CHAUDHURI v. STATE OF PUNJAB (2001) — a minister who has failed to get elected once within 6 months CANNOT be re-appointed for another 6-month term without election — plugged a loophole used in Punjab by Parkash Singh Badal. Note: Rajya Sabha vacancy is easier to engineer (party biennial elections + by-election to fill death/resignation-caused vacancy) than Lok Sabha seat — many non-MP ministers take the Upper House route. failing which he ceases to be a Minister.

cards.front:
Who administers the oath of office to the Prime Minister?

(A) Chief Justice of India
(B) PRESIDENT OF INDIA
(C) Speaker of Lok Sabha
(D) Vice-President
cards.back:
(B) PRESIDENT OF INDIA

Prime Minister & Cabinet — OATH OF OFFICE for the Prime Minister + Union Ministers — administered by the PRESIDENT of INDIA, at the Rashtrapati Bhavan. FORMS of the oath in the THIRD SCHEDULE of the Constitution. TWO oaths are administered: (1) OATH OF OFFICE — to bear true faith + allegiance to the Constitution, uphold sovereignty + integrity of India, faithfully + conscientiously discharge duties. (2) OATH OF SECRECY — not to directly or indirectly communicate any matter considered in Council, except as required for proper discharge of duties. Ceremony traditionally held at FORECOURT of Rashtrapati Bhavan; PM typically sworn first followed by Cabinet Ministers + MoS. MODI 2024: sworn in by President DROUPADI MURMU on 9 June 2024 — 3rd consecutive term (only other PM after Nehru to do so). OTHER CONSTITUTIONAL OATHS admin by President: Vice-President, Governors (to respective State Governors technically — PRESIDENT admins VP's oath + Governors take oath before the CJI of respective HC / senior-most HC judge), CEC, CAG, judges of SC (admin by President; CJI admins Supreme Court judge oath if CJI in office). CJI takes his/her oath from the PRESIDENT. Governor admins State CM + State Ministers' oaths. as per the Third Schedule of the Constitution.

cards.front:
The CABINET SECRETARIAT, which assists the Prime Minister + Council of Ministers, is headed by:

(A) Principal Secretary to the PM
(B) CABINET SECRETARY
(C) Home Secretary
(D) Attorney General
cards.back:
(B) CABINET SECRETARY

Prime Minister & Cabinet — CABINET SECRETARY — the HIGHEST-RANKING civil servant in India; head of the CABINET SECRETARIAT + secretary of the Cabinet + senior-most IAS officer; ex-officio CHAIRMAN of: (1) CIVIL SERVICES BOARD, (2) Committee of Secretaries, (3) ACC (Appointments Committee of the Cabinet) 'Establishment Officer' role. REPORTS TO: the Prime Minister (not to the President). TENURE: originally 2 years; extended up to 4 years by convention; longest-serving = P.K. Sinha (4 years, 2015-19). CURRENT: T.V. Somanathan (took over August 2024, previous Finance Secy). ROLE: (a) coordinates inter-ministerial issues; (b) circulates cabinet papers + draft notes; (c) monitors implementation of cabinet decisions; (d) heads emergency-response coordination (e.g., during COVID-19, Ukraine evacuation). CABINET SECRETARIAT IS DIFFERENT from PMO (Prime Minister's Office) — PMO is headed by PRINCIPAL SECRETARY TO THE PM (a separate role; currently P.K. Mishra of Modi govt; NSA Ajit Doval also sits in PMO structure). Cabinet Secretariat has Departments of: Cabinet Affairs, Coordination, + the National Security Council Secretariat (till recent). cards.front:
The Prime Minister of India is APPOINTED by the:

(A) Lok Sabha Speaker, presiding officer
(B) President of India under Article 75
(C) Election Commission of India directly
(D) Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
cards.back:
(B) President of India under Article 75

Prime Minister & Cabinet — Article 75(1) — 'The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President.' Convention: President appoints the leader of the majority party / coalition in Lok Sabha as PM. If no clear majority — President exercises discretion (e.g., Sanjiva Reddy → Charan Singh, 1979). PM need not be MP at appointment but must become one within 6 months (Article 75(5)). Manmohan Singh was a Rajya Sabha member, never won LS election.

cards.front:
Article 75 of the Constitution says that the COUNCIL OF MINISTERS is collectively responsible to:

(A) President of India and his cabinet
(B) House of the People (Lok Sabha)
(C) Both Houses of Parliament jointly
(D) Indian electorate via direct vote
cards.back:
(B) House of the People (Lok Sabha)

Prime Minister & Cabinet — Article 75(3) — 'Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the HOUSE OF THE PEOPLE.' Means: if LS passes a NO-CONFIDENCE motion, the WHOLE government must resign. Vajpayee govt fell by 1 vote in 1999 (269-270). PM personally responsible to LS. Note: Cabinet sails together, sinks together — collective responsibility is the cornerstone of parliamentary democracy. Rajya Sabha cannot remove government. Article 75(2) — 'Ministers hold office during the pleasure of President.'

cards.front:
The MINIMUM AGE qualification to become Prime Minister of India is:

(A) 21 years to qualify for office
(B) 25 years (LS) or 30 years (RS)
(C) 35 years to qualify for office
(D) Same as Indian voter, 18 years
cards.back:
(B) 25 years (LS) or 30 years (RS)

Prime Minister & Cabinet — PM must be a member of Parliament. Min age for: Lok Sabha = 25 years; Rajya Sabha = 30 years. So if PM is appointed via LS membership → 25; via RS → 30. Normally PM is from LS. Distractor 35 = President + Vice President min age. Note: Article 75(5) — non-MP can be appointed PM but must become MP within 6 months.

cards.front:
The PM is the head of the:

(A) State, with executive functions
(B) Government and Council of Ministers
(C) Indian Parliament both Houses
(D) Supreme Court of judicial branch
cards.back:
(B) Government and Council of Ministers

Prime Minister & Cabinet — PM = Head of GOVERNMENT (real executive). PRESIDENT = Head of STATE (nominal/ceremonial). PM chairs the Cabinet, allocates portfolios, removes ministers (advises Pres to). PM is the BRIDGE between President + Council, between government + Parliament, between government + the people. PM advises President on: appointments (Governors, AG, CAG, CEC, judges), dissolution of LS, summoning of sessions. India follows the BRITISH parliamentary model where PM = real chief executive.

The first PM to LOSE A NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION in Lok Sabha was:

(A) Indira Gandhi after the Emergency time
(B) Morarji Desai in 1979 (resigned after)
(C) Vajpayee in the 1999 vote loss

Then Charan Singh became PM (only ~24 days, never faced LS — resigned). Vajpayee (1996, 13 days, resigned without facing vote; 1999 — actually LOST by 1 vote, government fell). cards.front:
Which Article CAPS the size of the Council of Ministers?

(A) Article 75(1A) — 15% of LS strength
(B) Article 74 — Council to aid Prez
(C) Article 76 — Attorney General role
(D) Article 80 — Rajya Sabha members
cards.back:
(A) Article 75(1A) — 15% of LS strength

Prime Minister & Cabinet — Article 75(1A) — added by 91st AMENDMENT (2003): total Council of Ministers (including PM) shall not exceed 15% of total LS membership. With LS = 543, max ministers = 81. Rationale: prevent jumbo cabinets (Rajiv Gandhi had 60+ in 1989; UPA-1 had ~80). Same Amendment 91st added Article 75(1B) — defected MP cannot be made minister. Distractor 1: Article 74 says PM advises President (binding after 42nd Amend). Distractor 3: AG. Distractor 4: RS composition.

cards.front:
On the resignation/death of the PM, the Council of Ministers automatically:

(A) Continues with senior-most as acting PM
(B) Is dissolved (PM = pivot of cabinet)
(C) Reorganizes by President's direct order
(D) Continues until next general election
cards.back:
(B) Is dissolved (PM = pivot of cabinet)

Prime Minister & Cabinet — Constitutional principle: PM is the keystone of the Council of Ministers. If PM resigns or dies → entire Council STANDS DISSOLVED automatically. President may ask the outgoing Council to continue as CARETAKER until a new government is formed. Examples: Nehru (died 1964) → Lal Bahadur Shastri became PM (Gulzarilal Nanda was acting PM for 13 days both times, in 1964 + 1966). After Indira (1984) → Rajiv. President swears in new PM, who then advises on Council. Distractor 1 partly true in practice via senior-most acting role, but Council itself dissolves.

cards.front:
The Chief Justice of India is APPOINTED by:

(A) The President of India
(B) The Prime Minister alone alone
(C) The Vice President of India alone
(D) Parliament by majority vote alone
cards.back:
(A) The President of India

Judiciary — Article 124(2): The Chief Justice of India is appointed by the PRESIDENT under his hand and seal. CONVENTION: the SENIOR-MOST judge of the Supreme Court is appointed CJI (the 'seniority principle'). The outgoing CJI traditionally recommends the next in line. KEY EVENT: Supersession Crisis 1973 — Indira Gandhi's govt SUPERSEDED 3 senior judges (J.M. Shelat, K.S. Hegde, A.N. Grover) to appoint A.N. Ray as CJI — sparking outrage that the seniority convention had been broken. Result: collegium system gradually emerged via judicial decisions (Three Judges Cases, 1981, 1993, 1998). MEMORANDUM OF PROCEDURE: outlines the CJI appointment process — currently being reviewed by NJAC (National Judicial Appointments Commission, struck down by SC in 2015). RETIREMENT AGE: 65 years (Article 124(2)(b)). RECENT CJIs: D.Y. Chandrachud (Nov 2022 - Nov 2024), Sanjiv Khanna (Nov 2024 - May 2025), B.R. Gavai (May 2025 onwards) — first Buddhist-Dalit CJI of India. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'who appoints CJI' is a SSC, UPSC, polity 1-mark guarantee.

cards.front:
What is the RETIREMENT AGE for a Supreme Court judge (including CJI)?

(A) 65 years for Supreme Court judges
(B) 62 years for Supreme Court alone
(C) 60 years (general civil service)
(D) 70 years (Constitutional officers)
cards.back:
(A) 65 years for Supreme Court judges

Judiciary — Article 124(2)(b): Supreme Court judges retire at AGE 65. HIGH COURT JUDGES retire at AGE 62 (Article 217(1)). DON'T CONFUSE — quick retirement-age table: SC Judges: 65; HC Judges: 62; Comptroller-Auditor-General (CAG): 65; UPSC Chairman/Member: 65; Election Commission of India members: 65 (or 6 yrs, whichever earlier); Lokpal: 70; CVC/CIC: 65 (or 5 yrs term). PROPOSALS to RAISE retirement age: there's been periodic debate about raising HC age to 65 (matching SC) — would help reduce pendency by retaining experienced judges. NOT YET enacted. POST-RETIREMENT: SC judges often serve in tribunals, commissions of inquiry, arbitration boards. Some controversy about 'post-retirement plums' for cooperative judges (e.g., chairing the Press Council, Law Commission, NHRC). NOTABLE: under Article 128, the President can recall a retired SC judge to TEMPORARILY hear cases — used rarely. PYQ FREQUENCY: SC vs HC retirement ages is a top-3 polity confusion — 1-2 Qs per cycle in CGL, UPSC. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests precise constitutional ages.

cards.front:
The CJI is described as the 'MASTER OF THE ROSTER' because he/she:

(A) Allocates cases to Supreme Court benches
(B) Manages the SC's payroll alone (option here)
(C) Decides all administrative matters.
(D) Appoints High Court judges directly.
cards.back:
(A) Allocates cases to Supreme Court benches

Judiciary — MASTER OF THE ROSTER — administrative power of the CJI to ALLOCATE CASES to specific benches and judges. This is exclusive prerogative; no judge can decide his own case-bench composition. ROSTER PRACTICE: CJI publishes a 'subject-roster' assigning categories (criminal, constitutional, tax, environment, etc.) to specific judges. JUSTICE J. CHELAMESWAR PRESS CONFERENCE (12 Jan 2018): four senior-most SC judges (Chelameswar, Gogoi, Lokur, Kurian Joseph) PUBLICLY criticized then-CJI Dipak Misra over allegations of biased case-assignments — historic event in Indian judiciary. SC subsequently affirmed (Asok Pande v. SC of India, 2018) that 'master of roster' is the CJI's settled prerogative — but with constitutional accountability. ANALOGUE: HC Chief Justices have similar roster power for their courts. ADMINISTRATIVE POWERS of CJI: (1) Roster allocation. (2) Constituting Constitution Benches (5+ judges). (3) Convening Full Court meetings. (4) Heading the Collegium for HC/SC judge appointments. (5) Heading the SC administration. PYQ ANGLE: 'master of roster' is a top UPSC, IIBF/ICAI legal-section MCQ.

cards.front:
In the COLLEGIUM SYSTEM, the CJI heads a body that recommends:

(A) Appointment and transfer of judges
(B) Removal of judges from office.
(C) Salary increases for the SC alone
(D) Constitutional amendments for Parliament
cards.back:
(A) Appointment and transfer of judges

Judiciary — COLLEGIUM SYSTEM — judicial body of senior judges that RECOMMENDS appointments, elevations, and transfers of HC and SC judges to the President. EVOLUTION VIA THREE JUDGES CASES: 1ST JUDGES CASE (1981) — 'consultation' by President meant only consultation, not concurrence with CJI. 2ND JUDGES CASE (1993) — CJI's opinion has primacy; need consultation with 2 senior-most SC judges. 3RD JUDGES CASE (1998) — collegium = CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges (for SC appointments). FOR HC APPOINTMENTS: CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges + HC Chief Justice + 2 senior-most HC judges. NJAC v. COLLEGIUM (2015): SC struck down 99th Constitutional Amendment that would have replaced collegium with NJAC (govt + judges + civil society) — restoring collegium as supreme. CRITICISMS of collegium: lack of transparency, no formal selection criteria, accusations of nepotism. 2024-25 CJI Khanna initiative: publicizing collegium reasoning more transparently. REMOVAL of JUDGES is a SEPARATE process (Article 124(4)) — by President via PARLIAMENTARY IMPEACHMENT (special majority + addressing both houses on grounds of 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'). PYQ FREQUENCY: collegium concepts are tested in UPSC, judicial-services exams.

cards.front:
Who was the FIRST WOMAN judge of the Supreme Court of India?

(A) Justice M. Fathima Beevi (appointed 1989)
(B) Justice Sujata Manohar alone alone
(C) Justice Ruma Pal alone alone (option here)
(D) Justice Ranjana Desai alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Justice M. Fathima Beevi (appointed 1989)

Judiciary — JUSTICE M. FATHIMA BEEVI was appointed to the Supreme Court of India in OCTOBER 1989 — the FIRST WOMAN to hold this position. She served until April 1992. BACKGROUND: born 1927 in Pathanamthitta, Kerala; first woman to top the Bar Council Examination in India; Kerala HC judge before SC elevation. She later served as Governor of Tamil Nadu (1997-2001). MILESTONES IN INDIAN WOMEN JUDICIARY: (1) Anna Chandy — first woman HIGH COURT judge (Kerala HC, 1959). (2) Fathima Beevi — first woman SC judge (1989). (3) Justice R. Banumathi (2014-2020) — second woman after Fathima Beevi to retire. (4) Justice Indira Banerjee (2018-2022). (5) Justice Hima Kohli, B.V. Nagarathna, Bela Trivedi (all elevated 2021). NOTABLE: B.V. Nagarathna is set to become the FIRST WOMAN CHIEF JUSTICE OF INDIA (Sept 2027 - Oct 2027 tenure of ~1 month). REPRESENTATION: only ~11% of HC judges are women; 4 women SC judges as of 2025. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'firsts' in judiciary appear in CGL, UPSC, IBPS GA — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Who was the FIRST CHIEF JUSTICE OF INDIA after the Constitution came into force?

(A) Harilal Jekisundas Kania (Jan 1950)
(B) M. Patanjali Sastri alone alone
(C) Mehr Chand Mahajan alone alone
(D) B.K. Mukherjea alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Harilal Jekisundas Kania (Jan 1950)

Judiciary — JUSTICE H.J. KANIA (Harilal Jekisundas Kania) was the FIRST CJI of India, sworn in on 26 January 1950 — the day the Constitution came into force. Tragically, he died in office on 6 November 1951 — the only CJI to have died while in office. BACKGROUND: born 1890 in Ahmedabad; Bombay HC judge before being elevated. CHRONOLOGY OF FIRST FEW CJIs (memorize for UPSC): (1) H.J. Kania — 1950-1951. (2) M. Patanjali Sastri — 1951-1954. (3) Mehr Chand Mahajan — 1954. (4) B.K. Mukherjea — 1954-1956. (5) Sudhi Ranjan Das — 1956-1959. CURRENT CJI (April 2026): B.R. Gavai (sworn in May 2025; retires Nov 2025). FIRSTS: Indian-origin CJI: Justice K.G. Balakrishnan (Dalit, 2007-2010); Justice Ranganath Misra (1990-91, longer tenure ~ 2 years). LONGEST-SERVING CJI: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud (1978-1985, ~7 years 3 months — record). SHORTEST: Justice K.N. Singh (just 17 days, Nov 1991). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'first CJI' is a perennial UPSC, CGL fact.

cards.front:
Who can act as CJI in the absence of the CJI (e.g., during illness or foreign visit)?

(A) Senior-most judge of the Supreme Court
(B) Attorney General of India alone.
(C) Solicitor General of India alone.
(D) Chief Justice of Delhi HC alone.
cards.back:
(A) Senior-most judge of the Supreme Court

Judiciary — Article 126: When the office of CJI is VACANT (between resignations) or when CJI is absent or otherwise unable to perform duties (illness, foreign visit, leave), the President may appoint a JUDGE of the Supreme Court — by convention, the SENIOR-MOST judge — to act as CJI. PRACTICAL EXAMPLE: when CJI Sanjiv Khanna was on leave in 2025, the next senior-most judge presided over Court 1 in his absence. ARTICLE 127 (Ad-hoc judges): if there's a quorum problem at SC, the CJI (with President's prior consent) can request a HIGH COURT judge to sit as 'ad-hoc' SC judge — used rarely (e.g., Justice U.U. Lalit's elevation through this route). ARTICLE 128 (Recall retired judges): the CJI can request retired SC/HC judges (with their consent + President's permission) to sit as judges of the SC for SPECIFIC cases — used for high-profile constitutional benches. INTERESTING: Acting CJI carries the same powers as a full CJI but only for the duration of acting tenure; doesn't count toward retirement age extension. PYQ ANGLE: Articles 126, 127, 128 appear in UPSC CSE, HJS exams.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a type of writ that a High Court can issue under Article 226?

(A) Habeas Corpus
(B) Mandamus
(C) Quo Warranto
(D) Summary judgment
cards.back:

'Summary judgment' is a civil-procedure concept (Order 37 CPC), NOT a constitutional writ.

cards.front:
The jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 to issue writs extends to:

(A) Only to protect Fundamental Rights
(B) To protect both Fundamental Rights AND for any other purpose
(C) Only against State authorities
(D) Only within the territorial boundaries of the State
cards.back:

Judiciary — Article 226 is BROADER than Article 32 of the Supreme Court. This is why more cases go to HCs than directly to the SC under Art 32. HCs can also reach persons/authorities outside their territorial limits if the cause of action arose within.

cards.front:

cards.front:
The SUPREME COURT OF INDIA came into existence on:

(A) 15 August 1947
(B) 28 JANUARY 1950
(C) 26 January 1950
(D) 26 November 1949
cards.back:
(B) 28 JANUARY 1950

Judiciary — SUPREME COURT of INDIA — established 28 JANUARY 1950 (2 days after Constitution came into force). ESTABLISHMENT: Articles 124-147 of the Constitution (Part V, Chapter IV). Replaced the FEDERAL COURT of INDIA (est. 1 Oct 1937 under Govt of India Act 1935) + abolished JUDICIAL COMMITTEE of PRIVY COUNCIL (London, UK) as final court of appeal. Initial SITTING: Old Parliament House's 'Chamber of Princes' (Delhi). Moved to CURRENT building on Tilak Marg (designed by Ganesh Bhikaji Deolalikar, India's first CPWD chief architect, in 1958) — scales of justice form-like plan, main dome, 27m high. FIRST CJI: HARILAL JEKISUNDAS KANIA (26 Jan 1950 – 6 Nov 1951). STRENGTH: originally CJI + 7 judges = 8 total; raised over time — 1956 (10), 1960 (13), 1977 (17), 1985 (25), 2008 (30), 2019 (34 — 1 CJI + 33 judges, current strength). Art 124(1) — 'Supreme Court shall consist of CJI + not more than [33] other judges'. APPOINTMENT: by PRESIDENT under Art 124 — based on COLLEGIUM RECOMMENDATION since Second + Third Judges Cases (1993, 1998) — CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges. ELIGIBILITY: (a) Indian citizen; (b) HAS served as HC judge for 5 years; OR (c) advocate of HC for 10 years; OR (d) 'distinguished jurist' in President's opinion (this route NEVER used). RETIREMENT AGE: 65 YEARS. SALARY: CJI ₹2.80 lakh/month + allowances; judges ₹2.50 lakh + allowances (drawn from Consolidated Fund of India — not subject to parliamentary vote). OATH administered by President. REMOVAL by PARLIAMENTARY IMPEACHMENT (Art 124(4)) — 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'; special majority; procedure in Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968. Justice V. Ramaswami (1991-93) + Justice Soumitra Sen (2011) are partial impeachment cases; no judge yet removed by successful impeachment. CURRENT CJI (2025-26): Justice Sanjiv Khanna (11 Nov 2024 – 13 May 2025); next DY Chandrachud retired. 2 days after Constitution; replaced Federal Court (1937); first CJI = Harilal J. Kania.

cards.front:
Which ARTICLE of the Constitution provides the SUPREME COURT with power to issue WRITS for enforcement of FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS?

(A) Article 226
(B) ARTICLE 32
(C) Article 136
(D) Article 143
cards.back:
(B) ARTICLE 32

Judiciary — ARTICLE 32 — RIGHT to CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES — the procedural right to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B.R. AMBEDKAR called it 'the HEART AND SOUL OF THE CONSTITUTION'. Unlike most Fundamental Rights, Art 32 IS ITSELF a Fundamental Right — so Parliament cannot restrict it like any ordinary law; needs constitutional amendment. FIVE WRITS under Art 32 (+ Art 226 for HCs): (1) HABEAS CORPUS ('produce the body') — against illegal detention; compels authority to produce a detained person + justify detention. CANNOT be suspended even during Emergency post-44th Amendment. (2) MANDAMUS ('we command') — compels a public official to perform a statutory duty he/she has refused to perform. Can't be issued against President, Governor, Parliament. (3) PROHIBITION — issued by higher court to LOWER court / tribunal to STOP hearing a case beyond its jurisdiction. Preventive. (4) CERTIORARI ('to certify') — higher court QUASHES an order of lower court/tribunal already passed beyond its jurisdiction. Curative. (5) QUO WARRANTO ('by what authority') — questions the legal authority of a person holding a public office — to remove unauthorised occupant. DIFFERENCES Art 32 vs Art 226: (a) Art 32 = SC; Art 226 = HC; (b) Art 32 only for FRs; Art 226 for FRs + 'any other purpose' (broader); (c) Art 226 has territorial jurisdiction over the state + neighbouring areas; Art 32 pan-India; (d) HC wider power of PIL. PIL (PUBLIC INTEREST LITIGATION) — evolved in 1980s by Justice P.N. Bhagwati + V.R. Krishna Iyer; relaxed LOCUS STANDI (standing) so ANY public-spirited citizen can file petition on behalf of affected. Landmarks: S.P. Gupta, Hussainara Khatoon (under-trial prisoners), Asiad workers' case, Bandhua Mukti Morcha, Olga Tellis. PIL CAN BE CURATIVELY ABUSED — 'Publicity Interest Litigation', private agendas disguised — SC has cautioned (e.g., Ashok Kumar Pandey 2014). 'Heart + Soul of the Constitution' per Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; guarantees Right to Constitutional Remedies (a Fundamental Right itself).

cards.front:
The BASIC STRUCTURE DOCTRINE of the Indian Constitution was propounded in which landmark case?

(A) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
(B) KESAVANANDA BHARATI v. STATE OF KERALA (1973) — 13-judge bench held Parliament cannot amend Constitution to destroy its 'basic structure'
(C) Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967)
(D) Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
cards.back:
(B) KESAVANANDA BHARATI v. STATE OF KERALA (1973) — 13-judge bench held Parliament cannot amend Constitution to destroy its 'basic structure'

Judiciary — KESAVANANDA BHARATI v. STATE OF KERALA (1973) — MOST FAMOUS case in Indian constitutional history. 13-JUDGE SC bench — the LARGEST bench ever. 7-6 VERDICT delivered on 24 April 1973 (marathon 68-day hearing). Petitioner: Swami KESAVANANDA BHARATI of Edneer Mutt (Kerala); challenged Kerala Land Reforms Act acquiring his monastery's land. HELD: (1) Parliament has WIDE powers to amend the Constitution (Art 368); (2) BUT Parliament CANNOT amend the Constitution to destroy its BASIC STRUCTURE / FEATURES / FRAMEWORK; (3) OVERRULED GOLAKNATH (1967 — which had said Parliament could NOT amend FRs); (4) BUT LIMITED the amending power to those amendments that do not alter the 'basic structure'. Core features of BASIC STRUCTURE (non-exhaustive — evolved case by case): (a) Supremacy of Constitution; (b) sovereign + democratic + republican nature; (c) SECULARISM (S.R. Bommai 1994); (d) FEDERALISM; (e) separation of powers; (f) JUDICIAL REVIEW; (g) FREE + FAIR ELECTIONS; (h) rule of law; (i) FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (partially); (j) unity + integrity of India; (k) PARLIAMENTARY system; (l) independence of judiciary; (m) welfare state (socialist); (n) equality; (o) dignity of individual. SUBSEQUENT cases elaborating: (1) INDIRA GANDHI v. RAJ NARAIN (1975) — struck down 39th CAA which had validated Indira's election retrospectively — added 'free + fair elections' to basic structure. (2) MINERVA MILLS v. UoI (1980) — struck down parts of 42nd CAA that curbed judicial review + gave DPSPs primacy over FRs; confirmed judicial review + harmony between FRs + DPSPs as basic structure. (3) S.R. BOMMAI (1994) — secularism = basic. (4) I.R. COELHO v. State of TN (2007) — 9th Schedule laws (since 24 April 1973) subject to judicial review if they violate basic structure. PRE-KESAVANANDA history: (a) SHANKARI PRASAD (1951) — Parliament CAN amend FRs; (b) SAJJAN SINGH (1965) — reaffirmed; (c) GOLAKNATH (1967 11-judge) — REVERSED — Parliament CANNOT amend FRs; (d) Kesavananda restored Parliament's amending power BUT with 'basic structure' limitation. Kesavananda is the DNA of Indian Constitutionalism.

cards.front:
The COLLEGIUM SYSTEM for appointment of Supreme Court + HC judges evolved from the:

(A) Original Constitution (1950)
(B) Second Judges Case (1993) + Third Judges Case (1998) — CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges for SC appts; CJI + 2 senior-most for HC
(C) 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014)
(D) Sarkaria Commission
cards.back:
(B) Second Judges Case (1993) + Third Judges Case (1998) — CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges for SC appts; CJI + 2 senior-most for HC

Judiciary — COLLEGIUM SYSTEM — institutional mechanism for JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS to Supreme Court + High Courts in India. ORIGINAL CONSTITUTION Art 124: President appointed judges IN CONSULTATION with CJI (not bound to accept CJI advice). EVOLUTION: (1) FIRST JUDGES CASE / S.P. GUPTA v. UoI (1981) — held 'consultation' did NOT mean 'concurrence' — EXECUTIVE had primacy in appointments; CJI's view was merely consultative. (2) SECOND JUDGES CASE / Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. UoI (1993) — REVERSED — held 'consultation' meant 'concurrence'; CJI's opinion on appointments had PRIMACY. Introduced COLLEGIUM of CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges for SC appointments. (3) THIRD JUDGES CASE / In re Presidential Reference (1998) — EXPANDED collegium to CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges for SC appts; CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges from parent HC for HC judge appointment. ADDED that CJI's opinion must be formed after due consultation with collegium; individual opinion doesn't bind. (4) 99th CAA 2014 + NATIONAL JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS COMMISSION (NJAC) ACT 2014 — Parliament unanimously replaced collegium with NJAC (CJI + 2 senior SC judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent persons chosen by CJI+PM+LoP). (5) FOURTH JUDGES CASE / SC Advocates-on-Record Association v. UoI (2015) — STRUCK DOWN 99th CAA + NJAC Act as UNCONSTITUTIONAL by 4-1 majority; held collegium = basic structure; judicial independence essential. RESTORED collegium system. CRITICISM of collegium: (a) OPAQUE, non-transparent, no written rules; (b) 'judges appointing judges' — closed club; (c) favouritism / nepotism (judges promoting own kin); (d) MoP (Memorandum of Procedure) amendments by govt — unresolved. MEMO OF PROCEDURE — procedural rules governing collegium-executive interaction; still under discussion. Executive can return a recommendation ONCE; if re-sent, binding (per 3rd Judges). PRESENT: Collegium recommendations + executive either accepts or returns. Appointments often delayed — TNL tensions recent years. CALLS for transparent body like NJAC revived; but judiciary rejects anything that compromises 'basic structure' independence.

cards.front:
Which Article of the Constitution enables the Supreme Court to grant SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL against any judgment of any court or tribunal?

(A) Article 32
(B) ARTICLE 136
(C) Article 143
(D) Article 139
cards.back:
(B) ARTICLE 136

Judiciary — ARTICLE 136 — SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL — gives SC DISCRETIONARY power to grant SPECIAL LEAVE (SLP — Special Leave Petition) to appeal from ANY JUDGMENT / DECREE / determination / sentence / order (civil, criminal, or other) of any court or tribunal in India (except military courts/tribunals). UNIQUE FEATURES: (1) PLENARY power — covers all types of cases. (2) DISCRETIONARY — SC need not accept an SLP. (3) Can be filed after HC judgment or directly from tribunals (in certain cases). (4) TIME LIMIT: 90 days from HC judgment (criminal 60). (5) Not a 'right of appeal' — only a 'leave to appeal'. (6) MOST-FILED PETITION in SC; forms ~90% of SC caseload. SC EVOLVED GUIDELINES to manage Art 136 flood — Pritam Singh (1950), Nihal Singh (1965), Mathai @ Joby (2005), Mathai Samuel (2020). SC generally entertains SLP only in matters of CONSTITUTIONAL IMPORTANCE, SUBSTANTIAL QUESTION OF LAW, OR gross miscarriage of justice; not as routine appeal. OTHER SC JURISDICTIONS: (1) ORIGINAL JURISDICTION — Art 131 — disputes between (a) Govt of India + 1 or more states; (b) states inter se. Exclusive jurisdiction. (2) WRIT JURISDICTION — Art 32 — Fundamental Rights enforcement. (3) APPELLATE JURISDICTION: (a) CONSTITUTIONAL (Art 132) — appeal from HC if HC certifies substantial Q of law of constitutional interpretation. (b) CIVIL (Art 133) — if substantial Q of law of general importance. (c) CRIMINAL (Art 134) — from HC in certain cases (death sentence confirmation etc). (d) Tribunals (Art 136). (4) ADVISORY JURISDICTION — Art 143 — President may refer to SC question of law + get opinion; SC discretion to answer. Major referrals: Delhi Laws case (1951), Kerala Education Bill (1958), Berubari (1960), Keshav Singh (1965), Presidential Poll (1974), Ayodhya Reference (1993). (5) JUDICIAL REVIEW — Art 13 — unwritten; SC can strike down laws inconsistent with Constitution. (6) OTHER — Art 129 (Court of Record — contempt powers), Art 142 (complete justice). FOR LAW STUDENTS: Art 136 = 'grinding mill' of SC. 'Special Leave Petition' (SLP); discretionary, extraordinary jurisdiction; SC's most-used civil + criminal appellate power.

cards.front:
The FIRST WOMAN judge of the Supreme Court of India was:

(A) Leila Seth
(B) Justice M. FATHIMA BEEVI
(C) Indira Banerjee
(D) B.V. Nagarathna
cards.back:
(B) Justice M. FATHIMA BEEVI

Judiciary — JUSTICE M. FATHIMA BEEVI (1927-2023) — FIRST woman judge of the Supreme Court of India. APPOINTED 6 October 1989 (retired 29 April 1992). ALSO: first Muslim woman judge in higher judiciary; first woman judge of Kerala HC (1983). LATER: Governor of Tamil Nadu (25 Jan 1997 – 1 Jul 2001). Born Kerala, studied law at Govt Law College Trivandrum, topped BL examination (first woman to do so in Kerala). Pursued career through subordinate judiciary then district court then Kerala HC. After retirement, served on National Human Rights Commission. Died 23 Nov 2023, age 96. WOMEN JUDGES of Supreme Court since: (1) FATHIMA BEEVI (1989-92); (2) SUJATA V. MANOHAR (1994-99); (3) RUMA PAL (2000-06 — 5 years 10 months, longest-serving woman SC judge); (4) GYAN SUDHA MISRA (2010-14); (5) RANJANA DESAI (2011-14); (6) R. BANUMATHI (2014-20); (7) INDU MALHOTRA (2018-21 — first woman directly from Bar / advocate appointment); (8) INDIRA BANERJEE (2018-22); (9) HIMA KOHLI (2021-24); (10) B.V. NAGARATHNA (2021-present — projected to become first female CJI in Sept 2027); (11) BELA M. TRIVEDI (2021-present). TOTAL: ~11 women judges of SC till 2025; out of ~268 total SC judges since 1950. Ratio: ~4% overall; currently ~8% active. WOMEN CJIs: NONE yet in India. NAGARATHNA is slated to be India's first female CJI (35 days, 24 Sep–29 Oct 2027, per seniority). LEILA SETH (not SC) — first woman CJ of any HC (Himachal Pradesh HC 1991); also part of Justice Verma Committee (2013 anti-rape law reforms); mother of Vikram Seth (author). WOMEN CJ of HCs: Leila Seth (HP), Anna Chandy (Kerala HC 1959 — first woman HC judge in India, not CJ), Gita Mittal (J&K HC CJ), Manjula Chellur (Kerala-Calcutta-Bombay HCs CJ), Indira Banerjee (Madras HC CJ before SC). Women JUDGES in HCs ~15%. Gender diversity in judiciary still a WORK IN PROGRESS. appointed 6 October 1989; later Governor of TN (1997-2001).

cards.front:
JUDICIAL REVIEW in India is:

(A) Absent
(B) The POWER of courts to REVIEW legislative + executive actions + declare them unconstitutional if they VIOLATE the Constitution
(C) Only for tax laws
(D) Only in HC, not SC
cards.back:
(B) The POWER of courts to REVIEW legislative + executive actions + declare them unconstitutional if they VIOLATE the Constitution

Judiciary — JUDICIAL REVIEW — power of judiciary to review the constitutional validity of LAWS passed by legislature + EXECUTIVE ACTIONS; declare them invalid if inconsistent with Constitution. Derived from U.S. MARBURY v. MADISON (1803, Chief Justice John Marshall) — though implicitly present in British constitutionalism, judicial review as doctrine was an American innovation. SOURCES in Indian Constitution: (1) ART 13 — any law (pre + post 1950) in violation of FRs is VOID to the extent of inconsistency. (2) ART 32 — writs to enforce FRs (SC's 'guaranteed' power). (3) ART 131 — original jurisdiction (Centre-state + states). (4) ART 132-136 — appellate jurisdiction. (5) ART 226 + 227 — HC's writ + superintendence. (6) ART 246 + 7th Schedule — review of legislative competence (Centre vs State). (7) ART 254 — Centre-State law conflict. (8) BASIC STRUCTURE DOCTRINE — review of amendments (Kesavananda 1973). GROUNDS FOR STRIKING DOWN: (a) beyond legislative COMPETENCE (ultra vires); (b) violation of FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS; (c) violation of BASIC STRUCTURE (for constitutional amendments); (d) procedural illegality; (e) arbitrariness (Royappa 1974, Maneka 1978, Ajay Hasia); (f) unreasonableness (Wednesbury UK test, adopted with modifications); (g) violation of Art 14 + proportionality. LANDMARK USES: A.K. Gopalan 1950, Golaknath 1967 (FRs not amendable), Kesavananda 1973, Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain 1975 (election validation), Maneka Gandhi 1978 (expanded Art 21), Minerva Mills 1980, S.R. Bommai 1994 (Art 356), Shayara Bano 2017 (triple talaq struck down), Puttaswamy 2017 (Privacy = FR), Sabarimala 2018 (Art 17 + temple entry, still under review), NJAC 2015 (collegium restored), Navtej Johar 2018 (Sec 377 decriminalised), Joseph Shine 2018 (Sec 497 adultery struck), Indra Sawhney 1992 (Mandal, 50% ceiling — now under EWS review), Aadhaar 2018 (Puttaswamy-II). FRAMERS intended judicial review — Dr Ambedkar said 'I can't conceive of any better provision for protection of the Constitution than to give Supreme Court the power of judicial review.' COUNTER-MAJORITARIAN check in democracy; balance with democratic legitimacy has been subject of debate (judicial activism vs restraint). a basic structure feature.

cards.front:
CONTEMPT OF COURT in India is classified into:

(A) Only civil
(B) CIVIL (willful disobedience of court order) + CRIMINAL (scandalising / lowering authority of court); under Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
(C) Only criminal
(D) Constitutional + statutory
cards.back:
(B) CIVIL (willful disobedience of court order) + CRIMINAL (scandalising / lowering authority of court); under Contempt of Courts Act, 1971

Judiciary — CONTEMPT OF COURT — Art 129 of the Constitution makes the SUPREME COURT a 'COURT OF RECORD' with power to punish for CONTEMPT OF ITSELF. Art 215 does the same for HCs. Statutory law: CONTEMPT OF COURTS ACT, 1971. TWO TYPES: (1) CIVIL CONTEMPT — WILLFUL disobedience of any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ, or process of court, or willful breach of undertaking given to court. Remedial in nature — aims to get compliance. (2) CRIMINAL CONTEMPT — 'scandalising' the court, interfering with due course of judicial proceedings, or obstructing administration of justice. Punitive in nature — aims to protect dignity of courts. DEFENCES: (a) innocent publication / distribution; (b) FAIR + ACCURATE REPORT of judicial proceedings; (c) FAIR CRITICISM of judicial act (as long as not malicious + does not impair court's authority); (d) TRUTH — added as defence by 2006 Amendment (truth can be pleaded if in 'public interest' + 'bona fide'). PUNISHMENT: up to 6 MONTHS imprisonment +/or ₹2,000 fine. HIGHER PUNISHMENT requires separate procedure. NOTABLE CONTEMPT CASES: (1) 2020 — PRASHANT BHUSHAN (advocate) held GUILTY of criminal contempt for 2 tweets critical of SC + CJI Bobde; fined ₹1; refused to apologise. Became media flashpoint on FoE vs contempt. (2) 2002 — ARUNDHATI ROY (author) held in contempt for her criticism of SC on Narmada judgment; 1-day symbolic imprisonment. (3) 2006 — EDITOR of Times of India. (4) EX-CM MAMATA BANERJEE (warning). TENSIONS: (a) FREE SPEECH vs judicial reputation; (b) 'scandalising' broad + subjective; (c) increasingly criticised — UK abolished 'scandalising' contempt in 2013; LCI Report 274 recommended similar for India; (d) but contempt deemed necessary for rule of law. CIVIL vs CRIMINAL contempt often OVERLAP in practice. Judiciary generally EXERCISES SELF-RESTRAINT but enforces when required. Sub-judice RULE + GAG orders — related but separate concerns.

cards.front:
The SUPREME COURT's power to do 'COMPLETE JUSTICE' in any cause or matter is found in:

(A) Article 32
(B) ARTICLE 142
(C) Article 129
(D) Article 144
cards.back:
(B) ARTICLE 142

Judiciary — ARTICLE 142 — UNIQUE POWER of the Supreme Court to do 'COMPLETE JUSTICE'. Article 142(1): 'The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India.' Article 142(2): similar powers over securing attendance, production of documents, etc. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) gives SC EXTRAORDINARY power beyond procedural laws; allows equitable + creative remedies even where existing law is silent; (2) NO other country's supreme court has such broad textual power (US SC relies on common law + statutes). LANDMARK USES of Art 142: (1) BHOPAL GAS TRAGEDY (1989) — SC awarded $470 million compensation as a lump-sum settlement against Union Carbide; controversial because it overrode pending tort claims. (2) BABRI MASJID / AYODHYA verdict (9 Nov 2019) — 5-judge bench used Art 142 to award disputed 2.77-acre site to Hindus for Ram Mandir + 5-acre alternative site to Muslims for mosque, beyond strict legal title. (3) CAUVERY WATER DISPUTE — allocation + enforcement orders. (4) VINEETA SHARMA v. RAKESH SHARMA (2020) — equal coparcenary rights to daughters. (5) NAZ FOUNDATION / NAVTEJ JOHAR (2018) — decriminalisation of Sec 377; passed remedial directions. (6) NINJA case (restoration of wife's property). (7) MC MEHTA environmental cases — Ganga, Yamuna, Delhi air. (8) STATE OF UP v. RAJESH YADAV (2010) — reservation in promotions remedial. (9) TATA ELECTRIC v. REGULATORY COMMISSION — electricity pricing. LIMITATIONS (per A.R. Antulay v. RS Nayak 1988, Delhi Judicial Service 1991, others): (a) Art 142 cannot be used to supplant EXPRESS statutory provisions — only to supplement; (b) not a 'get out of jail free' card; must be invoked for legitimate public interest; (c) cannot override CONSTITUTION or fundamental rights; (d) cannot ignore general statutory mandates (R. RESHMA v. SC 2019 clarified). CRITICS argue Art 142 is sometimes OVERUSED (judicial overreach into policy). Defenders argue it's necessary for structural justice in complex public-law cases. allows SC to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice; used in Ayodhya (2019), Bhopal gas (1989), Cauvery dispute, etc.
