cards.front:
The FIRST CHIEF JUSTICE of INDIA was:

(A) M. Hidayatullah
(B) HARILAL JEKISUNDAS KANIA (26 Jan 1950 – 6 Nov 1951)
(C) B.K. Mukherjea
(D) Y.V. Chandrachud
cards.back:
(B) HARILAL JEKISUNDAS KANIA (26 Jan 1950 – 6 Nov 1951)

Judiciary — HARILAL JEKISUNDAS KANIA (3 Nov 1890 – 6 Nov 1951) — FIRST CHIEF JUSTICE of INDIA. Sworn in by President Rajendra Prasad on 26 January 1950. Served 21 months (Jan 1950 – Nov 1951). Died in office at age 61 of heart attack — only CJI to die in office. Born Surat, Gujarat. Studied at Government Law College, Bombay; practiced at Bombay HC; appointed Chief Justice of Bombay HC (1947); Federal Court judge (1948); elevated to first CJI (1950). Succeeded by M. PATANJALI SASTRI. NOTABLE CJIs chronologically (highlights): (1) Harilal Kania (1950-51); (2) M. Patanjali Sastri (1951-54); (3) Mehr Chand Mahajan (1954, brief); (4) B.K. Mukherjea (1954-56); (5) S.R. Das (1956-59); (6) B.P. Sinha (1959-64); (7) P.B. GAJENDRAGADKAR (1964-66); (8) Amal Kumar Sarkar (1966); (9) Koka Subba Rao (1966-67) — resigned to contest Presidential elections; (10) K.N. Wanchoo (1967-68); (11) M. HIDAYATULLAH (1968-70) — acting President twice; (12) J.C. Shah (1970-71); (13) S.M. Sikri (1971-73) — delivered KESAVANANDA BHARATI judgment; (14) A.N. RAY (1973-77) — SUPERSEDED 3 senior judges for CJI; controversial; (15) M.H. Beg (1977-78); (16) Y.V. CHANDRACHUD (1978-85) — LONGEST-SERVING CJI (7 years 4 months); father of DY Chandrachud; (17) P.N. BHAGWATI (1985-86) — PIL pioneer; (18) R.S. Pathak (1986-89); (19) E.S. Venkataramiah (1989, 6 months); (20) Sabyasachi Mukharji (1990, died in office; 2nd CJI to die in office); ...(45) R.M. Lodha (2014); (46) H.L. Dattu (2014-15); (47) T.S. Thakur (2015-17); (48) J.S. Khehar (2017) — first Sikh CJI; (49) Dipak Misra (2017-18); (50) Ranjan Gogoi (2018-19) — Ayodhya judge; (51) S.A. Bobde (2019-21); (52) N.V. Ramana (2021-22); (53) U.U. cards.front:
The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on:

(A) 26 January 1950
(B) 28 January 1950
(C) 15 August 1947
(D) 26 November 1949
cards.back:
(B) 28 January 1950

Judiciary — Supreme Court — inaugurated on 28 January 1950 (two days after the Constitution came into force). Replaced the Federal Court of India (set up 1937 under the Government of India Act 1935) and the Privy Council (London). First sitting at the Chamber of Princes, Parliament House. Moved to its present building (Tilak Marg, Delhi) in 1958. First Chief Justice — H.J. Kania. Building shape — symbolic of scales of justice. Apex court of India; final court of appeal. cards.front:
The current sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court of India (judges including the CJI) is:

(A) 21
(B) 34 (CJI + 33 other judges; raised from 31 by amendment in 2019)
(C) 26
(D) 50
cards.back:
(B) 34 (CJI + 33 other judges; raised from 31 by amendment in 2019)

Judiciary — Initial strength (1950) was 8 (CJI + 7), raised to 11 (1956), 14 (1960), 18 (1978), 26 (1986), 31 (2009), 34 (2019). Current — 34 judges (1 CJI + 33). Parliament is empowered to fix the number by law.

cards.front:
The 'collegium system' for appointment of judges is:

(A) Provided expressly in the Constitution
(B) A judge-led process evolved through SC judgments — Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998)
(C) An Act of Parliament
(D) Adopted from the British system
cards.back:
(B) A judge-led process evolved through SC judgments — Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998)

Judiciary — Collegium — not a constitutional body; evolved through SC interpretations of Article 124 + 217: First Judges Case (1981) — Centre dominant. Second Judges Case (1993) — judiciary primacy; collegium of CJI + 2 senior-most judges. Third Judges Case (1998) — collegium expanded to CJI + 4 senior-most for SC appointments. NJAC (National Judicial Appointments Commission) — 99th CAA (2014) tried to replace collegium with a 6-member commission (3 judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent persons); STRUCK DOWN by SC in 2015 (4-1 majority, 4th Judges Case) on 'basic structure' grounds (judicial independence). Collegium remains the operative mechanism, but is widely criticised for opacity. Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) — governs the process.

cards.front:
The 'basic structure doctrine', that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is not absolute, was laid down by the Supreme Court in:

(A) Shankari Prasad case (1951)
(B) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), 13-judge Bench, 7-6 majority
(C) Golaknath case (1967)
(D) Maneka Gandhi case (1978)
cards.back:
(B) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), 13-judge Bench, 7-6 majority

Judiciary — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — landmark; 13-judge bench (largest ever); 7-6 majority. Held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution INCLUDING Fundamental Rights, but CANNOT alter the BASIC STRUCTURE of the Constitution. Basic features (illustrative, evolved over time): supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, democracy, judicial review, free + fair elections. Earlier cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) — Parliament can amend FRs; Golaknath (1967) — Parliament cannot amend FRs (overruled by 24th CAA). Minerva Mills (1980) — reaffirmed basic structure; struck down 42nd CAA's attempt to give Parliament unlimited amending power.

cards.front:
The 'curative petition' before the Supreme Court was conceptualised in which case to allow correction of judgments after the dismissal of a review petition?

(A) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
(B) Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)
(C) Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
(D) Indra Sawhney case (1992)
cards.back:
(B) Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)

Judiciary — Curative petition — last resort after a review petition is dismissed. Conceptualised in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002). Grounds: (1) violation of natural justice; (2) bias of a judge that came to light later. Heard by a bench of 3 senior-most judges (with the original judges if available). Examples of high-profile curative petitions: Nirbhaya case (rejected — death penalties confirmed); Bhopal Gas victims; Sahara case; recent same-sex marriage curative (rejected). Vishaka — laid down sexual harassment guidelines (later replaced by POSH Act 2013). Maneka Gandhi — expanded Article 21 (procedure must be fair, just, reasonable). Indra Sawhney — 27% OBC reservation, 50% cap.

cards.front:
Article 32 of the Constitution provides for the:

(A) Election of the President
(B) Right to constitutional remedies (writs) — moving the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights
(C) Powers of the High Courts
(D) Emergency provisions
cards.back:
(B) Right to constitutional remedies (writs) — moving the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights

Judiciary — Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies. Empowers individuals to move the Supreme Court directly when their FRs are violated. Dr B.R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Five Writs (also available under Article 226 to High Courts): (1) HABEAS CORPUS — produce the body (against illegal detention); (2) MANDAMUS — we command (to compel a public official to perform duty); (3) PROHIBITION — bars a lower court from acting beyond jurisdiction; (4) CERTIORARI — to be informed (quash an order of a lower court); (5) QUO WARRANTO — by what authority (challenge appointment to a public office). HC jurisdiction (Art 226) is wider — also for legal rights, not only FRs.

cards.front:
The retirement age of a Judge of the Supreme Court of India is:

(A) 60 years
(B) 65 years
(C) 62 years
(D) 70 years
cards.back:
(B) 65 years

Judiciary — Retirement: SC Judge — 65 years (Article 124(2) proviso). HC Judge — 62 years (Article 217). District Judge — 60 years (varies; service rules). UPSC member — 65 years. CAG — 65 years. Election Commissioners — 65 years. Salary of judges — fixed by Parliament; charged on Consolidated Fund of India (cannot be voted on); cannot be reduced after appointment except during a financial emergency. Removal — only by impeachment (Article 124(4)) on grounds of 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'; needs 2/3 majority of present-and-voting + absolute majority of total strength in EACH House. No SC judge has been impeached so far (V. Ramaswami, 1993, narrowly survived in Lok Sabha after Congress abstained).

cards.front:
The 'Basic Structure' doctrine of the Indian Constitution was propounded by the Supreme Court in:

(A) Golaknath case (1967)
(B) Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)
(C) Minerva Mills case (1980)
(D) Shankari Prasad case (1951)
cards.back:
(B) Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)

Judiciary — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — a 13-judge bench (largest ever at the time) held by 7-6 that Parliament's power under Art 368 does not extend to altering the Basic Structure of the Constitution. Golaknath (1967) had earlier held that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights, but was overruled. Minerva Mills (1980) strengthened the Basic Structure doctrine further. Shankari Prasad (1951) had held the opposite — that amendments could abridge FRs.

Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to:

(A) Transfer cases between High Courts
(B) Review its own judgments

cards.front:
The first Chief Justice of independent India was:

(A) M. C. Mahajan
(B) H. J. Kania
(C) Patanjali Shastri

cards.back:

Judiciary — Harilal J. Kania served as the first Chief Justice of India from 26 January 1950 till his sudden death in November 1951. He was succeeded by M. Patanjali Sastri. Mehr Chand Mahajan (not 'M.C. Mahajan' — same person) was CJI from 1954 and is also known for leading Kashmir's accession negotiations. The Supreme Court of India itself was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.

cards.front:
The Chief Minister of an Indian state is APPOINTED by:

(A) The Governor of the state
(B) The President of India alone
(C) The State Legislative Assembly directly
(D) The Prime Minister of India.
cards.back:
(A) The Governor of the state

State Government — Article 164(1): 'The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the GOVERNOR.' Convention: the Governor invites the leader of the majority party (or coalition) in the LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY to form government. KEY DISTINCTIONS: (1) Governor's appointment is FORMAL — actual CM is decided by ELECTORAL VERDICT. (2) If no clear majority — Governor's DISCRETION matters; he/she may invite the largest single party or pre-poll alliance leader (refer Sarkaria, Punchhi Commission guidelines). (3) CM need not be an MLA at the time of appointment — but must become one within 6 MONTHS (Article 164(4)). FAMOUS CASES: Mamata Banerjee (West Bengal 2021) and Yogi Adityanath (UP 2017) were not MLAs when sworn in; both contested by-elections within 6 months. SAME PROVISION FOR PM: Article 75(1) — PM appointed by President, similar discretion. EXAM ANGLE: 'who appoints CM' is a 1-mark CGL/UPSC staple — appears in 50% of polity papers. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests basic federal-architecture knowledge — Governor as the constitutional head of state government.

cards.front:
What is the MAXIMUM time within which a Chief Minister must become a member of the State Legislature after appointment?

(A) Six months from oath of office
(B) Three months alone alone alone
(C) Twelve months alone alone alone
(D) Until next general election alone
cards.back:
(A) Six months from oath of office

State Government — Article 164(4): 'A Minister who for any period of SIX consecutive months is not a member of the Legislature of the State shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister.' This applies to the CM and all state ministers. PRECEDENT — S.R. CHAUDHURI v. STATE OF PUNJAB (2001): SC ruled that a non-member CANNOT be re-appointed minister after 6 months without first getting elected — closing a loophole used in Punjab where Tej Prakash Singh was made minister without election multiple times. SAME RULE AT CENTRE: Article 75(5) — for Union Ministers including PM. RECENT EXAMPLES: Mamata Banerjee (May 2021 — sworn in CM, won Bhabanipur by-election Sept 2021); Yogi Adityanath (Mar 2017 — won UP MLC seat from BJP within months). RAJASTHAN 2003: Vasundhara Raje was MLA before sworn-in; comfortable. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests precise constitutional time limits — high-yield for UPSC Prelims, SSC CGL, RBI Grade B.

cards.front:
The Chief Minister of a state holds office at the:

(A) Pleasure of the Governor (constitutional)
(B) Pleasure of the President alone
(C) Pleasure of the Legislative Assembly
(D) Discretion of the Speaker (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Pleasure of the Governor (constitutional)

State Government — Article 164(1): 'The Ministers shall hold office during the PLEASURE of the Governor.' But this 'pleasure' is exercised on the AID AND ADVICE of the Council of Ministers (Art 163), and is constrained by parliamentary democracy norms. EFFECTIVE MEANING: a CM stays in office as long as he/she enjoys the CONFIDENCE of the Legislative Assembly (majority support). If a no-confidence motion passes, CM must resign or recommend dissolution. GOVERNOR'S POSITION: by convention, Governor cannot remove a CM who commands a majority — even in 'pleasure' there's an implicit democratic constraint. POLITICAL CASES: (1) Karnataka 2018 — Governor's invitation to BJP's Yeddyurappa despite Cong-JD(S) alliance majority; SC intervened. (2) Maharashtra 2019 — Fadnavis's pre-dawn swearing-in; resigned within days when majority unclear. SARKARIA COMMISSION (1988) recommended limiting Governor's discretionary powers to prevent partisan abuse. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests the nuance between LEGAL FRAMEWORK ('pleasure') and POLITICAL REALITY ('confidence').

cards.front:
Which article makes it a duty of the CM to communicate cabinet decisions to the Governor?

(A) Article 167 of the Constitution
(B) Article 163 alone alone alone
(C) Article 164 alone alone alone
(D) Article 168 alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Article 167 of the Constitution

State Government — Article 167: It is the DUTY of the Chief Minister to: (a) COMMUNICATE to the Governor of the state all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the state and proposals for legislation. (b) FURNISH such information relating to administration as the Governor may CALL FOR. (c) Submit any matter on which a Minister has decided but the Council has not considered, when so required by the Governor — for consideration by the Council. KEY DUTIES OVERVIEW: (1) Liaison between Governor and Cabinet. (2) Lead Council of Ministers (chair Cabinet meetings). (3) Allocate portfolios. (4) Recommend resignation of any Minister to the Governor. (5) Lead the State in Inter-State Council and NITI Aayog meetings. PARALLEL: Article 78 imposes the SAME duty on the PM vis-à-vis the President. EXAM ANGLE: 'Article 167 = CM's duty' is a UPSC Prelims favourite — appears every 2-3 years. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests precise article-number recall.

cards.front:
Who was the FIRST FEMALE Chief Minister of any Indian state?

(A) Sucheta Kripalani of Uttar Pradesh
(B) Indira Gandhi (was Prime Minister)
(C) Mayawati of Uttar Pradesh state
(D) J. Jayalalithaa of Tamil Nadu state
cards.back:
(A) Sucheta Kripalani of Uttar Pradesh

State Government — SUCHETA KRIPALANI was the FIRST WOMAN to become CM of an Indian state — she led UTTAR PRADESH from 2 OCTOBER 1963 to 13 March 1967 as a Congress leader. BACKGROUND: born 1908 in Ambala (Punjab); freedom-fighter, educator; member of the Constituent Assembly; sang 'Vande Mataram' in the Assembly on 14 Aug 1947 night. HUSBAND: J.B. Kripalani (Congress President 1946-47). LEGACY: Kripalani is celebrated as a women's rights pioneer; UP Legislature has a portrait of her. SUBSEQUENT FIRSTS: Nandini Satpathy (Odisha, 1972) — second woman CM. Shashikala Kakodkar (Goa, 1973). Anwara Taimur (Assam, 1980). J. Jayalalithaa (Tamil Nadu, 1991). Mayawati (UP, 1995, first Dalit woman CM). Sheila Dikshit (Delhi, 1998 — longest-serving woman CM, 15 years). Mamata Banerjee (West Bengal, 2011). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'first woman CM' appears in CGL, IBPS, RRB GK 2-3× per year. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests significant historical political milestones — high-frequency factual recall.

PYQ FREQUENCY: 'first woman CM' appears in CGL, IBPS, RRB GK 2-3× per year. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests significant historical political milestones — high-frequency factual recall.

cards.front:
In a Union Territory, who appoints the Chief Minister where the UT has a Legislative Assembly?

(A) The Lieutenant Governor (or Administrator)
(B) The President of India alone too
(C) The Prime Minister of India alone
(D) The Home Minister of India alone
cards.back:
(A) The Lieutenant Governor (or Administrator)

State Government — UNION TERRITORIES with Legislative Assemblies — Delhi, Puducherry, J&K (post 2019 reorganization) — have a CM appointed by the LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR (LG) or Administrator. The framework is Article 239AA (Delhi-specific) and the Government of UT Act 1963 (for Puducherry). DELHI'S UNIQUE STATUS (NCT-Delhi): Article 239AA gives Delhi a special hybrid status — CM and elected legislature, but key subjects (police, public order, land) remain with LG/Centre. Source of frequent friction (Kejriwal vs LGs of Delhi). 2023-24 Centre-State Acts further empowered LG over services. PUDUCHERRY: smaller UT, similar arrangement. J&K (POST AUG 2019): downgraded from state to UT with legislature; first CM elections held in Oct 2024 (Omar Abdullah). UTs WITHOUT LEGISLATURE: Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep, Chandigarh, Dadra-Nagar-Haveli & Daman-Diu, Ladakh — have an LG/Administrator only, no CM. EXAM ANGLE: 'who appoints CM in UTs' tests federal nuance — comes up in UPSC Prelims and CGL. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing UT vs State distinctions.

cards.option2: The Prime Minister of India alone
cards.option3: The Home Minister of India alone

cards.front:
What is the MINIMUM AGE qualification to become a Chief Minister of an Indian state?

(A) 25 years (same as Legislative Assembly)
(B) 30 years (Council of States) alone
(C) 21 years (post-1989 amendment) alone
(D) 35 years (same as President) alone
cards.back:
(A) 25 years (same as Legislative Assembly)

State Government — Article 173: a person is qualified for the State LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY if 25 YEARS or above. Since the CM must be (or become) a member of the State Legislature, the IMPLICIT minimum age = 25. For LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL membership: 30 years. AGE THRESHOLDS — quick quiz: Lok Sabha MP: 25; Rajya Sabha MP: 30; State LA MLA: 25; State LC MLC: 30; CM: 25 (effectively); PM: 25 (must be LS) or 30 (if RS); President: 35; Vice-President: 35; Governor: 35. YOUNGEST CMs (significant cases): Akhilesh Yadav became UP CM at 38 (2012, then youngest UP CM); Pinarayi Vijayan (Kerala 2016, age 71 — example of older). RECORD: Sashidhar Jadhav (Andhra/Telangana 2014 swearing — different system). VOTER AGE 18 (61st Amendment 1989): voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 — same Constitutional Amendment, but candidacy age 25 unchanged. EXAM ANGLE: 'minimum age for CM' commonly mixes up with President (35) — top-3 confusion in UPSC prep.

cards.front:
The GOVERNOR of a State is APPOINTED by:

(A) The Chief Minister of the State
(B) The PRESIDENT OF INDIA
(C) The people, directly elected
(D) The Supreme Court
cards.back:
(B) The PRESIDENT OF INDIA

State Government — GOVERNOR of a STATE — Executive head of a State; titular / ceremonial counterpart of the President at state level. APPOINTMENT: ARTICLE 155 — appointed by the PRESIDENT (on the advice of Prime Minister / Union Govt). PROCESS: President issues a warrant (sign + seal) of appointment. Not elected. QUALIFICATIONS: Art 157 — (1) CITIZEN of India; (2) aged 35 YEARS or more; (3) must NOT hold any office of profit; (4) NOT member of either House of Parliament / State Legislature (if he/she is, must resign before assuming office). CONVENTIONS (not binding): (a) Governor should NOT be from the state he/she governs (to ensure impartiality); (b) CM's opinion 'should' be consulted — not binding. OATH (Art 159) — administered by the CHIEF JUSTICE OF the State's HIGH COURT (or senior-most HC judge if CJ unavailable). TERM (Art 156): 5 years, holds office at the pleasure of the President — meaning President can dismiss anytime (political instrument of Centre). Can resign by writing to the President. Can be re-appointed. Same person can be Governor of 2 or more states (Art 153 post-7th CAA 1956). REMUNERATION: Rs 3.5 lakh/month (as of 2018) + free accommodation (RAJ BHAVAN) + medical + allowances. PRIVILEGES: parliamentary + civil immunity for official acts (Art 361) — cannot be called to court during tenure for personal acts; civil proceedings only after 2-month notice. CURRENT (2026): varying by state. CAUTION: Governors have been politically controversial — accused of being 'extended arm of Centre' (Bommai case 1994 + recent WB-Bihar-Kerala-TN standoffs on Bill assent delays). under warrant under his hand + seal, usually on advice of the Union government.

cards.front:
The Governor is called the 'EXTENDED ARM OF THE CENTRE' because:

(A) He represents Parliament
(B) He is APPOINTED by + holds office at the PLEASURE of the PRESIDENT (i.e., Centre); performs DUAL role
(C) He directly serves the Home Minister
(D) He is appointed by the Governor General
cards.back:
(B) He is APPOINTED by + holds office at the PLEASURE of the PRESIDENT (i.e., Centre); performs DUAL role

State Government — GOVERNOR — DUAL CAPACITY: (1) CONSTITUTIONAL HEAD of the STATE (analogous to President at centre); (2) REPRESENTATIVE of the CENTRE / UNION GOVERNMENT. This dual role is built into the Constitution + has been a flashpoint of centre-state tensions. 'EXTENDED ARM of the CENTRE' — phrase arises because: (a) APPOINTMENT + REMOVAL by President (practically by Central ruling party); no fixed term, holds office at 'pleasure of the President' (Art 156); (b) Governor reserves Bills for Presidential consideration (Art 200 + 201) — particularly contentious; (c) Governor recommends PRESIDENT'S RULE (Art 356) to the President — misused historically (e.g., pre-1994 — struck down S.R. Bommai case); (d) acts on 'DISCRETIONARY' powers beyond ministerial advice (Art 163); sometimes guided by Centre. CRITICISMS (Sarkaria Commission 1988, Punchhi Commission 2010, ARC-II reports): (a) partisan appointees — often retired politicians from ruling party — Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer called them 'LACKEYS' of ruling party; (b) dismissed when Centre changes — 8 governors dismissed 1989 (V.P. Singh), 4 in 2004 (UPA), multiple in 2014 (NDA); (c) undue delays in assenting to State Bills (e.g., 2023 Tamil Nadu Governor RN Ravi + Kerala Governor Arif Mohammed Khan controversies — SC rulings on Bill assent timelines, Nov 2023 + April 2024). RECOMMENDATIONS for REFORM: (a) ELIMINATE 'pleasure' tenure, fix 5-year term; (b) appointment on consultation with state CM (NCRWC 2002 — mandatory); (c) non-politician persons of eminence; (d) timeline for Bill assent. NONE fully implemented. SC rulings: Nabam Rebia (Arunachal 2016) — Governor should not become a power unto himself. Rameshwar Prasad (Bihar 2005) — Governor's Report on imposition of Art 356 subject to judicial review. representative of Centre + constitutional head of state.
cards.option2: He directly serves the Home Minister
cards.option3: He is appointed by the Governor General

cards.front:
The Governor's DISCRETIONARY POWERS include:

(A) Signing all Bills without judgment
(B) Appointing CM in hung legislatures
(C) Appointing SC judges
(D) Levying taxes
cards.back:
(B) Appointing CM in hung legislatures

State Government — GOVERNOR's DISCRETIONARY POWERS — Art 163(1) + (2). NOT OBLIGATED to act on CM's advice in these cases. TYPES: (1) CONSTITUTIONAL DISCRETION — explicit in Constitution: (a) RESERVATION of BILLS passed by State Legislature for consideration of the President (Art 200-201) — e.g., Bills affecting HC powers, compulsory Bills, derogation from Constitution. (b) RECOMMEND IMPOSITION OF PRESIDENT'S RULE (Art 356 + Governor's Report). (c) SEEKING information from CM about administration of state affairs (Art 167). (d) Special responsibilities regarding SCHEDULED AREAS + TRIBAL AREAS (5th Schedule — Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand; 6th Schedule — Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram). (e) Governor of ASSAM — discretion re: Tribal Belt, Hill Areas (para 12 of 6th Schedule). (f) Special: NAGALAND (Art 371A), SIKKIM (Art 371F), ARUNACHAL PRADESH etc. (2) SITUATIONAL DISCRETION — not explicit but needed in certain political situations: (a) APPOINTMENT of CHIEF MINISTER in a HUNG ASSEMBLY (no clear majority). E.g., 2017 Goa Congress-BJP tussle, 2018 Karnataka, 2022 Maharashtra. (b) DISMISSING state CoM when it loses confidence + refuses to resign. (c) DISSOLVING State Legislative Assembly on losing majority / advising alternative government. CASE LAW: (1) S.R. BOMMAI v. UoI (1994) — 9-judge SC bench; Art 356 subject to judicial review; floor test must be in assembly, not Raj Bhavan. (2) NABAM REBIA v. Deputy Speaker (Arunachal 2016) — unanimous SC ruling — Governor cannot decide whether to convene/prorogue House or advance assembly session without CoM advice. (3) RAMESHWAR PRASAD v. UoI (2005) — Bihar — Governor Buta Singh's report on Art 356 quashed. (4) SHAMSHER SINGH v. State of Punjab (1974) — reaffirmed Governor bound by CoM advice except for limited discretion. Governors have become increasingly controversial post-2019 in several BJP-opposition ruling states. constitutional + situational discretion. reserving Bills for President's consideration; recommending President's Rule.

cards.front:
When a Bill passed by a State Legislature is sent to the Governor, he can:

(A) Only give assent
(B) FOUR options (Art 200)
(C) Veto permanently
(D) Only send it back
cards.back:
(B) FOUR options (Art 200)

State Government — Article 200 — Governor's powers when a Bill is presented for assent: (1) ASSENT — signs, becomes law. (2) WITHHOLD ASSENT — 'absolute veto' (rare; rarely justifiable for ordinary bills). (3) RETURN the Bill (if NOT a Money Bill) for RECONSIDERATION with a message suggesting amendments; 'suspensive veto' — if the state legislature re-passes (with or without amendments), the Governor MUST give assent. No re-return. (4) RESERVE the Bill for the PRESIDENT's consideration (mandatory in certain cases, e.g., Bills affecting HC powers; derogatory to Constitution; land acquisition compensation below a level). KEY ISSUE: the Constitution does NOT specify a TIME LIMIT within which the Governor must decide — led to unconstitutional DELAYS in bill clearance (years in some cases — TN, Kerala, Telangana). SC INTERVENTION: (a) State of Telangana v. Governor (2023) — SC said delay cannot be indefinite. (b) State of Punjab v. Governor (Nov 2023) — 'Governor is not unelected authority above elected legislature'; must decide in reasonable time. (c) State of Kerala v. Governor + State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor RN Ravi (Apr 2024) — SC issued DIRECTIONS with timelines for Governor to act on state Bills. PROSPECTIVE OVERRULING + constitutional guidelines. ART 201 — once reserved for President, President can: give assent; withhold; direct Governor to return for reconsideration; if re-passed, President can still sit on it (no time limit in Constitution). MONEY BILLS in states (Art 207-209) — originate in Legislative Assembly only; Governor's options on a Money Bill = assent OR withhold (cannot return for reconsideration); can reserve in principle but never done on money bills. RECENT CONTROVERSIES: NEET state bills, anti-conversion bills, online gaming bills — Governors sat on them for months/years. assent; withhold assent; return for reconsideration (except money bills); reserve for President's consideration.

cards.front:
Which of the following ARTICLES deals with the APPOINTMENT of the Chief Minister + Council of Ministers of a State by the Governor?

(A) Article 74
(B) ARTICLE 164
(C) Article 75
(D) Article 163
cards.back:
(B) ARTICLE 164

State Government — ARTICLE 164 — STATE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. (1) CM appointed by the GOVERNOR (constitutional convention: leader of majority party in Legislative Assembly). (2) Other Ministers appointed by Governor on the advice of the CM. (3) Ministers hold office during 'pleasure' of Governor (in practice, until CM's confidence holds). (4) CoM collectively responsible to LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY (Art 164(2)) — must resign if loses floor test. (5) 91st CAA 2003 — State CoM size (including CM) capped at 15% of Legislative Assembly strength; minimum 12 (for small states). (6) Ministers must be members of either House within 6 MONTHS (Art 164(4)) similar to Art 75(5). (7) Salary + allowances per Legislature. Special positions: SCs/STs welfare minister mandatory in some states (Art 164(1), now covers Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, MP, Odisha post-changes). Tribal Welfare Minister (Chhattisgarh + Jharkhand); Tribal + SC + OBC Welfare (MP + Odisha). Related Articles: (a) Art 163 — CoM to AID + ADVISE Governor, except in discretionary matters; Art 163(2) — question whether matter is discretionary is finally determined by Governor (not judicially reviewable on merits, but existence subject to judicial review — Shamsher Singh + Samsher Singh). (b) Art 165 — Advocate-General of State (analog of Attorney-General). (c) Art 166 — conduct of business of Govt of State (in Governor's name); Business Rules made by Governor. (d) Art 167 — CM's duties to Governor — communicate decisions, furnish info, submit matters. COMPARISON with Centre: Art 74 (CoM to aid President), Art 75 (appointment/tenure), Art 76 (AG), Art 77 (conduct of business), Art 78 (PM's duties). State articles roughly parallel. CM appointed by Governor; other ministers on advice of CM; CoM collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly.

cards.front:
The VERY FIRST WOMAN to be APPOINTED as GOVERNOR of an Indian state was:

(A) Indira Gandhi
(B) SAROJINI NAIDU
(C) Sucheta Kripalani
(D) Pratibha Patil
cards.back:
(B) SAROJINI NAIDU

State Government — SAROJINI NAIDU (1879-1949) — 'NIGHTINGALE OF INDIA' (Bharat Kokila); poet, freedom fighter, first WOMAN PRESIDENT of INC (Kanpur session 1925, first Indian woman), first WOMAN GOVERNOR of a state (United Provinces, now UP, from 15 Aug 1947 till her death 2 March 1949). BIRTH: 13 February 1879 in HYDERABAD. WOMEN'S DAY in INDIA is her birth anniversary (13 Feb, National Women's Day). Educated Madras, Girton College Cambridge, King's College London. POETRY: Published first collection 'The Golden Threshold' (1905), later 'The Bird of Time' (1912), 'The Broken Wing' (1917). Praised by Gosse + Edmund Blunden. NATIONALIST: joined INC ~1904; close to Gandhi + Gokhale. Led women's delegation to Montagu 1917. Signed Non-Cooperation (1920), Salt Satyagraha (1930), Quit India (1942) — jailed multiple times. LEGACY: Sarojini Naidu College for Women, Hyderabad; Sarojini Nagar (Delhi + Lucknow); Marine Drive (Cuffe Parade, Mumbai) — 'Queen's Necklace' officially Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Road. OTHER WOMEN FIRSTS: (1) first FEMALE PM = INDIRA GANDHI (1966). (2) first FEMALE PRESIDENT = PRATIBHA PATIL (2007-12); second = DROUPADI MURMU (2022-present). (3) first FEMALE CM = SUCHETA KRIPALANI (UP, 1963-67). (4) first FEMALE SUPREME COURT JUDGE = Justice M. FATHIMA BEEVI (1989). (5) first FEMALE IPS = Kiran Bedi (1972). (6) first FEMALE IAS = Anna Rajam Malhotra (1950). (7) first FEMALE FOREIGN SECRETARY = Chokila Iyer (2001). (8) first Indian WOMAN in SPACE = KALPANA CHAWLA (NASA, 1997; died 2003 Columbia disaster); Sunita Williams followed (2006, 2012, 2024-25 ISS stay). (9) first FEMALE SPEAKER of Lok Sabha = MEIRA KUMAR (2009-14). Notable Governors: LAKSHMI SAHGAL (INA); VIJAYA LAKSHMI PANDIT (Maharashtra 1962-64, 1st woman UN GA President 1953). INDIRA GANDHI famously Delhi University student + women's representative. 'Nightingale of India'; poet + freedom fighter; Governor of United Provinces / UP, 1947-49.

LEGACY: Sarojini Naidu College for Women, Hyderabad; Sarojini Nagar (Delhi + Lucknow); Marine Drive (Cuffe Parade, Mumbai) — 'Queen's Necklace' officially Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Road. OTHER WOMEN FIRSTS: (1) first FEMALE PM = INDIRA GANDHI (1966). (2) first FEMALE PRESIDENT = PRATIBHA PATIL (2007-12); second = DROUPADI MURMU (2022-present). (3) first FEMALE CM = SUCHETA KRIPALANI (UP, 1963-67). (4) first FEMALE SUPREME COURT JUDGE = Justice M. FATHIMA BEEVI (1989). (5) first FEMALE IPS = Kiran Bedi (1972). (6) first FEMALE IAS = Anna Rajam Malhotra (1950). (7) first FEMALE FOREIGN SECRETARY = Chokila Iyer (2001). (8) first Indian WOMAN in SPACE = KALPANA CHAWLA (NASA, 1997; died 2003 Columbia disaster); Sunita Williams followed (2006, 2012, 2024-25 ISS stay). INDIRA GANDHI famously Delhi University student + women's representative. 'Nightingale of India'; poet + freedom fighter; Governor of United Provinces / UP, 1947-49.

cards.front:
The S.R. BOMMAI v. UNION OF INDIA (1994) landmark Supreme Court judgment was primarily about:

(A) Fundamental Duties
(B) Limits on MISUSE of ARTICLE 356 (President's Rule)
(C) Education as a Fundamental Right
(D) Reservation policy
cards.back:
(B) Limits on MISUSE of ARTICLE 356 (President's Rule)

State Government — S.R. BOMMAI v. UNION OF INDIA (1994) 3 SCC 1 — seminal 9-judge SC bench decision (7-2). BACKGROUND: S.R. Bommai, CM of Karnataka (1988-89), was ousted when Governor P. Venkatasubbaiah imposed Art 356 on 21 April 1989, without giving Bommai a chance to prove majority on the floor. Similar Art 356 impositions followed (Meghalaya, Nagaland, Karnataka, MP, Rajasthan, HP) — several reversed judicially. SC's KEY HOLDINGS: (1) Art 356 IS JUSTICIABLE / SUBJECT TO JUDICIAL REVIEW — Governor's report + Presidential proclamation can be struck down by SC. (2) FLOOR TEST must be held in the Legislative Assembly, NOT by the Governor in Raj Bhavan. The question of whether CM enjoys majority can ONLY be decided by Assembly. (3) If proclamation is struck down, SC can REVIVE the dismissed government + Legislative Assembly (strong remedy); can order fresh elections if feasible. (4) SECULARISM is a BASIC FEATURE of the Constitution — its violation by state government can be grounds for Art 356 (important ruling post-Babri, 1992 — Art 356 imposed on BJP-ruled UP, MP, Rajasthan, HP after Dec 1992; SC upheld). (5) Proclamation must be based on relevant material; BONA FIDE + not malafide. (6) Within 2 MONTHS proclamation must be approved by BOTH Houses of Parliament (simple majority); can be for 6 months at a time, max 3 years. (7) Till Parliamentary approval, NO irreversible action (like dissolving Assembly) should be taken — or if dissolved, can be revived. IMPACT: Art 356 impositions DRASTICALLY REDUCED post-Bommai (pre-1994 ~100+ impositions; post-1994 ~30). Cases reversed: Uttarakhand 2016, Arunachal 2016. Bommai is part of the 'basic features' + 'federalism' canon of Indian constitutional law; along with Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Maneka Gandhi (1978), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007), K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), it forms top SC rulings. PM RAO + Home Minister S.B. Chavan had imposed Art 356 in 1992 on BJP states. Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommendations largely vindicated by Bommai. made proclamation JUDICIALLY REVIEWABLE; floor test must be in Assembly, not Raj Bhavan.

cards.front:
The Governor does NOT have which of the following powers?

(A) Legislative power to summon/prorogue/dissolve Legislative Assembly
(B) Executive powers under Article 154
(C) JUDICIAL power to pardon death sentences under Article 161
(D) Financial power to recommend money bills
cards.back:
(C) JUDICIAL power to pardon death sentences under Article 161

State Government — GOVERNOR's PARDONING POWER — Art 161 — LIMITED compared to President's pardoning power (Art 72). (1) GOVERNOR CAN (Art 161): grant PARDONS (except death sentence), REPRIEVES (stay), RESPITES, REMISSIONS of punishment; COMMUTE sentences (including DEATH sentences). So Governor CAN commute a DEATH SENTENCE to life, but CANNOT completely pardon/absolve a DEATH sentence (only President can). (2) Scope: limited to offences against laws to which the EXECUTIVE POWER OF THE STATE EXTENDS. Cannot pardon court-martial offences. (3) PRESIDENT can PARDON a death sentence — Art 72(1)(c). GOVERNOR'S OTHER POWERS: (1) EXECUTIVE (Art 154-155): all executive actions in Governor's name; appointment of Advocate-General, State Election Commissioner, State Public Service Commission chairman + members, Vice-Chancellors of some universities, etc. (2) LEGISLATIVE (Art 168): part of State Legislature; summons + prorogues + dissolves Assembly; gives message to Legislature; Ordinances (Art 213 — when Legislature not in session); nomination of MLCs (Art 171 — 1/6 of Legislative Council from literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service). Can't be MLA/MLC/MP concurrently. (3) FINANCIAL (Art 202-203): annual state budget laid on his recommendation; MONEY BILLS (Art 207) can be introduced only on Governor's recommendation. Governor's approval needed for supplementary grants. (4) JUDICIAL: Art 161 pardoning power; Art 217 — CJ of SC consulted for appointment of HC judges (collegium system). (5) DIPLOMATIC / MILITARY: NONE (these are exclusively President/Centre). Special discretionary powers for Governors of NE states, Schedule 5/6 areas. COMPARING Art 72 (President) vs Art 161 (Governor): pardon death sentence = only President; pardon court-martial = only President; both = pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation. limited — CANNOT pardon death; can commute/reprieve/respite.
cards.option1: Legislative power to summon/prorogue/dissolve Legislative Assembly
cards.option3: Financial power to recommend money bills

cards.front:
The same person can be appointed as GOVERNOR of TWO OR MORE STATES per:

(A) Only Article 155
(B) Art 153
(C) Article 200
(D) Article 356
cards.back:
(B) Art 153

State Government — ARTICLE 153 (first proviso) — 'Nothing in this article shall prevent the appointment of the SAME person as Governor for TWO OR MORE STATES'. Added by the 7TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 1956 (which also introduced the States Reorganisation on linguistic lines). RATIONALE: for efficiency + to manage small states / UTs that don't warrant separate full-time governors. EXAMPLES (historically + currently): (1) Small NORTHEASTERN STATES often share a Governor — Mizoram + Arunachal Pradesh + Nagaland at different times have had common Governors. (2) GOA + TELANGANA have shared Governors in recent years. (3) ASSAM Governor is also Governor of Meghalaya during transitional phases. UNION TERRITORIES: have ADMINISTRATORS (not Governors) except Delhi + Puducherry + J&K which have Lieutenant Governors — the LT GOVERNOR (LG) of DELHI + J&K + PUDUCHERRY differ from state Governors in specifics. LG of DELHI = most politically contentious (2015 onwards Kejriwal vs LG disputes; ultimately SC ruled in 2023 that except for land, police + public order, elected govt has executive authority; Centre countered via Govt of NCT of Delhi Amendment Act 2023 — raging dispute). LGs of UTs = Andaman + Nicobar, Puducherry, Chandigarh (same as Punjab Governor ex-officio), Dadra + Nagar Haveli + Daman + Diu, Lakshadweep. Each Administrator appointed by President. TERM: no fixed; 'pleasure of the President'. Note: GOVERNORS of STATES have charge; LIEUTENANT GOVERNORS of UTs + Administrators have charge on behalf of President. OATH: for Governor = from State HC CJ; for LG = from same or Central authorities. SALARY + allowances for Governor/LG is charged upon CONSOLIDATED FUND of INDIA (not State) — Art 158(3) — so State Legislature cannot debate/vote reduction. allows a Governor of one state to concurrently hold charge of another state (e.g., small NE states often share a Governor); first proviso, added by 7th CAA 1956.

cards.front:
The SARKARIA COMMISSION (1988) + the PUNCHHI COMMISSION (2010) both studied + recommended reforms on:

(A) Electoral reforms only
(B) CENTRE-STATE relations
(C) Education policy
(D) Tax reforms only
cards.back:
(B) CENTRE-STATE relations

State Government — SARKARIA + PUNCHHI COMMISSIONS on CENTRE-STATE RELATIONS: (1) SARKARIA COMMISSION (1983-1988) — chaired by JUSTICE R.S. SARKARIA (retired SC judge). Set up by Indira Gandhi govt 1983 during federal tensions (Punjab, AP, Assam movements). Submitted REPORT in JANUARY 1988 to PM RAJIV GANDHI. Comprehensive 19-chapter review. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) Strong Centre but decentralisation where possible; (b) RESIDUARY POWERS (Art 248) — concurrent rather than Union-only (not accepted); (c) ART 356 used only as LAST RESORT after exhausting all other options — proclamation should be based on material grounds + subject to judicial review (later upheld in BOMMAI 1994); (d) GOVERNOR should be 'eminent person' NOT from ruling party, CONSULT CM before appointment — not a binding norm yet; (e) Governor's removal + short tenures curtailed; (f) INTER-STATE COUNCIL (Art 263) to be revitalised — set up 1990 under V.P. Singh; (g) Revenue distribution reformed — implemented via Finance Commissions; (h) planning decentralised (pre-GST centralisation). (2) PUNCHHI COMMISSION (2007-2010) — chaired by JUSTICE MADAN MOHAN PUNCHHI (former CJI). Set up by UPA-I. Submitted 7-volume REPORT in MARCH 2010. Went further than Sarkaria. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) FIXED 5-YEAR TERM for Governors; remove 'pleasure' doctrine; NO REMOVAL without cause (address through Presidential process); (b) panel of 5 names for CM appointment in hung assembly; (c) a process for REMOVAL of Governors (impeachment by State legislature); (d) Treaty-making power — states should have voice in matters affecting them; (e) localise some all-India service cadre; (f) give MARGINAL states more say in national decisions; (g) coordinated response to internal security issues. IMPLEMENTATION: both Commissions' recommendations only PARTIALLY implemented. Inter-State Council has met only sporadically. Governors' politicisation persists. CENTRE-STATE tensions remain (GST compensation, law + order, disaster relief, CAG audits). including Governor's role, Art 356, Inter-State Council, residuary powers, legislative + administrative relations.

cards.front:
GOVERNOR of a STATE is APPOINTED by:

(A) President of India (Article 155)
(B) Chief Minister of the state
(C) Vice President of India here
(D) State Legislative Assembly elected
cards.back:
(A) President of India (Article 155)

State Government — Article 155 — Governor APPOINTED by PRESIDENT (de facto on Cabinet's advice — typically Home Ministry recommends, PM approves). Holds office during PLEASURE OF PRESIDENT (no fixed term; 5 yrs is normal but can be removed earlier). Article 153 — there shall be a Governor for each STATE. 7th Amendment 1956 → SAME PERSON can be Governor of MULTIPLE states. INSIGHT: although called 'state's' executive, Governor is CENTRE'S nominee → causes federal tension; SARKARIA (1988) + PUNCHHI (2010) Commissions recommended Governors should NOT be active politicians, consult CM, etc. — often violated in practice. APPOINTMENT criteria (Art 157): citizen of India + 35 yrs old. Convention: not a state native (to maintain neutrality). LT. GOVERNOR — for some UTs (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K, Ladakh, A&N).

cards.front:
MINIMUM AGE qualification for Governor of a state is:

(A) 35 years (Article 157)
(B) 30 years (RS member age)
(C) 25 years (LS member age)
(D) 40 years (incorrect age)
cards.back:
(A) 35 years (Article 157)

State Government — Article 157 — Governor must: (a) be Indian citizen; (b) be ≥ 35 years old. SAME age as President + Vice President. INSIGHT — PARALLEL OFFICES: Article 153 + 154 — Governor as state's executive head; Article 163 — Council of Ministers to AID + ADVISE Governor (analogous to Pres-PM at centre). Key DIFFERENCES from President: (1) Governor APPOINTED by Pres (Pres elected); (2) Governor has DISCRETIONARY powers in some cases (Article 163 — discretion; Pres has none post-42nd Amendment); (3) Governor can be transferred / removed at any time; Pres can only be impeached. CONVENTIONS — Governor not from same state, not active politician (often broken).

cards.front:
Governor's PARDONING POWER (Article 161) does NOT extend to:

(A) Death sentences + court-martial cases
(B) Sentences for ordinary state offences
(C) Reducing punishment for felons here
(D) Granting respite for short period
cards.back:
(A) Death sentences + court-martial cases

State Government — Governor (Art 161) can PARDON, COMMUTE, REMIT, REPRIEVE for offences against STATE LAWS — but: (a) CANNOT pardon DEATH SENTENCES (only PRESIDENT can; Art 72); (b) CANNOT pardon COURT-MARTIAL cases (only Pres). MERCY petitions for death go to Pres. Compare PRESIDENT (Art 72): can pardon any offence under Union law, court-martial, death sentences. So PRES has WIDER pardoning power than Governor. KOEHLER vs STATE OF ORISSA (1956) — clarified state-Pres pardoning division. INSIGHT — Pres / Governor pardoning is NOT a judicial review; it's an executive grace. Also: NABAM REBIA case (2016, SC, Arunachal) — limited Governor's discretionary powers further; he must act on CM's advice except in defined situations.

cards.front:
Governor APPOINTS the CHIEF MINISTER of the state. CM is:

(A) Leader of majority party in state assembly
(B) Always the senior-most MLA from any party
(C) Person directly elected by state's voters
(D) President's nominee for state ministership
cards.back:
(A) Leader of majority party in state assembly

State Government — CM = LEADER of majority party / coalition in STATE ASSEMBLY. Governor APPOINTS (mostly ceremonial; conventionally invites majority leader). DISCRETION used when no clear majority — Governor can use judgement (notable: Karnataka 2018, Maharashtra 2019 — both controversial). CM holds office during PLEASURE OF GOVERNOR (= until loses confidence in Assembly). NABAM REBIA (2016) limited Governor's power to dismiss CM with floor-test confirmation. CM must be MLA / MLC; if not, must become one within 6 months. Articles 163 + 164 govern state Council of Ministers. Compare CENTRE: PM appointed by Pres similarly; same logic.

cards.option2: Person directly elected by state's voters

cards.front:
PRESIDENT'S RULE in a state (Article 356) is imposed when:

(A) Governor reports state's constitutional machinery has FAILED
(B) CM resigns from his post for any reason (option here)
(C) Floods / natural disasters strike that state
(D) State demands more central funds urgently (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Governor reports state's constitutional machinery has FAILED

State Government — Article 356 (President's Rule) — invoked when Governor reports (or Pres satisfied) that STATE GOVT cannot function as per Constitution (e.g., loss of majority, communal riots, breakdown of law + order). Pres takes over state's functions; legislative powers go to Parliament. INITIAL PERIOD: 6 months. Extendable up to 3 YEARS with parliamentary approval (every 6 months). HISTORY — used extensively (often controversially). Most P-Rule states: UP, Bihar, Punjab. CONTROVERSY: BOMMAI CASE (1994) — SC limited misuse, made it judicially reviewable. 'Floor test' must be done in Assembly before dismissal of state govt. Article 365 — refusal to comply with central directives can trigger. Distractor 1 (CM resignation) → Governor invites alternative leader, NOT President's Rule directly.

cards.option2: Floods / natural disasters strike that state
cards.option3: State demands more central funds urgently (option here)

cards.front:
Salary of GOVERNOR is charged on the:

(A) Consolidated Fund of the state (no Pres veto)
(B) Consolidated Fund of India (centre pays)
(C) President's discretionary fund (Cabinet)
(D) Special trust fund of state legislature
cards.back:
(A) Consolidated Fund of the state (no Pres veto)

State Government — Governor's SALARY + ALLOWANCES = CHARGED on CONSOLIDATED FUND of the STATE (Article 202(3)) — i.e., paid by the state, NOT central govt. NOT subject to vote of state legislature → ensures financial INDEPENDENCE. (Just discussed, not voted upon.) CURRENT salary: ~₹3.5 lakh/month + allowances (raised from ₹1.10 lakh in 2018). Compare: PRESIDENT (~₹5 lakh/month, charged on Consolidated Fund of INDIA); CJI similar. INSIGHT — 'CHARGED' expenditure (also includes salaries of judges, Speaker, CAG, AG) is NON-VOTABLE — protected from political pressure. Voted expenditure (most other) needs annual parliamentary approval via Appropriation Bill.
cards.option3: Special trust fund of state legislature

cards.front:
Governor of MORE THAN ONE state is permissible per:

(A) 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956
(B) Original Constitution provision (1950)
(C) 73rd Amendment, on Panchayati Raj
(D) 42nd Amendment, the 'mini-Constitution'
cards.back:
(A) 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956

State Government — 7th AMENDMENT (1956) — among other things, allowed SAME PERSON to be appointed Governor of TWO OR MORE states. Done to handle small states + special situations. EXAMPLES: Governor of Punjab often Administrator of Chandigarh too; sometimes one Governor handles multiple NE states. CONTEXT — 7th Amendment also implemented STATES REORGANISATION ACT 1956 (linguistic states), abolished classification of states (Part A, B, C, D), redesigned framework. KEY AMENDMENTS to remember: 1st (1951, land reforms, 9th Schedule); 7th (1956, states reorg); 42nd (1976, 'mini-Constitution', Emergency-era); 44th (1978, undid Emergency excesses); 73rd-74th (1992, Panchayats + Municipalities); 86th (2002, Right to Education); 91st (2003, anti-defection); 101st (2016, GST); 103rd (2019, EWS reservation).

cards.front:
When is a state GOVERNOR justified in using DISCRETIONARY POWERS?

(A) Hung assembly — choosing CM candidate
(B) Routine bill assent (must follow CM)
(C) Daily administrative matters always
(D) Approving state cabinet decisions
cards.back:
(A) Hung assembly — choosing CM candidate

State Government — GOVERNOR's DISCRETIONARY POWERS arise in SITUATIONS where the Constitution doesn't bind him to act on Council of Ministers' advice. KEY CIRCUMSTANCES: (1) HUNG ASSEMBLY (no party with majority) — Governor decides which leader to invite to form government. (2) Loss of MAJORITY — Governor can dismiss CM and ask for floor test. (3) Recommendation of PRESIDENT'S RULE under Article 356 — Governor's discretion (in practice, advised by Centre). (4) Reservation of bills for President's consideration (Art 200). (5) Receiving REPORTS from constitutional functionaries. (6) Discretion in administering 5th/6th schedule areas (tribal). (7) Discretion in NE states (e.g., Nagaland — Governor has 'special responsibility' for law-and-order, Art 371A). KEY ARTICLES: Art 163(1) — 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion' — clear that some discretion exists. ROUTINE FUNCTIONS — Governor MUST act on CABINET ADVICE per Article 163: bill assent, appointments, etc. NOTABLE CASES: (a) Bommai Case (1994) — limited Art 356 misuse; floor test must precede CM dismissal. (b) Karnataka 2018 — Governor invited single largest party (BJP, no majority); SC ordered immediate floor test. PYQ FREQUENCY: Governor's discretion in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Article 163 of the Indian Constitution deals with:

(A) Council of Ministers to aid Governor
(B) Removal of Governor from office
(C) Appointment of Chief Minister
(D) Powers of state legislature now
cards.back:
(A) Council of Ministers to aid Governor

State Government — ARTICLE 163 — 'COUNCIL OF MINISTERS to AID and ADVISE the GOVERNOR': (1) There SHALL BE a Council of Ministers headed by CM to aid and advise Governor in exercise of his functions, EXCEPT in so far as the Governor is required to exercise his functions in his discretion. (2) If a question arises whether a matter is one in which Governor must use discretion — Governor's decision is FINAL and CANNOT BE QUESTIONED IN COURT. (3) Question of whether ministers gave advice CANNOT be inquired into in any court. KEY: Art 163 is ANALOGOUS TO ART 74 for the President at Centre — but PRESIDENT has FAR LESS discretion (74 was AMENDED in 1976 + 1978 to make presidential aid-and-advice BINDING; Art 163's wording for Governor is somewhat MORE FLEXIBLE). RELATED ARTICLES: (a) ART 153 — there shall be Governor for each state. (b) ART 154 — executive power of state vested in Governor. (c) ART 155 — appointed by President. (d) ART 156 — holds office during President's pleasure (5 years term but removable). (e) ART 161 — pardoning power. (f) ART 200 — assent to bills (can return non-money bill once for reconsideration). (g) ART 213 — promulgate ordinances. PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 163 in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
When a state bill is RESERVED for President's consideration under Article 200, the President has the option to:

(A) Give assent or withhold or return
(B) Give assent only without choice
(C) Send the bill back to bench again
(D) Appoint a Governor for ruling there
cards.back:
(A) Give assent or withhold or return

State Government — ARTICLE 200 — Governor has 4 options on a state bill: (1) ASSENT (becomes law). (2) WITHHOLD ASSENT (bill dies, but rare — undemocratic). (3) RETURN to legislature for reconsideration (NOT money bill) — if state passes again, Governor must assent. (4) RESERVE for President's consideration (e.g., bills affecting HC powers, related to property acquisition). After RESERVATION (Art 201): PRESIDENT can: (a) Give assent → bill becomes state law. (b) Withhold assent → bill dies. (c) DIRECT GOVERNOR to RETURN to state legislature. State legislature reconsiders; if passes again with/without amendments, sends back to Governor → who reserves for President AGAIN → President's option remains the same. KEY: there's NO TIME LIMIT for President to act on reserved bills — leading to long delays in some cases. CONCERN: bills can sit indefinitely, blocking state legislation. RECENT CONTROVERSIES: (1) TAMIL NADU 2023 — multiple state bills pending at Governor's desk (NEET exemption etc.); SC asked Governor to act 'promptly'. (2) KERALA 2023-24 — Governor sat on bills; CM Vijayan moved SC. STATES WITH MAJOR FRICTION (recently): TN, Kerala, Punjab, Telangana, WB. CONSTITUTION REVIEW COMMITTEE recommended TIME-LIMITS, but not yet enacted. PYQ ANGLE: Governor's bill-veto power tested in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC.
cards.option2: Send the bill back to bench again
cards.option3: Appoint a Governor for ruling there

cards.front:
Under Article 213, when can a Governor PROMULGATE AN ORDINANCE?

(A) When state legislature is not in session
(B) Anytime he sees a need to use it
(C) Even when assembly is in session
(D) Only with Cabinet's prior consent
cards.back:
(A) When state legislature is not in session

State Government — ARTICLE 213 — Governor can PROMULGATE ORDINANCES (state-level laws) ONLY WHEN: (1) the state legislature is NOT IN SESSION, AND (2) the Governor is satisfied that immediate action is necessary. ORDINANCE-MAKING is on the ADVICE of Council of Ministers (not pure discretion, but technically Governor's act). KEY CONDITIONS: (a) Bill MUST be placed before legislature within 6 WEEKS of next session — else lapses. (b) Maximum life of ordinance: ~6 weeks + session period (about 7-8 months) before it must be passed as legislation or lapse. (c) PROHIBITED ON: bills that would have required PRIOR PRESIDENTIAL SANCTION (e.g., bills on certain subjects in 7th Schedule); such ordinances also require pre-clearance. ANALOGOUS for CENTRE: PRESIDENT has same power under Article 123. NOTABLE CASES: (1) DC WADHWA case (1986): SC condemned 're-promulgation' of ordinances (without going to legislature) — called it 'fraud on the Constitution'. (2) KRISHNA KUMAR SINGH v. STATE OF BIHAR (2017): SC reaffirmed re-promulgation is impermissible. ORDINANCE 'RAJ': in 1990s-2010s, some governors re-promulgated same ordinance dozens of times — practice now stopped. RECENT: Bihar's 2023 reservation increase via ordinance was challenged. PYQ FREQUENCY: ordinance-making power is a top UPSC, MPSC polity MCQ — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.option2: Even when assembly is in session

cards.front:
The S.R. BOMMAI CASE (1994) is associated with which constitutional matter?

(A) Limits on President's Rule (Art 356)
(B) Reservation policy in jobs and education
(C) Right to Information enforcement
(D) Free speech rights (Article 19)
cards.back:
(A) Limits on President's Rule (Art 356)

State Government — S.R. BOMMAI v. UNION OF INDIA (1994) — landmark 9-judge SC bench judgment that PUT LIMITS on Article 356 (President's Rule). BACKGROUND: Karnataka CM SR BOMMAI was DISMISSED in 1989 over alleged loss of majority; SC eventually held this dismissal UNCONSTITUTIONAL. KEY HOLDINGS: (1) Floor test of majority must occur on the floor of HOUSE — NOT determined by Governor's subjective opinion. (2) President's Rule under Art 356 is JUSTICIABLE (court can review). (3) Material on which Centre bases Art 356 must be RELEVANT and BONA FIDE. (4) Until Parliament approves, the Assembly is only SUSPENDED, not dissolved — so possible to revive. (5) Federal balance is BASIC STRUCTURE — Art 356 must be used SPARINGLY. (6) SECULARISM is BASIC STRUCTURE — Art 356 can be invoked against state governments violating secularism. IMPACT: misuse of Art 356 dropped sharply after Bommai. Art 356 imposed: (a) ~125 times before 1994. (b) ~30 times since 1994 — and most reviewed by SC. RELATED PRECEDENTS: KESAVANANDA BHARATI (1973) — basic structure doctrine. INDIRA NEHRU GANDHI v. RAJ NARAIN (1975) — election cases. RAMESHWAR PRASAD (2006) — Bihar Assembly dissolution case. PYQ FREQUENCY: Bommai case in UPSC, MPSC, polity GS — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Who appoints the Governor of a state in India?

(A) President of India (warrant)
(B) Prime Minister directly here
(C) Chief Minister of the state
(D) State legislative assembly votes
cards.back:
(A) President of India (warrant)

State Government — ARTICLE 155: GOVERNOR APPOINTED by the PRESIDENT OF INDIA (under his hand and seal). In practice, PM and Cabinet recommend; President formally appoints. ARTICLE 156: tenure 5 YEARS, but holds office DURING PRESIDENT'S PLEASURE — meaning the Centre can REMOVE the Governor at any time. ARTICLE 157: QUALIFICATIONS — citizen of India, age 35+, NOT a member of Parliament/state legislature. ARTICLE 158: emoluments + restrictions — cannot hold office of profit, no other paid employment. KEY APPOINTMENT CONVENTIONS (mostly observed but not legally binding): (1) Governor should ideally NOT be from the SAME state. (2) Outgoing CMs of OTHER states often appointed (controversial). (3) State CM's views should be CONSULTED before appointment. (4) Governor should not be a partisan figure. CONTROVERSIAL APPOINTMENTS — RECENT DEBATES: governors with strong RSS/political backgrounds appointed to opposition-ruled states; alleged conflict with state government. SARKARIA COMMISSION (1988): recommended detailed guidelines for Governor appointment + functioning — non-partisan figures, 5-year fixed term, etc. PUNCHHI COMMISSION (2010): reiterated; recommended state legislature should be consulted. NEITHER FULLY IMPLEMENTED. PYQ FREQUENCY: Governor appointment in UPSC, MPSC, SSC CGL polity 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
In which special situation does the Governor of NAGALAND have extra discretionary powers?

(A) Law and order (Article 371A)
(B) Standard education matters here
(C) Health policy (state subject)
(D) Tourism promotion functions
cards.back:
(A) Law and order (Article 371A)

State Government — ARTICLE 371A — special provisions for NAGALAND. Includes the GOVERNOR's DISCRETIONARY responsibility for LAW AND ORDER for so long as 'situation requires'. KEY 371A PROVISIONS: (1) Acts of Parliament re: religious/social practices, customary law, civil/criminal procedure, ownership of land/resources DO NOT APPLY to Nagaland WITHOUT Naga Legislative Assembly's resolution. (2) Governor has SPECIAL RESPONSIBILITY for law and order until determined otherwise by President. (3) Governor's individual judgment — NOT bound by Council of Ministers — in this domain. SIMILAR SPECIAL ARTICLES: (1) Art 371 — special arrangements for Maharashtra, Gujarat. (2) Art 371B — Assam (tribal areas). (3) Art 371C — Manipur. (4) Art 371D — Andhra Pradesh + Telangana (employment, education). (5) Art 371F — Sikkim (special protections for Sikkimese culture). (6) Art 371G — MIZORAM (similar to Nagaland). (7) Art 371H — Arunachal Pradesh (Governor's special law-and-order role). (8) Art 371I — Goa. (9) Art 371J — Hyderabad-Karnataka. CONTEXT: NORTH-EAST states often have UNIQUE histories, ethnicities, autonomy demands → constitutional special provisions. NAGALAND specifically: 1963 constituted as state; 16-point agreement with Centre included this Governor role. PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 371 family in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

(B) President of India
(C) Chief Minister
(D) Supreme Court
cards.back:
(B) President of India

State Government — Article 155 — Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. NOT elected (unlike the President himself). Holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156(1)) — can be removed any time. Term — 5 years (Art 156(3)) or until pleasure withdrawn. Salary fixed by Parliament (Art 158(3)) — currently ~₹3.5 lakh/month. Same person can be Governor of two or more states (7th Amendment, 1956).

cards.front:
The minimum age qualification for being appointed as Governor is:

(A) 25 years
(B) 35 years
(C) 40 years
(D) 30 years
cards.back:
(B) 35 years

State Government — Article 157 — qualifications: (1) citizen of India; (2) at least 35 years of age. Article 158 conditions: (i) not a member of Parliament or State Legislature; (ii) not hold any other office of profit. Two unique conventions (not law): the Governor should be from outside the State and major political appointments should follow consultation with the CM (often ignored). The 35-year rule matches the President's age requirement.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a 'discretionary' power of the Governor — exercised without aid and advice of the Council of Ministers?

(A) Routine assent to ordinary State Bills
(B) Reserving a State Bill for the President's consideration (Art 200)
(C) Making appointments to the State Public Service
(D) Promulgating ordinances on the CM's advice
cards.back:
(B) Reserving a State Bill for the President's consideration (Art 200)

State Government — Discretionary powers (constitutional, non-discretionary acts → on CM's advice): (1) Reserving certain State Bills for the President — Art 200 (mandatory if bill threatens HC powers; discretionary otherwise); (2) Recommending President's Rule under Art 356; (3) Discharging functions as Administrator of an adjoining UT (when applicable); (4) Seeking information from the CM under Art 167; (5) Special responsibilities assigned by President (e.g., Art 371 provisions for Maharashtra/Gujarat/Nagaland). All other functions follow the cabinet's advice.
cards.option1: Routine assent to ordinary State Bills
cards.option2: Making appointments to the State Public Service
cards.option3: Promulgating ordinances on the CM's advice

All other functions follow the cabinet's advice.

cards.front:
The Governor's pardoning power under Article 161 differs from the President's (Art 72) in that the Governor:

(A) Has wider scope than the President
(B) CANNOT pardon a death sentence; CANNOT grant pardon in court-martial cases
(C) Can pardon any offence anywhere in India
(D) Has no pardoning power at all
cards.back:
(B) CANNOT pardon a death sentence; CANNOT grant pardon in court-martial cases

State Government — Two key restrictions on Article 161: (i) Governor can grant Pardon, Reprieve, Respite, Commutation, Remission for offences against State law — but NOT for death sentences (only President under Art 72 can). (ii) Cannot exercise pardoning power in cases of court-martial. Both Governor and President exercise this power on aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Maru Ram, Kehar Singh, Epuru Sudhakar judgments). Note: Governor CAN suspend a death sentence to enable a mercy petition to the President.
cards.option1: Has wider scope than the President
cards.option2: Can pardon any offence anywhere in India
cards.option3: Has no pardoning power at all

Both Governor and President exercise this power on aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Maru Ram, Kehar Singh, Epuru Sudhakar judgments). cards.front:
An ordinance issued by the Governor under Article 213 must be approved by the State Legislature within:

(A) 30 days from the start of the next session
(B) 6 weeks from the start of the next session — else it lapses
(C) 60 days from issue
(D) Six months from issue
cards.back:
(B) 6 weeks from the start of the next session — else it lapses

State Government — Article 213 — parallel to Article 123 for the President. Ordinance ceases to operate 6 weeks after the State Legislature's reassembly. Effective max life ≈ 6 months recess + 6 weeks ≈ 7.5 months. Must be tabled before the legislature when it reconvenes; can also be withdrawn by Governor any time. Some bill-types require prior instructions from the President before the Governor can issue an ordinance (under State List items reserved for Centre's view). Subject to judicial review.
cards.option1: 30 days from the start of the next session

Some bill-types require prior instructions from the President before the Governor can issue an ordinance (under State List items reserved for Centre's view). Subject to judicial review.

cards.front:
When a State Bill is reserved by the Governor for the President's consideration under Article 200, the President can:

(A) Only assent — no other option
(B) Assent, withhold assent, or return the bill (only for non-Money Bills) for reconsideration by the State Legislature
(C) Send it to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion
(D) Convert it into an ordinance
cards.back:
(B) Assent, withhold assent, or return the bill (only for non-Money Bills) for reconsideration by the State Legislature

State Government — Article 201 — three options for the President on a reserved bill: (1) assent; (2) withhold assent (effectively veto, no time-limit — pocket veto possible); (3) direct the Governor to return it (not Money Bill) to the State Legislature for reconsideration; if the legislature passes it again with or without modifications, the President is NOT bound to assent (unlike Parliament's repeat-passage of an ordinary bill returned to Lok Sabha by the President). Note: this triple-tier reservation is a unique federal feature.
cards.option2: Send it to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion

cards.front:
The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and Punchhi Commission (2010) recommended that the Governor's appointment should:

(A) Be by direct election
(B) Be made by the President in consultation with the Chief Minister of the concerned State
(C) Be by the Vice-President
(D) Require Supreme Court approval
cards.back:
(B) Be made by the President in consultation with the Chief Minister of the concerned State

State Government — Sarkaria Commission (Centre-State relations, 1988) — recommended (i) Governor should be an eminent person, NOT belonging to ruling party at Centre; (ii) appointment in consultation with the State CM; (iii) fixed term except in extreme cases; (iv) reasoned removal. Punchhi Commission (2010) reaffirmed and added impeachment-like procedure. Most recommendations remain unimplemented; Article 156 still says 'pleasure of the President'. NCRWC (2002) and SC ruling in B.P. Singhal (2010) are related authorities.

cards.front:
How many Indian states currently have a bicameral legislature (Vidhan Sabha + Vidhan Parishad)?

(A) Four states
(B) Six states
(C) Eight states
(D) Ten states
cards.back:
(B) Six states

State Government — Six bicameral states (as of 2025): Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh. All others are unicameral. Creating or abolishing a Vidhan Parishad requires a state-legislature resolution followed by a Parliament Act (Art 169). J&K had a Council until 2019 reorganisation.

cards.front:
The normal term of a Vidhan Sabha (State Legislative Assembly) is:

(A) Four years
(B) Five years
(C) Six years
(D) Seven years
cards.back:
(B) Five years

State Government — Art 172 — Vidhan Sabha has a 5-year term unless dissolved earlier by the Governor on the CM's advice, or during President's Rule. Strength: 60 to 500 members (Art 170). Smaller states have fewer: Sikkim 32, Goa 40, Mizoram 40. Rajya Sabha / Vidhan Parishad are permanent bodies with 6-year member terms.

cards.front:
Which of the following is true of the Vidhan Parishad (State Legislative Council)?

(A) It is dissolved with the Vidhan Sabha
(B) One-third of its members retire every two years
(C) One-half of its members retire every three years
(D) All members are directly elected by the people
cards.back:
(B) One-third of its members retire every two years

State Government — Like Rajya Sabha, the Vidhan Parishad is a permanent body — 1/3 retire every 2 years, each member serves 6 years. Max strength = 1/3 of the Vidhan Sabha. Composition: 1/3 by MLAs, 1/3 by local bodies, 1/12 by teachers, 1/12 by registered graduates, the rest nominated by the Governor (literature, science, art, social service).
cards.option1: It is dissolved with the Vidhan Sabha
cards.option2: One-half of its members retire every three years
cards.option3: All members are directly elected by the people

cards.front:
The minimum age to be elected as an MLA (Vidhan Sabha member) is:

(A) 21 years
(B) 25 years
(C) 30 years
(D) 35 years
cards.back:
(B) 25 years

State Government — Art 173 — MLA minimum age is 25, same as Lok Sabha MP. MLC / Rajya Sabha MP — 30. President, Vice-President, Governor — 35. Voting age — 18 (reduced from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988).
cards.storedExplanation: Art 173 — MLA minimum age is 25, same as Lok Sabha MP. MLC / Rajya Sabha MP — 30. President, Vice-President, Governor — 35. Voting age — 18 (reduced from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988).

cards.front:
The Governor of a state is appointed by the:

(A) Prime Minister
(B) President of India
(C) Chief Minister of the state
(D) MLAs of the state assembly
cards.back:
(B) President of India

State Government — Art 155 — Governors are appointed by the President. Art 156 — holds office during the pleasure of the President (no formal removal procedure; 5-year term by convention). Must be a citizen of India aged 35+. Oath of office administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court (Art 159).
cards.storedExplanation: Art 155 — Governors are appointed by the President. Art 156 — holds office during the pleasure of the President (no formal removal procedure; 5-year term by convention). Must be a citizen of India aged 35+. Oath of office administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court (Art 159).

cards.front:
The retirement age of a High Court judge is:

(A) 60 years
(B) 62 years
(C) 65 years
(D) 70 years
cards.back:
(B) 62 years

State Government — HC judges retire at 62 (raised from the original 60 by the 15th Amendment, 1963). SC judges retire at 65. HC judges are appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI, the HC Chief Justice, and the Governor of the state (Art 217).
cards.storedExplanation: HC judges retire at 62 (raised from the original 60 by the 15th Amendment, 1963). SC judges retire at 65. HC judges are appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI, the HC Chief Justice, and the Governor of the state (Art 217).

cards.front:
Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States (Art 246) is laid down in which Schedule of the Constitution?

(A) Fourth Schedule
(B) Seventh Schedule
(C) Eighth Schedule
(D) Eleventh Schedule
cards.back:
(B) Seventh Schedule

State Government — Seventh Schedule contains three lists — Union List (~100 subjects: defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy), State List (~61: police, land, public health), Concurrent List (~52: both may legislate, Union prevails on conflict). Fourth = Rajya Sabha seat allocation; Eighth = scheduled languages (22); Eleventh = panchayat subjects (29, via 73rd Amendment).
