cards.front:
Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is the office of the Attorney General of India established?

(A) Article 75
(B) Article 76
(C) Article 148
(D) Article 165
cards.back:
(B) Article 76

Constitutional Bodies — Article 76 of the Constitution provides for the appointment of the Attorney General of India — the highest law officer of the country. Article 75 deals with the appointment of the PM and Council of Ministers; Article 148 deals with the CAG; Article 165 establishes the office of the Advocate General for States — the three most common distractors for this question.
cards.storedExplanation: Article 76 of the Constitution provides for the appointment of the Attorney General of India — the highest law officer of the country. Article 75 deals with the appointment of the PM and Council of Ministers; Article 148 deals with the CAG; Article 165 establishes the office of the Advocate General for States — the three most common distractors for this question.

cards.front:
Who appoints the Attorney General of India?

(A) The Chief Justice of India
(B) The Parliament by a special majority
(C) The President of India on the advice of the Union Cabinet
(D) The Prime Minister in consultation with the Law Minister
cards.back:
(C) The President of India on the advice of the Union Cabinet

Constitutional Bodies — Under Article 76(1), the Attorney General is appointed by the President — who, per Article 74, acts on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers (effectively the Cabinet). The CJI has no role; Parliament does not elect the AG; the PM recommends through the Cabinet rather than independently.
cards.option2: The Parliament by a special majority
cards.option3: The Prime Minister in consultation with the Law Minister
cards.storedExplanation: Under Article 76(1), the Attorney General is appointed by the President — who, per Article 74, acts on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers (effectively the Cabinet). The CJI has no role; Parliament does not elect the AG; the PM recommends through the Cabinet rather than independently.

cards.front:
What qualification is required for appointment as the Attorney General of India, as per Article 76?

(A) Must be qualified for appointment as a judge of a High Court
(B) Must be qualified for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court
(C) Must have at least 15 years of practice in the Supreme Court
(D) Must be a sitting or retired judge of the Supreme Court
cards.back:
(B) Must be qualified for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court

Constitutional Bodies — Article 76(1) requires that a person must be qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court — i.e., be a citizen of India, and either have been a HC judge for 5 years, an HC advocate for 10 years, or be a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. The AG need not currently be a judge, and there is no fixed year requirement for practice.
cards.option1: Must be qualified for appointment as a judge of a High Court
cards.option2: Must have at least 15 years of practice in the Supreme Court
cards.option3: Must be a sitting or retired judge of the Supreme Court
cards.storedExplanation: Article 76(1) requires that a person must be qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court — i.e., be a citizen of India, and either have been a HC judge for 5 years, an HC advocate for 10 years, or be a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. The AG need not currently be a judge, and there is no fixed year requirement for practice.

cards.front:
What is the term of office of the Attorney General of India?

(A) 6 years or till 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
(B) 5 years, co-terminus with the Lok Sabha
(C) Not fixed by the Constitution
(D) Till 62 years of age
cards.back:
(C) Not fixed by the Constitution

Constitutional Bodies — The Constitution does not fix a term for the AG. Article 76(4) states the AG holds office 'during the pleasure of the President'. In practice, the AG resigns when the government that appointed them changes. Fixed 6-year/65-year terms apply to the CAG, not the AG. The AG's tenure is NOT tied to the Lok Sabha. holds office during the pleasure of the President.
cards.option1: 6 years or till 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
cards.option2: 5 years, co-terminus with the Lok Sabha
cards.storedExplanation: The Constitution does not fix a term for the AG. Article 76(4) states the AG holds office 'during the pleasure of the President'. In practice, the AG resigns when the government that appointed them changes. Fixed 6-year/65-year terms apply to the CAG, not the AG. The AG's tenure is NOT tied to the Lok Sabha. holds office during the pleasure of the President.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a duty of the Attorney General of India under Article 76?

(A) Give advice to the Government of India on legal matters referred to him
(B) Perform such other duties of a legal character as assigned by the President
(C) Discharge the functions conferred on him by or under the Constitution or any other law
(D) Prosecute government servants in criminal cases of corruption
cards.back:
(D) Prosecute government servants in criminal cases of corruption

Constitutional Bodies — Article 76(2) lists three duties — legal advice, assigned legal duties, and constitutional/statutory functions. Prosecution of government servants in corruption cases is handled by the CBI under the Prevention of Corruption Act, not by the AG. The AG is counsel for the government, not a prosecutor of its employees.
cards.option1: Give advice to the Government of India on legal matters referred to him
cards.option2: Perform such other duties of a legal character as assigned by the President
cards.option3: Discharge the functions conferred on him by or under the Constitution or any other law
cards.storedExplanation: Article 76(2) lists three duties — legal advice, assigned legal duties, and constitutional/statutory functions. Prosecution of government servants in corruption cases is handled by the CBI under the Prevention of Corruption Act, not by the AG. The AG is counsel for the government, not a prosecutor of its employees.

cards.front:
Which of the following rights does the Attorney General of India enjoy with respect to Parliament?

(A) Right to vote in both Houses
(B) Right to speak and take part in proceedings of both Houses and their committees, but not to vote
(C) Right to introduce bills in the Lok Sabha only
(D) No rights — AG is an executive officer only
cards.back:
(B) Right to speak and take part in proceedings of both Houses and their committees, but not to vote

Constitutional Bodies — Article 88 gives the Attorney General the right to speak in and take part in the proceedings of either House of Parliament, any joint sitting, and any parliamentary committee of which he may be named a member — WITHOUT the right to vote. This parallels the same right extended to Ministers (Article 88). The AG is NOT a Member of Parliament.
cards.option1: Right to vote in both Houses
cards.option2: Right to introduce bills in the Lok Sabha only
cards.option3: No rights — AG is an executive officer only
cards.storedExplanation: Article 88 gives the Attorney General the right to speak in and take part in the proceedings of either House of Parliament, any joint sitting, and any parliamentary committee of which he may be named a member — WITHOUT the right to vote. This parallels the same right extended to Ministers (Article 88). The AG is NOT a Member of Parliament.

cards.front:
Which of the following statements about the Attorney General of India's private practice is correct?

(A) The AG is barred from all private practice during the term of office
(B) The AG can engage in private practice, but cannot advise or brief against the Government of India
(C) The AG can appear against the Government of India but cannot accept private corporate work
(D) The AG can take only international arbitration work privately
cards.back:
(B) The AG can engage in private practice, but cannot advise or brief against the Government of India

Constitutional Bodies — The AG is NOT a full-time salaried government servant. He retains the right to private practice but — as per conventions and the 1987 Law Commission note — cannot advise or hold brief against the Government of India, or against any PSU/statutory body where the GoI is also a party, or defend an accused in criminal proceedings without government permission. This distinguishes the AG from full-time officers like the Solicitor General of earlier decades.
cards.option1: The AG is barred from all private practice during the term of office
cards.option2: The AG can appear against the Government of India but cannot accept private corporate work
cards.option3: The AG can take only international arbitration work privately
cards.storedExplanation: The AG is NOT a full-time salaried government servant. He retains the right to private practice but — as per conventions and the 1987 Law Commission note — cannot advise or hold brief against the Government of India, or against any PSU/statutory body where the GoI is also a party, or defend an accused in criminal proceedings without government permission. This distinguishes the AG from full-time officers like the Solicitor General of earlier decades.

cards.front:
Who, among the following, ranks immediately below the Attorney General in the hierarchy of Government law officers?

(A) Additional Solicitor General
(B) Solicitor General of India
(C) Standing Counsel for the Government
(D) Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs
cards.back:
(B) Solicitor General of India

Constitutional Bodies — The order is: Attorney General → Solicitor General → Additional Solicitors General → Standing/Panel counsels. The Solicitor General (and the Additional SGs) are statutory posts, unlike the AG which is constitutional. The Secretary of Legal Affairs is an administrative post in the Ministry of Law & Justice, not a 'law officer'.
cards.storedExplanation: The order is: Attorney General → Solicitor General → Additional Solicitors General → Standing/Panel counsels. The Solicitor General (and the Additional SGs) are statutory posts, unlike the AG which is constitutional. The Secretary of Legal Affairs is an administrative post in the Ministry of Law & Justice, not a 'law officer'.

cards.front:
Under Article 143 of the Constitution, the President may refer a question of law to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion. In such a reference, who typically represents the Government of India?

(A) The Prime Minister's Office's Legal Cell
(B) The Attorney General of India
(C) The Law Minister personally
(D) The Chief Justice of India
cards.back:
(B) The Attorney General of India

Constitutional Bodies — Presidential References under Article 143 are argued before the Supreme Court, and the Government of India is represented by the Attorney General as its chief law officer. Examples: Berubari Union Reference (1960), Kerala Education Bill Reference (1958), 2G Spectrum Reference (2012), Ayodhya Reference (1993) — AG led submissions in each. The CJI presides; he doesn't represent a party.
cards.option1: The Prime Minister's Office's Legal Cell
cards.storedExplanation: Presidential References under Article 143 are argued before the Supreme Court, and the Government of India is represented by the Attorney General as its chief law officer. Examples: Berubari Union Reference (1960), Kerala Education Bill Reference (1958), 2G Spectrum Reference (2012), Ayodhya Reference (1993) — AG led submissions in each. The CJI presides; he doesn't represent a party.

cards.front:
Who was the first Attorney General of India after the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950?

(A) C. K. Daphtary
(B) M. C. Setalvad
(C) Motilal Setalvad
(D) H. M. Seervai
cards.back:
(B) M. C. Setalvad

Constitutional Bodies — Motilal Chimanlal Setalvad — commonly written as M. C. Setalvad — served as the first Attorney General of India from 1950 to 1963, the longest tenure in the history of the office (13 years). 'Motilal Setalvad' (option C) is a redundant phrasing of the same name and is treated as a distractor. C. K. Daphtary succeeded him in 1963. H. M. Seervai was a jurist and Advocate General of Maharashtra, never AG of India.

Setalvad — served as the first Attorney General of India from 1950 to 1963, the longest tenure in the history of the office (13 years). 'Motilal Setalvad' (option C) is a redundant phrasing of the same name and is treated as a distractor. C. K. Daphtary succeeded him in 1963. H. M. cards.front:
The Advocate General of a State is provided for under which Article of the Constitution?

(A) Article 76
(B) Article 148
(C) Article 165
(D) Article 213
cards.back:
(C) Article 165

Constitutional Bodies — Article 165 establishes the office of the Advocate General for each State — the highest law officer at the State level, paralleling the Attorney General at the Union level. Article 76 is for the AG (Union). Article 148 covers the CAG. Article 213 empowers the Governor to promulgate ordinances, not a law-officer position.
cards.storedExplanation: Article 165 establishes the office of the Advocate General for each State — the highest law officer at the State level, paralleling the Attorney General at the Union level. Article 76 is for the AG (Union). Article 148 covers the CAG. Article 213 empowers the Governor to promulgate ordinances, not a law-officer position.

cards.front:
Who appoints the Advocate General of a State, and whose pleasure does he hold office during?

(A) Appointed by the President; holds office at the pleasure of the President
(B) Appointed by the Governor; holds office during the pleasure of the Governor
(C) Appointed by the Chief Minister; holds office till 65 years of age
(D) Elected by the State Legislature for a 5-year term
cards.back:
(B) Appointed by the Governor; holds office during the pleasure of the Governor

Constitutional Bodies — Under Article 165, the Governor appoints the Advocate General for the State, who holds office during the Governor's pleasure. The Governor acts on the advice of the State Council of Ministers (Article 163). Unlike the CAG, there is no fixed retirement age for the Advocate General. The President has no role — this is a State-level office.
cards.option1: Appointed by the President; holds office at the pleasure of the President
cards.option2: Appointed by the Chief Minister; holds office till 65 years of age
cards.option3: Elected by the State Legislature for a 5-year term
cards.storedExplanation: Under Article 165, the Governor appoints the Advocate General for the State, who holds office during the Governor's pleasure. The Governor acts on the advice of the State Council of Ministers (Article 163). Unlike the CAG, there is no fixed retirement age for the Advocate General. The President has no role — this is a State-level office.

cards.front:
What is the qualification required for appointment as Advocate General of a State?

(A) Must be qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court
(B) Must be qualified to be appointed a judge of a High Court
(C) Must have at least 20 years of legal practice in the State
(D) Must be a sitting MP/MLA of the ruling party in the State
cards.back:
(B) Must be qualified to be appointed a judge of a High Court

Constitutional Bodies — Article 165(1) states the Advocate General must be qualified to be appointed a judge of a High Court — i.e., a citizen of India who has held a judicial office for 10 years or been an advocate of an HC for 10 years. This is a LESSER threshold than that for the Attorney General (who needs SC judge eligibility — 5 years HC judge or 10 years HC advocate). The AG role is never political.

cards.front:
The remuneration of the Attorney General of India is determined by which authority?

cards.front:
Who was the Attorney General of India who served during the Emergency (1975–77) and signed the controversial ADM Jabalpur case affidavit on behalf of the government?

(A) M. C. Setalvad
(B) Niren De
(C) S. V. Gupte
(D) L. N. Sinha
cards.back:
(B) Niren De

Constitutional Bodies — Niren De served as AG of India from 1968 to 1977 (under Indira Gandhi). He is best remembered for his controversial submission in the ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) habeas corpus case during the Emergency, where he argued that a person whose fundamental right to life (Article 21) was suspended had no remedy — a position the SC later overruled in Puttaswamy (2017). M. C. Setalvad was the FIRST AG; S. V. Gupte (1977–79) succeeded De after Janata Party took office; L. N. Sinha served 1979–83.

cards.front:

(B) 1 and 2 only
(C) 2 and 3 only

(B) Only compliance audit

cards.front:

(B) Any academic post in a private university

cards.front:

cards.back:
(B) Sole auditor, Supplementary auditor, or Auditor by arrangement, depending on the PSU's structure

Constitutional Bodies — CAG's audit role for PSUs varies by structure: (a) for DEPARTMENTAL COMMERCIAL UNDERTAKINGS (e.g., Railways), CAG is the SOLE auditor; (b) for STATUTORY CORPORATIONS (e.g., LIC pre-2000, ONGC pre-1976), CAG's role depends on the enabling Act — sole, supplementary, or by arrangement; (c) for GOVERNMENT COMPANIES under Companies Act 2013 (Section 143(5)), CAG appoints the CA auditor and can conduct supplementary/test audits. So CAG's role is nuanced, not a one-size-fits-all.

cards.front:
The Election Commission of India is established under which Article of the Constitution?

(A) Article 324
(B) Article 148
(C) Article 280
(D) Article 312
cards.back:
(A) Article 324

Constitutional Bodies — ARTICLE 324 — 'Superintendence, direction and control of elections to be vested in an Election Commission'. The ECI supervises elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, offices of President + Vice-President. DOES NOT conduct local body elections (handled by STATE Election Commissions under Arts 243K + 243ZA — different body, added by 73rd + 74th CAA 1992). FOUNDED: 25 JANUARY 1950 — one day before Republic Day; this date is now celebrated as NATIONAL VOTERS' DAY since 2011. FIRST CEC: SUKUMAR SEN (IAS, 1950-58) — ran the massive 1st general election 1951-52 (17.3 crore eligible voters). CONSTITUTION-BODY CATEGORY: CONSTITUTIONAL body (unlike NITI Aayog, CBI, CVC which are statutory/executive). STRUCTURE: started with just CEC; became MULTI-MEMBER in Oct 1989; permanent 3-member since 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs — all equal status + equal vote). Decisions by majority if they disagree. ADMIN: secretariat at Nirvachan Sadan, New Delhi. APPOINTMENT: by PRESIDENT, per recent 2023 Act, on advice of 3-member panel (PM + LoP + Union Minister nominated by PM). TERM: 6 YEARS or until 65 — whichever earlier. REMOVAL: CEC can be removed ONLY by parliamentary IMPEACHMENT (like SC judge); ECs can be removed on CEC's recommendation.

cards.front:
The ELECTION COMMISSION of India became a MULTI-MEMBER body permanently from:

(A) 1950
(B) 1 OCTOBER 1993
(C) 1975
(D) 2003
cards.back:
(B) 1 OCTOBER 1993

Constitutional Bodies — ECI — MULTI-MEMBER status chronology: (1) 1950-1989: SINGLE-member body (only CEC). (2) 16 Oct 1989: Rajiv Gandhi government appointed two ECs making it a 3-member body for the first time (controversial — seen as PM's attempt to undermine independent CEC RVS Peri Sastri). (3) 2 January 1990: V.P. Singh's Janata Dal government ABOLISHED the two EC posts — returned to single-member. (4) 1 OCTOBER 1993: Narasimha Rao Cabinet permanently made ECI a 3-member body — CEC T.N. SESHAN was making aggressive moves solo, so adding 2 ECs was seen as a CHECK on him; SESHAN (CEC 1990-96) challenged the constitutionality; SC upheld it in T.N. SESHAN v. UNION OF INDIA (1995). Today's structure: 1 CEC + 2 ECs; all have EQUAL voting power; decisions by majority. RANK: CEC = rank of SC judge (salary, status); EC = rank of SC judge now too (after 2022 equalisation). ALL Commission members appointed by the President. T.N. SESHAN's tenure (1990-96) TRANSFORMED the ECI: enforced MODEL CODE OF CONDUCT strictly, issued voter ID cards (EPIC), cracked down on electoral malpractices (booth capturing, paid news, bribery). Called the 'Indian Eliot Ness'; RAMON MAGSAYSAY award 1996. Died Nov 2019. under PM Narasimha Rao (after brief multi-member 1989-90 phase + reversal).

(A) 26 January
(B) 25 JANUARY
(C) 15 August
(D) 1 October
cards.back:

Constitutional Bodies — NATIONAL VOTERS' DAY (NVD) — celebrated on 25 JANUARY every year to mark the FOUNDATION DAY of the ECI (25 January 1950, one day before Republic Day). OBJECTIVE: (1) encourage young voters (aged 18+) to ENROL in electoral rolls + collect their voter ID (EPIC); (2) spread electoral awareness + participation. CONDUCTED at booth level across 10+ lakh polling stations on 25 Jan every year. EACH YEAR has a theme — 'Nothing Like Voting, I Vote for Sure' etc. BEST ELECTORAL PRACTICES AWARDS: presented to states, DEOs, NGOs + media on NVD. SVEEP (Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation) is the ECI's flagship programme for voter awareness. WORLD ELECTION: India is the LARGEST democracy — 2024 Lok Sabha elections had 96.88 crore registered voters (~97 crore), 64.64 crore voted (turnout ~66.14%). The 2024 election was the largest democratic exercise in human history. First general elections 1951-52 had 17.3 crore voters + took 4 months. Voter ID (EPIC) first issued 1993 under CEC T.N. Seshan. Voting age lowered from 21 to 18 by 61st CAA (1989) — effective from 1989 general election. foundation day of ECI (established 25 Jan 1950, one day before Republic Day).

EVOLUTION: first adopted in Kerala during 1960 assembly elections; gradually accepted by all major parties; formalised by ECI in its present form in 1991 (T.N. Seshan-era strict enforcement). STATUS: NOT a law; not enforceable in courts; moral + political commitment among parties. But ECI ENFORCES it via its Art 324 powers — can de-register parties, disqualify candidates for grave violations. OPERATES from the date of ELECTION ANNOUNCEMENT (not notification) until the election process is completed. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) Parties/candidates must not (a) aggravate communal tensions; (b) use/abuse govt machinery for party work; (c) make promises using taxpayers' money just before election; (d) criticise private lives of opponents. (2) RULING PARTY under special restrictions: no new project announcements, no transfers of key officials without ECI clearance, no use of govt guest houses for party events, no use of govt funds for vehicles/ads. VIOLATIONS: 'censure', FIR under RPA/IPC, notice-issuing for explanation. HISTORIC CASES: 2019 MCC violations against Modi + Rahul over speeches; 2022 Yogi 'Abba Jaan' speech violation. Some parties have demanded MCC be given LEGAL TEETH; ECI opposes — flexibility + speed more valuable. morally binding, not legally enforceable; enforced by ECI.

cards.front:
ELECTRONIC VOTING MACHINES (EVMs) were FIRST USED in a general election in India in:

(A) 1982 (Parur assembly by-election in Kerala)
(B) 2004
(C) 1996
(D) 1989
cards.back:
(B) 2004

Constitutional Bodies — EVM CHRONOLOGY in India: (1) 1977 — EVM concept developed by ECI with Electronics Corp. of India (ECIL) + Bharat Electronics (BEL). (2) 1982 — FIRST USE: PARUR assembly constituency BY-election in Kerala (50 polling stations). Result was challenged in court (AC George v. State — SC ruled EVM use was ultra vires; Parliament needed to amend RPA). (3) 1989 — RPA amended to legally permit EVMs. (4) 1998 — EVMs used in select constituencies of Rajasthan, MP, Delhi. (5) 1999 — used in 46 Lok Sabha constituencies. (6) 2001 — first FULL STATE election: Tamil Nadu (also Kerala, Puducherry, WB). (7) 2004 GENERAL ELECTION — FIRST FULL LOK SABHA election conducted entirely on EVMs (all 543 seats). ALL ELECTIONS since 2004 have used EVMs. (8) 2013 — VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) introduced in Nagaland by-election; 2019 LS was the first GE with VVPAT at ALL booths. COMPONENTS: Control Unit (with Presiding Officer) + Ballot Unit (in the voting compartment); max 16 candidates per BU; up to 4 BUs cascadable for 64 candidates; machines run on batteries (no mains power needed). TAMPERING: ECI maintains EVMs are STANDALONE (not networked) + one-time programmable (OTP chips) + tamper-evident. SC has repeatedly upheld integrity. CRITICS demand return to ballot papers. TOTAL EVMs deployed 2024 GE: ~55 lakh units. first GENERAL ELECTION where EVMs were used NATIONWIDE; EVMs had been used in phases from 1999.

cards.front:
NOTA (None Of The Above) option on EVMs was introduced following a 2013 Supreme Court judgment. Which case?

(A) Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
(B) PEOPLE'S UNION FOR CIVIL LIBERTIES (PUCL) v. UNION OF INDIA (2013)
(C) Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
(D) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cards.back:
(B) PEOPLE'S UNION FOR CIVIL LIBERTIES (PUCL) v. UNION OF INDIA (2013)

Constitutional Bodies — PUCL v. UNION OF INDIA (27 Sep 2013) — landmark SC judgment directing ECI to include a NOTA (None Of The Above) button on EVMs + ballot papers to enable voters to reject ALL candidates. Based on the FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT under Art 19(1)(a) (speech + expression — vote = expression) + Right to negative vote. FIRST USE: 2013 state assembly elections (Delhi, Chhattisgarh, MP, Rajasthan, Mizoram). NOTA SYMBOL: a ballot paper with a CROSS marked through it, designed by NID Ahmedabad. EFFECT: currently purely SYMBOLIC — even if NOTA gets more votes than any candidate, the candidate with the highest NON-NOTA votes still wins. Parties with NOTA-HIGH constituencies see political pressure. Some countries (Russia, Ukraine had 'against all' option earlier). 2024 Lok Sabha: Indore saw Congress candidate withdraw late → NOTA got 2.18 LAKH votes (second place; highest NOTA vote share ever in a single LS seat — 14%). ECI has proposed binding NOTA — if NOTA wins, election be re-held with new candidates — but PARLIAMENT has not legislated this. MAHARASHTRA State Election Commission (for local body polls) has made NOTA the de-facto 'fictional elected candidate' — if NOTA leads, re-polling. Goa ordered similar in 2023. NOTA turnout typically 1-2% nationally; rises to 4-5% in constituencies with weak candidates. SC directed ECI to provide NOTA on ballot paper / EVM.

cards.front:
The minimum age to CONTEST a Lok Sabha election is:

(A) 18 years
(B) 25 YEARS
(C) 21 years
(D) 30 years
cards.back:
(B) 25 YEARS

Constitutional Bodies — AGE REQUIREMENTS to CONTEST Indian elections — per the Constitution: (1) LOK SABHA + State Legislative Assembly: 25 years (Art 84(b), 173(b)). (2) RAJYA SABHA + State Legislative Council: 30 years (Art 84(b) for RS; Art 173(b) for LC). (3) PRESIDENT of India: 35 years (Art 58(1)(b)). (4) VICE-PRESIDENT of India: 35 years (Art 66(3)(b)). (5) GOVERNOR of State: 35 years (Art 157). VOTING age: 18 YEARS (reduced from 21 by 61st CAA 1989 by Rajiv Gandhi government). OTHER DISQUALIFICATIONS for contesting (Art 102 + RPA 1951): (a) unsound mind declared by competent court; (b) undischarged insolvent; (c) holding office of profit under Government; (d) non-citizen of India; (e) conviction for certain offences (RPA Sec 8 — if convicted >2 years jail, disqualified for 6 years after release; Lily Thomas v. UoI, 2013 — SC ruled conviction causes IMMEDIATE disqualification from membership, not just contesting). (f) Failure to lodge election expenses. (g) disqualification under ANTI-DEFECTION LAW (10th Schedule). NO EDUCATIONAL qualification mandated at central level for LS/Assembly; some states have imposed them for PANCHAYAT elections (SC upheld Haryana's min qualification in 2015 Rajbala case — controversially). as per Article 84(b) of the Constitution + Section 4 of the RPA 1951.

cards.front:
The CURRENT ceiling on ELECTION EXPENDITURE for a Lok Sabha candidate (as of 2022 revision) is:

(A) ₹10 lakh
(B) ₹95 LAKH (bigger states) / ₹75 LAKH
(C) ₹1 crore
(D) No ceiling
cards.back:
(B) ₹95 LAKH (bigger states) / ₹75 LAKH

Constitutional Bodies — ELECTION EXPENDITURE LIMITS — set by ECI via Conduct of Election Rules 1961, periodically revised. CURRENT limits (revised Jan 2022 based on ECI committee): (1) LOK SABHA — ₹95 LAKH (big states: AP, UP, TN, Maha, etc.) / ₹75 LAKH (small states + UTs: Goa, Sikkim, Arunachal, etc.). (2) VIDHAN SABHA — ₹40 LAKH (big states) / ₹28 LAKH (small states). Earlier 2014-2022: ₹70L LS big, ₹54L LS small. RATIONALE: account for inflation, rising campaign costs (media, GPS-tagged vehicles, mobile app costs). REPORTING: candidates must LODGE EXPENDITURE within 30 days of result; penalty for not doing so = disqualification for 3 years. TRACKING: ECI deploys Flying Squads, Video Surveillance Teams, Static Surveillance Teams, Accounting Teams. SEIZED cash/liquor/freebies during 2024 LS: ~₹10,000+ crore (highest ever). POLITICAL PARTIES: NO CEILING on party expenditure (only candidate; a loophole parties exploit heavily for 'party publicity'). Voluntary disclosure norms by ECI + IT returns filing. ELECTORAL BONDS (2018-2024) were struck down by SC in Feb 2024 (ADR v. UOI) — anonymity + unlimited corp donations unconstitutional; ordered SBI to disclose donor list. REGISTERED PARTIES: over 2,500 (as of 2024); only ~6 national + 50+ state parties. revised by ECI Jan 2022 from earlier ₹70/54 L; smaller states.

cards.front:
The VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) was introduced to:

(A) Replace EVMs
(B) PROVIDE A PAPER RECORD of each EVM vote, visible to the voter briefly, to allow VERIFICATION + audit in case of disputes
(C) Speed up counting
(D) Track voter identity
cards.back:
(B) PROVIDE A PAPER RECORD of each EVM vote, visible to the voter briefly, to allow VERIFICATION + audit in case of disputes

Constitutional Bodies — VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) — an ATTACHMENT to the EVM that prints a PAPER SLIP showing the voter's choice (candidate name + party symbol) for ~7 SECONDS after the voter presses the EVM button. Slip is visible through a TRANSPARENT window, then drops into a SEALED BOX (voter does not take it). PURPOSE: (a) allow voter to VERIFY her vote was recorded correctly; (b) provide a PAPER AUDIT TRAIL for manual recount in case of dispute; (c) address EVM-tampering allegations. HISTORY: (1) 2010 ECI ordered trials. (2) 2013 FIRST USED in Nagaland (Noksen AC by-election). (3) SEP 2013: SC in Subramanian Swamy v. ECI ruled VVPAT is 'indispensable for free + fair elections'. (4) 2019 Lok Sabha — first GENERAL ELECTION with VVPAT at ALL booths. (5) 2019 SC direction: 5 VVPAT SLIPS per assembly segment to be manually counted + matched with EVM — now standard. 2024 FURTHER PILs for 100% VVPAT-EVM matching were DISMISSED by SC (Apr 2024) — ruled existing 5-booth sample sufficient; 100% match not needed. VVPAT UNITS: ~17 lakh deployed in 2024 GE. MANUFACTURED by BEL + ECIL. NOT connected to any network; thermal printer with special ink; requires dry + dust-free storage.

cards.front:
The Election Commission of India became a multi-member body permanently from:

(A) 1950
(B) 1 October 1993 (T.N. Seshan era)
(C) 1969
(D) 2009
cards.back:
(B) 1 October 1993 (T.N. Seshan era)

Constitutional Bodies — ECI — single-member body (CEC alone) from 1950 to 1989. Briefly became 3-member in 1989 (Dinesh Goswami's reforms), reverted to single in 1990, and made permanently 3-member from 1 October 1993 — during T.N. Seshan's tenure. Currently 1 CEC + 2 ECs. CEC and ECs have equal say; majority decision rules. CEC removable only by impeachment (Articles 324(5), same as SC judge). ECs removable on CEC's recommendation.

cards.back:

Constitutional Bodies — T.N. Seshan — 10th CEC (December 1990 – December 1996). Reforms: enforcement of Model Code of Conduct, voter ID cards (EPIC), action against booth capturing, enforcement of expenditure limits, mandatory affidavits. First CEC — Sukumar Sen (1950-58). cards.front:
Recognition of a political party as a 'NATIONAL party' by ECI requires the party to fulfill ANY ONE of the following — which is INCORRECT?

(A) Has 2% LS seats from at least 3 states
(B) Recognised as state party in at least 4 states
(C) Has at least 200 MPs across LS + RS
(D) Has secured 6% valid votes in 4 states + 4 LS seats
cards.back:
(C) Has at least 200 MPs across LS + RS

Constitutional Bodies — ECI conditions for NATIONAL party (any one): (1) 6% valid votes in any 4 states + ≥4 LS seats; (2) 2% LS seats from at least 3 different states (current requirement = 11 LS seats from 3 states); (3) recognised as state party in at least 4 states. There is NO 200-MP threshold. Currently ~6 national parties: BJP, Congress, BSP, NPP, AAP, CPI-M (varies as ECI reviews periodically). 'State party' has separate criteria. Reserved election symbols are tied to recognition.

cards.front:
The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body created by which Article?

(A) Article 280, providing for the Finance Commission
(B) Article 324, providing for the Election Commission
(C) Article 148, dealing with the Comptroller & Auditor General
(D) Article 76, dealing with the Attorney General of India
cards.back:

Constitutional Bodies — Article 324 — Election Commission of India (ECI). Established 25 January 1950 (the day before India became a republic). National Voters' Day celebrated annually on 25 Jan. Independent constitutional body. Conducts elections to Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies + Councils, Office of President + Vice-President. State elections (panchayats, municipalities) are the State Election Commissions' job under Articles 243K and 243ZA — separate bodies, not ECI.

(B) Multi-member: CEC + 2 Election Commissioners (since 1993)
(C) Five Election Commissioners decided by ruling party
(D) Three Election Commissioners chosen by Supreme Court alone
cards.back:

cards.front:
The CHIEF ELECTION COMMISSIONER (CEC) can be REMOVED FROM OFFICE:

(A) By the President alone at his sole discretion at any time
(B) Only by the procedure used to remove a Supreme Court judge
(C) By the Prime Minister together with cabinet approval
(D) By a vote of two-thirds of the ruling party in Parliament
cards.back:
(B) Only by the procedure used to remove a Supreme Court judge

Constitutional Bodies — Article 324(5) — CEC can be removed only via the SAME procedure as a Supreme Court Judge — i.e., by IMPEACHMENT: requires majority of total membership of EACH House of Parliament + 2/3 of those present and voting. Grounds: PROVED MISBEHAVIOUR or INCAPACITY. Strong protection ensures independence. ELECTION COMMISSIONERS (other than CEC) — can be removed only on the recommendation of the CEC (a weaker protection). Distractor 1 wrongly gives President discretion. Distractors 3, 4 wrongly involve cabinet / ruling-party power.

(C) Comes into force only on polling day every election cycle

cards.front:
VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) was introduced in Indian elections to:

(A) Replace the EVM completely with paper ballots once again
(B) Provide a paper-slip record verifying each EVM vote cast
(C) Speed up the counting of votes after polling concludes
(D) Allow voting from home through a paper postal ballot
cards.back:
(B) Provide a paper-slip record verifying each EVM vote cast

Constitutional Bodies — VVPAT — paper slip showing the candidate name + symbol of the chosen vote, visible behind a glass for ~7 seconds, then deposited in a sealed box. Allows post-election verification — EC mandated since 2019, slips from 5 randomly chosen polling stations per assembly constituency are matched against EVM count. Reasoning: address allegations about EVM tampering. SC (Apr 2024) — declined 100% VVPAT verification but kept the 5/constituency rule. Distractor 1 — VVPAT supplements EVM, doesn't replace. Distractor 3 — actually adds time. Distractor 4 — different mechanism (postal ballot for absentee voting).

cards.front:
The first Chief Election Commissioner of India was:

(A) T.N. Seshan, the famous reformist CEC of the early 1990s
(B) Sukumar Sen, who oversaw the first general election in 1951-52
(C) M.S. Gill, who later became a Union Cabinet Minister
(D) James Michael Lyngdoh, of the Bihar 2005 election fame
cards.back:
(B) Sukumar Sen, who oversaw the first general election in 1951-52

Constitutional Bodies — Sukumar Sen (ICS officer) — FIRST CEC of India, 1950-1958. Conducted the FIRST GENERAL ELECTIONS (1951-52) — a logistical marvel: 173 million eligible voters, only 15% literate, 224,000 polling booths, 2 million ballot boxes, ~16,500 candidates for 489 LS seats. He pioneered the use of separate ballot boxes and party symbols (necessary for illiterate voters). T.N. SESHAN (CEC 1990-96) — 10th CEC, transformed the office: introduced voter ID cards, enforced MCC strictly. Lyngdoh (2001-04) — known for free + fair Bihar 2005 polls.

cards.front:
NOTA (None Of The Above) was introduced as a voting option in Indian general elections starting from:

(A) 2009 Lok Sabha elections, on initial Supreme Court suggestion
(B) 2013 state elections, after Supreme Court order in PUCL v. Union of India
(C) 2019 Lok Sabha elections, with new EVM design changes
(D) 2024 elections, as part of pandemic-era voting reforms
cards.back:
(B) 2013 state elections, after Supreme Court order in PUCL v. Union of India

Constitutional Bodies — NOTA — introduced 2013 (Sept 2013 SC ruling in PUCL v. Union of India). First used in November 2013 state elections (Chhattisgarh, MP, Rajasthan, Mizoram, Delhi). Allows voters to formally REJECT all candidates without spoiling the ballot. SYMBOL — a stylised ballot paper with a black cross. NOTA votes don't elect anyone (highest non-NOTA vote-getter wins) — essentially a 'protest' vote. Recently the SC reaffirmed (2024) that NOTA majority doesn't trigger re-election in single-candidate constituencies, though the ECI introduced 're-election' if NOTA wins, in some specific conditions.

The 'NOTA' (None of the Above) option on Indian electronic voting machines was introduced on the directive of the Supreme Court in:

The 'Anti-Defection Law' was added to the Constitution by the:

cards.front:
The 'NOTA' (None Of The Above) option on Indian ballots was introduced after which Supreme Court judgment?

(A) Indra Sawhney 1992
(B) PUCL v Union of India 2013
(C) Kesavananda Bharati 1973
(D) Vishakha 1997
cards.back:

The NATIONAL HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION (NHRC) of India was established in:

(A) 1950, alongside the framing of the Indian Constitution
(B) 1993, under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
(C) 2005, alongside the Right to Information Act, 2005

cards.back:

Constitutional Bodies — NHRC established by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHR Act). Inaugurated on 12 October 1993; HQ at New Delhi. STATUTORY (not constitutional) body. Mandate: investigate human rights violations by public officials, intervene in court proceedings, study international treaties, promote awareness. Powers: civil court for evidence-gathering; recommendations are not binding but carry moral weight. India became a signatory to the Paris Principles (1991) on national human rights institutions, which prompted setting up NHRC.

cards.front:
The NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW) was established under:

(A) Article 15(3) of the Constitution of India
(B) National Commission for Women Act, 1990
(C) Domestic Violence Act enacted in the year 2005
(D) Right to Information Act of the year 2005
cards.back:
(B) National Commission for Women Act, 1990

Constitutional Bodies — NCW — created by the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. Began functioning January 1992. Headquarters: New Delhi. Statutory body (not constitutional). Functions: investigate constitutional + legal safeguards for women, recommend remedial action, take up complaints, fund research, review existing laws. Composition: Chairperson + 5 members (each with relevant experience), all appointed by Centre. Article 15(3) PERMITS special provisions for women + children but is not the legal basis for NCW. The Domestic Violence Act 2005 is enforced by Protection Officers + magistrates, not by NCW itself.
cards.option1: Article 15(3) of the Constitution of India
cards.option2: Domestic Violence Act enacted in the year 2005
cards.option3: Right to Information Act of the year 2005

cards.front:
The recommendations of the NHRC are:

(A) Legally binding on the Centre and on every state government
(B) Non-binding but generally acted upon as moral persuasion
(C) Equivalent to a Supreme Court order in every legal sense
(D) Binding only on Union Territories under direct Centre rule
cards.back:
(B) Non-binding but generally acted upon as moral persuasion

Constitutional Bodies — NHRC recommendations are NOT legally binding — only persuasive. Government must respond within 1 month explaining if it accepts or rejects. NHRC can move the courts (via Section 18 of the Act) and approach the Supreme Court / High Courts directly for enforcement of human rights. Critics call NHRC a 'toothless tiger' for this reason. Distractor 3 — only the SC's own orders are binding. Distractor 4 — UT vs state distinction doesn't change the binding nature.

cards.option2: Equivalent to a Supreme Court order in every legal sense
cards.option3: Binding only on Union Territories under direct Centre rule

cards.front:
Which of these is NOT among the major functions of the NCW?

(A) Investigating and reporting on women's safeguards under law
(B) Issuing legally binding rulings against the perpetrators
(C) Looking into individual complaints of women's rights violations
(D) Recommending amendments to laws for better gender protection
cards.back:
(B) Issuing legally binding rulings against the perpetrators

Constitutional Bodies — NCW does NOT issue legally binding rulings against perpetrators (it can only investigate, recommend, refer to police/courts). Distractor 1 = real function. Distractor 3 = real function (NCW receives complaints, especially via its Complaint and Counselling Cell). Distractor 4 = real function (e.g., NCW's recommendations led to changes in dowry, sexual-harassment laws). The Commission also reports annually to Parliament.

cards.front:
STATE HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSIONS (SHRCs) — separate from NHRC — were also provided for under the 1993 Act. SHRC chairperson must be:

(A) A retired Indian Civil Service officer of cabinet rank
(B) A retired chief justice or judge of a High Court
(C) Senior member of the state's ruling political party only
(D) Director general of police of the concerned state
cards.back:
(B) A retired chief justice or judge of a High Court

Constitutional Bodies — SHRC Chairperson — retired Chief Justice of HC or Judge of HC (eligibility expanded by 2019 Amendment). Members: judicial member + 1 person with HR knowledge. SHRCs handle violations under STATE LIST + CONCURRENT LIST subjects; NHRC handles UNION LIST (and concurrent issues that the state has not addressed). NHRC can transfer cases to SHRC; SHRC can refer matters to NHRC. As of 2024, ~26 states have established SHRCs.

cards.front:
Who APPOINTS the Solicitor General of India?

(A) Appointments Committee of Cabinet (ACC)
(B) President directly via notification
(C) Supreme Court of India only
(D) Bar Council of India panel
cards.back:
(A) Appointments Committee of Cabinet (ACC)

Constitutional Bodies — The SOLICITOR GENERAL OF INDIA (SG) is appointed by the APPOINTMENTS COMMITTEE OF THE CABINET (ACC) — chaired by the PRIME MINISTER, includes the Home Minister + Minister of Law & Justice. This is DIFFERENT from the ATTORNEY GENERAL (AG), who is appointed DIRECTLY BY THE PRESIDENT (Article 76). KEY DISTINCTION: AG is a CONSTITUTIONAL POST (Article 76); SG and Additional SG are STATUTORY/Government posts (NOT mentioned in the Constitution). HIERARCHY of GOVERNMENT LAW OFFICERS: (1) ATTORNEY GENERAL of India (Art 76) — top-most. (2) SOLICITOR GENERAL of India — second-rank. (3) ADDITIONAL SOLICITORS GENERAL (currently 4-6 positions). (4) ASSISTANT SOLICITORS GENERAL (HCs). (5) Standing Counsels, government counsels at HC/SC. ROLE OF SG: assists the AG, represents the Government of India in important cases, prepares legal opinions on complex government matters. CURRENT SG (as of April 2026): Tushar Mehta (since 2018, longest-serving SG in recent times). PREDECESSORS: Ranjit Kumar (2014-17), Mohan Parasaran (2013-14), Gopal Subramanium (2009-11). TENURE: typically 3 years; renewable. PYQ FREQUENCY: SG-AG distinction is a top UPSC, MPSC polity MCQ — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The Solicitor General of India is which RANK among government law officers?

(A) Second (after Attorney General only)
(B) First and topmost rank position
(C) Third (after AG and Add SGs)
(D) Equal in rank with the AG himself
cards.back:
(A) Second (after Attorney General only)

Constitutional Bodies — GOVERNMENT LAW OFFICERS HIERARCHY: (1) ATTORNEY GENERAL of INDIA (AG) — TOP, constitutional post (Art 76). (2) SOLICITOR GENERAL of INDIA (SG) — SECOND. (3) Additional Solicitors General (ASGs). (4) Assistant SGs (at HC level). KEY ROLE OF SG: ASSISTS the AG; takes the lead in complex constitutional matters. The SG often appears in court when the AG is unavailable or when the case is delegated. STATUS: SG-AG are not in a 'reporting' relationship — both are independent law officers, but in PROTOCOL the AG outranks SG. AG'S STATUS: equivalent to a Cabinet Minister (Art 76); attends Parliament (right of audience) but not a Member; cannot vote. SG: NO right to attend Parliament. EMOLUMENTS: AG draws salary equal to SC judge (~Rs 2.5 lakh/month + perks); SG ~similar but a step lower. CURRENT (2026): AG = R. Venkataramani (since Sept 2022); SG = Tushar Mehta. CASES SG DEFENDED: Article 370 abrogation (Kashmir), CAA, Sabarimala temple-entry case, electoral bonds, Ayodhya verdict assistance. PYQ FREQUENCY: hierarchy of law officers is 1× per UPSC, MPSC, state PSC cycle.
cards.option3: Equal in rank with the AG himself

cards.front:
The post of Solicitor General of India is mentioned in which document?

(A) Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987
(B) Article 76 of Constitution of India (option here)
(C) Indian Penal Code, 1860 sections (option here)
(D) Code of Civil Procedure 1908 here (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987

Constitutional Bodies — The SG and ASGs are governed by the LAW OFFICERS (CONDITIONS OF SERVICE) RULES, 1987 — a STATUTORY framework, NOT a constitutional one. CONTRAST: ATTORNEY GENERAL is created by ARTICLE 76 of the Constitution (a constitutional post). KEY IMPLICATION: SG can be APPOINTED, SUSPENDED, or REMOVED by the executive (ACC) at its discretion — no constitutional protection. AG, by contrast, is a constitutional post but holds office DURING THE PLEASURE of the PRESIDENT (effectively the Cabinet) — also removable, but historically AG resignation accompanies a change of government. ELIGIBILITY for SG/ASG (per Rules): must be qualified to be a JUDGE of HIGH COURT — ie, advocate of HC for ≥10 years OR has held judicial office for ≥10 years. CONVENTION: SG is usually elevated AG when AG retires (e.g., Mukul Rohatgi, K.K. Venugopal had similar trajectories). LAW MINISTRY: oversees law officers' day-to-day functioning. CURRENT ASGs (2026): N. Venkataraman (revenue/tax cases), Vikramjit Banerjee, Aishwarya Bhati (first woman ASG, 2021), among others. PYQ ANGLE: 'is SG constitutional or statutory?' is a UPSC PT topic — 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.option3: Code of Civil Procedure 1908 here (option here)

cards.front:
Who is the FIRST and ONLY constitutional law officer mentioned in the Indian Constitution?

(A) Attorney General (Article 76)
(B) Solicitor General of India here
(C) Chief Justice of India alone
(D) Chairman of Bar Council India
cards.back:
(A) Attorney General (Article 76)

Constitutional Bodies — ARTICLE 76 — only the ATTORNEY GENERAL OF INDIA is mentioned in the Constitution as the first law officer of the Government of India. KEY PROVISIONS of Art 76: (1) President APPOINTS AG. (2) Must be qualified to be a SC judge (ie, citizen, age ≥ 35, HC judge for 5 yrs OR HC advocate for 10 yrs). (3) Holds office during PRESIDENT'S PLEASURE. (4) Receives such REMUNERATION as the President may determine. (5) DUTY: to give legal advice to GOI on matters referred by President; appear in SC on behalf of GOI. (6) Has RIGHT OF AUDIENCE in ALL COURTS in India. (7) MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT-LIKE PRIVILEGES: can take part in Parliamentary proceedings (BOTH HOUSES + committees) but CANNOT VOTE. He's NOT an MP. AG'S RANK: equivalent to Cabinet Minister; precedes State Chief Justices; accompanies PM/President at protocol events. RESTRICTIONS on AG: cannot advise / hold brief AGAINST GOI; cannot accept Cabinet posts; can hold private practice if permitted. CONTRAST WITH ADVOCATE GENERAL (states, Article 165) — analogous role at state level; appointed by Governor. SG/ASG/State Standing Counsels: NOT mentioned in Constitution. PYQ FREQUENCY: AG vs other law officers is a perennial UPSC, MPSC topic.

cards.front:
Which Article of the Constitution provides for an ADVOCATE GENERAL at the STATE level?

(A) Article 165 (state-level law officer)
(B) Article 76 (centre-level officer)
(C) Article 124 (Supreme Court topic)
(D) Article 233 (district judge topic)
cards.back:
(A) Article 165 (state-level law officer)

Constitutional Bodies — ARTICLE 165 — provides for an ADVOCATE GENERAL OF THE STATE — analogous to Attorney General at the Central level, but for state governments. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) Appointed by GOVERNOR. (2) Must be qualified to be a HIGH COURT judge. (3) Holds office during GOVERNOR'S PLEASURE. (4) Receives such remuneration as Governor determines. (5) DUTY: legal advice to STATE GOVT on matters referred to him. (6) RIGHT OF AUDIENCE: can address state legislative assembly + committees but CANNOT VOTE. CONTRAST: AG (Centre, Art 76) vs Advocate General (State, Art 165). FUNCTIONALLY analogous; CONSTITUTIONALLY parallel. ADVOCATE GENERAL OF STATE rank: equivalent to State Cabinet Minister. STATE LAW OFFICERS HIERARCHY: (1) Advocate General. (2) Additional Advocates General. (3) Government Pleaders / Standing Counsels. SAMPLE current (2026): different per state. STATE — RECENT TRENDS: many states have started appointing senior counsels with strong constitutional reputations to AG roles, recognizing the need for elite legal representation. KEY DISTINCTIONS — AG of India vs SG: AG = Art 76 constitutional; SG = statutory under 1987 Rules. AG of state (Advocate General) = Art 165 constitutional. PYQ ANGLE: this Article-distinction is a top UPSC, state PSC polity MCQ.

cards.front:
Can the Solicitor General of India have a PRIVATE LEGAL PRACTICE alongside his official duties?

(A) No — restricted from private practice
(B) Yes, freely without any restrictions
(C) Yes, only in Supreme Court alone
(D) Only with Bar Council prior consent
cards.back:
(A) No — restricted from private practice

Constitutional Bodies — Per the LAW OFFICERS (CONDITIONS OF SERVICE) RULES, 1987 — the SOLICITOR GENERAL of INDIA is generally PROHIBITED from private legal practice while holding office. RESTRICTIONS on SG: (1) Cannot advise or hold brief AGAINST the Government of India in any case. (2) Cannot defend ACCUSED persons in criminal cases (without Govt permission). (3) Cannot accept appointment as a director in any company without Govt permission. (4) Cannot be an active member of a political party. CONTRAST WITH ATTORNEY GENERAL: Art 76 traditionally allowed AG private practice (subject to no conflict-of-interest with GOI), but in practice modern AGs typically don't accept private briefs while holding office. WHY THESE RESTRICTIONS: to PREVENT CONFLICT OF INTEREST between government work and private clients. HISTORICAL CONTEXT: in the early decades of the republic, M.C. Setalvad (first AG) maintained private practice; modern norms have tightened. POST-RETIREMENT: SG/AG often return to elite private practice in Supreme Court — high-value litigation work. KNOWN ELITE LAWYERS post-retirement: Soli Sorabjee, K. Parasaran, Mukul Rohatgi, KK Venugopal — all back in active practice. PYQ ANGLE: rare but appears in HJS exams.
cards.option2: Yes, only in Supreme Court alone
cards.option3: Only with Bar Council prior consent

cards.front:
Which is true about the eligibility for APPOINTMENT as Solicitor General of India?

(A) Must be qualified to be HC judge
(B) Must be a former judge of SC
(C) Must have served as MP earlier
(D) Age limit of 65 yrs maximum
cards.back:
(A) Must be qualified to be HC judge

Constitutional Bodies — ELIGIBILITY for SG/ASG: must be QUALIFIED TO BE A HIGH COURT JUDGE — per Article 217 (HC judges qualifications): (a) is or has been a judge of a HC for ≥ 5 yrs, OR (b) has been an ADVOCATE of HC (or two HCs in succession) for ≥ 10 yrs. ELIGIBILITY for AG (Art 76): must be qualified to be a SUPREME COURT JUDGE — per Art 124: (a) HC judge for 5 yrs OR HC advocate for 10 yrs OR distinguished jurist (in opinion of President). NOTE: the eligibility criteria for AG and SC judges are SIMILAR; AG is one rung higher in protocol. NO AGE LIMIT specified in the rules for SG (in practice, appointees are typically 50-65). KEY DIFFERENCE FROM JUDGES: AG/SG can be re-appointed; judges generally cannot be reappointed after retirement (unless ad hoc, Art 128). FAMOUS PRACTITIONERS who became LAW OFFICERS: Sorabjee, Salve, Rohatgi, Venugopal, Tushar Mehta — all came from elite private practice. CASE LOAD: AG/SG handle ~50-100 important cases at any time. SUPPORT: SG draws on the Solicitor General's Office (a team of junior counsels, secretarial staff at Ministry of Law). PYQ FREQUENCY: eligibility specifics are tested 1× per UPSC, MPSC cycle.
cards.option1: Must be a former judge of SC
cards.option2: Must have served as MP earlier

cards.front:
The Anti-Defection law was added to the Constitution by which Constitutional Amendment?

(A) 44th Amendment, in 1978 after the Emergency
(B) 52nd Amendment, in 1985 by the Rajiv Gandhi government
(C) 73rd Amendment, in 1992 for panchayati raj reforms
(D) 91st Amendment, in 2003 strengthening the existing rules
cards.back:
(B) 52nd Amendment, in 1985 by the Rajiv Gandhi government

Emergency & Anti-Defection — 52nd Amendment, 1985 — added the TENTH SCHEDULE to the Constitution. Aim: prevent 'aaya ram gaya ram' political defections that had destabilised governments since the 1960s. The 91st Amendment (2003) significantly strengthened the law — abolished the 'split' provision (1/3 defection allowed) and barred defectors from holding ministerial / paid offices for the rest of the term. Distractor 1 = 44th amendment was about restoring rights changed during Emergency. Distractor 3 = 73rd was about panchayats. Distractor 4 = 91st only AMENDED an existing law, didn't create it.
cards.option2: 73rd Amendment, in 1992 for panchayati raj reforms
cards.option3: 91st Amendment, in 2003 strengthening the existing rules

cards.front:
Under the 10th Schedule, a member of Parliament can be DISQUALIFIED for defection on which ground?

(A) Voting against the Prime Minister's personal preference
(B) Voluntarily giving up party membership or defying party whip
(C) Switching constituencies between two general elections
(D) Failing to attend the parliamentary session for one whole month

(B) Voluntarily giving up party membership or defying party whip

cards.front:
The Indian Constitution provides for THREE types of Emergencies. Article 352 covers:

(A) Financial Emergency
(B) NATIONAL EMERGENCY
(C) State Emergency (President's Rule)
(D) Health Emergency
cards.back:
(B) NATIONAL EMERGENCY

Emergency & Anti-Defection — THREE TYPES OF EMERGENCIES under Indian Constitution (Part XVIII, Articles 352-360): (1) ARTICLE 352 — NATIONAL EMERGENCY on grounds of WAR, EXTERNAL AGGRESSION, or ARMED REBELLION (44th Amend 1978 replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' to raise the bar). (2) ARTICLE 356 — STATE EMERGENCY / PRESIDENT'S RULE — 'failure of constitutional machinery in a state'. (3) ARTICLE 360 — FINANCIAL EMERGENCY — due to threat to financial stability of India. PROCLAIMED 3 TIMES so far nationally (Art 352): (a) 1962 Sino-Indian war (till 1968), (b) 1971 Indo-Pak War (till 1977), (c) 25 June 1975 — Indira Gandhi's INTERNAL EMERGENCY (for 21 months till 21 March 1977). Article 356 used 100+ times (controversial). Article 360 NEVER used (never proclaimed financial emergency). Borrowed from the WEIMAR CONSTITUTION (Germany). war, external aggression, armed rebellion.

cards.front:
The NATIONAL EMERGENCY (Art 352) can be proclaimed by the President only on the WRITTEN recommendation of:

(A) Prime Minister
(B) Union CABINET
(C) Parliament
(D) Attorney General
cards.back:
(B) Union CABINET

Emergency & Anti-Defection — PROCEDURE for National Emergency (post-44th Amendment 1978 safeguards): (1) Proclamation by the President, ONLY upon WRITTEN recommendation of the UNION CABINET (the whole cabinet, not just PM — raised bar). (2) Must be APPROVED by BOTH Houses of Parliament within ONE MONTH by SPECIAL MAJORITY (2/3 of members present + voting AND majority of total membership). (3) Once approved, operates for 6 MONTHS; can be extended every 6 months with fresh parliamentary approval. (4) Can be REVOKED by the President at any time by subsequent proclamation. (5) LOK SABHA can pass a RESOLUTION disapproving → Emergency must be revoked (simple majority suffices for disapproval). These safeguards were introduced BECAUSE of abuses during Indira Gandhi's Emergency (1975-77) — PM had ADVISED Emergency single-handedly, without Cabinet consultation (called a Cabinet meeting only AFTER the proclamation was signed). President FAKHRUDDIN ALI AHMED famously signed at midnight 25 June 1975 — the 'darkest day' of Indian democracy per critics. as modified by the 44th Amendment, 1978.

cards.front:
During a National Emergency under Article 352, which Fundamental Rights can NEVER be suspended?

(A) Article 19 (freedoms)
(B) Articles 20 and 21 — Protection against double jeopardy/ex-post facto/self-incrimination + Right to Life & Personal Liberty (NEVER suspendable post-44th Amendment)
(C) Article 14 (equality)
(D) Article 25 (freedom of religion)
cards.back:
(B) Articles 20 and 21 — Protection against double jeopardy/ex-post facto/self-incrimination + Right to Life & Personal Liberty (NEVER suspendable post-44th Amendment)

Emergency & Anti-Defection — Article 359 (as amended by 44th Amendment 1978): during National Emergency, President can suspend enforcement of any Fundamental Right EXCEPT Articles 20 and 21. (1) ART 20 — Protection: no ex-post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination. (2) ART 21 — Right to Life and Personal Liberty. These are NEVER suspendable. Art 19 rights (freedoms) — automatically suspended when Emergency declared on grounds of WAR or EXTERNAL AGGRESSION (restored post-Emergency); on grounds of ARMED REBELLION, they're NOT auto-suspended. Other FRs (14, 22, 25, 29, 32 etc.) — their enforcement can be suspended by Presidential order. WHY this SAFEGUARD for Arts 20 + 21: the 1975-77 Emergency saw the SC in ADM JABALPUR v. SHIVKANT SHUKLA (1976) rule 4-1 that even Art 21 (right to life) could be suspended (Justice HR Khanna's lone dissent — he was subsequently superseded for the CJI post). This SHAMEFUL decision was overturned by K.S. PUTTASWAMY v UNION (2017) — Right to Privacy case. 44th Amendment specifically amended Art 359 to prevent such suspensions again. Also 44th made it clear mere declaration of Emergency doesn't auto-suspend FRs — need specific Presidential order per Art 359.

cards.front:
PRESIDENT'S RULE (Article 356) imposes direct Central rule on a state. Maximum duration:

(A) 6 months only (no extension)
(B) Initially 6 months
(C) Indefinite
(D) 1 year maximum
cards.back:
(B) Initially 6 months

Emergency & Anti-Defection — ARTICLE 356 — President's Rule / 'State Emergency' imposed when 'the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution'. Grounds: no party has majority, coalition collapses, CM-Governor rift, constitutional breakdown. PROCEDURE: Proclamation by President based on REPORT from GOVERNOR. Must be approved by BOTH Houses of Parliament (SIMPLE MAJORITY) within 2 MONTHS. Once approved, operates for 6 MONTHS. EXTENDABLE with parliamentary approval every 6 months, but MAX 3 YEARS total (Art 356(4)). Beyond 3 years requires specific conditions: emergency under Art 352 in force OR Election Commission certifies elections can't be held. Effects: (a) Governor runs the state on behalf of President; (b) Parliament assumes State Legislature functions; (c) State assembly may be dissolved. 100+ impositions since independence — often MISUSED politically. SARKARIA COMMISSION (1988) recommended restraint. S.R. BOMMAI v. UNION OF INDIA (1994) — landmark case — held Art 356 subject to JUDICIAL REVIEW; floor test of majority should be in Assembly, not Raj Bhavan; SC can strike down dismissals. Most recent: Uttarakhand 2016 (struck down by HC), Arunachal 2016 (struck down by SC). extendable up to 3 YEARS total (with conditions per Article 356(4) & (5)).

cards.front:
The INTERNAL EMERGENCY of 25 June 1975 – 21 March 1977 was proclaimed by:

(A) President Rajendra Prasad
(B) President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
(C) President V.V. Giri
(D) President Zail Singh
cards.back:
(B) President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed

Emergency & Anti-Defection — INTERNAL EMERGENCY — proclaimed on 25 June 1975 by PRESIDENT FAKHRUDDIN ALI AHMED (5th President, 1974-77) on the advice of PM INDIRA GANDHI. DURATION: 21 months (25 June 1975 – 21 March 1977). BACKGROUND: (1) 12 June 1975 — Allahabad HC (Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha) found Indira Gandhi GUILTY of electoral malpractice in Raj Narain v. Indira Gandhi case (Rae Bareli 1971 election), set aside her election, barred her from office for 6 years; (2) Opposition + JAYAPRAKASH NARAYAN called for her resignation, launched 'Sampoorna Kranti' (Total Revolution) movement — even exhorted police + army to disobey unconstitutional orders; (3) To stay in power, Indira advised Emergency on grounds of 'INTERNAL DISTURBANCE' — signed by Ahmed that night, Cabinet informed only next morning. FEATURES: press censorship, arrest of opposition leaders (Vajpayee, Advani, JP, Morarji Desai, Raj Narain), forced sterilisations under Sanjay Gandhi (Delhi slum demolitions at Turkman Gate), 20-point programme, 42nd Amendment passed with extensive changes. 1977 ELECTION: INDIRA lost — JANATA PARTY government (Morarji Desai 1st non-Congress PM). Janata passed 44th Amendment (1978) reversing major Emergency excesses. 'INDIAN DEMOCRACY'S DARKEST HOUR' — per many historians; but supporters argue it stabilised economy. on PM Indira Gandhi's advice.

cards.front:
Financial Emergency under Article 360 has been PROCLAIMED in India how many times since 1950?

(A) Once — 1991 during BoP crisis
(B) NEVER — Article 360 has not been invoked even in 1991 BoP crisis
(C) Three times
(D) Once — 1962 Chinese aggression
cards.back:
(B) NEVER — Article 360 has not been invoked even in 1991 BoP crisis

Emergency & Anti-Defection — FINANCIAL EMERGENCY (ART 360) — has NEVER BEEN PROCLAIMED in Indian history (as of 2026). Even during severe crises like the 1991 BoP crisis (India had reserves for just ~2 weeks of imports; gold pledged to Bank of England to raise $600 million), Art 360 was not invoked. Grounds for Art 360: 'threat to the financial stability or credit of India or any part thereof'. PROCEDURE: Presidential proclamation, approved by BOTH Houses of Parliament by simple majority within 2 months. Once approved, operates UNTIL REVOKED (no max duration — unusual feature). EFFECTS: (1) Union can give directions to States; (2) Salaries + allowances of State employees (including HC + SC judges) can be reduced; (3) Money bills + financial bills may be reserved for Presidential consideration. Article 360 is viewed as a LAST RESORT — invoking it signals international financial distress + could trigger loss of sovereign rating, capital flight. COMPARATIVE: US uses Federal Reserve tools + Congress; many countries have defaulted (Argentina, Sri Lanka 2022, etc.) without invoking a similar clause. 1991 India TACKLED via IMF loan + structural adjustment programme (Manmohan Singh as FM, LPG reforms) — WITHOUT a formal Art 360.

cards.front:
The concept of Emergency provisions in the Indian Constitution was borrowed from which country's constitution?

(A) USA
(B) WEIMAR GERMANY
(C) UK
(D) USSR
cards.back:
(B) WEIMAR GERMANY

Emergency & Anti-Defection — EMERGENCY PROVISIONS in the Indian Constitution borrowed primarily from the WEIMAR CONSTITUTION of Germany (1919, Republic of Weimar between 1919-33). Weimar's Article 48 gave the President (Hindenburg) power to use emergency decrees — used extensively in the 1920s-30s, most infamously by Hitler to seize dictatorial power after 1933 Reichstag fire. This DARK HISTORY was fresh in Constituent Assembly members' minds when they debated Emergency provisions. Some, like H.V. Kamath, opposed these provisions as potentially dangerous. Dr. AMBEDKAR defended them: 'The Constitution as framed requires the presence of a strong Executive in the center, whenever needed to be able to preserve the stability of the country and unity of the federation.' He acknowledged the risk but argued safeguards (parliamentary approval + judicial review) would suffice. The 1975-77 Emergency VINDICATED the worst fears — Emergency WAS misused. 44th Amendment 1978 strengthened safeguards substantially. Emergency provisions in India are thus MORE ELABORATE than most democracies. 'PRESIDENT'S RULE' (Art 356) concept also has echo of central emergency provisions in the Gov of India Act 1935 (sec 93). 1919 Weimar Constitution.

During a NATIONAL EMERGENCY under Art 352, which Fundamental Rights REMAIN PROTECTED (cannot be suspended even via Art 359)?

(B) Articles 20 and 21 (protection against arbitrary conviction + right to life/personal liberty)

Financial Emergency under Article 360 has been proclaimed in India:

(B) Never

(D) Three times

The 1991 crisis was handled through IMF assistance and the opening-up reforms, not via Art 360.

During a National Emergency, most Fundamental Rights can be suspended — but which rights are protected under Article 20 and Article 21 and cannot be suspended?

(A) Right to property
(B) Protection in conviction and right to life/liberty
(C) Right to freedom of speech
(D) Right to constitutional remedies
cards.back:

Emergency & Anti-Defection — The 44th Amendment (1978) guarantees that Art 20 (protection against retrospective criminal laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination) and Art 21 (right to life and personal liberty) can never be suspended, even during a National Emergency. Before 1978 all Fundamental Rights could be suspended. The right to property was removed from the list of FRs in 1978 and is now a legal right under Art 300A.

cards.front:
The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) replaced which phrase in Article 352?

(A) 'External aggression' with 'war'
(B) 'Internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'
(C) 'War' with 'armed aggression'
(D) 'Proclamation' with 'notification'
cards.back:
(B) 'Internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'

Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) became constitutionally mandated through the:

(A) 42nd Amendment, 1976

Mandatory three-tier system (village + intermediate + district) for states with population > 20 lakh. 5-year tenure. Direct elections. Reservation for SC/ST/Women (1/3 → 50% in 20 states). 73rd's urban counterpart — 74th Amendment (Part IX-A, 12th Schedule, 18 subjects) — added municipalities. Both came into force on the same day — 1 June 1993.

cards.front:
The minimum age to contest a Panchayat / Municipality election is:

(A) 18 years
(B) 21 years
(C) 25 years
(D) 30 years
cards.back:
(B) 21 years

Local Self-Government — Article 243F (Panchayats) and Article 243V (Municipalities) — qualifications: (1) registered as voter (so 18 years voting age); (2) attained 21 years of age. cards.front:
The 'Three-Tier' Panchayati Raj structure consists of:

(A) Gram Panchayat, MLA, MP
(B) Gram Panchayat (village) + Panchayat Samiti / Mandal Parishad (block) + Zila Parishad (district)
(C) Tehsil, District, State
(D) Ward, Constituency, State
cards.back:
(B) Gram Panchayat (village) + Panchayat Samiti / Mandal Parishad (block) + Zila Parishad (district)

Local Self-Government — Three-tier system mandated by 73rd Amendment (states with population > 20 lakh). VILLAGE level — Gram Panchayat (head — Sarpanch). BLOCK level — Panchayat Samiti / Janpad / Mandal Parishad. DISTRICT level — Zila Parishad / Zila Panchayat (head — Adhyaksha or President). States < 20 lakh population may have only village + district levels. Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended 3-tier; Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) — 2-tier (Mandal + Zila); only the former was institutionalised.

The State Election Commission (different from ECI) handles elections to:

(C) Rajya Sabha
(D) President of India

The 74th Amendment Act 1992 introduced THREE types of Urban Local Bodies. They are:

(A) Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad
(B) Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area)
(C) Town, City, Megacity
(D) Cantonment Board, NDMC, MCD

(B) Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area)

cards.front:
The first state to introduce the 3-tier Panchayati Raj system on 2 October 1959 (Gandhi Jayanti) — preceding the 73rd Amendment — was:

(A) Karnataka
(B) Rajasthan (Nagaur district)
(C) Madhya Pradesh
(D) Tamil Nadu

Local Self-Government — Rajasthan's Nagaur district — PM Nehru launched first 3-tier Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959. Andhra Pradesh — second (1959). Karnataka was a pioneer in implementing reforms in early 1980s under CM Ramakrishna Hegde. Pre-73rd Amendment, Panchayats existed under State laws (often weak, irregular elections). The Constitution merely had Article 40 (DPSP — 'organise village panchayats') — non-justiciable. 73rd Amendment elevated PRIs to constitutional status.

cards.front:
The 74TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1992) gave constitutional status to:

(A) Urban local bodies (municipalities)
(B) Panchayati Raj rural bodies
(C) Universities and colleges only
(D) Cooperative societies completely
cards.back:
(A) Urban local bodies (municipalities)

Local Self-Government — 74TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT (1992) — gave CONSTITUTIONAL STATUS to URBAN LOCAL BODIES (Municipalities). Came into effect 1 JUNE 1993. ADDED PART IXA + 12TH SCHEDULE + Articles 243P to 243ZG. PARALLEL: 73RD AMENDMENT (also 1992) — for PANCHAYATI RAJ (rural local govt); Part IX + 11th Schedule. THREE-TIER MUNICIPAL STRUCTURE under 74th: (1) NAGAR PANCHAYAT (for AREAS in TRANSITION from rural to urban — population threshold variable). (2) MUNICIPAL COUNCIL (for SMALLER URBAN areas). (3) MUNICIPAL CORPORATION (for LARGER urban areas — typically million-plus cities; e.g., Mumbai's BMC, Delhi's MCD, Chennai Corporation, Kolkata Corporation, Bengaluru BBMP, Hyderabad GHMC). KEY MANDATORY PROVISIONS: (1) ELECTIONS every 5 YEARS; reservation for SC/ST/Women (33% women, since 1992; many states 50%). (2) STATE ELECTION COMMISSION (SEC) conducts elections. (3) STATE FINANCE COMMISSION (every 5 years) recommends financial devolution. (4) WARD COMMITTEES in larger cities. (5) DISTRICT PLANNING COMMITTEE + METROPOLITAN PLANNING COMMITTEE for area-wise plans. (6) 18 SUBJECTS in 12th Schedule (urban planning, water, sanitation, public health, etc.). PROBLEMS: states can VARY IMPLEMENTATION; municipal finances weak; mayors often ceremonial (executive power with State-appointed Commissioner). UPSC angle: 73RD-74TH amendments core GS-2 topic; LOCAL GOVT, decentralization. PYQ FREQUENCY: 74th Amendment in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which is the LARGEST type of urban local body for major cities like Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru?

(A) Municipal Corporation (millon+ cities)
(B) Nagar Panchayat (very small towns)
(C) Municipal Council (mid-size towns)
(D) Township Authority (rare type)
cards.back:
(A) Municipal Corporation (millon+ cities)

Local Self-Government — MUNICIPAL CORPORATION — LARGEST TYPE of urban local body, for cities with population typically > 10 lakh (1 million). Notable examples: (1) BRIHANMUMBAI MUNICIPAL CORPORATION (BMC) — Mumbai; biggest municipal budget in Asia (~₹50,000 crore/year); founded 1888. (2) MUNICIPAL CORPORATION OF DELHI (MCD) — unified back in 2022 (after 2012 trifurcation). (3) BBMP (Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike) — Bengaluru. (4) GHMC (Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation). (5) KMC (Kolkata Municipal Corporation) — founded 1876, oldest. (6) Chennai Municipal Corp — founded 1688 (oldest in India, established by Madras Province council). (7) PCMC (Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corp), AMC (Ahmedabad MC), SMC (Surat MC). KEY OFFICIALS: (1) MAYOR — political head; ceremonial in most cases. (2) MUNICIPAL COMMISSIONER — IAS officer; executive head; APPOINTED by state govt. (3) DEPUTY MAYOR. (4) STANDING COMMITTEE (executive body). (5) WARD COMMITTEES. (6) ELECTED COUNCILLORS — represent wards. KEY POWERS of CORPORATION: water supply, sewage + sanitation, solid-waste management, public health, building permissions, property tax collection, parks, primary education, primary health centres. CHALLENGES: revenue dependency on state grants; political tussles between Mayor + state govt + Commissioner; population pressure. UPSC angle: URBAN GOVERNANCE + smart cities mission + AMRUT scheme. PYQ FREQUENCY: municipal corporation structure in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
How many SUBJECTS are listed in the 12TH SCHEDULE (functions of municipalities)?

(A) 18 subjects (urban planning, water, etc.)
(B) 29 subjects (that's 11th Schedule)
(C) 10 subjects (under-counted)
(D) 25 subjects (over-counted)
cards.back:
(A) 18 subjects (urban planning, water, etc.)

Local Self-Government — 12TH SCHEDULE — added by 74th Amendment 1992; lists 18 SUBJECTS that may be entrusted to MUNICIPALITIES by state legislatures. KEY SUBJECTS (memorize categories — UPSC PT favorite): (1) URBAN PLANNING + town planning. (2) Regulation of land-use + building. (3) Planning for economic + social development. (4) Roads + bridges. (5) WATER SUPPLY (domestic, industrial, commercial). (6) Public health, sanitation, conservancy + solid waste management. (7) Fire services. (8) Urban forestry, ecology, environment. (9) Safeguarding interests of WEAKER SECTIONS (SCs, STs, PHs). (10) SLUM IMPROVEMENT + upgradation. (11) URBAN POVERTY ALLEVIATION. (12) PARKS, gardens, playgrounds. (13) PROMOTION of cultural, educational, aesthetic aspects. (14) BURIAL + cremation grounds. (15) CATTLE pounds + prevention of cruelty to animals. (16) Vital statistics — registration of BIRTHS + DEATHS. (17) Public amenities — STREET LIGHTING, parking, bus stops. (18) Regulation of SLAUGHTER HOUSES + tanneries. CONTRAST WITH 11TH SCHEDULE (PANCHAYATS, 73rd Amendment): 29 subjects — includes agriculture, animal husbandry, fisheries, social forestry, drinking water, fuel + fodder, roads, rural electrification, etc. KEY DIFFERENCE: 12th Schedule subjects are 18 + URBAN focused; 11th Schedule subjects are 29 + RURAL focused. cards.front:
Reservation for WOMEN in municipal bodies under 74th Amendment is:

(A) At least 1/3 of total seats
(B) Less than 10% of seats
(C) Half of all seats compulsorily
(D) No reservation required by law
cards.back:
(A) At least 1/3 of total seats

Local Self-Government — Article 243T (74th Amendment): not less than 1/3 of TOTAL SEATS in municipalities reserved for WOMEN, including SC/ST women (1/3 within each reservation category). Many state laws have INCREASED women's reservation to 50% — including: BIHAR (2007 — first), KARNATAKA, JHARKHAND, KERALA, MAHARASHTRA, RAJASTHAN, GUJARAT, ANDHRA PRADESH, UTTARAKHAND, ODISHA, TAMIL NADU, MADHYA PRADESH, HIMACHAL PRADESH, CHATTISGARH. RESERVATION FOR SC/ST: in proportion to their POPULATION in the area; rotated by seats. RESERVATION FOR OBC: state-by-state (e.g., Maharashtra, Karnataka have 27%; not constitutional mandatory). KEY REASONS: women's representation historically poor; reservation aimed at empowerment + decision-making access. IMPACT — STUDIES: women panchayat/municipal leaders prioritize: WATER (drinking water, public taps), SANITATION (toilets, drainage), CHILD welfare, education, ANGANWADIs. NATIONAL TRAJECTORY: women MPs/MLAs ~14-15% (low); 73rd-74th have created ~14 lakh women representatives at PRI/ULB level — the LARGEST cohort of elected women globally. NARI SHAKTI VANDAN ADHINIYAM (106TH AMENDMENT) — Sept 2023 — passed by Parliament: 33% reservation for WOMEN in LOK SABHA + STATE LEGISLATURES; effective POST-DELIMITATION (Census-based, expected 2027-29). UPSC angle: gender + governance + women's empowerment, GS-2 + GS-1 social issues. PYQ FREQUENCY: women's reservation in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
WHO conducts MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS in a state?

(A) State Election Commission (SEC)
(B) Election Commission of India only
(C) State government directly here
(D) Mayor of the corporation only
cards.back:
(A) State Election Commission (SEC)

Local Self-Government — STATE ELECTION COMMISSION (SEC) — conducts municipal + panchayat elections; created under 74th + 73rd Amendments (Articles 243K, 243ZA). NOT to be confused with ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA (ECI) — which conducts only PARLIAMENTARY + STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY + STATE LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL + Office of PRESIDENT/VP elections. KEY POWERS of SEC: (1) Superintendence, direction, conduct of all local body elections. (2) Preparation of voter rolls. (3) Demarcation of constituencies. (4) Election dispute resolution. (5) Each state has its own SEC; some UTs share with neighboring states. STATE ELECTION COMMISSIONER: appointed by GOVERNOR; tenure 5 years (or as state law); REMOVAL only in same manner as HIGH COURT JUDGE (i.e., difficult — to ensure independence). KEY: SECs have STATE-LEVEL constitutional protection. INDIA's MULTI-LEVEL elections oversight: (1) ECI (Centre) — Lok Sabha + Vidhan Sabha elections. (2) SEC (State) — Panchayat + Municipal elections. CHALLENGES: (1) State govts SOMETIMES delay/postpone local elections through legislation or administrative decisions. (2) SC has held — 5-year-cycle is MANDATORY; cannot extend without due reason. UPSC ANGLE: ELECTION COMMISSIONS + DEMOCRACY HEALTH; recent issues like delayed local elections in some states (e.g., Karnataka BBMP elections delayed several years). PYQ FREQUENCY: ECI vs SEC distinction in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.
