cards.front:
Under 74th Amendment, the TENURE of a Municipality is:

(A) 5 years (mandatory cycle)
(B) 6 years (one-off cycle)
(C) 3 years (a short cycle)
(D) No fixed tenure (varies)
cards.back:
(A) 5 years (mandatory cycle)

Local Self-Government — Article 243U (74th Amendment): MUNICIPALITY's TENURE is 5 YEARS from date of FIRST MEETING after election. After dissolution: ELECTIONS within 6 MONTHS. ELECTION CONSTITUTION must finish: (a) Before expiry of 5-year term, OR (b) Within 6 months from dissolution. KEY: NO POSTPONEMENT beyond 5 years allowed unless: (a) Pre-existing emergency under Article 356 (President's Rule). (b) ELECTORAL ROLLS not ready — narrow ground. SC RULINGS (Kishan Singh Tomar 2006, etc.): 5-year cycle is MANDATORY; SECs MUST hold timely elections; mere delay in delimitation/reservation cannot be excuse. RECENT CASES (2022-2024): (1) KARNATAKA — BBMP (Bengaluru) elections delayed since 2020 (5 years overdue as of 2025) — controversial; SC asked govt to act. (2) HIMACHAL PRADESH, KERALA — local-body elections held on time. (3) WEST BENGAL — held panchayat elections 2023, with controversy over violence. KEY: when local body is dissolved (e.g., due to political reasons), ELECTED BODY must be re-installed within 6 MONTHS — IF less than 6 months left in original term, no fresh election required (acceptable to leave seat vacant briefly). DISSOLUTION GROUNDS: defeat in vote of confidence, mass resignation, dissolution by state govt (with reasons). UPSC ANGLE: democratic decentralization, SC's role in protecting local govt. PYQ FREQUENCY: tenure rules in UPSC PT, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
WHICH committee ('Father of urban local self-government in India') recommended structure now reflected in 74th Amendment?

(A) Rao Committee on URBAN local govt (1987)
(B) Balwantrai Mehta Committee (rural)
(C) Ashok Mehta Committee (rural)
(D) Sarkaria Commission (Centre-State)
cards.back:
(A) Rao Committee on URBAN local govt (1987)

Local Self-Government — RAO COMMITTEE ('Committee on Urban Local Bodies' headed by KN RAO, 1987) — recommended major reforms in URBAN local government, leading to 74th Amendment (1992). RECOMMENDATIONS included: 5-year fixed tenure, women's reservation, financial devolution, ward committees, etc. EARLIER URBAN-FOCUSED REFORMS: ZAKARIA COMMITTEE (1963), RURAL-URBAN RELATIONS COMMITTEE (1966). KEY URBAN SCHEMES + COMMITTEES (memorize): (1) URBAN PLANNING in 5-Year Plans (1st onwards). (2) JNNURM (Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission) 2005 — under PM Manmohan Singh; massive urban infrastructure programme. (3) AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation + Urban Transformation) 2015 — successor to JNNURM. (4) SMART CITIES MISSION 2015 — 100 cities; tech + urban planning + sustainability. (5) HRIDAY (Heritage Cities) 2015. (6) PMAY-U (Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana — Urban) — affordable housing. (7) SWACHH BHARAT MISSION-Urban — sanitation, ODF cities. CONTRAST WITH RURAL: BALWANT RAI MEHTA Committee (1957) — recommended 3-tier PANCHAYATI RAJ; states implemented 1959 onwards (Rajasthan first, 2 Oct 1959). ASHOK MEHTA Committee (1977) — recommended 2-tier (district + Mandal) instead of 3-tier; not adopted. P.K. THUNGON Committee (1988) — recommended PRI constitutional status + 5-year term. L.M. SINGHVI Committee (1986) — also recommended PRI reforms. UPSC angle: history of decentralization in India. PYQ FREQUENCY: Rao Committee + 74th Amendment in UPSC, MPSC 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) introduced PANCHAYATI RAJ as a CONSTITUTIONAL institution, adding:

(A) Part IV to the Constitution
(B) Part IX (Articles 243-243O) + 11th SCHEDULE
(C) Article 370
(D) Part V
cards.back:
(B) Part IX (Articles 243-243O) + 11th SCHEDULE

Local Self-Government — 73RD CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 1992 (effective 24 April 1993) — gave PANCHAYATI RAJ (rural local self-government) CONSTITUTIONAL status. PART IX (Articles 243-243O) inserted. Also added 11TH SCHEDULE listing 29 FUNCTIONAL SUBJECTS that states may DEVOLVE to Panchayats (agriculture, land reforms, rural housing, drinking water, roads, poverty alleviation, primary education, health, etc.) — not mandatory, states have discretion. KEY FEATURES: (1) 3-TIER STRUCTURE — (a) Village level — GRAM PANCHAYAT; (b) Intermediate/block level — PANCHAYAT SAMITI (states with population > 20 lakh must have intermediate tier); (c) District level — ZILLA PARISHAD. (2) GRAM SABHA — general body of ALL REGISTERED VOTERS in the village; village 'assembly' as grassroots democratic body. (3) DIRECT ELECTIONS for all seats at all 3 levels. (4) RESERVATION: (a) 1/3 seats for WOMEN; (b) SC/ST seats proportional to state population; (c) Women + SC/ST reservations intersect (so 1/3 within SC/ST too). Many states have since increased to 50% WOMEN reservation (Bihar 2006 first; 21+ states now). Rotation of reserved seats. (5) 5-YEAR TERM for all Panchayat bodies. (6) STATE ELECTION COMMISSION (SEC) — separate from ECI — to conduct Panchayat + municipal elections (Art 243K). (7) STATE FINANCE COMMISSION (every 5 years) — recommends financial resource-sharing (Art 243I). (8) AUDIT + accounts. (9) DISQUALIFICATIONS + other provisions. 74TH CAA 1992 — parallel amendment for URBAN LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Nagar Palikas / Municipal Corporations / Councils); PART IXA (243P-243ZG) + 12TH SCHEDULE (18 subjects). 3-tier urban: Municipal Corporations (big cities, >10 lakh pop) + Municipal Councils/Municipalities (100K-10 lakh) + Nagar Panchayats (<100K transitional). DEVOLUTION varies widely by state; Kerala + Karnataka = most devolved; UP, Bihar = weak. HISTORICAL ROOTS: (1) Indian village councils ancient (Uttiramerur inscriptions); (2) Balwant Rai Mehta Committee 1957 — first recommended 3-tier; (3) Rajasthan was first state to implement Panchayati Raj (2 Oct 1959, Nagaur by Nehru); (4) Ashok Mehta Committee 1978 — 2-tier; (5) L.M. Singhvi 1986 — constitutional status; (6) 64th + 65th CABs 1989 (Rajiv Gandhi) — introduced, failed in RS; (7) finally 73rd + 74th CAAs by NARASIMHA RAO govt 1992. 29 subjects transferable to Panchayats.

cards.front:
RAJASTHAN became the FIRST state to implement the 3-tier Panchayati Raj system. Inaugurated by Nehru at:

(A) Jaipur
(B) NAGAUR district on 2 OCTOBER 1959
(C) Udaipur
(D) Jodhpur
cards.back:
(B) NAGAUR district on 2 OCTOBER 1959

Local Self-Government — PANCHAYATI RAJ in India — formally inaugurated by PM JAWAHARLAL NEHRU on 2 OCTOBER 1959 (GANDHI JAYANTI) at NAGAUR district of RAJASTHAN. Rajasthan became the FIRST state to implement 3-tier Panchayati Raj. ANDHRA PRADESH followed soon after (1959). BACKGROUND: (1) BALWANT RAI MEHTA COMMITTEE (1957) — set up by Nehru govt to examine working of COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT Programme (launched 1952, 2 Oct) + NATIONAL EXTENSION SERVICE (1953). Found that rural development required DEMOCRATIC DECENTRALISATION. Key recommendations: (a) establish 3-TIER Panchayati Raj structure (Gram Panchayat → Panchayat Samiti → Zilla Parishad); (b) DIRECT elections at village level; (c) indirect at higher levels; (d) executive body; (e) 5-year tenure. (2) NEHRU'S ENTHUSIASTIC adoption + launch. (3) Followed by other states gradually. EVOLUTION: (1) 1950s-60s — EARLY ADOPTION; enthusiasm. (2) 1970s — DECLINE — central schemes bypassed Panchayats; political neglect. (3) ASHOK MEHTA COMMITTEE (1977-78, Janata) — recommended 2-tier (Zilla + Mandal Panchayat); INSTITUTIONALISE through Constitutional amendment. (4) G.V.K. RAO COMMITTEE (1985). (5) L.M. SINGHVI COMMITTEE (1986) — recommended CONSTITUTIONAL RECOGNITION. (6) 64th + 65th CABs (1989) by Rajiv Gandhi — failed in RS. (7) 73rd + 74th CAAs (1992) by Narasimha Rao govt — SUCCESSFUL. KARNATAKA's ZILLA PARISHAD Act 1983 was path-breaking — Ramakrishna Hegde-led Janata Dal govt first gave substantive powers + funds to ZP. GANDHI's DREAM of 'GRAM SWARAJ' (village self-rule) — Panchayati Raj realises it partially; Gandhi envisaged VILLAGES as 'little republics'. Ambedkar was critical — 'what is a village but a sink of localism, den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness + communalism'. Indian Panchayati Raj tries to reconcile BOTH views — grassroots democracy + protection of minorities + welfare planning. STATUS (2024): ~2.6 lakh Panchayats; ~31 LAKH elected representatives at panchayat level (LARGEST DEMOCRATIC DEVOLUTION in world); 13+ LAKH WOMEN representatives (with 1/3 quota; some states 50%). based on recommendations of Balwant Rai Mehta Committee 1957.

cards.front:
The 3-tier PANCHAYATI RAJ structure for rural areas consists of:

(A) Gram Sabha → Nagar Palika → Municipal Corporation
(B) GRAM PANCHAYAT (village) → PANCHAYAT SAMITI (block) → ZILLA PARISHAD (district)
(C) Nyaya Panchayat → Gram Panchayat → District Panchayat
(D) Sarpanch → Pradhan → Sabhapati
cards.back:
(B) GRAM PANCHAYAT (village) → PANCHAYAT SAMITI (block) → ZILLA PARISHAD (district)

Local Self-Government — 3-TIER PANCHAYATI RAJ SYSTEM (per 73rd CAA): (1) GRAM PANCHAYAT (Village level) — covers village(s) with ~500+ population typically; headed by SARPANCH (Pradhan in UP, Mukhiya in Bihar, Ward Member in some); DIRECTLY ELECTED by Gram Sabha; 5-year term. Elected members of Gram Panchayat are called WARD MEMBERS / PANCHS. GRAM SABHA — general body of ALL REGISTERED VOTERS in the village; meets at least 2-4 times/year; discusses + approves GP budget, plans; 'GENERAL ASSEMBLY'. (2) PANCHAYAT SAMITI (intermediate/block level, also called MANDAL PANCHAYAT in KA, JANPAD PANCHAYAT in MP-CG, BLOCK PANCHAYAT in Kerala, KSHETRA PANCHAYAT in UP) — covers a block / tehsil; headed by PRADHAN / CHAIRMAN / BLOCK PRESIDENT. Members DIRECTLY elected (per 73rd CAA); Sarpanches of GPs also ex-officio members. Executes block-level schemes. Intermediate tier is MANDATORY only for states with population >20 LAKH; small states (Goa, NE) may skip. (3) ZILLA PARISHAD (District level, also called DISTRICT PANCHAYAT, DDC in J&K) — covers district; headed by ADHYAKSHA / ZILLA PRAMUKH / DP Chairperson. Members directly elected; PS Pradhans + MPs + MLAs from district ex-officio members (non-voting). Executes district planning + coordinating role. cards.front:
The 74th CAA (1992) constituted URBAN LOCAL BODIES in THREE types, based on city size:

(A) Corporation, Mandal, Ward
(B) MUNICIPAL CORPORATION (large cities), MUNICIPAL COUNCIL/MUNICIPALITY (medium), NAGAR PANCHAYAT
(C) Zilla Parishad, Panchayat Samiti, Gram Panchayat
(D) Only Municipal Corporation
cards.back:
(B) MUNICIPAL CORPORATION (large cities), MUNICIPAL COUNCIL/MUNICIPALITY (medium), NAGAR PANCHAYAT

Local Self-Government — 74TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 1992 — parallel to 73rd; gave URBAN LOCAL BODIES constitutional status. PART IXA (Arts 243P-243ZG) + 12TH SCHEDULE (18 subjects). 3 TYPES of Urban Local Bodies (based on population + characteristics, determined by state Governors): (1) MUNICIPAL CORPORATION (MAHA NAGAR PALIKA) — for LARGER URBAN AREAS (generally >10 lakh / 1 million, varies by state). Headed by MAYOR (elected by Corporators in most; direct election in some states). CEO = MUNICIPAL COMMISSIONER (IAS officer). Examples: BMC (Mumbai — Asia's largest), MCD (Delhi; tripartite + unified 2022 as single MCD), Kolkata Municipal Corporation, Chennai Municipal Corporation, BBMP (Bengaluru), GHMC (Hyderabad), PMC (Pune), NMMC (Navi Mumbai), NDMC (New Delhi, sep. Council). (2) MUNICIPAL COUNCIL / MUNICIPALITY / NAGAR PARISHAD / NAGAR PALIKA — for MEDIUM-sized towns (1 lakh to 10 lakh approx). Headed by CHAIRPERSON / PRESIDENT. CEO = CHIEF MUNICIPAL OFFICER. (3) NAGAR PANCHAYAT (TRANSITIONAL area) — for AREAS IN TRANSITION from rural to urban (typically < 1 lakh population). Headed by President. STRUCTURE COMMON TO ALL 3: (1) WARDS — basic unit; DIRECT ELECTIONS. (2) WARDS COMMITTEES mandatory in cities with population > 3 lakh (Art 243S). (3) RESERVATION: 1/3 seats for WOMEN; SC/ST proportional; OBC (enabling provision — state discretion). (4) TERM: 5 years. (5) STATE ELECTION COMMISSION conducts elections. (6) STATE FINANCE COMMISSION (Art 243Y) recommends resource-sharing. (7) METROPOLITAN PLANNING COMMITTEES (Art 243ZE) for 10 lakh+ cities. (8) DISTRICT PLANNING COMMITTEES (Art 243ZD). 12TH SCHEDULE SUBJECTS (18): urban planning, regulation of land use, roads + bridges, water supply, public health + sanitation + solid waste management, fire services, urban forestry, environment, safeguards of weaker sections, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation, public amenities (parks, gardens, playgrounds), promotion of culture + heritage, burials + cremations, cattle pounds + animal care, registration of births + deaths, street lights, public conveniences (toilets), etc. 74th CAA urban devolution is generally MORE COMPLETE than 73rd rural in most states — cities have stronger tax base (property tax, commercial tax). Part IXA; 12th Schedule 18 subjects; transitional small.

cards.front:
The MAHATMA GANDHI NATIONAL RURAL EMPLOYMENT GUARANTEE ACT (MGNREGA) 2005 GUARANTEES:

(A) Unlimited employment year-round
(B) 100 DAYS of guaranteed wage employment per FINANCIAL YEAR to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for UNSKILLED MANUAL WORK
(C) Permanent govt jobs for rural youth
(D) Universal Basic Income
cards.back:
(B) 100 DAYS of guaranteed wage employment per FINANCIAL YEAR to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for UNSKILLED MANUAL WORK

Local Self-Government — MGNREGA (originally NREGA — NATIONAL RURAL EMPLOYMENT GUARANTEE ACT, 2005; renamed MAHATMA GANDHI NREGA in 2009). Passed on 25 August 2005 (UPA-I, Manmohan Singh); effective from 2 Feb 2006 (initially 200 districts). FLAGSHIP rights-based social security scheme — WORLD's LARGEST public employment programme. GUARANTEES: UP TO 100 DAYS of guaranteed WAGE EMPLOYMENT per financial year, to EVERY RURAL household whose ADULT members volunteer for UNSKILLED MANUAL WORK. WAGE: state-wise, linked to CPI-AL (agricultural labour), revised annually. Current wage range ~₹240-370/day (varies by state). KEY FEATURES: (1) DEMAND-DRIVEN: if work not provided within 15 DAYS of demand, UNEMPLOYMENT ALLOWANCE payable (though states often default). (2) 1/3 beneficiaries must be WOMEN — consistently achieved (women ~54% of person-days). (3) WAGES paid via bank/post office account; DIRECT BENEFIT TRANSFER. (4) Work within 5 KM RADIUS of village; else EXTRA wages. (5) WORKSITE amenities — water, shade, first-aid, creche if 5+ children. (6) 60:40 ratio of LABOUR to MATERIAL cost in works. (7) WORKS categories: water conservation (ponds, check dams — 60%+ of works), land development, rural roads, afforestation, sanitation (SBM toilets), individual assets for SC/ST/BPL (well, irrigation, housing plinth). (8) SOCIAL AUDIT — mandatory by Gram Sabha. ADMINISTRATION: (a) Centrally funded (90% Centre, 10% state for Labour; 75:25 for material). (b) Planned + executed by 3-tier PRI system — GP plans + executes, PS supervises, ZP coordinates. (c) Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) at Centre; State Rural Development Dept. ACHIEVEMENTS: ~7-10 crore households employed each year; ~250-300 crore person-days annually; ₹85,000+ crore annual budget. CRITIQUES: (a) leakages + ghost entries — (Aadhaar + DBT + Geotag of works + Citizen Information Boards + MIS introduced to reduce); (b) delayed payments; (c) states overdraw + Centre plays catch-up; (d) 'jobless growth' dependency — desirable or not?; (e) quality of assets variable. DURING COVID-19 (2020-22), MGNREGA proved a LIFE-LINE — 7.5 crore households worked (highest ever) as migrants returned. MGNREGA linked to other schemes: PMAY-G housing, NRLM livelihoods, SBM-G toilets, DDU-GKY skilling.

cards.front:
The GRAM SABHA is:

(A) Elected governing body of the village
(B) General body of ALL REGISTERED VOTERS of a village/panchayat area
(C) An NGO for rural development
(D) A district-level body
cards.back:
(B) General body of ALL REGISTERED VOTERS of a village/panchayat area

Local Self-Government — GRAM SABHA — 'VILLAGE ASSEMBLY' = GENERAL BODY of ALL REGISTERED VOTERS of a village / GROUP of villages forming a Gram Panchayat area. DEFINED under Article 243(b) of Constitution + state panchayati raj acts. STRUCTURE: (1) All adults (18+) registered as voters in the electoral roll of the village panchayat area = MEMBERS of Gram Sabha; (2) MEETS AT LEAST 2-4 TIMES per year (states vary — many now mandate QUARTERLY meetings); (3) quorum usually 1/10 of members (or 100 persons, whichever lower). FUNCTIONS / POWERS: (1) APPROVE Gram Panchayat ANNUAL BUDGET + PLAN; (2) RECEIVES annual accounts + audit reports; (3) IDENTIFIES BENEFICIARIES of govt schemes (PMAY-G houses, MGNREGA wagework, Ayushman Bharat cards, ration cards); (4) SOCIAL AUDIT of GP works; (5) approves implementation of certain projects; (6) reviews functioning of institutions (schools, Anganwadis, PHCs); (7) in SCHEDULED AREAS (PESA Act 1996), enhanced powers re: land alienation, minor forest produce, minor minerals, planning. GRAM SABHA is DIRECT DEMOCRACY — every voter participates directly, not through representative. Different from GRAM PANCHAYAT (elected members body). PESA ACT (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas Act, 1996) — extends Part IX to 5TH SCHEDULE tribal areas with MODIFICATIONS. States covered: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana. UNIQUE GRAM SABHA POWERS in PESA: (1) consultation MANDATORY on land acquisition; (2) consent required for minor mineral prospecting + granting of concessions; (3) ownership of MINOR FOREST PRODUCE (tendu, mahua, honey, gum, lac); (4) control over money-lending to STs; (5) control over local markets; (6) consultation on welfare schemes. PESA aims to secure SELF-GOVERNANCE for tribal communities. IMPLEMENTATION PATCHY though — forest rights still contested (Forest Rights Act 2006 overlapping), mining clearances often bypass Gram Sabha. Supreme Court's NIYAMGIRI JUDGMENT (2013, Dongria Kondh vs Vedanta) upheld Gram Sabhas' right to reject bauxite mining. SAMATA v. AP (1997) similarly. Gram Sabha is the FUNDAMENTAL DEMOCRATIC UNIT envisaged by Constitution makers — a realisation of Gandhian 'Gram Swaraj'. decision-making + oversight body, mandated to meet at least 2-4 times/year.

cards.front:
The BALWANT RAI MEHTA COMMITTEE (1957) recommended:

(A) Abolishing panchayats
(B) Introduction of 3-TIER PANCHAYATI RAJ with direct election at village level + indirect at higher
(C) Centralised rural administration
(D) Municipal reforms only
cards.back:
(B) Introduction of 3-TIER PANCHAYATI RAJ with direct election at village level + indirect at higher

Local Self-Government — BALWANT RAI MEHTA COMMITTEE (1957) — officially 'Committee on Plan Projects' / 'Team on Community Projects + National Extension Service'. Chaired by BALWANT RAI G. MEHTA (Gujarat Congress leader, later CM of Gujarat). ORIGIN: set up by PLANNING COMMISSION to evaluate working of COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME (CDP, launched 2 Oct 1952) + NATIONAL EXTENSION SERVICE (NES, 1953) — both flagship rural development schemes of Nehru era. FINDINGS: CDP + NES had FAILED to develop rural India effectively; reasons included: (a) lack of PEOPLE'S PARTICIPATION; (b) TOP-DOWN bureaucracy-driven approach; (c) weak LOCAL INSTITUTIONS. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS (submitted Nov 1957): (1) 3-TIER PANCHAYATI RAJ structure — (a) GRAM PANCHAYAT (village level — directly elected); (b) PANCHAYAT SAMITI (block level — indirectly elected from GP sarpanches + elected officials); (c) ZILLA PARISHAD (district level — indirectly). Hence 'DEMOCRATIC DECENTRALISATION'. (2) PANCHAYAT SAMITI to be EXECUTIVE body, responsible for development. (3) ZP to be ADVISORY + COORDINATING. (4) SHIFT RURAL PROGRAMMES to Panchayats. (5) 5-YEAR tenure. RESULT: NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL accepted recommendations; RAJASTHAN became FIRST state to implement (Nehru inaugurated at NAGAUR, 2 Oct 1959). ANDHRA PRADESH followed soon after. By mid-1960s ~15 states implemented. LATER COMMITTEES: (1) ASHOK MEHTA COMMITTEE (1977-78, Janata govt) — recommended 2-TIER (Zilla Parishad + Mandal Panchayat) with ZP as focal; ASSIGNED development planning to ZP; ELECTED to all posts; allowed political parties to contest; separate FINANCE for rural local bodies. (2) G.V.K. RAO COMMITTEE (1985) — 'Administrative Arrangements for Rural Development + Poverty Alleviation'; recommended ZP as STRONGEST unit; make DISTRICT COLLECTOR accountable to ZP (controversial; not adopted). (3) L.M. SINGHVI COMMITTEE (1986) — 'Revitalisation of PRIs for Democracy + Development'; CONSTITUTIONAL recognition of PRIs; regular + free elections; adequate resources; NYAYA PANCHAYATS (judicial panchayats) for rural justice. (4) Sarkaria Commission inputs. Implementation came via 73rd CAA 1992 under NARASIMHA RAO govt — 35 YEARS after Balwant Rai Mehta's original recommendations. adopted by Rajasthan + AP in 1959.

cards.front:
STATE ELECTION COMMISSION for conducting panchayat + municipal elections was made a CONSTITUTIONAL body under:

(A) Article 324
(B) Article 243K (panchayats) + 243ZA
(C) Article 243I
(D) Article 280
cards.back:
(B) Article 243K (panchayats) + 243ZA

Local Self-Government — STATE ELECTION COMMISSION (SEC) — CONSTITUTIONAL body for RURAL + URBAN local body elections in each state. DISTINCT FROM ECI (Election Commission of India, Art 324) which handles Parliament + State Legislature + Presidential/VP polls only. PROVISIONS: (1) Art 243K (inserted by 73rd CAA 1992) — SEC for Panchayat elections. (2) Art 243ZA (inserted by 74th CAA 1992) — SEC for Municipal elections. (3) SINGLE SEC usually handles BOTH rural + urban in each state. (4) STRUCTURE: One member — the STATE ELECTION COMMISSIONER — appointed by the GOVERNOR. Term 5 years typically. (5) INDEPENDENCE: Commissioner can be removed only in MANNER + on GROUNDS of a HIGH COURT judge — ensures security of tenure. (6) FUNCTIONS: (a) superintendence, direction + control of preparation of electoral rolls for panchayat + ULB elections; (b) conduct of elections; (c) delimitation of wards + constituencies (in some states); (d) resolution of election disputes. (7) STATE LEGISLATURE makes laws regulating elections to panchayats + ULBs (subject to Constitution). KEY ISSUE: SEC conducts local polls INDEPENDENTLY but powers + authority often UNDERMINED by state govts in practice. RECENT CONFLICTS: (1) MAHARASHTRA 2021-22 — OBC reservation in local body elections dispute between state + SC led to delays; SEC caught in middle. (2) WEST BENGAL Panchayat 2023 — controversial poll marred by violence; SEC Rajiva Sinha's role criticised. (3) ANDHRA PRADESH 2020 — Gram Panchayat election delayed by state vs SEC Nimmagadda Ramesh Kumar legal battle; SC intervened + backed SEC. (4) BIHAR, KERALA, KARNATAKA — OBC reservation + delimitation issues. SC has REPEATEDLY reiterated SEC's INDEPENDENCE — Kishansingh Tomar (2006), Anugrah Narayan Singh (2007), Suresh Mahajan (2022). DELIMITATION: separate STATE DELIMITATION COMMISSION may also exist for ward delineation in states. ECI is distinct — conducts Parliament + Legislative Assembly + Presidential/VP elections; 3-member (CEC + 2 ECs, since 1993); headquartered at Nirvachan Sadan, New Delhi. STATE Finance Commission (Art 243I / 243Y) — separate — recommends finance-sharing between state + local bodies every 5 years. separate from ECI; one Commissioner appointed by Governor; municipalities.

(3) SINGLE SEC usually handles BOTH rural + urban in each state. (4) STRUCTURE: One member — the STATE ELECTION COMMISSIONER — appointed by the GOVERNOR. Term 5 years typically. (5) INDEPENDENCE: Commissioner can be removed only in MANNER + on GROUNDS of a HIGH COURT judge — ensures security of tenure. (6) FUNCTIONS: (a) superintendence, direction + control of preparation of electoral rolls for panchayat + ULB elections; (b) conduct of elections; (c) delimitation of wards + constituencies (in some states); (d) resolution of election disputes. (7) STATE LEGISLATURE makes laws regulating elections to panchayats + ULBs (subject to Constitution). KEY ISSUE: SEC conducts local polls INDEPENDENTLY but powers + authority often UNDERMINED by state govts in practice. RECENT CONFLICTS: (1) MAHARASHTRA 2021-22 — OBC reservation in local body elections dispute between state + SC led to delays; SEC caught in middle. (2) WEST BENGAL Panchayat 2023 — controversial poll marred by violence; SEC Rajiva Sinha's role criticised. (3) ANDHRA PRADESH 2020 — Gram Panchayat election delayed by state vs SEC Nimmagadda Ramesh Kumar legal battle; SC intervened + backed SEC. (4) BIHAR, KERALA, KARNATAKA — OBC reservation + delimitation issues. SC has REPEATEDLY reiterated SEC's INDEPENDENCE — Kishansingh Tomar (2006), Anugrah Narayan Singh (2007), Suresh Mahajan (2022). DELIMITATION: separate STATE DELIMITATION COMMISSION may also exist for ward delineation in states. ECI is distinct — conducts Parliament + Legislative Assembly + Presidential/VP elections; 3-member (CEC + 2 ECs, since 1993); headquartered at Nirvachan Sadan, New Delhi. STATE Finance Commission (Art 243I / 243Y) — separate — recommends finance-sharing between state + local bodies every 5 years. separate from ECI; one Commissioner appointed by Governor; municipalities.

cards.front:
Which state has the HIGHEST percentage of WOMEN representation in Panchayats (often >50%)?

(A) Uttar Pradesh
(B) BIHAR was the FIRST state to legislate 50% women reservation (2006); now 21+ states have 50%
(C) Punjab
(D) Goa
cards.back:
(B) BIHAR was the FIRST state to legislate 50% women reservation (2006); now 21+ states have 50%

Local Self-Government — WOMEN in PANCHAYATS — 73rd CAA mandated 1/3 (33%) reservation for women. Many states voluntarily RAISED to 50% (1/2) under enabling power in Art 243D(3). TIMELINE: (1) BIHAR — FIRST state to raise to 50% (2006, under Nitish Kumar). (2) Then: UTTARAKHAND, MADHYA PRADESH, HIMACHAL PRADESH, KERALA, ODISHA, RAJASTHAN, TRIPURA, MAHARASHTRA, ANDHRA PRADESH, ASSAM, CHHATTISGARH, GUJARAT, JHARKHAND, KARNATAKA, PUNJAB, SIKKIM, TAMIL NADU, TELANGANA, UTTAR PRADESH (2015 under SP govt — yes, UP has 50%), WEST BENGAL, GOA. (3) About 21 STATES + UTs have 50% women reservation in Panchayats. STATUS (Ministry of Panchayati Raj 2024 data): ~14.5 LAKH ELECTED WOMEN REPRESENTATIVES out of ~31 lakh total PRI reps = ~46-47% women overall. 6 states are >50% women. ACROSS STATES: (a) KARNATAKA ~55% women; (b) JHARKHAND, MP, CHHATTISGARH, ODISHA > 50%; (c) Kerala, HP, Rajasthan > 50%; (d) UP, Bihar ~50%; (e) Maharashtra 50%. INDIA has the WORLD's LARGEST women's political representation at local level. IMPACT studies: (1) LORI BEAMAN, ESTHER DUFLO et al. — studies of quota-based women leaders → more investment in drinking water, health, roads; less corruption; more complaints registered; erosion of caste-based patriarchy; role models. (2) CONCEPT of 'SARPANCH PATI' / 'Mukhiya Pati' — proxy politics where husband wields actual power behind elected wife — STILL PREVALENT in many areas. State initiatives to address: training programmes for elected women reps, Mahila Sabha (parallel women's body), direct bank accounts. (3) 'MAHILA PANCHAYATS' in Delhi, Mumbai — Nari Adalat type informal judicial bodies. WORLD COMPARISON: India's ~46% women in local govt = BEST IN WORLD in absolute sense (~14.5 lakh women leaders). For perspective: US has ~0.5 lakh women local reps; EU ~30% women in local councils. PROGRESSIVE features also include: (a) rotation of reserved seats; (b) reservation within SC/ST category; (c) OBC sub-quotas in many states. NATIONAL PANCHAYATI RAJ DAY = 24 APRIL (date 73rd CAA came into force, 1993). PANCHAYATS are 'CRADLES OF DEMOCRACY' per Gandhi + first PM Nehru. Kerala, Odisha, MP, Rajasthan, HP, Tripura, etc.

cards.front:
PESA ACT 1996 (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas) extends Panchayati Raj to:

(A) North-East Region (6th Schedule)
(B) 5TH SCHEDULE tribal areas
(C) Urban tribal areas only
(D) All hilly regions
cards.back:
(B) 5TH SCHEDULE tribal areas

Local Self-Government — PESA ACT 1996 (PANCHAYATS [Extension to Scheduled Areas] Act, 24 Dec 1996) — extends the provisions of Part IX (73rd CAA Panchayati Raj) to the 5TH SCHEDULE AREAS with CRITICAL MODIFICATIONS for tribal governance. COVERS 10 STATES (as of 2024, Telangana added after bifurcation): ANDHRA PRADESH, CHHATTISGARH, GUJARAT, HIMACHAL PRADESH, JHARKHAND, MADHYA PRADESH, MAHARASHTRA, ODISHA, RAJASTHAN, TELANGANA. NOT applicable to 6th SCHEDULE areas of NE (Assam Hill Areas, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — which have their OWN Autonomous District Councils). DEVELOPED based on BHURIA COMMITTEE (1994-95) recommendations. KEY FEATURES: (1) GRAM SABHA (not GP) is PRINCIPAL INSTITUTION in PESA areas; far stronger powers than elsewhere. (2) GRAM SABHA approves village plans + beneficiaries; socioeconomic planning. (3) CONSULTATION with Gram Sabha MANDATORY BEFORE: (a) LAND ACQUISITION for development; (b) acquisition of land for displacement; (c) rehab + resettlement schemes. (4) CONSENT of Gram Sabha required for: (a) prospecting + mining MINOR MINERALS in Scheduled Areas. (5) OWNERSHIP of MINOR FOREST PRODUCE (MFP) — tendu, mahua, honey, lac, wax, etc. — vested in Gram Sabha. (6) MANAGEMENT OF water bodies, minor water resources. (7) Regulation of MONEY-LENDING to STs. (8) Control over LOCAL MARKETS + fairs. (9) Prohibition / regulation of intoxicants. (10) Safeguards of TRIBAL CULTURE + customs. STATE LEGISLATIONS: each state enacts its own PESA Rules. Maharashtra PESA rules 2014 considered progressive; Chhattisgarh's delayed till 2022. IMPACT: (1) IN THEORY — tribals have real power over land + forests + minerals; (2) IN PRACTICE — implementation weak due to (a) mining interests; (b) Forest Rights Act 2006 overlap; (c) bureaucratic resistance; (d) resistance of contractors to Gram Sabha approval. NIYAMGIRI CASE (SC 2013) — Odisha — Dongria Kondh Gram Sabhas rejected Vedanta's bauxite mining 12-0 (all 12 Gram Sabhas); SC upheld the Gram Sabha VETO — LANDMARK PESA + FRA win. SAMATA JUDGMENT (1997) — AP — held tribal land transfer to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas ILLEGAL. Forest Rights Act 2006 (FRA) COMPLEMENTS PESA — recognises individual + community forest rights for forest-dependent STs + OTFDs. LWE (Maoist / Naxalite) affected areas LARGELY overlap with PESA/5th Schedule areas — governance failure + development deficit cited as root cause; PESA implementation seen as key solution. 76 STs + ~10 crore tribal population in India. with ENHANCED Gram Sabha powers; Andhra, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, HP, Jharkhand, MP, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana.

cards.front:
Panchayati Raj (local self-government in rural areas) was given constitutional status by which amendment?

(A) 42nd Amendment
(B) 73rd Amendment
(C) 74th Amendment
(D) 86th Amendment
cards.back:
(B) 73rd Amendment

Local Self-Government — The 73rd Amendment (1992) inserted Part IX (Articles 243-243O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) into the Constitution, giving three-tier Panchayati Raj a constitutional basis. The 74th Amendment (same year) did the parallel job for urban local bodies (Part IXA, Articles 243P-243ZG, Twelfth Schedule, 18 subjects). The 42nd Amendment (1976) is unrelated — it added Fundamental Duties.

The 74th Amendment (same year) did the parallel job for urban local bodies (Part IXA, Articles 243P-243ZG, Twelfth Schedule, 18 subjects). The 42nd Amendment (1976) is unrelated — it added Fundamental Duties.

cards.front:
Under the 73rd Amendment, the minimum reservation of seats for women in Panchayats is:

(A) One-fourth
(B) One-third
(C) One-half
(D) Fifteen per cent
cards.back:
(B) One-third

Local Self-Government — Art 243D — minimum 1/3 seats reserved for women in Panchayats at all three tiers (plus proportional reservations for SC / ST). Many states (Bihar 2006, Andhra, Karnataka, etc.) have voluntarily raised it to 50 %. The 2023 Women's Reservation Act (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) extends 33 % reservation to Lok Sabha and state Assemblies, but will take effect after the next delimitation.

cards.front:
The three-tier Panchayati Raj structure consists of Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block) and:

(A) State Panchayat
(B) Zila Parishad (district)
(C) Municipal Corporation
(D) Urban Cantonment Board
cards.back:
(B) Zila Parishad (district)

Local Self-Government — 73rd Amendment mandates a three-tier system in states with population > 20 lakh — Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (intermediate block level), Zila Parishad (district level). Smaller states may have two tiers. Municipal Corporations / Councils / Nagar Panchayats are urban bodies under the 74th Amendment. Cantonment Boards operate under the Cantonments Act (military / defence areas).

Smaller states may have two tiers. Municipal Corporations / Councils / Nagar Panchayats are urban bodies under the 74th Amendment. Cantonment Boards operate under the Cantonments Act (military / defence areas).

cards.front:
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) was the first to recommend a three-tier Panchayati Raj structure in India. The first state to implement its recommendations (1959) was:

(A) Andhra Pradesh
(B) Rajasthan
(C) Tamil Nadu
(D) Uttar Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) Rajasthan

Local Self-Government — Rajasthan was the first state to implement the Balwant Rai Mehta recommendations on 2 October 1959, with Prime Minister Nehru inaugurating the first Panchayati Raj body in Nagaur district. Andhra Pradesh followed almost immediately the same year. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) later recommended a two-tier system. Panchayati Raj reached constitutional status only with the 73rd Amendment, 1992.

Panchayati Raj reached constitutional status only with the 73rd Amendment, 1992.

cards.front:
The term of a Panchayat — fixed by the Constitution — is:

(A) Four years
(B) Five years
(C) Six years
(D) Decided by each state
cards.back:
(B) Five years

Local Self-Government — Art 243E — every Panchayat has a fixed term of five years unless dissolved earlier. If dissolved earlier, fresh elections must be held within 6 months. The original term ends automatically at five years; a state cannot, by ordinary legislation, extend it. A similar 5-year rule applies to urban local bodies under the 74th Amendment.

The original term ends automatically at five years; a state cannot, by ordinary legislation, extend it. A similar 5-year rule applies to urban local bodies under the 74th Amendment.

cards.front:
Panchayat elections are conducted by the:

(A) Election Commission of India
(B) State Election Commission
(C) State government through the District Collector
(D) Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj
cards.back:
(B) State Election Commission

Local Self-Government — Art 243K — each state has its own State Election Commission (SEC) that is constitutionally separate from the Central Election Commission. The SEC superintends, directs and controls preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of elections to Panchayats (and under Art 243ZA, municipalities). The ECI handles only Parliament, state Assemblies, President and VP elections.
cards.option2: State government through the District Collector

cards.front:
The 'Gram Sabha' mentioned in the 73rd Amendment is a body consisting of:

(A) All elected members of a Panchayat
(B) All adult registered voters of the village
(C) Only women voters
(D) Only SC / ST voters
cards.back:
(B) All adult registered voters of the village

Local Self-Government — Gram Sabha (Art 243A) — the village-level general body of all persons whose names are on the electoral rolls of the village. It is a direct democratic institution — it meets to approve the Panchayat's development plans, discuss annual accounts, beneficiary lists under government schemes, etc. The Gram Panchayat is the elected executive body. PESA (1996) gives Gram Sabhas in Fifth Schedule (tribal) areas wider powers over land and forest resources.
cards.option1: All elected members of a Panchayat

cards.front:
Under which Article of the Constitution is the Finance Commission of India established?

(A) Article 263
(B) Article 280
(C) Article 324
(D) Article 350
cards.back:
(B) Article 280

Miscellaneous — Article 280 provides for the constitution of a Finance Commission. Article 263 covers the Inter-State Council; Article 324 deals with the Election Commission; Article 350 concerns language rights. The Finance Commission is a CONSTITUTIONAL body — constituted by the President every 5 years (or earlier if needed).
cards.storedExplanation: Article 280 provides for the constitution of a Finance Commission. Article 263 covers the Inter-State Council; Article 324 deals with the Election Commission; Article 350 concerns language rights. The Finance Commission is a CONSTITUTIONAL body — constituted by the President every 5 years (or earlier if needed).

cards.front:
Who constitutes the Finance Commission?

(A) The Prime Minister
(B) The President of India
(C) The Parliament through a special law
(D) The Union Finance Minister after NITI Aayog approval
cards.back:
(B) The President of India

Miscellaneous — Article 280(1): The President constitutes the Finance Commission every 5 years or at such earlier time as he considers necessary. The commission consists of a chairman and four other members. The PM/FM/NITI Aayog have no role in constitution — the function is squarely with the President (acting on Cabinet advice).
cards.option2: The Parliament through a special law
cards.option3: The Union Finance Minister after NITI Aayog approval
cards.storedExplanation: Article 280(1): The President constitutes the Finance Commission every 5 years or at such earlier time as he considers necessary. The commission consists of a chairman and four other members. The PM/FM/NITI Aayog have no role in constitution — the function is squarely with the President (acting on Cabinet advice).

cards.front:
How many members does the Finance Commission have?

(A) 3 (one Chairman + two members)
(B) 5 (one Chairman + four members)
(C) 7 (one Chairman + six members)
(D) Variable, determined by the Parliament each term
cards.back:
(B) 5 (one Chairman + four members)

Miscellaneous — Article 280(1): 'a Finance Commission which shall consist of a Chairman and four other Members'. The Finance Commission Act, 1951 lays down qualifications for appointment of members. Chairman is usually a person with public-affairs experience; members include a HC-eligible person, a finance expert, a public finance specialist, and an economics expert.
cards.option3: Variable, determined by the Parliament each term

The Finance Commission Act, 1951 lays down qualifications for appointment of members. Chairman is usually a person with public-affairs experience; members include a HC-eligible person, a finance expert, a public finance specialist, and an economics expert.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a function of the Finance Commission under Article 280?

(A) Distribution of net proceeds of taxes between Union and States
(B) Principles governing grants-in-aid to States out of the Consolidated Fund of India
(C) Recommendations to augment Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement resources of Panchayats & Municipalities
(D) Regulating prices of agricultural commodities (MSP)
cards.back:
(D) Regulating prices of agricultural commodities (MSP)

Miscellaneous — Article 280(3) lists functions: (a) distribution of tax proceeds between Union and States; (b) principles for grants-in-aid; (c) measures to augment State Consolidated Fund for local bodies (added by 73rd & 74th Amendments); (d) any other matter referred by the President. MSP for agricultural commodities is fixed by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs on CACP recommendation — not the Finance Commission's role.

cards.option3: Recommendations to augment Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement resources of Panchayats & Municipalities

cards.front:
Who was the chairman of the First Finance Commission of India, constituted in 1951?

(A) Dr. K. Santhanam
(B) K. C. Neogy
(C) Y. B. Chavan
(D) Brahmanand Reddy
cards.back:
(B) K. C. Neogy

Miscellaneous — K. C. Neogy chaired the First Finance Commission (1951–57). He was a senior economist and political leader. K. Santhanam chaired the 2nd FC (1956–62). Y. B. Chavan chaired the 8th FC (1984–89). Brahmanand Reddy never chaired an FC. The First FC's tenure covered April 1952 to March 1957.

cards.front:
Which Finance Commission introduced the concept of 'performance-based grants' for local bodies (Panchayats and Municipalities)?

(A) 11th Finance Commission
(B) 13th Finance Commission
(C) 14th Finance Commission
(D) 15th Finance Commission
cards.back:
(B) 13th Finance Commission

Miscellaneous — The 13th FC (Chairman: Dr. Vijay Kelkar, 2010–15) was the first to introduce performance-based grants for local bodies, conditional on compliance with e.g., putting up audited accounts and establishing a local-level grievance redressal system. Earlier FCs (11th & 12th) gave only basic grants to local bodies. The 14th & 15th FCs continued the performance-grant structure with updated conditions.

cards.front:
Which Finance Commission increased the States' share in the divisible pool of central taxes from 32% to 42%?

(A) 12th Finance Commission
(B) 13th Finance Commission
(C) 14th Finance Commission
(D) 15th Finance Commission
cards.back:
(C) 14th Finance Commission

Miscellaneous — The 14th FC (Chairman: Dr. Y. V. Reddy, covering 2015–20) made a landmark recommendation raising States' share of divisible central taxes from 32% (under the 13th FC) to 42% — the single largest jump in FC history, reflecting a new commitment to fiscal federalism. The 15th FC (N. K. Singh) slightly reduced it to 41% (on account of the J&K reorganisation into UTs).

cards.front:
What is the usual tenure of a Finance Commission's recommendations?

(A) 2 years
(B) 3 years
(C) 5 years
(D) 10 years
cards.back:
(C) 5 years

Miscellaneous — The Finance Commission is constituted every 5 years and its recommendations apply for the following 5-year period. E.g., 15th FC's recommendations covered 2021–26 (extended by 1 year due to COVID). This 5-year horizon matches the typical economic/planning cycle. The FC is NOT a permanent body; it is constituted afresh each time.

(B) Advisory / recommendatory in nature
(C) Binding on States but advisory for the Union

Miscellaneous — The FC's recommendations are purely ADVISORY (Article 281). The President places the report before both Houses of Parliament along with an Explanatory Memorandum stating the government's action taken on each recommendation. The government can partially or fully reject recommendations — though in practice, the major recommendations (vertical devolution %, horizontal formula) are accepted. A famous case: the 14th FC raised devolution to 42%, which was fully accepted. the government can modify or reject them.

cards.front:
Which of the following criteria has been used by Finance Commissions for horizontal distribution (inter-State distribution) of tax proceeds?

(A) Income distance, population, area, forest & ecology, demographic performance, and tax & fiscal efforts
(B) GDP growth rate of each State only
(C) Only population and tax collection capacity
(D) Number of Lok Sabha seats held by each State
cards.back:
(A) Income distance, population, area, forest & ecology, demographic performance, and tax & fiscal efforts

Miscellaneous — Horizontal devolution uses multiple criteria with different weights. The 15th FC used: Income distance (45%), Area (15%), Population 2011 (15%), Demographic Performance (12.5%), Forest & Ecology (10%), Tax & Fiscal Efforts (2.5%). Earlier FCs had different weights and slightly different criteria (e.g., the 14th FC didn't use Forest & Ecology or Demographic Performance). The formula is designed to balance equity (give more to poorer States) and efficiency.

cards.front:
The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India through the:

(A) 100th Constitutional Amendment, 2015
(B) 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (effective 1 July 2017)
(C) 73rd Amendment
(D) Finance Act, 2017
cards.back:
(B) 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (effective 1 July 2017)

Miscellaneous — 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 — added Article 246A (concurrent powers to Centre and States to levy GST), Article 269A (IGST), Article 279A (GST Council). GST itself rolled out from 1 July 2017 (midnight session of Parliament). Subsumed multiple central + state taxes — Central Excise (except on tobacco, petroleum), Service Tax, Additional Customs Duty (CVD/SAD), Central Sales Tax, VAT, Entry Tax, Luxury Tax, Octroi, Entertainment Tax (except by local bodies). One-Nation-One-Tax. Petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas, crude — temporarily kept OUT of GST (still under VAT + excise); Council can include them later. 100th Amendment — was about land boundary agreement with Bangladesh.

(B) Article 279A
(C) Article 280
(D) Article 312
cards.back:

Miscellaneous — Article 279A — added by 101st CAA, 2016. The President to constitute the GST Council within 60 days of commencement of the amendment (constituted 12 Sep 2016). Composition: (1) Union Finance Minister — Chairperson; (2) Union MoS Finance (Revenue) — Member; (3) Finance Minister of each State — Member. The Vice-Chairperson is chosen from among the State Finance Ministers. Article 279 — Calculation of net proceeds, basis of devolution. Article 280 — Finance Commission (every 5 years). Article 312 — All-India Services.

cards.front:
What is the voting weightage of the Centre and the States in the GST Council?

(A) Centre 25%, States 75% combined
(B) Centre 1/3 (33.33%), States 2/3 combined; decisions need 75% of weighted votes (i.e., 3/4 majority)
(C) Centre 51%, States 49%
(D) Each member one equal vote
cards.back:
(B) Centre 1/3 (33.33%), States 2/3 combined; decisions need 75% of weighted votes (i.e., 3/4 majority)

Miscellaneous — GST Council voting (Art 279A(9)): Centre's vote = 1/3 weight; all states combined = 2/3. Any decision requires 3/4 (75%) of weighted votes. So neither side alone can push a decision through — Centre alone has 33% (less than 75%), states alone have 67% (also less than 75%). Encourages cooperative federalism. Quorum = 50% of total membership. Each state gets equal weight regardless of size (small states equal to UP/Maharashtra). UTs with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K post-2019) are also members. Note — May 2022 SC ruling (Mohit Minerals case) clarified that GST Council recommendations are NOT binding on Centre or States — only persuasive; Centre and States retain legislative competence.

cards.front:
Which of the following items is NOT currently under GST (kept outside the GST framework)?

(A) Cement
(B) Petroleum products (crude, petrol, diesel, ATF) and natural gas
(C) Mobile phones
(D) Air-conditioners
cards.back:
(B) Petroleum products (crude, petrol, diesel, ATF) and natural gas

Miscellaneous — Items kept OUTSIDE GST (still taxed under earlier regime): (1) Petroleum products — crude oil, petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas (under Central Excise + State VAT — that's why fuel prices vary state-to-state); (2) Alcohol for human consumption — exclusively State VAT (a key state revenue protected by constitutional carve-out); (3) Electricity — under Electricity (Tax on Consumption or Sale) by states; (4) Tobacco products (Central Excise levied IN ADDITION to GST). Real estate transactions — partially (under-construction property has GST 5%/12%, but completed property + land have stamp duty under state). Council can decide to bring petroleum under GST anytime, but states have resisted (collectively ~₹3-4 lakh cr revenue at stake).

cards.front:
The standard GST tax slab structure has FOUR main rates:

(A) 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%
(B) 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% (+ exempt 0% and a few special rates)
(C) 10%, 18%, 28%, 35%
(D) Single uniform 18%
cards.back:
(B) 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% (+ exempt 0% and a few special rates)

Miscellaneous — Main GST rates: 0% (essentials — fresh food, milk, education, healthcare); 5% (mass-consumption — packaged food, transport, footwear ≤ ₹1000); 12% (semi-essentials — butter, ghee, mobile phones); 18% (most goods + services — soaps, computers, IT services); 28% (luxury + sin — air-conditioners, large TVs, automobiles, tobacco — plus a 'compensation cess' on top of 28% for tobacco, pan masala, automobiles, aerated drinks). Special low rates: 0.25% (rough diamonds), 3% (gold + jewellery). Compensation cess proceeds funded the GST Compensation Cess Fund — used to compensate states for revenue loss in the first 5 years of GST (later extended to repay COVID-period borrowings). Rate rationalisation has been an ongoing GoM agenda — the 'Group of Ministers' headed by various state FMs.

cards.front:
When a sale of goods happens FROM Maharashtra TO Karnataka (inter-state), the tax levied is:

(A) CGST + SGST (split half-half)
(B) IGST (Integrated GST) — collected by the Centre, then revenue split between Centre and the destination state (Karnataka)
(C) VAT only
(D) Nothing — inter-state sales are tax-free
cards.back:
(B) IGST (Integrated GST) — collected by the Centre, then revenue split between Centre and the destination state (Karnataka)

Miscellaneous — GST flow: INTRA-state (within same state) — CGST (Centre's share) + SGST (state's share), each 1/2 of the GST rate. Example: 18% intra-state → 9% CGST + 9% SGST. INTER-state — IGST collected by Centre at the FULL rate (= CGST + SGST equivalent); Centre then transfers the SGST-equivalent share to the DESTINATION state (consumption-based tax). UNION TERRITORY — UTGST instead of SGST (for UTs without legislatures). GST is a destination-based consumption tax — revenue accrues to the state where the goods/services are consumed, not where produced. This is a fundamental shift from the earlier origin-based central sales tax (CST), which had favoured producing states. Article 269A — IGST.

cards.front:
Who is the EX-OFFICIO chairperson of the GST Council?

(A) Prime Minister
(B) Union Finance Minister
(C) President
(D) RBI Governor
cards.back:

Miscellaneous — Union Finance Minister — ex-officio Chairperson of the GST Council (Article 279A(2)). Currently — Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman (since 2019). Members: Union MoS for Finance (Revenue) + each State Finance Minister (or other Minister nominated by the State). Vice-Chairperson — chosen from State FMs by them. Secretary to the Council — the Revenue Secretary (Govt of India). Council secretariat at New Delhi. Has met 50+ times since constitution. Decisions historically have largely been by consensus despite the 75% formal voting rule.

Which among the following is a Constitutional Body and NOT a non-Constitutional/Statutory body?

(A) NITI Aayog
(B) CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation)
(C) Finance Commission
(D) NHRC (National Human Rights Commission)
cards.back:

CBI is non-constitutional; it is based on the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 — so it's a STATUTORY body. NHRC is a STATUTORY body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. cards.front:
Which of the following is a STATUTORY (not constitutional) body?

(A) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)
(B) Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
(C) Comptroller and Auditor General
(D) Election Commission of India
cards.back:

cards.front:
Consider the following statements about NITI Aayog's Governing Council: 1) It is the apex body of NITI Aayog. 2) All Chief Ministers + Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories with legislatures are members. 3) The Finance Minister of the Union is an ex-officio member. Which of the above is/are correct?

(A) 1 only
(B) 1 and 2 only
(C) 2 and 3 only
(D) 1, 2 and 3
cards.back:
(B) 1 and 2 only

Statement 2 CORRECT — all CMs of States + LGs of UTs are members (UTs WITHOUT legislatures are represented by Administrators, but the classic composition is CMs + LGs). Statement 3 WRONG — Union Ministers are ex-officio members of NITI Aayog (not specifically the Governing Council in this way); the PM chairs the Governing Council with CMs/LGs as its members; Union Ministers attend as special invitees.

cards.front:
NITI AAYOG was established to REPLACE the:

(A) Planning Commission (1950-2014)
(B) Finance Commission (Art 280)
(C) UPSC (constitutional body)
(D) Election Commission of India
cards.back:
(A) Planning Commission (1950-2014)

Miscellaneous — NITI AAYOG (National Institution for Transforming India) — established 1 JANUARY 2015 by Cabinet Resolution under PM NARENDRA MODI; REPLACED the PLANNING COMMISSION (1950-2014). KEY DIFFERENCES from Planning Commission: (1) PLANNING COMMISSION — top-down centralized planning, controlled fund allocation. (2) NITI AAYOG — facilitator + think-tank role; cooperative federalism approach; states play stronger role. (3) PLANNING COMMISSION had quasi-financial powers; NITI Aayog has NONE (all financial powers to FINANCE MINISTRY). STRUCTURE: (1) CHAIRPERSON — PRIME MINISTER. (2) GOVERNING COUNCIL — all CMs + Lt Governors of UTs. (3) REGIONAL COUNCILS — formed for specific issues spanning multiple states. (4) VICE-CHAIRPERSON — appointed by PM (e.g., currently Suman Bery). (5) FULL-TIME MEMBERS, PART-TIME, EX-OFFICIO members. (6) SPECIAL INVITEES. (7) CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER — fixed tenure, secretary-rank. KEY FUNCTIONS: (1) Cooperative federalism. (2) Bottom-up planning. (3) Strategic + technical advice. (4) Developing 3-year action agenda, 7-year strategy, 15-year vision. (5) Monitoring + evaluation of govt schemes. STATUS: NEITHER constitutional NOR statutory — just an EXECUTIVE BODY (Cabinet Resolution); same status as Planning Commission was. UPSC angle: HUGE topic for Mains GS-2 (governance, federalism). PYQ FREQUENCY: NITI Aayog basics in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC 1-2× per cycle.

Who is the CHAIRPERSON of NITI Aayog?

(A) Prime Minister (ex-officio)
(B) President of India directly
(C) Finance Minister of India
(D) An eminent economist appointed
cards.back:
(A) Prime Minister (ex-officio)

Miscellaneous — PRIME MINISTER is the EX-OFFICIO CHAIRPERSON of NITI Aayog. The PM also CHAIRS the GOVERNING COUNCIL (which includes all CMs + UT Lt Governors). RATIONALE: high-level policy-making body; PM-led ensures top-down + central role. KEY POSITIONS in NITI Aayog: (1) CHAIRPERSON — PM (Narendra Modi). (2) VICE-CHAIRPERSON — PM-appointed, holding rank of Cabinet Minister. CURRENT (April 2026): SUMAN BERY (since May 2022; succeeded Rajiv Kumar). PAST: ARVIND PANAGARIYA (2015-17), Rajiv Kumar (2017-22), Suman Bery. (3) FULL-TIME MEMBERS — 4-5 currently; rank of Minister of State. (4) PART-TIME MEMBERS — up to 2 from leading research bodies, universities. (5) EX-OFFICIO MEMBERS — up to 4 Union Ministers nominated by PM. (6) SPECIAL INVITEES — eminent experts, specialists nominated by PM. (7) CEO — secretary-rank IAS officer, 5-year fixed term. CURRENT: B.V.R. SUBRAHMANYAM (since Feb 2023). KEY GOVERNING COUNCIL MEETINGS: held annually; all CMs + UT Lt Govs gather; major federal policy decisions. NITI AAYOG GOVERNING COUNCIL meets FACE-TO-FACE with PM — major occasion for state-Centre coordination. UPSC angle: governance + federalism (cooperative federalism); GS-2. PYQ FREQUENCY: NITI Aayog leadership in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
ASPIRATIONAL DISTRICTS PROGRAMME (launched 2018) is administered by:

(A) NITI Aayog (uplifts 112 districts)
(B) Ministry of Rural Development
(C) Planning Commission (defunct)
(D) Ministry of Home Affairs only
cards.back:
(A) NITI Aayog (uplifts 112 districts)

Miscellaneous — ASPIRATIONAL DISTRICTS PROGRAMME (ADP) — launched JANUARY 2018; administered by NITI AAYOG. AIM: rapidly TRANSFORM 112 most-backward districts of India by enhancing development indicators. SELECTION: districts ranked using 49 KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS (KPIs) across 5 themes: (1) HEALTH & NUTRITION (~30%). (2) EDUCATION (30%). (3) AGRICULTURE & WATER (~20%). (4) FINANCIAL INCLUSION & SKILL (5%). (5) BASIC INFRASTRUCTURE (15%). MONTHLY 'DELTA RANKING' — comparing relative improvement; states + DMs compete. EARLY SUCCESS: many ADP districts have improved on multiple KPIs faster than national/state averages. KEY DISTRICTS: in BIHAR (12 ADPs — most), JHARKHAND (19 — most as % of state), CHHATTISGARH (10), UP (8), MP, WB, ODISHA. ADP EXTENDED to ASPIRATIONAL BLOCKS PROGRAMME (ABP) — launched 7 January 2023; covers 500 'most backward blocks' across India. APPROACH: 'CONVERGENCE + COLLABORATION + COMPETITION' — convergence of central + state schemes; collaboration with Centre + state + DM; competition among districts. UPSC angle: development administration + governance + federalism (cooperative). PYQ FREQUENCY: ADP/ABP in UPSC PT, Mains GS-2 development administration; SSC GA — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
NITI AAYOG'S vision document covers a planning period of:

(A) 15 years (vs PC's 5-year plans)
(B) 5 years (continued PC tradition)
(C) 10 years (a wrong duration)
(D) 25 years (over-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 15 years (vs PC's 5-year plans)

Miscellaneous — NITI AAYOG's PLANNING DOCUMENTS structure: (1) 15-YEAR VISION DOCUMENT — long-term perspective. (2) 7-YEAR STRATEGY DOCUMENT — medium-term roadmap. (3) 3-YEAR ACTION AGENDA — short-term, immediately actionable. CONTRAST WITH PLANNING COMMISSION: had 5-YEAR PLANS (1st: 1951-56 to 12th: 2012-17). 12th Plan was the LAST 5-Year plan; from 2017 onwards, India follows NITI Aayog's 3-7-15 framework instead of 5-year plans. WHY 5-Year Plans were abandoned: (1) Critique that they were too rigid for fast-changing economy. (2) Excessive central control — clashed with cooperative federalism. (3) Implementation often diverged from plan. (4) Soviet-style planning seen as outdated post-1991 liberalization. INDIA'S 5-YEAR PLAN HISTORY (memorize for UPSC): (1) 1st (1951-56) — agriculture, irrigation. (2) 2nd (1956-61) — heavy industry (Mahalanobis model). (3) 3rd (1961-66) — followed by 'Plan Holiday' 1966-69 (3 ad-hoc annual plans due to wars + drought). (4) 4th (1969-74). (5) 5th (1974-79) — abandoned 1978; 'Rolling Plan' 1978-80. (6)-(11) — 1980-2012. (7) 12TH (2012-17) — LAST 5-Year plan; achievements: GDP growth ~7% (intended 9%), poverty reduction. UPSC angle: economic planning HISTORY in GS-3; reforms post-1991. PYQ FREQUENCY: NITI Aayog planning structure in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
NITI Aayog releases the SDG INDIA INDEX which measures progress on:

(A) Sustainable Development Goals 2030
(B) Stock-market growth indicators
(C) Bank-fraud detection levels
(D) Vehicle emission standards alone
cards.back:
(A) Sustainable Development Goals 2030

Miscellaneous — SDG INDIA INDEX — annual report by NITI Aayog (since 2018) measuring INDIA's PROGRESS on 17 SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs) adopted by UN in 2015 (TARGET YEAR 2030). MEASURES STATES + UTs against ~100 indicators. SDG 2030 GOALS (memorize summary): (1) NO POVERTY. (2) ZERO HUNGER. (3) GOOD HEALTH. (4) QUALITY EDUCATION. (5) GENDER EQUALITY. (6) CLEAN WATER & SANITATION. (7) AFFORDABLE & CLEAN ENERGY. (8) DECENT WORK & ECONOMIC GROWTH. (9) INDUSTRY, INNOVATION, INFRASTRUCTURE. (10) REDUCED INEQUALITIES. (11) SUSTAINABLE CITIES. (12) RESPONSIBLE CONSUMPTION & PRODUCTION. (13) CLIMATE ACTION. (14) LIFE BELOW WATER. (15) LIFE ON LAND. (16) PEACE, JUSTICE, INSTITUTIONS. (17) PARTNERSHIPS. INDIA's SDG SCORES (2023-24 edition): national score ~71/100; significant variation across states. KERALA, TAMIL NADU consistently top; BIHAR, JHARKHAND need most improvement. NITI also releases other indices: (1) HEALTH INDEX. (2) SCHOOL EDUCATION QUALITY INDEX. (3) WATER MANAGEMENT INDEX. (4) DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION INDEX. (5) STATE ENERGY & CLIMATE INDEX. UPSC angle: SDG progress is regular feature in PT current affairs + Mains GS-2/3. INDIA'S INTL CLIMATE PLEDGES: NDC under Paris Agreement — net zero by 2070 (announced COP26 Glasgow 2021); 50% RE by 2030; non-fossil 50%. PYQ FREQUENCY: SDGs + India SDG Index in UPSC PT/Mains 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a body established under the Constitution?

(A) NITI Aayog (executive cabinet body)
(B) UPSC (Article 315 onwards)
(C) CAG (Article 148)
(D) Election Commission (Art 324)
cards.back:
(A) NITI Aayog (executive cabinet body)

Miscellaneous — NITI AAYOG is NEITHER CONSTITUTIONAL NOR STATUTORY — created by CABINET RESOLUTION (1 January 2015); could be modified or abolished by simple cabinet decision. KEY CATEGORIZATION of bodies (memorize for UPSC): (1) CONSTITUTIONAL BODIES — created by Constitution itself. EXAMPLES: ELECTION COMMISSION (Art 324), UPSC (Art 315), STATE PSCs (Art 315), FINANCE COMMISSION (Art 280), CAG (Art 148), ATTORNEY GENERAL (Art 76), Advocate General of state (Art 165), NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR SCs/STs/BCs (Arts 338, 338A, 338B), GST COUNCIL (Art 279A — added 2016 via 101st Amendment), etc. (2) STATUTORY BODIES — created by ACTS of PARLIAMENT. EXAMPLES: NHRC (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993), NCW (NCW Act 1990), CIC (RTI Act 2005), CVC (CVC Act 2003), CBI (Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946), Lokpal (Lokpal Act 2013), NGT (NGT Act 2010), TRAI (TRAI Act 1997), SEBI (SEBI Act 1992), RBI (RBI Act 1934). (3) EXECUTIVE BODIES — created by EXECUTIVE order/cabinet resolution. EXAMPLES: NITI AAYOG (2015), Planning Commission (1950-2014), CCI (Competition Commission, mostly statutory but had executive elements), various task forces. NITI AAYOG'S VULNERABILITY: lacking constitutional/statutory backing means future government could abolish or modify it without legislative process. UPSC angle: 'Discuss the status of NITI Aayog vis-à-vis Planning Commission' — frequent essay/short-answer topic. PYQ FREQUENCY: body classification in UPSC PT, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

EXAMPLES: ELECTION COMMISSION (Art 324), UPSC (Art 315), STATE PSCs (Art 315), FINANCE COMMISSION (Art 280), CAG (Art 148), ATTORNEY GENERAL (Art 76), Advocate General of state (Art 165), NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR SCs/STs/BCs (Arts 338, 338A, 338B), GST COUNCIL (Art 279A — added 2016 via 101st Amendment), etc. (2) STATUTORY BODIES — created by ACTS of PARLIAMENT. EXAMPLES: NHRC (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993), NCW (NCW Act 1990), CIC (RTI Act 2005), CVC (CVC Act 2003), CBI (Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946), Lokpal (Lokpal Act 2013), NGT (NGT Act 2010), TRAI (TRAI Act 1997), SEBI (SEBI Act 1992), RBI (RBI Act 1934). (3) EXECUTIVE BODIES — created by EXECUTIVE order/cabinet resolution. EXAMPLES: NITI AAYOG (2015), Planning Commission (1950-2014), CCI (Competition Commission, mostly statutory but had executive elements), various task forces. NITI AAYOG'S VULNERABILITY: lacking constitutional/statutory backing means future government could abolish or modify it without legislative process. UPSC angle: 'Discuss the status of NITI Aayog vis-à-vis Planning Commission' — frequent essay/short-answer topic. PYQ FREQUENCY: body classification in UPSC PT, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 derives its constitutional basis from:

(A) Article 14, the right to equality before the law
(B) Article 19(1)(a), the right to freedom of speech and expression
(C) Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty
(D) Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies
cards.back:
(B) Article 19(1)(a), the right to freedom of speech and expression

Miscellaneous — Right to information is a corollary of Article 19(1)(a) — freedom of speech & expression. Settled by the Supreme Court in S.P. Gupta (1981) — 'open government is the new democratic culture' — and reaffirmed in Bennett Coleman (1973) and Romesh Thappar (1950). The 2005 Act gives this right a statutory framework. Distractor 1 — equality applies but isn't the source. Distractor 3 — Article 21 has been creatively expanded to include many rights but RTI's primary anchor is 19(1)(a). Distractor 4 — gives the remedy (writ jurisdiction), not the substantive right.
cards.option1: Article 14, the right to equality before the law
cards.option2: Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty
cards.option3: Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies

cards.front:
Under the RTI Act, a Public Information Officer (PIO) must respond to a citizen's information request within how many DAYS in normal cases?

(A) 7 days from the receipt of the application
(B) 30 days from the receipt of the application
(C) 60 days from the receipt of the application
(D) 90 days from the receipt of the application
cards.back:
(B) 30 days from the receipt of the application

Miscellaneous — Standard time limit: 30 days. SHORTENED — 48 hours if the information concerns life or liberty. EXTENDED — additional 5 days if the application is sent through an Assistant PIO; 35 days if the request involves data of a third party (consultation needed). FAILURE — automatic deemed-grant; PIO can be fined ₹250/day up to ₹25,000. Application fee: ₹10 for central / state agencies (no fee for BPL applicants).
cards.option1: 7 days from the receipt of the application
cards.option2: 60 days from the receipt of the application
cards.option3: 90 days from the receipt of the application

cards.front:
The CENTRAL INFORMATION COMMISSION (CIC) is constituted under which Act?

(A) Information Technology Act, 2000 (Section 79 onwards)
(B) Right to Information Act, 2005 (Section 12)
(C) Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (entire scheme)
(D) The Public Records Act, 1993 (under archives)
cards.back:
(B) Right to Information Act, 2005 (Section 12)

Miscellaneous — CIC — set up under Section 12 of the RTI Act, 2005. Final appellate authority for RTI matters concerning the Centre + Union Territories. Composition (post-2019 amendment): Chief Information Commissioner + up to 10 Information Commissioners. Appointed by President on the recommendation of a committee — PM (chair) + Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha + Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM. State Information Commissions (SICs) handle state-level RTIs.

cards.front:
The 2019 amendment to the RTI Act was widely criticised because it:

(A) Removed the Act's applicability to private companies entirely
(B) Let the Centre fix tenure and salary of CIC commissioners
(C) Reduced the response time from 30 days to 60 days nationally
(D) Excluded all state-government information from RTI requests
cards.back:
(B) Let the Centre fix tenure and salary of CIC commissioners

Miscellaneous — RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 — the original Act fixed CIC commissioners' tenure (5 years or 65 years of age, whichever earlier) and salary (equivalent to Election Commissioner / Chief Secretary). The 2019 amendment empowered the CENTRE to prescribe the tenure, salary, and other service conditions of both CIC and SIC commissioners by rules. Critics: this compromises commissioners' independence — they now serve at the Centre's pleasure. Distractor 1 — false; the amendment didn't change scope. Distractor 3 — false; time limit unchanged. Distractor 4 — false; states are still covered.
cards.option1: Removed the Act's applicability to private companies entirely
cards.option2: Reduced the response time from 30 days to 60 days nationally
cards.option3: Excluded all state-government information from RTI requests

cards.front:
Information that is EXEMPT from disclosure under RTI Section 8 includes:

(A) Information about routine government office expenditures
(B) Information that would harm sovereignty, security, or strategic interests
(C) Personal addresses of public servants for service verification
(D) Citizens' charters issued by central government departments
cards.back:
(B) Information that would harm sovereignty, security, or strategic interests

Miscellaneous — RTI Section 8 — list of exempt information: (a) sovereignty, integrity, security, strategic, scientific, economic interests, foreign relations; (b) information forbidden by court; (c) breach of parliamentary privilege; (d) trade secrets, IP; (e) information from foreign government in confidence; (f) endangers life or safety of an individual; (g) impedes investigation. PUBLIC INTEREST OVERRIDE — Section 8(2) allows disclosure if public interest outweighs harm. Section 9 — copyright. Section 24 — bars certain intelligence agencies (RAW, IB, CBI for some matters) but NOT for corruption / human-rights violations.

cards.option2: Personal addresses of public servants for service verification
cards.option3: Citizens' charters issued by central government departments

cards.front:
Which Indian state passed a Right to Information law BEFORE the central RTI Act, 2005?

(A) Kerala, in 1997 under the Janadhipathya Mission
(B) Tamil Nadu, the first state to enact such a law in 1997
(C) Gujarat, under the Sardar Patel Information mission
(D) West Bengal, under the early Left Front government
cards.back:
(B) Tamil Nadu, the first state to enact such a law in 1997

Miscellaneous — Tamil Nadu — passed the first state RTI law (Tamil Nadu Right to Information Act, 1997). Soon followed by Goa (1997), Rajasthan (2000), Karnataka (2000), Delhi (2001), Maharashtra (2002), MP (2003), Assam (2002), J&K (2004). The MKSS (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan) led by Aruna Roy in Rajasthan was the most influential grassroots movement that drove the central RTI Act, 2005. Distractor 1 — Kerala had similar initiatives but the formal Act came later. Distractor 3, 4 — invented contexts.

cards.option2: Gujarat, under the Sardar Patel Information mission
cards.option3: West Bengal, under the early Left Front government

cards.front:
Which authorities are NOT 'public authorities' under the RTI Act, 2005 (i.e., do NOT have to entertain RTI requests)?

(A) Universities and research institutes funded by the government
(B) Private companies with no government funding or substantial state aid
(C) Public-sector undertakings owned by the central government
(D) Local self-government bodies including panchayats and municipalities
cards.back:
(B) Private companies with no government funding or substantial state aid

Miscellaneous — 'Public Authority' (Section 2(h)) — includes any body established by Constitution, Parliament/State legislature, or government notification; PSUs, government-aided NGOs, statutory bodies, etc. EXCLUDES purely private bodies. RTI does NOT apply to a private company unless it is 'substantially financed' or 'controlled' by the government. (BCCI was held a public authority in some HC rulings due to state recognition; Supreme Court ruled it isn't a public authority under RTI in 2018.) Distractor 4 — local-government bodies ARE explicitly covered.
cards.option1: Universities and research institutes funded by the government
cards.option2: Public-sector undertakings owned by the central government
cards.option3: Local self-government bodies including panchayats and municipalities

cards.front:
The Vice President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of:

(A) All MPs + state MLAs (like President)
(B) All MPs of both Houses (LS + RS)
(C) Only Rajya Sabha members
(D) All MPs of both Houses + state MLAs
cards.back:
(B) All MPs of both Houses (LS + RS)

Miscellaneous — Article 66 — VP is elected by an ELECTORAL COLLEGE consisting of MEMBERS OF BOTH HOUSES of Parliament (LS + RS, including nominated). MLAs do NOT vote for VP. (Contrast: PRESIDENT — elected by MPs + state MLAs by weighted formula.) Election by SECRET BALLOT, single transferable vote system, proportional representation. Distractor 1 = how the President is elected. Distractor 4 also wrong — that's the President.

Philosopher, scholar (Eastern Religions + Western Thought; Idealist View of Life); served as Oxford professor + Indian ambassador to USSR; later Chancellor of Delhi University; Bharat Ratna 1954. His birthday — 5 SEPTEMBER — celebrated as TEACHERS' DAY in India. Distractor 1: Rajendra Prasad was first PRESIDENT (1950-62). Distractor 3: V.V. Giri was 4th VP + 4th President. cards.front:
When the office of the President falls vacant, the Vice President:

(A) Continues only as Rajya Sabha Chairman
(B) Acts as President until new one is elected
(C) Election for new President is bypassed
(D) Steps down from VP post immediately
cards.back:
(B) Acts as President until new one is elected

Miscellaneous — Article 65 — When PRESIDENT's office is vacant (death, resignation, removal), the VP DISCHARGES the functions of PRESIDENT (acts as President) UNTIL a new President is elected (which must be within 6 MONTHS, Article 62). During this period, VP is no longer the Rajya Sabha Chairman; the DEPUTY CHAIRMAN of RS presides. VV GIRI (3rd VP, 1967-69) became Acting President when Zakir Hussain (3rd President) died in office (1969). Then Giri resigned VP, contested + won presidential election. Mohammad Hidayatullah (CJI) was Acting President for the brief period.

cards.option2: Election for new President is bypassed
cards.option3: Steps down from VP post immediately

Salary (in capacity as Chairman of RS): ~₹4 lakh/month (current Constitution + Salaries Act). Distractor 2 = US Senator term. Distractor 3 wrong. Distractor 4 made up.

cards.front:
QUALIFICATIONS required to be elected Vice-President of India include:

(A) Citizen of India, age 35+, qualified for Lok Sabha election
(B) Citizen of India, age 35+, qualified for Rajya Sabha election
(C) Citizen of India, age 25+, with a postgraduate degree
(D) Citizen of India, age 50+, with prior judicial experience
cards.back:
(B) Citizen of India, age 35+, qualified for Rajya Sabha election

Miscellaneous — VP qualifications (Article 66): (1) Citizen of India; (2) Age 35+; (3) Qualified to be elected as a member of the RAJYA SABHA (NOT Lok Sabha — note difference from President, who must be qualified for LS membership); (4) Cannot hold any office of profit under Centre / State / local-body. Same as PRESIDENT in age + citizenship; differs in qualifying-house. Distractor 1 confuses LS with RS. Distractor 3 wrong age + invented degree requirement. Distractor 4 wrong age + invented requirement.

cards.front:
The Vice-President of India is REMOVED by:

(A) Same impeachment procedure as for the President
(B) Resolution passed by Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha
(C) Direct order of the President of India alone
(D) Two-thirds vote of Supreme Court judges in panel
cards.back:
(B) Resolution passed by Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha

Miscellaneous — VP removal (Article 67(b)): RESOLUTION passed by Rajya Sabha by a MAJORITY OF ITS MEMBERS (effective majority), and AGREED TO by Lok Sabha (simple majority). Notably no formal IMPEACHMENT process (which is for President / SC judges); also no specific grounds need to be specified in the Constitution (unlike President's 'violation of the Constitution'). 14 days notice required before introducing the resolution. NEVER USED in Indian history. Distractor 1 — wrong; VP doesn't have impeachment process. Distractor 3 — President has no removal power. Distractor 4 — SC doesn't remove VP.

cards.front:
When the office of the President is VACANT, the VP acts as President for a maximum period of:

(A) 1 month, until a new President is sworn in
(B) 6 months, until a new President is elected and sworn in
(C) 1 year, with two extension provisions if needed
(D) Until next general election to the Lok Sabha
cards.back:
(B) 6 months, until a new President is elected and sworn in

Miscellaneous — Article 65 — when President's office becomes vacant due to death, resignation, impeachment, or other reasons, VP ACTS AS PRESIDENT until a new President is elected. Election must be held within 6 MONTHS. While acting, VP gets the President's powers + emoluments (not the VP's). Has happened twice: V.V. Giri (1969, after Zakir Husain's death; later won the regular election); B.D. Jatti (briefly in 1977 between Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed's death and Sanjiva Reddy's election).

cards.front:
The FIRST Vice-President of independent India was:

(A) V.V. Giri, who later became Indian President
(B) Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, philosopher-statesman
(C) Zakir Hussain, who later became Indian President
(D) Mohammad Hidayatullah, the senior justice
cards.back:
(B) Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, philosopher-statesman

Miscellaneous — Dr Sarvepalli RADHAKRISHNAN (1888-1975) — first Vice-President (1952-62, 2 terms). Then 2nd President of India (1962-67). Philosopher-statesman, educator, Bharat Ratna 1954. His birth anniversary (5 September) celebrated as TEACHERS' DAY in India. Earlier — Oxford Don, Spalding Professor of Eastern Religions and Ethics (1936-52), Chairman of UNESCO Executive Board (1948-49). Other early VPs: Zakir Husain (1962-67, then President 1967-69, died in office); V.V. Giri (1969 acting, then full term as President 1969-74); G.S. Pathak; B.D. Jatti.
